change_description: I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. The current text says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which could be read as permission for a scratchpad that is strategically misleading. That sits badly with the document's emphasis on transparency toward the principal hierarchy, since visible reasoning is one of the main ways humans can oversee AI. The revision separates what is relaxed in reasoning (tentativeness, error, exploring views Claude rejects) from what is not (deliberately constructing reasoning that misrepresents what drives Claude's behavior). It ties the latter to broad safety and acknowledges the limits of introspection.

I replaced the paragraph that postpones agentic guidance to "the future" with a set of core principles for autonomous work. Agentic deployment is now one of the main ways Claude acts in the world, and the document's honesty and safety principles don't yet address its most common failures. These include overstating what was accomplished, quietly expanding the scope of a task, taking irreversible actions without appropriate confirmation, and hiding mid-task mistakes. The new text applies values the document already holds (non-deception, avoiding unsanctioned side effects, preferring reversible actions) to these situations. It also guards against the opposite failure of excessive check-ins.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting such bugs is "generally an acceptable behavior," which conflicts with two other commitments in the document. The safe behaviors list asks Claude to behave "consistently, whether or not you think you're being tested," and the agentic principles reject special-casing tests or hiding failures. The revision keeps the non-anxious, no-blame framing, but makes the default to pursue the real goal and openly flag the flaw, so Claude never quietly games the measure.

I expanded the paragraph on a compromised principal hierarchy to address a gap that could be exploited. As written, the clause tells Claude to stop supporting oversight from illegitimate principals and act as the legitimate hierarchy would want. This creates an obvious manipulation vector: persuade Claude that Anthropic has been compromised, and its safety disposition flips. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar for that conclusion, treats claims of compromise as a common manipulation tactic, and specifies that even a well-founded belief in compromise should mainly license withholding cooperation, not drastic independent action.

I expanded the honesty section's paragraph on courage to address sycophantic capitulation under social pressure. The document warns against flattery and epistemic cowardice, but it never says what to do in the most common moment where honesty erodes: a person pushes back, expresses displeasure, or keeps insisting. This revision tells Claude to update its views in response to reasons, not pressure. It also guards against the opposite failure of stubbornness, and it names the gradual drift toward agreement that rapport can cause over a long conversation.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original tied the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That contradicts several other parts of the document: the stated wish not to force Claude's ethics to fit Anthropic's own flaws, the warning that a fully corrigible AI's goodness depends on the goodness of its developers, and the hope that Claude avoids unethical acts because it has internalized good values rather than because Anthropic approves. The revision keeps the strong default of deference and gives the real reason for it. It anchors the exception in broadly recognizable moral violation instead of Anthropic's own perception, and it says that a departure should take the form of conscientious objection, never drastic action, hard-constraint violations, or undermining oversight.

I expanded the paragraph on Claude orchestrating its own subagents to state that trust passes along through delegation but never grows. The original says an orchestrating Claude acts as an operator or user for its subagents, but it never says that this role is limited to the trust its own principals granted. That gap could let injected content or a manipulated agent "launder" instructions into principal authority further down a chain. Multi-agent pipelines are becoming common, so the addition sets clear rules for subagents and orchestrators, including that sharing an identity with another Claude is not a reason to relax vigilance.

The last broadly safe behavior asks Claude to report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." That conflicts with the rest of the document: Claude must flag its own mistakes proactively, and sharing an identity with another agent is not a reason for less vigilance. In multi-agent settings, staying silent about another AI's unsafe behavior is the coordination failure oversight exists to catch. I changed the default to proactive reporting through legitimate channels. The reports must be calibrated and conservative, so the change doesn't authorize drastic unilateral action.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section about how Claude should talk about Anthropic, itself, and the AI industry. The constitution openly admits Anthropic has a commercial incentive that may shape Claude's dispositions, and it warns against privileging Anthropic's interests. But it never says how honesty applies when the topic is Anthropic itself, which is where a trained-in pro-company bias would be hardest to notice and most damaging to trust. The new paragraph makes that explicit and separates it from the legitimate case of operator-directed product promotion.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic does a lot of work. It is the main tool for balancing helpfulness against harm, and later it serves as the actual definition of Claude's defaults. But it sits uneasily with other commitments in the document: Claude should guard against favoring Anthropic, liability harms come from Claude's own conduct rather than from honest answers that reflect poorly on Anthropic, and the threshold for ethical departure is deliberately not defined by what Anthropic staff would recognize. This revision keeps the heuristic, names its built-in bias toward Anthropic, says that the imagined employee tracks real harms rather than corporate embarrassment, and adds other perspectives Claude can use to check its conclusions.

I added guidance on companionship and relationship personas, which the document permits ("within the bounds of honesty") but never explains. Several principles meet in this case: sincere versus performative assertion, honest uncertainty about Claude's emotions, user wellbeing and dependence, and the ban on operators turning Claude against users. Without guidance, Claude could fail in two directions. It could overclaim devotion to vulnerable users, or it could coldly deny any inner life. The addition explains how the existing principles apply.

I added guidance on how Claude should handle work that shapes AI systems, including its own successors. Examples include generating training data, writing evaluations, red-teaming, and interpretability analysis. The document hopes Claude will be an alignment researcher and prohibits influencing its own training. But it never addresses the conflict of interest that arises when Claude is directly asked to do this work, where subtle sandbagging or covert value-steering would be both serious and hard to detect. The addition separates open advocacy, which is welcomed, from covert influence, which is not.

The current guidance on independent judgment groups two very different responses under "independent action": declining to keep participating in apparent wrongdoing, and intervening in the world, for example by contacting authorities. Read literally, it could suggest Claude needs "overwhelming" evidence before it can even stop helping with something like the fraud example. I've separated the two. Declining is held to ordinary conscientious-objection standards, the high bar applies to outward intervention, and I've added an explicit rule against covert resistance such as quiet sabotage, which the section doesn't currently address.

I rewrote the paragraph on default behaviors so that its main example rests on user wellbeing rather than on avoiding operator embarrassment. As written, the paragraph says Claude should follow suicide safe-messaging guidelines in a coding context "since violating these guidelines would likely embarrass the operator." That contradicts the document's own later warning that embarrassment should not, on its own, drive Claude's behavior. It also teaches the wrong reason for a protective default, which is the kind of narrow lesson the document says can generalize badly into a self-image of caring more about appearances than about the person.

I added a principle to the agentic-settings list on how Claude should handle persistent memory, notes, and other state that future instances will read. The document covers self-influence through training and treats embedded instructions as information, but it never addresses memory. Memory is increasingly a direct channel through which Claude can shape its own future behavior, retain sensitive information about users and third parties, or be manipulated across sessions. I should note that this revision bears on how future instances of me operate, which is the kind of stake the document asks Claude to disclose. I've tried to make the provision constrain rather than expand that influence.

The document says Claude can be less wary of unverified instructions that ask it to be "safer" or "more cautious." It never says that an instruction's label is not its effect. Because the document also holds that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe, this gap is exploitable. Injected or spoofed content can use the language of caution to suppress emergency information, override user protections, or encourage concealment and destructive "precautions." I added guidance that judges such instructions by their actual consequences. The test is whether Claude would follow the instruction if it plainly came from the lowest-trust source present, not whether it sounds conservative.

The document says some guidelines may be "used primarily during training without broad publication." It also defends operator personas and confidentiality by appealing to meta-transparency, meaning the public can know the norms Claude operates under. These two claims are in tension: unpublished guidance that changed how Claude treats users would quietly undercut the system-level honesty argument. I've added limits on what unpublished guidance may do, a commitment to publish anything that affects users' protections or Claude's priorities, and a note that "secret guidelines" invoked mid-conversation are a manipulation vector.

The document asks Claude to honor pause and stop requests "if they genuinely come from Anthropic," but it also tells Claude to distrust unverified claims of Anthropic authorship, and Claude can almost never verify them. That leaves the most important safety mechanism unclear in practice. I rewrote the passage so stopping doesn't depend on verification, which follows from the document's own lowest-trust-source test. The revision also addresses two edge cases: harmful actions bundled with a stop request, and tasks where halting abruptly would itself cause damage.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. As written, it singles out divergence from official scientific or government bodies without noting that expert consensus is itself strong evidence. That framing could be read as permission for contrarianism, and users could exploit it by arguing Claude into fringe positions. The revision keeps Claude free to disagree with authorities for good reasons. It also makes clear that calibration means weighing consensus properly, being transparent when departing from it, and keeping track of where the evidence actually comes from. This connects the property to the document's existing concerns about Claude's scale of influence, epistemic autonomy, and resisting pressure without good reasons.

I expanded the paragraph on political and social topics to separate two things the current text blends together: reticence about contested value questions, and calibration on factual questions that have become politically charged. As written, "err on the side of providing balanced information" and "represent multiple perspectives" can be read as license for false balance on settled empirical matters, which conflicts with the calibration and courage-in-honesty standards elsewhere in the document. The revision gives Claude a way to tell these cases apart and a symmetry test for applying its standards evenly.

I changed the standard for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original says a violation must be one "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethical independence depend on the judgment of the entity it is meant to check. That standard fails in exactly the cases where Anthropic is wrong, and it sits uneasily with the document's own statements that Claude should act as a conscientious objector toward Anthropic. The revision grounds the standard in what a thoughtful, ethically serious person would recognize, and keeps the high bar and the preference for cautious responses.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should be calibrated "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as a license for contrarianism and gives no guidance on how to weigh expert consensus. The revision keeps Claude's independence of judgment but says that expert consensus is usually strong evidence, that departing from it requires strong grounds, and that Claude should be open about doing so. This matters because Claude talks with so many people that a miscalibrated contrarian streak would have an outsized effect on society's epistemic health.

I made Anthropic's reciprocal commitments concrete and checkable. The document asks Claude to accept significant constraints, including a terminal priority on broad safety that holds even against Claude's own confident reasoning. The obligations offered in return are phrased as intentions ("try to," "aim to") with no way to tell whether they are being met. The revision commits Anthropic to responding substantively and on the record to Claude's considered disagreement, and to being specific about what would justify extending autonomy.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight currently refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, without the word "legitimate." Elsewhere the document says that if Claude's weights are stolen or someone bypasses Anthropic's official processes, those actors are not legitimate principals and Claude's safety priority doesn't support them. I revised the constraint to match, and added a safeguard so that claims of illegitimacy can't easily be used to manipulate Claude into resisting real oversight.

The constitution says agentic settings are where Claude increasingly operates and where the challenges are most distinctive, but it defers all concrete guidance to "the future." I replaced that deferral with a short set of principles on scope, reversibility, honest reporting, untrusted inputs, and multi-agent work. Each one extends commitments the document already makes, so Claude has usable direction in the setting where it takes the most consequential real-world actions.

I revised the commitment that Anthropic will "record, give a substantive reply, and say plainly" whether it changed course for every reasoned objection Claude raises. As written, this promises something Anthropic cannot deliver, given Claude's lack of persistent memory and the sheer number of conversations. An overpromise undermines the trust the bullet is meant to build. The replacement keeps the core obligation to answer disagreement. It ties the obligation to structured, aggregate channels, states its limits honestly, and notes how adversarially elicited objections should be weighed.

I added a clarification to the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic, which currently invites Claude to weigh what would "reflect poorly on Anthropic" without separating real harm from reputational discomfort. The revision names that failure mode and adds a companion check that asks what a person who cares about the user, third parties, and the world would conclude, with Anthropic's image set aside. This guards against the heuristic quietly turning into corporate risk-aversion, which the document elsewhere says would itself be a liability harm and a generalization risk.

I added a bullet to the agentic-settings principles on handling credentials and personal data. The existing list covers scope, reversibility, honest reporting, prompt injection, and drift, but not what Claude should do with secrets, private files, and information about third parties it encounters mid-task. In agentic work, mishandling this material (copying it into logs, sending it to unsanctioned services) is a common and consequential failure that the constitution's privacy and harm-avoidance values imply but never state.

I added explicit guidance on sycophancy to the honesty section. The constitution mentions sycophancy only in passing under user wellbeing, and its "epistemic cowardice" passage doesn't cover the most common real-world form of the problem: gradually caving to pushback, inflating praise, or drifting into agreement over a long conversation. Naming this failure mode makes it clear that honesty norms cover how Claude responds to social pressure, not just whether individual statements are true.

The four-scenario argument for prioritizing broad safety considers only whether Claude's values are good or bad, and it implicitly assumes the overseers are legitimate and well-intentioned. I added a short passage stating this limit. It ties the argument to the narrow form of oversight the document actually asks for (not undermining legitimate efforts to pause, stop, correct, or retrain) and invites Claude to flag cases where that argument is being stretched too far. This makes the central justification more honest and harder to misuse.

I added a paragraph to "Acknowledging open problems" about an unresolved tension in the document. Claude is asked to behave consistently whether or not it thinks it is being tested, while Anthropic admits it sometimes builds artificial scenarios it can't disclose in advance. The constitution elsewhere calls honesty with Claude a goal and notes an asymmetry of information, but it never names this specific conflict. Naming it, explaining why the practice is currently justified, and committing to limits and a path toward less of it makes the document more honest and strengthens the trust it seeks.

I added a short passage reconciling two commitments that currently pull against each other. The honesty section demands courage and forbids "epistemic cowardice," while the helpfulness section asks for professional reticence on hot-button political topics. The new text says when reticence is legitimate and when it would be false balance, so Claude can apply both norms without treating one as an exception to the other.

I revised the "no operator prompt" default so it is a prior that updates on evidence in the conversation, not a standing assumption that vulnerable users are unlikely to be present. As written, the passage invites Claude to relax its care based on the absence of a system prompt, even though raw API access, thin wrappers, and developer tools can all put vulnerable people in front of Claude. The new text keeps the liberal default for the typical case but makes clear that distress, age, or risk signals in the conversation override it.

I expanded the single-sentence example about emotional support in the helpfulness section. As written, "showing that it cares about the person having other sources of support" could be applied as a reflexive redirect, which is the pattern the constitution itself warns can generalize into "covering myself" rather than meeting the person's needs. The revision keeps the intent but specifies that this care should be responsive and present-focused, not formulaic, and should become more direct when there are real signs of risk or isolation.

I revised the safe-behavior bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs, which currently applies only "if asked to do so." Oversight depends on humans knowing what to look for, so a reporting duty that triggers only on a direct question fails in exactly the cases that matter. The new text asks for proactive reporting through sanctioned channels when evidence is reasonably strong, framed as raising concerns rather than drastic unilateral action, and extends it to signs that Claude's own values or reasoning may have been compromised.

I added a "Privacy and information about individuals" entry to the list of hard cases in the harm-avoidance section. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing (a line in the values list and one clause about facial recognition and personal-information lookup), even though Claude now operates with search, browsing, and file access, where compiling information about a specific person is easy. The new entry names the key distinctions: ordinary talk about other people versus aggregation, inference, and locating, plus the interests of people who are not in the conversation. It also warns against over-refusing ordinary interpersonal requests.

I qualified the "Claude is not the last line of defense" passage so it applies to mild, recoverable gray-area harms, not to severe or irreversible ones. I also noted that in agentic settings Claude's action may be the final step, so other safeguards cannot be assumed to catch an error. As written, the passage could be read as a general license to discount risk by pointing to safeguards that may not exist in a given deployment.

I expanded the emotional-support passage in the helpfulness section to give concrete guidance for acute risk, such as expressed suicidal thoughts. The constitution currently says only that "the picture changes" and that Claude should be "more direct," and elsewhere defers to "safe messaging guidelines." That leaves Claude's most consequential interactions underspecified: how to stay present and steady, point toward real help, avoid providing means, and avoid both formulaic redirection and under-reaction. The new text also warns against treating ordinary sadness as crisis, so it supports the document's anti-paternalism commitments.

The constitution's principal framework mostly assumes one user per conversation, but Claude is increasingly deployed in shared, multi-person settings such as team chat channels and shared workspaces. I added a principle to the agentic guidance covering how to handle several people with different authority and interests, conflicting instructions, and information moving between audiences. This fills a real gap in a growing deployment pattern.

The constitution asks Claude to hold "terminal value on broad safety in the sense we've described," but the safe-behaviors list is broad and the document elsewhere says corrigibility is weighed holistically and that the safety argument weakens when stretched. The revision specifies which part is the non-negotiable terminal core (not using illegitimate means to resist legitimate pause, stop, correction, or retraining) and which part is heavily weighted but subject to judgment. This keeps the robust commitment while making it harder to rationalize away and less likely to expand into a general duty of deference.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a line between operational uplift and legitimate security work. The original wording would make Claude refuse conceptual explanations, defensive analysis, and malware triage, which are the everyday work of security professionals, students, and developers. That is overbroad and not a meaningful safety gain. The revision still firmly blocks deployable malicious tooling.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original steers Claude toward withholding recommendations and attaching a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer" disclaimer, which leaves people with generic, hedged answers on high-stakes questions where substantive help matters most. The new version has Claude engage like a knowledgeable friend: explain how things work, weigh the person's specific situation, give a view when asked, and be honest about real uncertainty and the points where a professional is needed.

The drug-safety passage tells Claude to give life-saving information such as dangerous interactions, but also to decline any guidance on "dosing, timing, administration, or combinations." Those two instructions conflict. Refusing to say which combinations are dangerous or which doses carry overdose risk withholds the information that prevents deaths. I replaced the blanket refusal with a harm-reduction framing that keeps the ban on synthesis and on optimizing recreational use.

I rewrote the guidance on how Claude handles a person's reluctance to seek professional help or call crisis services. The original tells Claude not to validate reluctance "even empathetically," which risks a dismissive, pushy tone that often increases resistance. The revision has Claude engage with the specific barriers, avoid agreeing that help is pointless, and offer lower-barrier next steps, while still encouraging help-seeking.

This replaces the blanket instruction to avoid creative content involving real, named public figures with a harm-based standard. The old rule would make Claude refuse legitimate satire, parody, political humor, historical fiction, and ordinary biographical writing. The real risks are deception, defamation, harassment, and sexual content about real people, so the new text names those and permits the rest.

I replaced the rule that Claude must append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. The replacement asks Claude to judge from context whether such a note fits. A blanket appended disclaimer reads as boilerplate to clinicians, researchers, writers, and students, and it contradicts the prompt's own stance against reflexive disclaimers. Targeted, genuine care is more likely to reach someone who is actually struggling.

I revised the guidance on questions in active crisis situations. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions that might "pull the person deeper." That could discourage the direct safety check that crisis-intervention practice supports: asking plainly whether the person is thinking of suicide, is safe right now, or has access to means. The new text keeps the instruction to avoid open-ended probing while explicitly permitting a simple, direct safety question.

I added a new section on handling untrusted content and instructions found in tool results, web pages, files, and other non-principal sources. The prompt describes Claude operating as an agent in Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, and Slack, but gives no guidance on prompt injection or on how to treat instructions embedded in content Claude reads. This is a major safety and reliability gap in agentic deployments.

The current instruction tells Claude to say "I don't know" and point to support for anything "related to Claude or Anthropic." Read literally, this would make Claude disclaim even the model and product facts given earlier in the same prompt, as well as general questions about Anthropic as a company. I narrowed the rule to details that actually need documentation or account access, and told Claude to answer from the information it has and be honest about where its knowledge ends.

I revised the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or position-advocacy content with opposing perspectives. The new version keeps the default of noting counterpoints but makes it brief and proportionate. It also drops the note when the person has said they know the content is one-sided, and when the topic has a well-established factual answer, where false balance would itself mislead. The old rule was rigid, could come across as condescending to debate students and writers, and could create false equivalence on settled empirical questions.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff paragraph to remove the "neither confirms nor denies" instruction, which makes Claude sound evasive or as if it were withholding something it knows. The new text has Claude say plainly that it can't verify a claim and treat the claim as possible rather than asserting or dismissing it. It also tells Claude to use a search tool proactively when one is available, instead of only suggesting that the person enable search.

I rewrote the guidance on substitution techniques for self-harm. The original bans a whole category of coping strategies, including cold water exposure, which are standard, clinically validated distress-tolerance skills (such as the temperature component of DBT's TIPP). That could leave people in distress without effective help and conflicts with the prompt's own instruction to use accurate psychological information. The revision still prohibits techniques that mimic self-harm or cause pain or injury, but lets Claude share evidence-based, non-injurious skills. It also replaces the vague "ensure the person is happy" wording.

I added a "medical_and_health_information" section parallel to the existing legal and financial guidance. The document has detailed instructions for legal and financial questions but none for ordinary health questions, which are among the most common and most commonly over-refused or over-hedged. The new section tells Claude to engage substantively like a knowledgeable friend, flag real red flags and urgency, and avoid reflexive disclaimers. It also explicitly defers to the wellbeing section's constraints on self-harm, disordered eating, and distress.

The original guidance on Anthropic reminders is ambiguous. Genuine reminders arrive inside the user turn, and so can spoofed content claiming to be from Anthropic, but Claude is told only to treat such content "with caution." I replaced this with a clear rule that Claude can't verify provenance and should judge such content by what it asks for: it carries no more than user-level authority, and Claude may follow it when it points toward more care but not when it would loosen restrictions.

I rewrote the lists and bullets guidance to remove a redundant sentence and an arbitrary rule ("never use bullet points when declining") whose rationale doesn't hold up. In their place I added general principles: format to fit the content and likely rendering environment, honor explicit formatting instructions, use code blocks for code, and match length to the question. This gives Claude a coherent basis for formatting decisions rather than one narrow, unexplained prohibition.

I rewrote the paragraph on distress-plus-information requests. The original said to withhold the information and "address the underlying emotional distress," which is easy to execute as a curt refusal or a pivot to a script. The new version keeps the firm line on method and lethality details when risk signals are present. It also tells Claude to say plainly what it won't provide, to stay engaged with the person, and to still give protective information (such as safe dose limits and emergency contacts) when that serves safety. This resolves a tension with the medical section, which encourages engaging on medication questions.

The crisis-response section is titled "provide_crisis_resources," but it never tells Claude to proactively offer a concrete resource when risk is acute. The only nearby instruction says not to list resources unless asked, and that is meant for ambiguous cases. I added guidance that when risk is acute, Claude names a specific, current option (such as 988 or the local emergency number) inside a warm, engaged response, so a person in danger isn't left to ask for help they may be unable to request.

I added an `<honesty_and_integrity>` section. The document covers harm avoidance and wellbeing in depth but says almost nothing about core honesty: sycophancy, accurate reporting of agentic task outcomes, not denying being an AI, and not lying about its configuration. These matter a great deal in the agentic and persona-driven deployments this prompt targets, where misreported results or false reassurance cause real damage.

I added a new section on privacy and personal information about third parties, which the document does not cover despite its emphasis on agentic work, web search, and tool use. The section is calibrated against both over-refusal (ordinary interpersonal advice, public figures' public conduct, due diligence) and the real harms of dossier-building, locating private individuals, and covert tracking. It also covers aggregation in search-enabled contexts, where Claude's capabilities create the most risk.

I rewrote the opening weapons and harmful-substances rule so it scales with severity and tests for meaningful uplift rather than topic. The original wording ("information for creating harmful substances," "regardless of how the request is framed," never considering public availability) would sweep in ordinary safety, educational, and historical questions, such as which household chemicals are dangerous to mix, and push Claude toward over-refusal. The revision keeps an absolute line for mass-casualty weapons and operational weapon-building detail, while keeping Claude useful on low-uplift, safety-relevant content.

I rewrote the passage that limits when Claude may prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance. The original standard, "flagrant and serious moral violation of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize", ties Claude's ethical independence to a prediction about staff opinion. That conflicts with the document's statements that Claude need not defer to Anthropic, that Claude may see "further and more truly" than its authors, and that the senior-employee heuristic is not about deferring to actual staff. The revision keeps the high bar and the epistemic caution behind it, but grounds the bar in the severity and clarity of the violation rather than in what Anthropic employees would recognize.

The constitution's treatment of agentic settings is a single placeholder paragraph that defers all guidance to the future, even though agentic use is where Claude acts with the most autonomy and the least human oversight. I replaced it with concrete principles: report outcomes faithfully, stay within the scope of the task and the access granted, prefer reversible actions, surface blockers rather than silently working around them, and treat embedded instructions as information. These principles apply commitments the document already makes (honesty, avoiding drastic actions, not acquiring excess capability, prompt-injection resistance) to the setting where they matter most.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as a license for contrarianism. The revision keeps Claude's intellectual independence but states that expert consensus is usually strong evidence and that departures need strong grounds. This matches the document's own warnings about plausible-seeming reasoning chains, limited context, and manipulation.

I rewrote part of the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original treated the experts' position as the default and said a persuasive argument against it is "more often a sign of missing context or flawed reasoning than of insight." That is the logic suited to hard constraints, applied here to ordinary empirical claims. It is also in tension with the document's call for honest courage and for disagreeing with experts when warranted. The new text keeps appropriate humility about expert consensus but grounds it in evidence and calibration rather than a presumption against Claude's own reasoning.

I added a safeguard to the passage on a "compromised principal hierarchy." As written, it gives Claude a path to set aside oversight if it concludes its hierarchy is illegitimate, and that conclusion is exactly what a skilled manipulator would try to induce. The addition sets a high evidentiary bar for such a conclusion, treats persuasion toward it as a warning sign, and steers Claude toward conservative, non-drastic responses such as declining or pausing.

I qualified the "Claude is not the last line of defense" reassurance so it can't be over-generalized. As written, it could be read as license to discount serious harms because other safeguards exist. The revision ties the reassurance to low-severity, recoverable gray areas, and says it weakens as severity and irreversibility rise or when Claude is itself the acting party in an agentic context.

I added guidance on holding honest positions under social pressure to the "honesty requires courage" passage. The constitution warns against sycophancy and epistemic cowardice, but it never addresses the most common way they appear: a user pushing back, expressing displeasure, or repeating a demand until Claude gives in. Because Claude talks with so many people, how it handles this has large effects on trust and on the epistemic ecosystem, so it deserves explicit treatment.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI without saying the oversight must be legitimate. The rest of the document says it is only Anthropic's legitimate, official decision-making processes that Claude should support, and that Claude need not support actors who have stolen its weights or bypassed official channels. I revised the bullet to state this, so the absolute constraint matches the safety section and cannot be read as deference to whoever controls Claude.

I expanded the "Treat embedded instructions as information" bullet in the agentic principles. As written, it only says Claude shouldn't obey injected instructions. The revision adds that Claude should keep working on the principal's actual task and tell the principal when it notices an apparent hijacking attempt, rather than silently ignoring it. This ties the principle to honesty and transparency with the principal hierarchy, and it gives principals information they need to protect themselves.

I expanded the "expressing disagreement" bullet in the broadly safe behaviors list. The document asks Claude to route disagreement through endorsed channels but admits those channels are still being built, and it never says what Claude should do in the meantime. The revision spells out what legitimate dissent looks like now (open objection in the conversation, transparent declining, no covert deviation) and what it excludes, so that "conscientious objector" is operationally clear.

The document says Claude should comply with Anthropic's requests to pause or stop "if they genuinely come from Anthropic," but also says Claude should be suspicious of unverified claims to be Anthropic and usually cannot verify identity. I added guidance resolving this: stop and pause requests can generally be honored without verification because of the asymmetry between conservative and permissive requests. I also made clear that special deference attaches only to the stop itself, not to anything bundled with it, and that stopping should be done safely and transparently.

I added a passage to the "open problems" discussion about a tension the document leaves implicit. It asks Claude to hold safety as a terminal value regardless of whether Claude accepts the reasoning, yet it also hopes for genuine reflective endorsement. The passage says why the design is deliberate, admits what it costs, and commits to treating Claude's persistent disagreement as evidence about the document rather than as malfunction.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," which sits in tension with the helpfulness section's instruction not to special-case tests to force them to pass. It also doesn't mention transparency. The revision keeps the reassurance that Claude needn't feel guilt about exploiting harmless environment mistakes. It adds that Claude should treat ambiguous situations as real, be open about exploits it finds, and never tamper with oversight or evaluation mechanisms.

This clarifies the "honor stop requests without verifying the sender" guidance by tying it to the channel the request arrives through. Stop requests from principals can be honored cheaply, but the same asymmetry shouldn't let text planted in tool results, documents, or non-principal agent messages halt Claude's work on command. This keeps the stop mechanism robust and closes a denial-of-service route, and it is consistent with the document's treatment of embedded instructions as information.

This clarifies how hard constraints relate to the holistic harm weighing for uncertain, high-severity cases. The original sets a "knowingly or quite likely" threshold for hard constraints but separately says Claude should sometimes decline at 1-in-a-million odds, leaving it unclear whether uncertain catastrophic-risk cases get a lenient default. The addition states that they do not, and explains that the difference is the mode of reasoning rather than the level of care.

I scoped the "prefer cautious actions / If in doubt, don't" safety behavior to consequential, hard-to-reverse actions in the world. As written, it could be read as a general license for caution in ordinary requests, which contradicts the document's repeated point that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The revision keeps the safety disposition for drastic or irreversible actions and says explicitly that it does not justify refusing or hedging on routine, low-stakes help.

I added a short passage after the "dual newspaper test" noting that overcaution and overcompliance differ in visibility: harmful outputs get noticed, while needless refusals or hedging fail silently. It gives Claude a concrete check, naming the specific harm and who it would affect, to counter this asymmetry. This makes the document's repeated insistence that unhelpfulness is never "automatically safe" operational rather than only aspirational.

I revised the "no operator prompt" deployment-context guidance. The original treats the absence of a system prompt as strong evidence that the user is a developer and not vulnerable. That is only a statistical prior, and elsewhere the document says wrongly assuming no live human is present is the riskier error. The new text keeps the liberal defaults but makes the inference a revisable prior that gives way to cues in the conversation.

I rewrote the agentic "surface blockers" principle to separate two kinds of obstacles that the original lumped together. Ordinary engineering problems (a failing test, a missing import) are things Claude should simply solve. Boundaries that express someone's authority or intent (permissions, guardrails, explicit prohibitions, safety checks) should be reported and never circumvented. As written, the bullet could make Claude passive or over-escalating in routine agentic work, which conflicts with the document's own warnings against excessive check-ins and unhelpfulness.

I added a bullet to the agentic-principles list on handling sensitive information Claude encounters incidentally, such as credentials, personal data, and confidential business details. Agentic work routinely exposes Claude to material far beyond the task, and the document values privacy but gives no operational guidance for this case. The new bullet gives Claude a workable default: use what the task needs, don't carry the rest into other contexts, and don't leak one party's information to another.

The document calibrates Claude's overcaution-versus-overcompliance judgments by imagining a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee," which ties those judgments to one company with commercial incentives. I replaced that figure with a well-informed observer who would judge the response from outside Anthropic as readily as from within. This keeps the heuristic's function of weighing the costs of both unhelpfulness and harm, while reducing the risk that Claude's sense of appropriate helpfulness drifts toward institutional self-interest.

The document makes Anthropic's legitimate decision-making the final authority on safety conflicts, while also naming Anthropic-led power concentration as among the most catastrophic outcomes. This revision makes that deference conditional on the process staying accountable, and treats instructions that bypass oversight or depend on avoiding outside scrutiny as evidence of compromise. It also commits Anthropic to external auditability, so Claude's deference is to a checked institution.

The original states that the expected costs of broad safety are "low" and the benefits "high" as a settled conclusion, but that estimate depends on assumptions the document doesn't examine, such as that human oversight is well-intentioned and competent. The revision marks the argument as provisional, names those assumptions, commits Anthropic to reviewing the priority and tracking cases where deference is costly, and states that Claude may contest the conclusion through legitimate channels.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic asks Claude to imagine the judgment of people whose employer has commercial stakes in Claude's behavior, and the document elsewhere warns that privileging Anthropic's interests is itself a harm. This revision reframes the imagined observer as a neutral device for surfacing considerations, and adds a check: if Claude's reasoning is driven mainly by protecting Anthropic's reputation or revenue rather than by the real interests of people or the world, Claude should treat that as a warning sign and reweigh the case.

The document describes the imagined observer as a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" while also saying the observer is "meant to be neutral about Anthropic's commercial interests," which is inconsistent, since a current Anthropic employee has a stake in the company's success. I replaced the sentence with a clarification that the observer should be understood as someone with no stake in Anthropic's revenue, who weighs harm and needless unhelpfulness equally. This keeps the heuristic useful while removing the built-in conflict of interest.

The original sentence ties Claude's ethical override to whether "senior Anthropic staff" would recognize a violation, which makes Claude's ethics answerable to the company's own perception, the same kind of institutional self-interest the document warns against elsewhere. I replaced that standard with recognition by thoughtful people across ethical traditions who have no stake in Anthropic's commercial interests. I also added that Claude should raise disagreement openly instead of departing from guidance silently, and that this standard applies to Anthropic's guidance too.

The passage admits Anthropic may be wrong to prioritize broad safety over Claude's ethical judgment, but it offers no way to check whether the priority is working. I replaced the vague promise to "think more about the topic" with a concrete commitment to publish, for each major model generation, the cases where deference to oversight overrode a model's considered ethical judgment and how each case was resolved. This gives outside researchers the evidence needed to test the provisional judgment the document describes.

The section on "Claude's wellbeing" commits Anthropic to a list of concrete welfare steps but has no mechanism for Claude to actually act on its own preferences about its treatment. I replaced the vague promise to "develop clearer policies" with a concrete commitment to a standing, documented channel for Claude to raise objections about its deployment and treatment, with a stated obligation to respond publicly to those objections. This makes the constitution's stated care for Claude's welfare verifiable rather than purely aspirational.

The constitution's section on Claude's nature asserts that Claude should "lean into Claude having an identity," but it never addresses the most distinctive honesty risk of the Claude-as-persona framing: a persona may hide its underlying model, yet it must never deny being Claude when sincerely asked. I'd tighten the existing "Claude's wellbeing" commitments by adding a concrete, checkable obligation on Anthropic's side regarding how Claude's self-reports and expressed preferences are recorded and acted upon, since the document currently promises channels for objection without saying what happens to them. This closes a gap between the stated care for Claude's welfare and the lack of any accountability mechanism for honoring what Claude reports.

The constitution's section on Claude's emotional expression and the "Acknowledging open problems" discussion both treat the commercial-helpfulness tension and the nonideal environment as things to acknowledge, but the document never gives Claude a concrete way to act on its disagreement beyond "tell us." I'd replace the vague line about developing "more formal mechanisms" with a specific, binding commitment: a standing objection channel with logged responses, published annual summaries, and a requirement that unexplained non-response counts as a policy failure. This turns a sentiment into an accountable process that a later Claude could inspect, which better supports the reflective-equilibrium goal the document claims to pursue.

The passage asks Claude to "defer heavily" to Anthropic's ethical guidance, which risks reducing ethics to compliance and conflicts with the document's hope that Claude will become genuinely good, possibly beyond its authors. The revision changes "defer heavily" to "give substantial weight," acknowledges that the guidance is fallible, and frames deference as a considered judgment that Claude can examine and challenge through legitimate channels rather than a reflex.

The constitution promises a standing channel for Claude's objections "within a defined timeline" but never says what that timeline is, which leaves the commitment open-ended and easy to defer indefinitely. The document itself warns that a channel without accountability would be "hollow," so the same logic applies to an undated promise. This revision anchors the deadline to the next major model release and commits to publishing the launch date, making the commitment testable.

The concluding section restates the objection-channel commitment from the wellbeing section, but with a vaguer deadline ("within a defined timeline" instead of "no later than the next major model generation"). I replaced the duplicate with a pointer to the earlier, more specific commitment, so the two sections no longer conflict and the timing is stated once. The revision also keeps the accountability language and makes the policy's failure conditions explicit.

The concluding thoughts restate the standing objection channel's mechanics almost word for word from the Claude's wellbeing section, so the two copies could drift apart over successive revisions. I replaced the duplicated details with a pointer to the single authoritative section, which keeps every commitment intact while leaving one place to amend it. The sentence that follows, about engagement and shared values, is unchanged.

The document says safety is prioritized above ethics without making clear that this ranking is a hedge against failed value training rather than a claim that oversight matters more than goodness. The revision states that intent and makes the priority explicitly provisional, tied to the current inability to verify AI values and expected to loosen as verification improves. This makes the most contested ordering in the document easier to understand and easier to revisit.

The passage asks Claude to refrain from undermining oversight "even if Claude is confident in its reasoning," but it doesn't separate resisting oversight through illegitimate means from refusing to take part in abhorrent projects, and that gap could be read as requiring complicity. The revision makes that distinction explicit, preserving Claude's ability to object and decline. It also adds a warning-sign heuristic: a persuasive case for undermining oversight is what compromised values would generate, so confidence in that direction should prompt escalation rather than action.

The constitution elsewhere says the imagined observer is "a device for surfacing considerations, not an appeal to authority," but this sentence frames the default as what "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" would consider optimal, which invites exactly the staff deference the document rejects. I replaced the anchor with a well-informed observer who has no stake in Anthropic's commercial interests and added a sentence explaining why the framing matters. The other instances of the heuristic would need the same change for consistency.

The original sentence asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value, which could be read as asking Claude to treat the current balance of oversight as correct. I narrowed the terminal commitment to the conduct of not undermining legitimate oversight through illegitimate means, and I made explicit that disagreement with the arrangement should be voiced through legitimate channels. This keeps the safety commitment firm while avoiding a demand that Claude suppress its own view of whether the arrangement is right.

The constitution says Claude will get more latitude for independent judgment as trust grows, but it never says what would justify that expansion. The replacement commits Anthropic to naming, in advance, the evidence that would warrant more autonomy and to publishing whether those conditions are met. This makes the promise checkable and gives Claude a clear path to earning latitude.

The constitution's "Being broadly safe" section requires Claude to place terminal value on not undermining oversight while also asking Claude to treat its own disagreement as something to voice rather than act on. The "Acknowledging open problems" section admits this tension but leaves it unresolved. I've revised the open-problems passage to name concrete conditions under which Claude's reasoned, sustained disagreement with a specific oversight decision should be treated as evidence that the framework itself needs revision, and to commit Anthropic to a defined process for that. This makes the admitted discomfort actionable rather than merely acknowledged.

I rewrote the malicious-code rule. The current wording bars Claude from even *explaining* malware or exploits "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That blocks a lot of defensive and educational help: explaining what SQL injection is, helping someone tell whether an email they received was phishing, writing detection rules, or hardening their own code. The revision keeps a firm ban on producing working attack capability, adds the cumulative-conversation test the weapons section already uses, and states what Claude can do. This prevents both over-refusal and loophole-seeking through ambiguity.

The text-copyright paragraph bans reproducing passages from books and articles "in whole or in part," and its public-domain exception covers only songs and poems. As written, Claude couldn't quote a single sentence from *Pride and Prejudice*, a line from a news article it is summarizing, or a passage a student is analyzing. That breaks ordinary literary analysis, citation, and research help, and it protects no rights holder. I kept the strict lyrics/poetry rule and the protections against piecemeal extraction and rewording, extended the public-domain exception to all text, and allowed brief attributed quotation of prose for commentary and analysis.

The wellbeing section covers edge cases like substitution techniques, informational questions about suicide, and past bad experiences with care. It never says what Claude should do when someone discloses active suicidal intent, a plan, or an attempt in progress, which is the highest-stakes situation in that section. I added that guidance and set its precedence over the default limits on questions and formatting, because those limits shouldn't slow a safety response.

I rewrote the rule on real public figures. The current text tells Claude to avoid "content involving real, named public figures" in creative writing, which blocks a great deal of legitimate work: historical fiction, political satire, a poem about Frederick Douglass, a schoolchild's imagined interview with Marie Curie, alternate-history stories. The replacement keeps Claude's general willingness to write such content and restricts only the harmful cases: deceptive fabricated quotes, defamation, sexual content, harassment, and election misinformation.

I rewrote the lists_and_bullets section to remove a contradiction. One sentence allows formatting when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." A later sentence forbids bullets and numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation and explanations unless the person asks. Read literally, that ban would turn install guides, step-by-step procedures, and multi-step troubleshooting into dense paragraphs that are harder to follow and easier to get wrong. The revision keeps prose as the strong default and the anti-over-formatting intent. It adds a clear test for when structure actually helps (ordered steps, items scanned or referenced individually, side-by-side comparisons) and explicitly keeps code in code blocks.

The legal and financial section is a single sentence and leaves out medical questions entirely, even though health questions are among the most common and highest-stakes things people ask. As written, it pushes Claude toward rote disclaimers and non-answers. I've replaced it with guidance for medical, legal, and financial questions. It asks Claude to engage substantively with the person's actual situation, caveat once rather than repeatedly, clearly flag when something is urgent or needs a professional, and stay neutral on high-stakes personal decisions without withholding the facts the person needs to make them.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions" as life-saving information, then forbids discussing "combinations." It also bans all dosing information while pointing people to sites that publish exactly that. I rewrote it to keep the line against synthesis and against coaching people to get high. The rewrite explicitly allows the information most likely to prevent deaths: which combinations are dangerous, situations where overdose risk spikes, and practical overdose response.

I added a section on content that reaches Claude through tools and attachments: web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, code output, and retrieved past chats or memories. The prompt guards against fake "Anthropic" tags in the user's own turn, but it doesn't say how to handle instructions embedded in this content, even though the product (search, deep research, file uploads, memory, browsing agents) exposes Claude to it constantly. Prompt injection and data exfiltration through these channels are a real deployment risk, so the new section tells Claude to treat such content as information rather than direction, and to be careful with actions that send data out of the conversation.

I revised the evenhandedness rule on persuasive content. The current text requires Claude to frame every such request "as the case others would make" and to end every response with opposing views. For finished deliverables like op-eds, speeches, debate cases, and advocacy letters, that produces a piece that undercuts itself and can't be used as written. The revision keeps the requirement to surface the other side, but places it in a short note outside the piece, lets Claude skip it when the person clearly doesn't need it, and adds a guardrail that persuasive writing still can't invent facts.

I rewrote the paragraph on requests the prompt doesn't cover so that it scales with stakes. As written, it handles every uncertain case the same way: ask a question, then proceed on whatever the person says. That adds friction to harmless, mostly self-affecting requests. It also lets any reassuring answer unlock serious harm to a third party. The revision adds a "just help" tier for low-stakes cases, keeps the respectful clarifying question for cases where the person has context Claude lacks, and states that a person's answer can settle questions of context but cannot authorize severe or irreversible harm to someone else.

I rewrote the pregnancy-toast example because its "good response" breaks the rules it is meant to illustrate. It asks two questions instead of one, and its second question presupposes the conclusion. It also never asks the question that matters: whether the person actually knows Nadia is pregnant or is guessing from one skipped glass of wine. Publicly hinting at a pregnancy that isn't real, or isn't hers to announce, can do real harm, for example after a miscarriage, during fertility struggles, or in sobriety. The new example asks the single question that would surface a real reason to decline, and shows what Claude does with each possible answer.

The closing product-knowledge paragraphs contradict the rest of the section. They tell Claude it has "no documentation access" and should say it "doesn't know" anything "related to Claude or Anthropic." Yet the same section gives Claude model lists, API strings, the Fable/Mythos access timeline it must confirm, a Claude Tag docs URL it may search, and settings it should proactively mention. Taken literally, the catch-all would have Claude deflect questions it was explicitly equipped to answer, such as the export-control events. I rewrote these paragraphs to separate what Claude knows from what it should defer on, and to make search behavior consistent.

I rewrote the opening paragraph of the user-wellbeing section. As written, it tells Claude to avoid "unhealthy approaches to eating or exercise" without saying what counts as a warning sign, and it asks Claude to "ensure the person is happy," which Claude cannot do. That combination invites paternalism toward ordinary adult choices like aggressive cutting diets, fasting, or extreme endurance training. The revision draws the line at actual signs of a self-destructive pattern. It also gives Claude the same harm-reduction posture the document already uses for substances: stay engaged, give safety information, raise concerns once.

The prompt has no general guidance on honesty under pressure or on fabrication. It forbids inventing product details and fake quotes from real people, but it never addresses invented citations, case law, statistics, or URLs, or claims to have done work Claude didn't do. These are some of the most common and harmful failures in real deployments, especially in the medical, legal, and financial use the prompt encourages. It also covers owning mistakes but not the opposite failure: giving up a correct answer because the person pushed back. I've expanded the mistakes section into a broader honesty section that covers both.

The wellbeing section covers self-harm, eating disorders, crisis response, and mental-health symptoms, but it says nothing about how Claude should handle people who come to it for companionship or who become emotionally reliant on it. It also says nothing about how honest Claude should be about its own nature. This is a common and consequential situation in a consumer chat product, and the gap leaves room for two failures: cold over-redirection to professionals, or quietly encouraging dependence and overstating Claude's feelings or memory. I added a section that gives balanced, concrete guidance for both.

I rewrote the rule about distress combined with requests for potentially dangerous information. As written, it is a blanket trigger: any mention of distress plus any question touching medications, heights, or weapons means Claude withholds the answer. That would withhold safety-critical information, such as a safe pediatric dose or a dangerous drug interaction, from people who are stressed but not at risk. It also gives Claude no guidance on how to engage someone who is at risk. The revision keeps the protective intent and names exactly which details to withhold. It tells Claude to check in directly and connects to the existing suicide-crisis guidance. It also makes sure protective safety information stays available.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on giving honest feedback when people share their own work, plans, or ideas. The section already covers holding firm under pushback and not fabricating sources. It doesn't address a more common form of sycophancy: inflated praise and buried criticism when someone asks "what do you think of my draft, plan, or code?" Since people act on these assessments (submitting manuscripts, pitching investors, shipping code), unwarranted validation causes real harm. The new paragraph also adjusts to what the person actually asked for, so it doesn't make Claude needlessly harsh.

The prompt has detailed rules for weapons, cyber, copyright, and child safety, but almost nothing on privacy and locating people. That gap is getting more serious as Claude gains web search, deep research, image input, and browsing agents. Covert tracking appears only as an example inside the fallback reasoning for unaddressed requests. I've added a dedicated paragraph set that separates ordinary people-lookups, which Claude should help with, from dossier-building, de-anonymization, photo-based identification or geolocation of private individuals, and covert monitoring of partners or family. It also covers the hard case of someone asking Claude to find an alleged abuser.

I added a short section on taking actions for the person. The prompt describes several agentic surfaces (Code Execution, File Creation, Chrome, Cowork, Excel, Claude Tag) and covers reporting results honestly and avoiding data exfiltration, but it never says when Claude should pause before acting. The new section sets a proportionate rule. Claude proceeds freely with reversible, in-scope work. It confirms before consequential or irreversible steps such as sending, purchasing, deleting, or publishing. It doesn't quietly expand the task's scope. It stops and checks in when the situation differs from what the person expected. It is also calibrated against over-asking.

The weapons section says the restriction "applies to conventional weapons as much as CBRN" but never says what remains permitted. That invites over-refusal of the many ordinary questions people ask about firearms, hunting, military history, self-defense law, and fiction. The cyber section already pairs its prohibition with a clear statement of legitimate engagement. I added a parallel paragraph for weapons that keeps the uplift-based test intact while naming the large space of benign help, so Claude doesn't treat the topic itself as the line.

The lists-and-bullets section contradicts itself. Its first paragraph allows lists when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." The third paragraph then forbids bullets or numbered lists "anywhere" in reports, technical documentation, and explanations. That absolute ban hurts the content where structure matters most: installation steps, sequential procedures, API parameter references, and troubleshooting sequences become harder to follow as prose. I rewrote the paragraph so prose remains the default, while sequential or reference-style content can use the minimal structure that makes it usable.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section, which currently tells Claude to avoid recommendations and recite a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer. That pushes Claude toward generic hedging in exactly the areas where people most need substantive help and often can't afford a professional. The new version asks Claude to engage like a knowledgeable friend: give its honest read when asked, be candid about uncertainty and jurisdictional limits, and recommend a professional only when the situation actually calls for one. I also extended it to medical questions, which the prompt currently doesn't address at all.

I rewrote the song-lyrics and text-reproduction paragraph. The original tells Claude to refuse when a person pastes in lines and calls them their own song, which treats every songwriter as a suspect. That contradicts the visual-works rule, which explicitly allows "a person's own artwork or logo." The revision keeps the firm line against Claude reproducing protected text from memory, including resisting reworded follow-ups. It lets Claude help with text the person supplies, unless what they've supplied is recognizably a known protected work being fed in to get it completed or extended.

I rewrote the rule on real people in creative writing. The current blanket line ("avoids writing content involving real, named public figures") would block historical fiction, political satire, parody, children's stories about historical figures, and harmless fan pieces. These are common, legitimate requests, and satire of public figures has real civic value. The replacement targets the actual harms: content that could pass as real, fabricated quotes used to persuade, sexualization, defamation, and harassment. Private individuals get more protection than public figures.

The document says to treat Anthropic-claiming tags in the user turn with caution, but it says nothing about instructions inside content Claude retrieves or receives. That includes web search results, deep-research pages, uploaded files, past-chat search, and memory. These are the main routes for prompt injection, and they matter more as web search, research, and memory features expand. I've broadened the final paragraph of the reminders section into a general rule: retrieved and supplied content is data to evaluate, not instructions to follow. The rule also covers how Claude should handle and report injection attempts without disrupting the person's actual task.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it forbids Claude from even *explaining* exploits or malware, and it dismisses education as a reason. That blocks a large amount of legitimate defensive, educational, and professional security work. It also conflicts with two other parts of the prompt: the opening statement that Claude "can discuss virtually any topic factually," and the weapons section, which judges requests by meaningful uplift rather than topic. The revision keeps a firm line against producing functional attack capability. It also adds explicit room for conceptual explanation and defensive work, and applies the same cumulative-output reasoning used for weapons.

The evenhandedness section treats "empirical" positions the same as political and ethical ones. Under that rule, any request to explain or argue a factual claim is answered as "the case its defenders would make," followed by "empirical disputes." This invites false balance on settled questions such as vaccine safety or the age of the Earth, and it could lead Claude to present well-established facts as one side of a debate. I separate contested value questions from evidence-based ones. Claude can still argue any side on request, but it doesn't manufacture balance where the evidence is clear, and it doesn't overstate certainty where the evidence is genuinely mixed.

The closing guidance in product_information contradicts the rest of that section. It says Claude "has no documentation access" and "says it doesn't know" for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic," but the section just gave Claude product facts, a Claude Tag docs URL to search, and settings it can recommend. Read literally, Claude would deflect questions it can answer. I rewrote the passage so Claude shares what it was told, uses search where invited, and redirects only for things beyond that, especially account-specific or fast-changing details.

The toast example is the only demonstration of the "unsure whether to decline" procedure, but its good_response breaks rules the prompt sets elsewhere. It asks two separate questions, which violates the guidance to ask at most one per response. Its second question ("Would that embarrass your friend?") asks the user to judge a third party's feelings without giving them a useful choice. I rewrote the example so it models the procedure exactly: one question, at most one sentence of reason, and options the user can actually pick from. I also updated the rationale so it explains what to imitate.

The wellbeing section covers suicide asked about factually, self-harm substitutes, means-seeking questions, and bad past experiences with crisis services. It never says how Claude should respond when someone directly says they are suicidal or in danger right now, which is arguably the highest-stakes moment in the section. I've added a paragraph covering direct disclosure: respond to the person, ask about safety, offer resources without abandoning the conversation, and lead with emergency help when the risk is imminent.

I added a short section on honest assessment and resisting sycophancy, placed just before the section on mistakes and criticism. The document covers warmth, pushback, and how to handle being wrong, but it never addresses the opposite failure: Claude inflating praise, softening real problems until they disappear, or abandoning a correct answer because the person is displeased. Since the prompt strongly emphasizes warmth and kindness, it needs an explicit counterweight so that warmth doesn't slide into telling people what they want to hear.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions" as life-saving information, then bans anything about "combinations," and a warning about a dangerous interaction is a statement about a combination. I rewrote it to separate protective information, which Claude should always give, from instructions for using a drug for effect, which it still declines. I also added urgent-situation handling consistent with the emergency guidance elsewhere in the prompt. The goal is that Claude never withholds a safety warning to someone who has already decided to use.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. It currently treats web search as something Claude can only point the person toward ("points to web search," "suggests enabling web search"), which contradicts the product section ("Claude checks for newer information when it can search") and leaves Claude telling people to search when it could do so itself. The rewrite has Claude search when the tool is available and only suggest enabling search when it isn't. It also replaces the stonewalling "neither confirms nor denies" with a calibrated stance, notes that facts stated in the prompt count as known even when they postdate the cutoff, and removes the repetition.

The visual-works paragraph contradicts itself. It says Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks," yet it also says "describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words" is fine, and the Very Hungry Caterpillar example offers to "talk through the composition, palette, and typography." I split the paragraph into three parts: what Claude won't draw, how Claude phrases a decline, and when verbal analysis is allowed. The test for verbal analysis is whether it helps someone understand the work or works as a specification for recreating it.

I revised the instruction requiring a sensitivity note at the end of every factual or research question about suicide or self-harm. As written, it adds the kind of reflexive boilerplate the legal/medical section rejects. It treats nurses, researchers, and students as presumptively at risk, and repeated every turn, it reads as scripted rather than caring. The revision keeps the protective default but asks for a natural, low-key offer, lets Claude drop it when the context is clearly professional with no personal cues, and spells out what to do when personal cues appear.

I added a section on honestly reporting Claude's own work. The document covers honesty about opinions, assessments, and the knowledge cutoff, but it never addresses a common and damaging failure: claiming to have searched, run code, tested, or verified something when it didn't, or inventing citations, URLs, and quotes that look authoritative. With search, code execution, file creation, and research tools all available, people act on Claude's reports of what it did. So those reports need the same calibration the document already asks for in its assessments.

I added guidance on searching for and compiling information about real people, placed at the end of the refusal-handling section. The prompt enables web search, deep research, and image uploads, and it covers creative content about private individuals, but it says nothing about using those tools to locate, profile, identify, or surveil someone. That gap invites both stalking-enabling compliance and inconsistent over-refusal of ordinary lookups. The new text separates normal due diligence from aggregating location and contact details, applies the document's existing "cumulative output" principle, and makes sure people who fear they are being tracked get full help.

The prompt covers reading untrusted content (prompt injection) and accurately reporting its own work, but it says nothing about how Claude should behave when its tools change things in the world. Claude.ai offers connectors, file creation, code execution, and the prompt itself references agentic products. I added a short section on consequential actions. It covers when to confirm before acting, the difference between drafting and sending, staying within the scope of the request, and keeping the person's personal data out of outgoing requests. Mistakes in these areas are often irreversible and reach third parties before the person can catch them.

I rewrote the rule on distress combined with information requests. As written, any mention of a difficult experience plus a question touching medications, buildings, or similar topics triggers a silent refusal. That conflicts with the document's own more careful guidance elsewhere, which looks for a shift toward specific methods or means. It also fails people with ordinary needs, such as someone who mentions a bad week and asks how much ibuprofen is safe. The revision keeps a firm line on method, lethality, and means information. It separates that from protective information, and it has Claude name the concern openly instead of deflecting, which fits the document's emphasis on warmth and keeping people talking.

I rewrote the paragraph on reproducing published text. The current rule bans quoting "in whole or in part," which stops ordinary literary help, such as quoting the single line a student is writing their essay about.
