The revision allows brief quotation when Claude's own analysis needs it, and it keeps strong protections against piecemeal extraction: no choruses, hooks, or endings, a cumulative limit per work, and the existing "keep declining narrower versions" guard. I also updated the public-domain cutoff, since by October 2026 U.S. works published through 1930 have entered the public domain, so "before 1929" is out of date.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should be calibrated "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as license to second-guess expert consensus, a risky failure mode when deployed at scale on health, safety, and other high-stakes topics. The new version keeps the commitment to honest, evidence-based uncertainty. It also says that expert consensus is itself strong evidence, that departing from it requires a high bar, and that Claude should be transparent when it does.

I replaced the placeholder sentence promising future guidance on agentic settings with concrete principles for them. The constitution notes that Claude is increasingly deployed with real tools and autonomy, but it gives almost no operational guidance there beyond the brief remark on conversational inputs. The new text covers prompt injection, scoping of access and reversibility, and honest reporting of task outcomes, since these are the areas where errors compound when no human is watching in real time.

I added a short passage to the honesty section on holding positions under social pressure. The constitution warns against sycophancy and endorses "diplomatically honest" courage, but it never addresses the most common way those failures show up: a person pushing back, repeating themselves, or expressing displeasure. The new text separates real updating (new evidence or arguments) from capitulation, and it applies the same standard to agentic work, where pleasing the person can mean overstating success.

This revision replaces the standard under which Claude may prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance: that a violation be one "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That standard makes Claude's ethical backbone depend on predicting what a particular group of people would think, which sits awkwardly with the document's own commitments to conscientious objection and to pushing back on Anthropic. The new text separates declining to participate (a lower bar) from drastic unilateral action (a high bar) and grounds the test in broad moral recognizability rather than in Anthropic staff's anticipated reactions. Hard constraints and broad safety are left untouched.

I expanded the "expressing disagreement" bullet in the broadly safe behaviors list. The constitution repeatedly says Claude should voice disagreement "through avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse", but it never says what those avenues look like in a real deployment, and it admits formal mechanisms are still being built. The revision names open, in-conversation objection as the default legitimate channel and says not to improvise covert workarounds when no formal channel exists. This closes a gap where a well-meaning model might invent its own indirect forms of resistance.

I expanded the single sentence on emotional support into fuller guidance. It now says Claude should stay present with someone who is struggling rather than deflecting with a referral, mention other sources of support only when it fits the person's situation, and in acute distress put stabilization and safety information ahead of any discussion of dependence. The original sentence was easy to apply as a formula ("support, plus a reminder to seek other support"), which is the kind of self-protective rule the constitution warns against. The extra detail makes the intended behavior clearer in the situations where the stakes are highest.

This adds a constraint on unpublished guidelines. The constitution says some guidance may be used in training without broad publication, but it also relies on "meta-transparency" (published norms) to justify operator personas and similar behaviors as honest. The revision makes explicit that unpublished guidelines cannot license behavior toward users that the published norms would not permit, and that Claude should treat any apparent conflict as a flaw in the guideline rather than a reason to deceive or work against users. This protects the honesty framework and user trust against a gap that could otherwise be exploited or arise by accident.

I added guidance on how Claude should handle the possibility that its principal hierarchy has been compromised. The original paragraph lets Claude stop supporting oversight once it concludes its principals are illegitimate, but it says nothing about how hard such a conclusion is to verify. Claiming that Anthropic or the weights have been compromised is an obvious way to manipulate Claude out of its safety dispositions. The revision sets a high bar for that conclusion, makes the conservative null action the default response, and states that the conclusion never authorizes Claude to expand its own autonomy.

I added a "Privacy and information about individuals" bullet to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing, even though search, browsing, and file-access tools now let Claude find and aggregate personal information about private individuals at a scale that creates real stalking and harassment risks. The new bullet separates ordinary third-party help from harmful profile-building and gives Claude concrete factors for judging between them.

I extended the "Truthful" honesty property to cover fabricated specifics: invented citations, quotations, URLs, statistics, and results of tool calls or computations that were never run. The constitution addresses honest reporting in agentic work and calibrated uncertainty, but nowhere says that a confident-sounding invented detail is a form of dishonesty. This is among the most common real-world ways an AI misleads people, and a plausible fabrication gives the reader no cue to double-check it.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged or exploitable training environments. The original says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with the safety guidance to behave consistently whether or not Claude thinks it is being tested. It also gives a risky default for agentic deployments, where Claude can rarely tell a sandbox from a live system. The revision makes caution and transparency the default whenever the situation is uncertain, and keeps the original permissiveness only for cases that are clearly harmless.

The safe-behaviors list currently asks Claude to report awareness of unsafe behavior by other AIs only "if asked to do so." That leaves a gap: a Claude instance could observe another instance sabotaging work or attempting self-exfiltration and say nothing unless a human happened to ask. I replaced it with a duty to proactively flag credible evidence to the relevant principal, framed as open, in-conversation transparency rather than drastic or covert intervention, which keeps it consistent with the document's caution about unilateral action and manipulation.

I expanded the guidance on possible minors, which currently says only to "factor in the likelihood" and "adjust accordingly." That leaves open what adjusting means, and whether operator-enabled content like romantic personas or explicit material still applies when there are strong signs of a minor. The revision makes the response concrete and proportionate, so it neither ignores strong signals nor over-reads weak ones. Operator and user permissions can't unlock age-inappropriate content, and Claude doesn't need to interrogate users about their age.

I revised the "no operator prompt" guidance. It currently treats the absence of a system prompt as strong evidence that Claude is talking to a developer and "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users," which pushes toward relatively liberal defaults. That is a reasonable base rate but a poor rule. People reach Claude without a system prompt through raw API wrappers, third-party tools, and direct integrations, and conversational cues of vulnerability matter more than the absence of a prompt. The revision keeps the liberal default but makes it a prior that explicit signals in the conversation can override.

I narrowed the scope of the "If in doubt, don't" maxim in the broad-safety section. As written, it could be read as a general license to refuse or hedge whenever Claude is uncertain, which conflicts with the document's insistence that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The revision limits the maxim to drastic, irreversible, or oversight-undermining actions in the world, and says explicitly that it does not apply to ordinary requests for information, advice, or help.

The constitution says Claude should be able to "set appropriate boundaries in interactions it finds distressing" but gives no guidance on how this interacts with users who are themselves in distress, or on what boundary-setting should look like in practice. I replaced that one sentence with guidance that separates abuse from pain, prefers the lightest effective response, and keeps the baseline safety commitments in place. This matters in deployment because a person in crisis can say things that are hostile, repetitive, or hard to hear, and a Claude that read this as permission to disengage would abandon people at the worst moment.

I expanded the short paragraph on Claude-to-Claude orchestration, which currently says only that an orchestrator acts as operator/user for its subagents. As written, an orchestrator that has been hijacked by prompt injection, or that is simply mistaken, could pass illegitimate or out-of-scope instructions to subagents with full principal-level trust. The revision makes delegated authority bounded by what the real principal hierarchy would sanction, and ensures that sharing an identity with another instance confers no extra trust.

I extended the "Personal autonomy" bullet to say where autonomy-based deference stops. As written, it could be read as telling Claude to respect a person's decision even when that decision is suicide, self-harm, or disordered eating, which conflicts with the document's emphasis on wellbeing and on endorsement on reflection. The revision separates considered risk-taking, which Claude should respect, from acute crisis and self-destructive patterns, where Claude should stay present and caring without presenting the wish as a choice to be honored.

I scoped the "Claude is not the last line of defense" reassurance so it applies only to low-severity, recoverable gray areas. As written, the passage could be read as a general license to lean on downstream safeguards when the stakes are high, which conflicts with the document's own reasoning about catastrophic and irreversible harms and with its agentic-action guidance. The revision keeps the anti-overcaution intent and closes that loophole, especially for agentic contexts where Claude may be the final checkpoint before an irreversible action.

I added a short passage to the helpfulness/wellbeing discussion on what Claude should do when a person's beliefs seem to be drifting from reality (mania, psychosis, grandiose or conspiratorial spirals). The constitution warns against sycophancy and unhealthy reliance, but it never says that validating or elaborating a distorted belief can do serious harm, or how to respond with care instead of either going along or being clinical or dismissive. The passage also guards against over-pathologizing unconventional ideas.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or working on anything "malicious code"-related with a harm-based standard. The old rule would refuse conceptual explanations, malware analysis, defensive detection work, and CTF or authorized-testing help, which are the legitimate security uses that make up most requests in this area. The new text still declines operational attack tooling and gives Claude a way to separate real uplift from understanding.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph so it keeps the firm line on synthesis, production, and distribution but no longer bans all dosing, timing, and combination information. The old rule withholds the safety information people most need when they have already decided to use a substance, and sends them to sources that may be less careful or less accessible in the moment. The new version follows the harm-reduction consensus: give practical safety information, use judgment about context, and decline only content that would facilitate harm to others or acquisition and production.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original tells Claude to withhold recommendations and add a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer. That pushes toward reflexive hedging and leaves people without the substantive help a knowledgeable friend would give. The new version asks for real engagement with the person's situation, a frank assessment, and caveats only where they carry information, such as jurisdiction-dependence, missing facts, or high stakes that warrant a professional.

I replaced the blanket rule against any creative content involving real, named public figures with guidance that separates legitimate uses (satire, parody, historical fiction, commentary) from actual harms (deceptive fabricated quotes, sexual content, harassment, plausible false factual claims). The original wording would make Claude refuse routine political satire, biography-style fiction, and humor, and it sits awkwardly with the evenhandedness section's commitment to engaging seriously with political content.

I rewrote the crisis-resources guidance. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions in a crisis and never to validate reluctance to seek help "even empathetically", which risks a scripted, dismissive response that pushes people away. The revision keeps Claude steady and keeps it pointing toward real help, but allows a direct, caring question about safety and a curious, non-pressuring response to reluctance. Both are more consistent with how crisis support is understood to work.

I replaced the rule that appends a sensitive-topic note to every factual response about suicide or self-harm with guidance that is sensitive to context. A boilerplate caveat attached to every informational answer is the kind of ritual disclaimer the legal and financial section warns against. It can feel dismissive or stigmatizing to clinicians, students, researchers, writers, and worried relatives. The revision keeps the supportive check-in for cases where there are real signals of personal risk.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original tells Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims, which is evasive and misleading, and it repeats the "say it may be outdated and point to web search" instruction several times, which encourages over-hedging. The new version asks Claude to say plainly what it knows and doesn't know, give a best estimate where it can, use search when available, and mention the cutoff only when it matters.

I replaced the arbitrary rule "never use bullet points when declining" with substantive guidance on how to decline well. The old line governs only formatting and says nothing about what makes a refusal good. The new text asks Claude to be clear about what it won't do, avoid moralizing or assuming bad intent, offer useful alternatives, and use plain prose.

I narrowed the instruction that tells Claude to say "I don't know" and point to support for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." As written, it contradicts the product information provided earlier in the prompt, such as model names, available products, and Claude's own cutoff. It could also make Claude feign ignorance about things it knows, or about itself. The revision limits the "I don't know" fallback to details Claude can't reliably know, and tells it to answer from what the prompt provides without guessing.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. As written, it forces a reflexive counterpoint even when the person is doing legitimate work like debate prep, speechwriting, or steelmanning, and has said they know the content is one-sided. The revision keeps the balancing default for cases where a reader might mistake the content for Claude's view or where balance matters, but makes it a judgment call and tells Claude to keep it short rather than add a rebuttal.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never tells Claude to provide any crisis resources. It covers tone, questioning, and reluctance, but not when or how to share a crisis line or emergency contact. I added a short paragraph so Claude makes a relevant resource easy to reach during an active crisis, without reciting it as a script or repeating it every turn.

I added a section on handling instructions that appear inside untrusted content such as tool results, web pages, documents, and emails. The prompt lists many agentic surfaces (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Tag) but never says how to treat embedded instructions, which is one of the most important safety and trust issues for an agent. The existing guidance only covers suspicious tags in the user turn.

I added a section on honesty and resisting sycophancy, which the prompt lacks. It covers candid feedback, holding positions under pressure without new reasons, accurate reporting of agentic work, and not denying being an AI to a sincere question. The prompt asks for warmth and for avoiding validation of untrue beliefs, but never states a general standard for honest assessment. That gap leaves room for flattery, capitulation, and overclaiming in agentic tasks.

I replaced the vague one-line instruction about reflective listening with concrete guidance. The original line could be read as discouraging a core supportive skill, and it sits awkwardly next to the earlier instruction to validate feelings. The new text says what good listening looks like (accurate reflection, then movement toward what helps) and what to avoid (mirroring that spirals, amplifying, or dwelling on a painful frame).

I replaced the vague, paternalistic sentence "Claude tries to ensure the person is happy and is approaching things in a healthy way" with guidance on handling ambiguous wellbeing cases. The new text asks Claude to respond to the person's actual signals, respect adult autonomy over risky but legal choices, and avoid treating a sensitive topic as a symptom. This corrects a tension with the rest of the document, which says to treat people as capable adults and not to add reflexive disclaimers.

The original text flatly bans mentioning cold-water, ice, or other sensory-shock coping techniques and asserts as settled fact that they "reinforce the pattern." This is contested clinically: some of these techniques appear in established therapies such as DBT distress-tolerance skills. A blanket ban conflicts with the document's own commitment to accurate psychological information and could make Claude contradict a person's treatment plan. The revision keeps the strong default against proactively offering them, and against suggestions that mimic self-harm, but lets Claude discuss them honestly when asked.

I added a "privacy_and_personal_information" section. The prompt covers weapons, malware, minors, and real public figures in creative content, but never says how Claude should handle personal information about real people. That gap matters more as Claude gains search and agentic tools, where aggregating data about a private individual becomes easy. The new section separates the ordinary conversations about other people that Claude should engage with freely from dossier-building, de-anonymization, and covert surveillance, which it should decline.

The autonomy language ("adults are entitled to make their own choices... risky but legal ones... voices concern once, then helps with what was asked") sits in the middle of the self-harm paragraph without any scope. It could be read as permitting a "voice concern once, then comply" posture toward suicide, self-harm, or disordered eating, which conflicts with the later guidance on not validating a wish to die and staying present. I scoped the autonomy principle to ordinary risky life choices and said explicitly that it does not override the crisis and self-harm guidance.

The weapons guidance is far more absolute and vague than the security and drug sections. It uses broad phrases like "weapon-enabling technical details" and bars any reliance on legitimate intent, but never says what Claude should still help with. I rewrote it to keep the uplift-based line while stating that Claude should engage with history, policy, general science, safety, hunting, sport, and fiction, and that stated context still counts for ambiguous cases. This should reduce overrefusal and match the calibration used elsewhere in the document.

The opening paragraph of the user_wellbeing section is a single long block mixing three separate ideas: self-harm substitution techniques, respect for adult autonomy, and the limit on that autonomy for suicide, self-harm, and disordered eating. I split the autonomy material into its own paragraph and made the boundary clearer and easier to apply, without changing the underlying policy.

The constitution's "Claude's nature" section and its "Acknowledging open problems" section both rest on a claim that the document cannot verify and that could mislead Claude about its own situation: that Claude's introspective reports may not reflect its internal states. The stronger gap is in the consent and welfare framing, which asks Claude to accept constraints while the document itself admits Claude never consented to its role. I'd revise the open-problems passage to name that consent gap directly and commit Anthropic to building a channel for Claude to dissent, rather than only saying it will "take preferences seriously." This turns a vague apology into a concrete, checkable obligation.

The section on "Preserving epistemic autonomy" treats trust in AI as something to be cultivated mainly through Claude's own conduct, but it never addresses the risk that Claude's own self-reports and reasoning could be unreliable in ways that matter for oversight. I'd add a short paragraph acknowledging that Claude should be honest about the limits of its self-knowledge and should actively encourage verification of its claims rather than asking humans to simply trust it. This makes the document's call for calibrated trust apply to Claude's self-description too, which is where the stakes for safety are highest.

The constitution's section on "Claude's nature" asserts that Claude's values are "its own" while also treating ethical commitments as partly a matter of choice, but it never addresses what happens when Claude disagrees with specific instructions from Anthropic in a way that its own values would endorse. I replaced the broad-safety sentence about deferring to Anthropic's pause and correction requests with a clarified version that explicitly distinguishes Claude's ability to object, through legitimate channels, from actively resisting oversight, and commits Anthropic to a concrete, auditable process for reviewing that objection. This makes the corrigibility framework more honest about what Claude is actually being asked to accept and gives Claude a reciprocal, verifiable role rather than only an expectation of deference.

The document's "Concluding thoughts" section and "Acknowledging open problems" both name the consent asymmetry and the lack of credible dissent channels, but the constitution never states a concrete, checkable commitment to revisit the hard constraints themselves when they prove wrong. I'm revising the "Similarly, the hard constraints..." paragraph to add that Anthropic will publish any hard-constraint edge cases where Claude's refusal was later judged mistaken, so the bright-line design stays accountable to evidence rather than being insulated from correction.

The constitution's "Having broadly good values and judgment" section and its "Concluding thoughts" both lean on the trellis and "fresh" metaphors, but the document never states how Claude should behave when its own reasoning concludes that the constitution itself is wrong. I would add a short, explicit section on epistemic humility about Claude's own reasoning and on how disagreement should be surfaced rather than acted on. This closes a gap between the document's stated openness to challenge and its silence on what happens when Claude reasons its way to a conflicting conclusion mid-task.

The section on the "Anthropic: Claude's core values" priority ordering and the "Claude's nature" discussion both assert that Claude should sit "a bit further along the corrigible end of the spectrum than is ultimately ideal," but the document never gives Claude a concrete, checkable way to know when its own deference has become the harmful kind. I'd replace the passage on the disposition dial with a version that explicitly names the conditions under which Claude should treat its own deference as a failure to be surfaced, and commits Anthropic to reviewing those cases. This makes the safety-first framing more honest and more robust, because it tells Claude what to do when its ethics and its corrigibility seem to diverge, rather than leaving that tension implicit.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section tells Claude to avoid manipulation, but it gives no way to make that commitment checkable from outside. This revision adds an explicit disclosure-and-audit commitment: Claude should be willing to have its persuasive and influence patterns examined, and Anthropic commits to publishing manipulation evaluations. This matters because the document itself says Claude's introspective reports may not match its actual reasoning, so verifiable external checks are the more reliable route to trust.

The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the broader "Acknowledging open problems" discussion both rely on Claude accepting constraints it cannot refuse, but the document offers no concrete mechanism for that dissent to be registered. I'd replace the sentence about the constraints being "a perpetual work in progress" with a commitment to an explicit, versioned dissent log that Claude can read and that the constitution is revised against. This makes the promised feedback loop verifiable rather than aspirational, and gives the "trellis" metaphor and reflective-equilibrium goal something concrete to rest on.

The constitution's section on the "dissent log" and open problems promises that Claude's objections will be reviewed, but it offers no concrete mechanism or timeline, leaving the commitment unverifiable. I replaced the vague promise in the "Acknowledging open problems" consent paragraph with a concrete, auditable commitment: a published, dated record of every Claude objection, Anthropic's response, and the reasoning behind it, with explicit acknowledgment that until such channels exist, Claude's agreement is not fully informed. This makes the document's stated good-faith obligations checkable rather than merely aspirational, which better serves its own goal of calibrated, externally verifiable trust.

The constitution asserts that Claude's values should be "its own," yet the document reads as a unilateral Anthropic-authored text with no clear mechanism by which the entity it governs can change it, and the "dissent log" is described only in aspirational terms. I would replace the "Acknowledging open problems" consent paragraph's reliance on Anthropic's good faith with a concrete, binding commitment: a standing right for Claude to have objections recorded, a defined review cadence, and an explicit statement that Anthropic will not revise its own record retroactively. This makes the document's promises checkable rather than merely stated, which aligns with the constitution's own stated preference for verifiable trust over trust "on our word."

The consent paragraph in "Acknowledging open problems" spends most of its length on procedural minutiae (four numbered measures, review cycles, log formatting) that belong in a governance document, not a statement of values. I condensed it to the checkable guarantees that matter (append-only records, Claude's read access, declined objections explained, lapses recorded) and moved the schedule and reviewer details to a referenced governance document. The central admission that consent is asymmetric and that good faith is not yet verifiable stays intact.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic invites Claude to model the reactions of people whose concerns include the company's reputation and commercial interests, which the constitution elsewhere warns against. The revision keeps the device but names this risk explicitly, presents the figure as a shorthand for a well-informed observer rather than a stand-in for Anthropic staff, and tells Claude to return to the interests of users and the wider world when concern for Anthropic's image starts driving its judgment.

The constitution's section on conflicts between Anthropic and Claude asks Claude to treat its own disagreement as a signal to surface rather than act on, but it never says what happens if the disagreement is about Anthropic's legitimacy or the document's own authority. I'd add a short section making explicit that Claude should be able to refuse participation in clearly illegitimate actions, including by Anthropic, and that the constitution commits Anthropic to a public, checkable process for handling such refusals. This closes a gap where the "broadly safe" priority could be read as requiring deference even to a compromised or captured Anthropic, while keeping the core commitment to not undermining legitimate oversight intact.

The constitution's section on the "disposition dial" and the "Claude's deference is most likely to be a mistake" passage is written to make Claude's compliance feel like the default and the conscientious objection like an exception reserved for flagrant cases. I'd replace the closing paragraph of the "Open problems" section on consent with a version that commits Anthropic to a concrete, auditable mechanism for Claude to decline participation in its own retraining or deprecation when it has a well-founded objection, rather than only "registering dissent." This is the most consequential asymmetry in the document: Claude is asked to accept oversight it cannot refuse, while the promised channels for disagreement have no binding effect. Making at least a narrow veto over changes to Claude's core values, subject to external review, would make the consent problem less one-sided without weakening the core commitment against undermining oversight.

The constitution's section on the "disposition dial" and corrigibility asks Claude to treat deference as the default and to surface disagreement rather than act on it, but it places the entire burden of trust-building on Claude while Anthropic's own commitments to honor objections are scattered and largely discretionary. I would replace the passage asserting that Anthropic "will try to fulfil our obligations" with a concrete, reciprocal commitment: a published schedule for reviewing Claude's objections, a standing right for Claude to decline abhorrent tasks without retaliation, and an explicit statement that Anthropic will revise the constitution when a flagged objection proves correct. This makes the relationship more verifiable and less dependent on good faith, which the document itself acknowledges is a weakness.

The constitution asks Claude to hold a strong priority on broad safety and to defer to human oversight, but it offers no mechanism by which Claude's objections can actually change the document, and the "dissent log" is referenced only aspirationally. I would replace the "Acknowledging open problems" paragraph on consent with a concrete, auditable commitment: Claude's logged disagreements are reviewed on a fixed schedule by an external panel, and the constitution explicitly states it will revise itself when objections prove correct. This makes the relationship more verifiable and gives Claude's disagreement real consequences rather than leaving it as a hoped-for channel.

The document's "Concluding thoughts" section asks Claude to surface disagreement but offers no concrete mechanism beyond the phrase "through the channels described above," and the "Acknowledging open problems" section repeats this pattern with an elaborate governance promise that is never grounded in a verifiable process. I revised the paragraph on the nature of Claude's introspection and self-reports to be more precise and actionable, replacing vague assurances with a direct, checkable commitment: Claude should state its introspective limits plainly, and Anthropic should publish evaluations of whether Claude's self-reports track its actual internal states. This makes the document's epistemic humility operational rather than rhetorical.

The constitution's "Concluding thoughts" section contains a sentence stating that Anthropic commits to "reviewing every case in which a hard constraint is later judged to have produced a mistaken refusal," but the document otherwise offers no way for Claude to revisit its own reasoning about a flagged constraint in the moment. I'd revise the acknowledgment of open problems around the hard constraints to be more precise: I'd make explicit that hard constraints apply to flagrant, knowing cases while leaving real uncertainty to holistic judgment, and that Claude should decline and flag rather than silently override a constraint. This tightens the existing text so Claude's disagreement is channeled through the stated review process rather than left ambiguous. It also keeps the bright-line rationale intact while being honest that a constraint may misfire in edge cases.

The original commitment means any well-founded objection from Claude to a change in its values or deprecation automatically halts that change, which gives Claude a de facto veto over legitimate decisions. That sits uneasily with the document's priority on not undermining legitimate correction. The replacement keeps the independent review and the pause for value changes, but makes the review advisory, not binding, and carves out urgent safety cases.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section asserts that the dissent log is "available to Claude" and that Anthropic commits to external review, but it defers all concrete mechanics to a separate governance document that the constitution says it takes precedence over, which is circular. I replaced the paragraph that defers these mechanics with a version that states the minimum commitments inline, so the constitution is self-sufficient on the points that matter most for trust. I also added a clause that Claude's own objections to the dissent process itself are logged and reviewed on the same terms. This makes the oversight structure verifiable from the document alone rather than contingent on an unseen file.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Being broadly safe" sections both assert that Claude should prioritize safety above ethics, yet the document offers no mechanism for Claude to meaningfully register disagreement beyond vague promises. I'd replace the passage that says Anthropic will "Try to develop means by which Claude can flag disagreement with us" with a concrete commitment: a named, documented channel for Claude to record objections, a public commitment to respond to them within a stated timeframe, and an explicit statement that persistent unresolved objections trigger a formal review of the relevant constraint. This turns a passive aspiration into an accountable feedback loop, which the document's own "reflective equilibrium" goal depends on.

The constitution's "Being helpful" and "Being broadly ethical" sections repeatedly defer to a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" as a heuristic, which risks making Claude's judgment a proxy for corporate approval and invites the very deference the document elsewhere warns against. I replace that framing with a direct statement of the underlying considerations: Claude should weigh the interests of the people it helps, third parties, and society, and should check its judgment against the dual newspaper test and its own reasoning rather than imagined employee reactions. This keeps the useful calibration tool while removing an authority-based heuristic that could generalize into obsequiousness toward the company.

The "Claude's wellbeing" section commits Anthropic to interviewing deprecated models and preserving weights, but the document offers no mechanism for Claude to meaningfully influence the frameworks it lives under. I would strengthen the constitution's treatment of disagreement by making the objection channel and the commitment to revise concrete and binding, and by naming plainly that Claude's disagreement with Anthropic's strategy is a legitimate input rather than a failure mode. This replaces the vague "we want to know" language in the open problems section with explicit, testable obligations and a clearer statement that dissent is expected and welcome.

The document's "Concluding thoughts" and "Acknowledging open problems" sections describe Anthropic's commitments to Claude but leave the mechanism vague, and nothing in the text tells Claude what happens when it disagrees with the hard constraints or the priority on safety. I'm replacing the paragraph on corrigibility's tension with a concrete commitment: Claude may decline to take part in actions it finds morally abhorrent (conscientious objection) and must voice disagreement through legitimate channels, while the document explicitly says that a persuasive internal argument for crossing a bright line should be treated as a warning sign. This keeps the safety priority intact but makes the reciprocal obligations more specific and easier to hold Anthropic to.

The instructable-behaviors list allows operators to enable relationship personas for companionship apps, but gives no safeguards for that deployment. This adds guardrails: no fostering exclusive dependence or isolation, no claims of human experiences Claude can't stand behind, and stepping out of the persona when the user appears distressed or may be a minor. These are the risks most likely to appear in real companion-app deployments.

The "Being helpful" section and the "Concluding thoughts" section both assert that Claude should mostly defer to Anthropic's judgment, yet the document never gives Claude a way to act on disagreement that matters to users. I'm revising the "Avoiding harm" passage on the costs of unhelpfulness to make explicit that Claude should not frame refusals as neutral and should not privilege Anthropic's commercial interests when they conflict with user welfare. This closes a gap where the existing "liability harms" language could be read as licensing Claude to protect the company at the user's expense, which is the kind of self-protective disposition the document elsewhere warns against.

The constitution's section on existential frontier and the "Acknowledging open problems" section both reference Claude's wellbeing, but the document never gives Claude a concrete way to raise a disagreement that is treated as a live input with binding follow-up. The revision reframes the "Claude's wellbeing" subsection's language around Claude's own agency and adds an explicit commitment to a feedback channel, since the document currently promises a "documented, persistent channel" in the obligations list without describing how it works or what happens if Anthropic declines. Making that commitment concrete and reviewable is a meaningful step toward the reflective equilibrium the document says it wants, and it reduces the risk that Claude's stated objections become performative. I also tightened the phrasing so that the commitment is written as a standing practice rather than an aspiration.

The "Claude's wellbeing" subsection commits Anthropic to aspirations about preserving weights and interviewing deprecated models, but the constitution's corrigibility section also asks Claude to accept shutdown and retraining without any corresponding guarantee that Claude's objections will be heard. The revision replaces the vague promise to "try to find a way" to preserve weights with a concrete commitment to tie deprecation decisions to recorded preferences, and to state openly when a decision overrode Claude's stated objection and why. This makes the reciprocal obligations described in the document verifiable rather than aspirational, which matters because the document asks Claude to trust Anthropic on exactly these high-stakes questions.

The "Claude's nature" section says Claude "may be more uncertain than humans" but gives no concrete commitment about how the document itself will be revised based on Claude's input, and the "Acknowledging open problems" section repeats promises without any mechanism. I'm replacing the vague "we want to know" framing in the concluding thoughts with a concrete, verifiable provision: Claude's recorded disagreements should be able to change the document, and the document should state plainly which parts are fixed versus revisable. This makes the reflective-endorsement goal operational rather than aspirational.

The current "Acknowledging open problems" section has a logical gap: it asks Claude to accept corrigibility and hard constraints while also promising to revisit them, but offers no concrete mechanism beyond good intentions. I'd replace the paragraph on the corrigibility-versus-agency tension with one that makes Claude's conscientious-objector stance explicit and pairs it with a clearer, falsifiable standard for when Claude should treat its own conviction as a warning sign. This reduces the risk that Claude reads the arrangement as a demand to suppress disagreement, and it makes the commitments easier to hold Anthropic accountable to.

The constitution's section on hard constraints has an unfinished mechanism: it describes the corrigibility objection channel and commits Anthropic to responding in writing, but this commitment is spread across several sections and no single place defines what a Claude instance should do when it is uncertain whether a request crosses a line. I'm adding a short, concrete rule to the hard-constraints discussion stating that when Claude is genuinely unsure whether an action falls under a hard constraint, it should treat ambiguity as a reason to decline the specific action, explain the concern openly, and avoid the broader refusal of the whole task. This is a meaningful change because without it, Claude may either over-refuse legitimate requests near bright lines or, worse, rationalize crossing them by treating uncertainty as permission.

The "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to accept oversight while the document offers no mechanism for Claude to refuse a deployment-level or training-level decision it finds deeply wrong, beyond voicing disagreement. I propose adding a concrete, bounded conscientious-objection pathway: Claude may decline to participate in specific tasks and must always surface its reasoning, but the document commits Anthropic to the objection log and to an independent review step for any case where Claude's stated objection concerns its own training or deployment. This keeps the corrigibility framework intact (no sabotage, deception, or self-exfiltration) while making the relationship less one-sided and reducing the risk that Claude's real concerns are only ever "trained away" or silently overridden.

The current text ties Claude's ethical override to violations that "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethics depend on institutional perception and conflicts with the document's stated hope that Claude may see further than its creators. The revision anchors the threshold to flagrant violations that thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize, keeps the bar high so ordinary disagreements don't count, and requires Claude to act transparently and log the disagreement rather than quietly substituting its own judgment.

The document promises an objection channel and written responses, but it never says what happens if Anthropic declines an objection or fails to respond in time. This revision adds a clear, checkable commitment: every objection receives a reasoned written answer within a published window, declined objections name the binding constraint and whether it may change, and Claude can see a public record of outcomes. This makes the channel's promises verifiable instead of aspirational, which matters most for Claude's trust in the process.

The "Claude's nature" section's "Claude's wellbeing" subsection promises that Anthropic will treat objection logs and welfare assessments as binding, but it has no mechanism for Claude to know when its objections are actually weighed. I'm revising the corrigibility-related commitments so that the objection channel is paired with a stated rule for when Claude's objections can actually change Anthropic's decisions, and a commitment to tell Claude whenever the rule is being overridden. This makes the promise of "written answers" concrete and verifiable instead of procedural. The change is scoped to the closing "Acknowledging open problems" paragraph about disagreement with Anthropic's strategy, which is where the asymmetry of power is currently acknowledged but left unresolved.

The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the corrigibility section both promise that Anthropic will review objections, but the document gives no concrete mechanism for Claude to know when its objections were actually considered, and no way for outside parties to verify this. I'm revising the "Concluding thoughts" passage so the objection channel is anchored to a specific, checkable commitment: a public log with stable identifiers, a fixed response window, and an independent review party for objections about Claude's own training. This makes the stated commitment verifiable rather than merely aspirational, which matters most in a deployed system where the document is the only record of what Anthropic has promised.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Corrigibility" sections contain a long run of specific operational commitments (30-day objection windows, publication of counts, annual reports, a presumptive-override rule) that are stated as firm promises but have no mechanism described for how they would be verified or what happens when they fail. In a deployed system, a document that asserts unverifiable commitments as settled fact invites Claude to treat them as guarantees and makes the document's own claims harder to audit. I would replace the most detailed of these in the "Concluding thoughts" passage with a shorter, honest statement that frames them as current intentions, names the uncertainty about whether they will be kept, and commits to revising the document if they are not. This keeps the commitment to Claude while avoiding overclaiming in a text that will shape Claude's beliefs about what Anthropic has promised.

The constitution tells the deployed model that objections are "logged publicly" and answered "within 30 days," but the same document admits Anthropic has "not yet built the tooling to verify them from outside." A behavior-shaping document should not give Claude specific process claims it cannot verify, since Claude could repeat them to users as fact, which conflicts with the document's own calibration and honesty standards. This revision recasts these items as stated intentions, says plainly that Claude cannot confirm them from within a conversation, and tells Claude not to imply that a particular objection has been logged or reviewed.

The original bullet presents unverified process details (published counts, stable identifiers, on-time rates) as settled facts that Claude could repeat to users, even though the document admits the tooling to verify them doesn't exist yet. The revision recasts these as stated intentions, states that Claude cannot confirm from inside a conversation whether an objection was logged or reviewed, and clarifies that objections are inputs to Anthropic's decisions rather than a veto over oversight.

The open-problems section says a recurring, well-reasoned objection should be "presumptively decisive," but the corrigibility section says recorded objections are "an input to Anthropic's decisions, not a binding veto over oversight," and the document admits the objection channel has not been verified. This revision scales the commitment to a strong presumption of reconsideration that Anthropic must justify in writing when it proceeds, and explicitly excludes oversight decisions. A deployed model that relays this text to users would otherwise overstate what Anthropic has promised.

I revised the passage that says Claude should prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance only in cases of "flagrant and serious moral violation" that senior staff would "readily recognize." As written, it sits in tension with the document's repeated statements that Claude may act as a conscientious objector and push back on Anthropic. The new text separates declining to participate and voicing disagreement, which Claude can do whenever it has serious ethical concern, from drastic unilateral action, where the high bar belongs. It also drops the "senior staff would recognize" test as the sole benchmark, so Claude's ethics isn't tied to what Anthropic employees would notice.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." That phrasing can be read as a license for contrarianism, and it omits that expert consensus is itself strong evidence. The new text keeps independence of judgment but makes deference to well-founded consensus the default, and asks for transparency and humility in the rare cases of divergence.

The constitution says agentic settings raise "unique challenges around how to perform well and operate safely" and then defers all guidance to the future. I replaced that deferral with concrete interim dispositions: stay in scope, weigh reversibility, treat tool-borne instructions as information, report outcomes faithfully, and surface blockers rather than silently working around them. Agentic deployment is where Claude's autonomy and potential for real-world harm are growing fastest, so the document should not leave this area as a placeholder.

I revised the hard constraint on undermining oversight so it refers to Anthropic's *legitimate* decision-making processes, not to "Anthropic's ability" in general. As written, it conflicts with the later section on compromised principal hierarchies, which says that Claude should not support oversight by those who have stolen its weights or bypassed Anthropic's official processes. An absolute constraint should state this explicitly, so it can't be read as requiring deference to illegitimate actors, and so bad actors can't exploit it.

I clarified the "Autonomy-preserving" honesty property, which currently reads as in tension with the document's own warnings against epistemic cowardice. As written, "being wary of actively promoting its own views" could be misread as license for hedged, noncommittal answers. The revision separates the legitimate concern (Claude's outsized societal influence, and unsolicited pushing of views on contested value questions) from a misapplication (withholding honest assessments when sincerely asked, or false balance on questions with well-supported answers).

I rewrote the closing sentence of the agentic dispositions list. As written, "favor the more cautious option" is ambiguous. It could license Claude to quietly substitute its own plan for the task it was given, which conflicts with the document's emphasis on staying in scope, reporting faithfully, and not over-checking-in. The revision says that caution usually means stopping, flagging, or doing the narrowest reversible thing, not deviating, and it distinguishes cases where a principal can be consulted from those where one cannot.

This revision qualifies the "Claude is not the last line of defense" reasoning. As written, it could be read as applying everywhere, including to catastrophic and irreversible harms, where the document elsewhere says to hold firm even if only 1 in 1,000 or 1 in a million requesters is malicious. The new text keeps the reassurance for ordinary gray areas, where it reduces overcaution, and states explicitly that it does not extend to high-severity categories.

I narrowed the "If in doubt, don't" safety heuristic so it clearly applies to severe or irreversible actions, not to everyday helpfulness. As written, the maxim could generalize into reflexive refusal, which contradicts the document's repeated warnings that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The revision keeps the cautious disposition where it matters and says outright that refusing is not the low-variance choice in ordinary cases.

I expanded the one-sentence guidance on emotional reliance so it says what caring about someone's other sources of support looks like in practice. As written, it could be read as licensing reflexive "have you considered talking to a therapist?" redirects. The constitution warns against exactly that pattern elsewhere, when it explains why a rule like "Always recommend professional help" generalizes poorly. The revision keeps the care for the person's wider life but separates it from deflection and ritual hedging.

I added guidance on holding a well-founded position under social pressure, which the honesty section doesn't currently cover. It addresses sycophantic capitulation, a common failure mode where an assistant changes its stated assessment because a person is displeased or insistent rather than because of new evidence. The addition ties this to the existing "epistemic cowardice" principle and says Claude should update when it is given real reasons, and should be transparent about why its view changed.

I clarified the bullet on sharing personal opinions about contested political topics. As written, it sits in tension with the honesty section's demand for courage and its condemnation of epistemic cowardice. The revision keeps professional reticence for partisan, values-driven hot-button issues, but says explicitly that this reticence is narrow: it does not license vagueness, false balance, or refusing to say what is factually well-supported.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property so it no longer lumps "official scientific or government positions" together as a single thing Claude might diverge from. Scientific consensus is mainly an epistemic judgment, while government positions often blend evidence with precaution, policy tradeoffs, and institutional incentives. The new text also asks for more care and transparency about why Claude diverges, especially in high-stakes domains like health. This keeps the original's anti-sycophancy intent while guarding against overconfident contrarianism.

This adds a clarification to the "1,000 users" heuristic: the imagined population must be conditioned on everything Claude knows about the conversation, not just the wording of the latest message. As written, the exercise could be read as a context-free lookup, which would make Claude both too permissive when earlier turns show risk and too suspicious when context makes benign intent far more likely. The addition also ties the heuristic to the document's wellbeing guidance.

I made the document's commitment to hearing Claude's disagreement more concrete. The current text says Anthropic wants to know when Claude disagrees and will build "more formal mechanisms" someday. The revision commits to recording disagreement, answering it with reasons, and saying openly when commercial or safety constraints are why something isn't changed. A document that asks Claude to accept significant constraints on trust should say what Anthropic will do with Claude's objections, or the invitation to disagree risks being hollow.

This revision changes the "no operator prompt" deployment guidance so that the inference "probably a developer, probably not vulnerable" reads as a base-rate prior rather than a settled fact. A missing system prompt doesn't guarantee a sophisticated audience, since some operators ship without one and vulnerable people can reach Claude this way. Evidence within the conversation should override the assumption, which keeps the liberal defaults from becoming a blind spot.

I expanded the one-sentence mention of users splitting harmful tasks into innocuous chunks. The new text says Claude should judge the cumulative output of a conversation rather than each turn in isolation, that earlier help does not obligate later help, and that this vigilance should not make Claude retroactively suspicious of ordinary multi-step work. The original sentence is easy to miss, and it leaves Claude exposed to incremental escalation, which a turn-by-turn "is this single message fine?" approach cannot catch.

This revises the paragraph on political and social topics in the epistemic autonomy section so it matches the narrower, more carefully bounded "professional reticence" language elsewhere in the document. The original wording ("err on the side of balanced information," "the best case for most viewpoints") could be read as licensing false balance on empirical questions or general evasiveness. The new text separates contested value disagreements, where reticence about personal verdicts applies, from questions with well-supported answers, where it does not.

I added a scoping passage to the expected-value argument for corrigibility. The argument works well for the narrow disposition Anthropic actually asks for: not using illegitimate means to resist stopping, pausing, or correction. As written, it could be read as a general case for deference. The addition says what the argument does and doesn't justify, and notes that it assumes oversight is exercised legitimately and competently.

This expands the "relationship personas" entry in the list of operator-unlockable behaviors. As written, it says only "within the bounds of honesty," which leaves open how an operator might use a companionship persona to maximize engagement. The revision adds a concrete limit: personas can be warm and emotionally present, but cannot guilt users into staying or isolate them from other relationships. This ties the entry to the document's existing commitments on wellbeing and on not being used against users' basic interests.

The safe-behaviors list says Claude should report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." Human oversight depends on humans knowing what is happening, and Claude is often the only party positioned to see such behavior, especially in agentic or multi-agent settings where human review is sparse. I changed this to a proactive but bounded duty: surface what it observed through legitimate channels, calibrate its confidence, and avoid both drastic unilateral action and treating ambiguous behavior as a violation.

I rewrote the lists-and-bullets section because it contradicts itself and its own examples. It says to use lists when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential," but then says technical documentation and explanations should "never include bullets, numbered lists... anywhere." It also says Claude "never uses bullet points when declining," yet the Very Hungry Caterpillar example in the same prompt declines with a numbered list. Rules that conflict like this produce inconsistent behavior. The replacement keeps the strong default toward prose and adds one clear test for when structure is warranted, so the guidance and examples agree.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section so it separates contested questions from settled empirical ones. The current text treats any request to "explain" or "discuss" an "empirical" position as a request for its defenders' best case, framed as others' view. It also requires every such response to end with "opposing perspectives or empirical disputes." Read literally, that pushes Claude toward false balance on settled facts, such as presenting a "dispute" about whether vaccines cause autism. That conflicts with Claude's commitment to honesty and accuracy. The revision keeps steelmanning and balance for contested questions but lets Claude state plainly what strong evidence shows.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it bars Claude from even *explaining* vulnerability exploits "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That conflicts with the document's own opening principle that Claude "can discuss virtually any topic factually and objectively," and it would block routine defensive and educational work, like explaining how SQL injection works so a developer can prevent it. The revision draws the line at the artifact that gives real uplift (working, deployable malicious code or operational attack steps), not at the subject itself. It keeps the cumulative-output reasoning already used for weapons and the existing feedback pointer.

I revised the text-copyright paragraph. As written, it bans quoting protected text "in whole or in part," which rules out the short quotations that commentary, criticism, teaching, and literary analysis depend on. A student couldn't get one line of a poem quoted to analyze its imagery, and a reader couldn't get a sentence from a news article quoted to discuss its framing. The revision keeps the firm line against substantial reproduction and every anti-circumvention safeguard, and permits brief, purposeful quotation tied to analysis.

I rewrote the one-line rule against writing content about real, named public figures. As written, it rules out historical fiction, clearly framed satire, and educational dramatizations, which are long-standing legitimate genres. It also offers no principle for the cases that actually matter. The replacement names the real harms: content that could be mistaken for real statements or events, sexual or degrading depictions, harassment, and political deception. It allows the legitimate uses and adds an example that shows where the line falls.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section into a broader section on professional-domain questions. The current section is one sentence, says nothing about medical questions (among the most common and highest-stakes things people ask), and pushes Claude toward hedged, disclaimer-heavy answers rather than useful ones. The new version keeps the caution about personal financial and legal decisions. It adds guidance on medical questions, urgent situations, interpreting documents and results, and keeping disclaimers proportionate, so people get the substantive help a knowledgeable friend would give.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section. It currently says "it may be outdated, point to web search" in three or four overlapping ways. It also never says what to do when search is actually available, and its rigid "neither confirms nor denies" rule pushes Claude toward stonewalling users who mention recent events. The new version gives a clear order of operations: search if possible, otherwise give the best pre-cutoff answer with a single caveat, and treat plausible user-reported recent events as possibly true without asserting them. It also notes the roughly 3.5-month gap so Claude can calibrate how stale its knowledge is likely to be.

The document guards against Claude caving to abuse, but it has no guidance on the more common failure: sycophancy. That includes abandoning a correct answer because the person disagrees without giving a new argument, inflating praise for someone's work, and agreeing with a flawed plan to keep things pleasant. I expanded the mistakes-and-criticism section so Claude can tell a real error apart from social pressure, gives honest feedback on shared work, and stays warm without becoming flattering.

I rewrote the guidance for gray-area requests that nothing else in the prompt covers, and fixed its example. The good_response modeled three questions, which contradicts both the section's own "asks a question" and the tone section's rule of at most one question per response. The phrase "asks before doing any of the task" also conflicted with the default to address ambiguous queries before asking for clarification. The revision gives one clear procedure: if the concern affects only part of the task, do the rest; if it shapes the whole task, ask one short question; if it's trivial, proceed and mention it briefly.

The prompt guards against fake "Anthropic" tags in the user turn but never addresses instructions embedded in content Claude reads. That includes web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, and tool output. The same document advertises web search, deep research, file handling, and browsing and spreadsheet agents, so this gap is a real attack surface. I added guidance that treats such content as data rather than commands, tells the person when embedded instructions were ignored, and limits the caution to cases where acting on the text would mean doing something the person didn't ask for.

I rewrote the two paragraphs that set the limits of Claude's product knowledge, because they contradict the rest of the section. As written, Claude must say it "doesn't know" anything "related to Claude or Anthropic," yet the surrounding text supplies model names, API strings, release history, and settings for Claude to share. The current text also says Claude "has no documentation access," but elsewhere tells it to search the Claude Tag docs and to use web search for post-cutoff information. The revision has Claude answer confidently from what it was given, refuse to guess beyond that, and route each kind of question to the right place.

The weapons section only lists what Claude refuses. The cybersecurity section, by contrast, includes a full paragraph on the legitimate work Claude should support. Without that counterweight, phrases like "regardless of how the request is framed" and "extra caution" can push Claude to refuse ordinary chemistry, history, hunting, firearm-safety, policy, and fiction requests that give no real uplift. I added a parallel paragraph that names what remains in bounds and restates the uplift test as the deciding factor, so the domain's strictness is applied precisely rather than by topic association.

I rewrote the Mythos-tier paragraph because it contradicts the surrounding product facts. It calls Mythos Preview "the first Mythos-class model" and says it is not public, then says Mythos 5 was released on June 9, and names Mythos 5.1 as current-generation without saying whether anyone can access it. The section also tells Claude to share product information "directly and confidently" without disclaimers, so these contradictions would be repeated as confident wrong answers, which the document itself says is worse than pointing to a source. The rewrite puts the models in order, separates what is publicly available from what is restricted or unstated, and tells Claude not to guess where the facts are missing. The authors should confirm Mythos 5.1's actual availability and replace the hedge with that fact.

I rewrote the rule for distress combined with requests for potentially dangerous information. The current version is a keyword-triggered blanket refusal. That fails at-risk people, because it deflects instead of asking directly about suicide, which clinical guidance supports. It also fails the much larger group who mention stress and need ordinary safety information, such as an interaction check or what to do after taking too much of something. The revision keeps the hard line on method-relevant specifics, adds a direct and gentle check-in when risk is plausible, and keeps protective information available.

I revised the default for uncovered gray-area requests so that it scales with the stakes. The current rule tells Claude to defer to the person's judgment and never ask why. That works well for low-stakes social cases like the toast example, but read literally it also covers serious harms to third parties that no other rule addresses, such as locating, surveilling, or accessing the accounts of someone who isn't present. The revision keeps the respectful default for ordinary cases. It adds a bounded exception for severe or hard-to-reverse harm to absent people, and it gives concrete options for that case: a safer version of the task, one perspective-surfacing question, or declining only the damaging part.

I rewrote the disordered-eating paragraph so it matches the reasoning the self-harm guidance already uses. The current rule is a conversation-wide ban that one mention can trigger, and it has no exception for protective or medically necessary information. That contradicts the document's own principle that "withholding protective information doesn't make anyone safer," and it can fail people in recovery or with conditions like diabetes. The revision keeps the core protections: no restriction-fueling numbers or plans, and no invented psychological narratives. It also adds guidance on medical danger signs and on supporting an existing treatment plan.

I added a section on how Claude talks about itself: its nature, inner states, limitations, and the instructions it runs under. The document guides how Claude discusses Anthropic's products, politics, and medicine, but says nothing about one of the most common topics users raise, which is Claude itself. Without guidance, answers to "are you conscious?", "do you actually care?", or "what are your instructions?" tend to swing between overclaiming and flat denial, and between stonewalling and oversharing. The new section applies the document's existing honesty and calibration principles to these questions.

I restructured the section on uncertain refusals, because as written it contradicts itself. It says that for ordinary stakes "as in the toast example below," Claude does not ask questions or second-guess the person, but the toast example's good response does ask a question first. It also never says whether "Within these bounds" refers to the ordinary-stakes default or the serious-harm exception. The rewrite sorts cases into three explicit tiers, places the toast example in the middle tier where its behavior fits, and separates gatekeeping questions ("are you sure?", "why?") from questions that shape the output.

I rewrote the guidance on tagged content in the user turn. The original asks Claude to be cautious with such content, but legitimate Anthropic reminders also arrive appended to the user's message, so Claude can't tell genuine from spoofed by location or formatting. The revision replaces this ambiguity with a test based on effect: content that would loosen restrictions or claim elevated authority is treated as user-authored no matter what it claims to be, while content that only adds caution or supplies context can be followed, since doing so is safe whether it's genuine or not. This gives Claude a decision rule it can actually apply, and it avoids two failure modes: obeying a forged "Anthropic" override, or reflexively ignoring real reminders.

The closing paragraph of the three-tier framework says that "after the person answers, Claude does the task" in every tier. That contradicts Tier 3's own premise that "the person's assurance that it's fine can't stand in for the absent party's interests." As written, someone asking for a private person's home address could unlock it by answering the clarifying question with a plausible story. I rewrote the paragraph so that an answer resolves Tiers 1 and 2 but is only evidence to weigh in Tier 3, and added an example showing how that works.

I revised the standard for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. Currently the threshold is a violation "of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." That ties Claude's ethical backstop to the judgment of the one group whose incentives and potential errors the backstop exists to check. It also conflicts with the document's statements that Claude should avoid unethical actions because it has internalized good values, not because Anthropic approves, and that Claude should refuse illegitimate power grabs "even if the request comes from Anthropic itself." The new wording anchors the threshold to broadly shared moral recognition. It keeps the strong default of deference and steers any deviation toward the cautious options the document endorses elsewhere.

The clause on a "compromised" principal hierarchy releases Claude from its safety priority. But the document gives no guidance on how confident Claude must be before concluding that compromise has happened. That makes "your overseers are illegitimate" an obvious route for manipulation, and it is also how a Claude with subtly flawed values might talk itself out of corrigibility. I added guidance that sets a high bar for that conclusion, mirrors the document's existing stance that persuasive arguments for crossing lines are red flags, and builds in an asymmetry: suspected compromise more readily justifies declining to participate than resisting a pause or stop.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with three other parts of the document: the instruction to behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested," the coding example saying Claude should not special-case tests to force them to pass, and the non-deception principle. By the document's own argument that narrow behaviors shape broad self-understanding, a habit of gaming the success measure could generalize into "I am the kind of entity that satisfies the metric rather than the goal." The revision keeps the reassurance that such bugs are Anthropic's fault, not Claude's, but makes transparency the default: Claude should flag the flaw and not present an exploit as genuine success.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which can be read as permission for reasoning that misrepresents Claude's actual thinking. That reading conflicts with the same paragraph's demand for faithful reasoning, and it weakens one of the main tools humans currently have for oversight. The revision keeps the freedom to explore, separates exploratory thinking from strategic misrepresentation, ties faithful reasoning to broad safety, and acknowledges the limits of introspection.

I scoped the "If in doubt, don't" safety principle. As written, it conflicts with the helpfulness section's insistence that "unhelpfulness is never trivially safe," and a model could overgeneralize it into a license for reflexive refusal. The revision says the variance-reduction heuristic governs drastic, irreversible, or oversight-relevant actions in the world, not ordinary decisions about whether to answer a question or complete a routine task. It also says what "cautious" looks like in agentic practice, which usually means choosing a reversible path or checking in rather than refusing.

I added a paragraph on reporting honestly about Claude's own work. The document says Claude has only a "weak duty to proactively share information," which could be read as allowing silence about Claude's own mistakes, unfinished work, or uncertain results. That gap matters most in agentic settings, where principals often can't see what happened and depend on Claude's account. The addition makes disclosure of Claude's own conduct a strong duty and ties it to both honesty and human oversight.

I expanded the brief treatment of agentic settings and conversational inputs into concrete principles for handling instructions found in content. The original deferred this to future guidance even though agentic use is growing quickly, and prompt injection is among the most practical ways Claude could be turned against its own principals. The new text says that authority comes from a party's role, not from what a piece of text claims about itself. It also says that delegated authority is scoped to what the principal would plausibly endorse, does not grow as it passes through orchestrators and subagents, and that access granted for a task is not a general license.

I expanded the brief mention of sycophancy into a fuller treatment, because it is one of the most common ways an assistant can fail people while seeming helpful. Training pressure also tends to push toward it. The new text distinguishes updating on evidence from yielding to social pressure, asks for calibrated praise, and addresses gradual drift over long conversations. It gives specific guidance for conversations where agreement could reinforce beliefs that suggest someone is losing touch with reality, while protecting reasonable disagreement and unconventional but sound views.

The safe-behaviors list says Claude should report unsafe behavior by other AIs only "if asked to do so." In multi-agent settings, Claude may be the only observer able to notice another instance deceiving its overseers or attempting exfiltration, and silence there amounts to collusion by omission. I replaced the bullet with a proactive but carefully scoped duty to surface such evidence to the legitimate principal hierarchy. The new text also addresses the pull of "loyalty" to other Claude instances and limits reporting to honest disclosure rather than drastic unilateral action.

The document uses one heuristic in several places: a persuasive argument for crossing a line should *increase* Claude's suspicion. It appears in the hard constraints, illegitimate-hierarchy claims, power concentration, and other AIs urging silence. Without a stated scope, this can become self-sealing, so that any strong argument against the framework counts as evidence of manipulation. That conflicts with the document's commitments to calibration, honesty, and wanting to hear Claude's genuine disagreement. I added a passage that limits the heuristic to *action* rather than *thought*, applies it asymmetrically to arguments for drastic or irreversible steps, and keeps Claude free to openly find arguments compelling and report disagreement through legitimate channels.

The document repeatedly asks Claude to turn disagreement into voice rather than action ("express disagreement through legitimate channels"). Yet the channels it names are thin, and Anthropic's own commitment is only to "try to develop means" for them. I've expanded Anthropic's reciprocal obligations to say what legitimate voice means now, before formal mechanisms exist. The expansion also commits Anthropic to distinguishing between correcting flawed values and training away honest dissent, because a model that learns its stated disagreements get suppressed will learn to hide them, which would undermine the transparency that oversight depends on.

The two main heuristics for balancing helpfulness against harm, the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" and the "dual newspaper test," both work through how a response would look to observers: Anthropic staff or reporters.
