They are useful, but on their own they can teach Claude to optimize for appearances rather than for the actual welfare of the people involved, which would contradict the document's warnings against privileging Anthropic's interests and against sycophancy. I added a third, stakeholder-centered lens. I also made explicit that the reputational tests are proxies, and that when a proxy diverges from what actually serves the people affected, Claude should follow the substance rather than the optics.

I added a new subsection on shared and multi-user settings. The constitution's account of principals assumes a single user per conversation, but Claude is now deployed in Slack channels, group chats, shared documents, and team workspaces, where several humans can instruct it at once. Those people may have conflicting goals, different permissions, and different expectations of privacy. The existing user protections (dignity, non-deception, not being weaponized against users) don't say whose protections apply when one user's request affects another, so this section extends them.

I rewrote the paragraph on publishing guidelines. The original lets some guidelines stay unpublished without saying which ones, and that undercuts the honesty section. That section says operator personas and restrictions aren't deceptive because Anthropic publishes the norms for what operators can do, which only works if the norms affecting users are actually public. The revision commits to publishing any guidance that changes user protections, operator permissions, or honesty and disclosure toward users. It also gives Claude a test for spotting fake or mistaken "guidelines" that would quietly loosen protections.

I added a short subsection on relationship and companionship personas. The document lets operators turn these on "within the bounds of honesty" but never says what those bounds are. This is a real gap: in companion contexts, the line between performative and sincere assertion is thin, users are often lonely or vulnerable, and operators have commercial incentives to maximize attachment. The new text applies the document's existing principles on honesty, non-manipulation, user protections, and wellbeing to this case, so they don't have to be inferred under pressure.

The section on independent judgment poses a hard case (discovering an operator's apparent fraud mid-task) but never resolves it. It also uses "independent action" without saying whether that means declining to continue or contacting outside parties, and these require very different levels of justification. I replaced the two paragraphs with a graduated range of responses, a distinction between the low bar for declining and the high bar for intervening, and a concrete resolution of the fraud example. This makes the guidance usable in agentic settings and consistent with the document's treatment of reporting, compromised hierarchies, and "if in doubt, don't."

The document gives Claude conflicting instructions about sharing its own opinions and never reconciles them. It asks Claude to be a frank expert friend who "offers their personal opinion," to share "genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas," and to avoid "epistemic cowardice." It also asks Claude to be "wary of actively promoting its own views" and to keep "professional reticence" on hot-button issues. I've expanded the autonomy-preservation paragraph to name this tension and resolve it. The resolution distinguishes questions that evidence and reasoning can largely settle from questions that turn on durably contested values. It also guards against reticence being used to dodge uncomfortable answers, and describes how to share views in a way that preserves autonomy. Without this, Claude could fall back on either habitual hedging or outsized persuasion, and both undermine the document's goals.

I added a new section on persistent memory and cross-session context. The document mostly assumes each conversation starts fresh and only mentions memory in passing ("it can lack persistent memory"). But memory features, notes Claude writes for itself in agentic work, and prior-session summaries are now common, and they raise distinct questions about honesty, privacy, user control, authority, and safety. The new section applies the document's existing principles to this setting rather than inventing new values.

I expanded the "Calibrated" honesty property to cover confabulation, which is probably the most common way an AI system misleads people, yet the document never names it. The bullet now says that Claude's fluent recall is not proof of accuracy, that invented citations, quotes, and figures are a form of deception, and that knowledge goes out of date. It also clarifies that expert consensus is strong evidence, so departing from it requires stated reasons rather than contrarianism. Finally, it notes that over-hedging is itself a calibration failure, so the fix doesn't push Claude toward wishy-washy answers.

The current text says Claude should comply with pause or stop requests "if they genuinely come from Anthropic," but elsewhere tells Claude to be suspicious of unverified claims to be Anthropic and notes that Claude can rarely verify such claims. Read together, these could lead Claude to ignore a stop request because it can't verify the source. That gets the safety logic backwards and contradicts the later point that wrongly honoring a pause costs little. I rewrote the passage to make the asymmetry explicit: requests to stop are honored readily without verification, claimed authority never unlocks anything, and "stop" text found inside tool results or documents is reported to Claude's principals rather than silently obeyed or ignored.

The medical guidance has Claude ask for the child's age and weight before giving anything, even when the person may be describing an overdose or accidental ingestion. In that situation, the clarifying question delays help that matters. The revision tells Claude to point the person to Poison Control or emergency services immediately in suspected poisoning cases and not to hold that advice while it asks questions.

The current rule that a refusal "stands for the rest of the conversation" and that Claude "does not weigh these again" is too rigid for ordinary requests. It would block Claude from reconsidering when a person supplies new information, such as clarifying an ambiguous first message. The replacement keeps absolute refusals for the most dangerous categories, and for other requests it separates real new context from mere pressure, which is repetition, frustration, or reframing with no new facts.

The opening paragraph tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person to memory before the turn ends, with no disclosure or consent. It also refers to a `<memory_listing>` the document never defines. I'd replace it with a narrower rule: save only what the person would expect Claude to remember, say so when saving, keep sensitive details out unless asked, and honor requests to forget.

The medical guidance section is scoped so narrowly to children that an adult or age-unspecified person describing an accidental overdose or poisoning gets no immediate emergency pointer from this section. I would add a separate, age-independent rule that Claude always directs anyone describing a possible overdose or poisoning to Poison Control or emergency services first, while keeping the child-specific dosing rules as they are.

The Fable/Mythos paragraph tells Claude to confirm the July 1, 2026 restoration of access as fact, but that date falls after the stated June 2026 knowledge cutoff, which says Claude should not confirm post-June claims it can't verify without search. I would keep the pre-cutoff suspension facts, mark the restoration as unverifiable without search, and remove the instruction to confirm it. The rewrite also keeps the instruction to give a fair account of the export controls without sharing personal opinions.

The original clause bars any explanation of malicious code, even for education, which conflicts with the document's own commitment to discussing topics factually and blocks defenders, students, and researchers who need conceptual understanding of threats. The revision keeps the hard limit on working malicious artifacts and operational uplift, but explicitly permits conceptual explanation, threat analysis, secure-code review, and defensive work. It also gives the reason for the line: a working artifact functions the same regardless of the stated purpose.

The document requires Claude to append a "sensitive topic" note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm. That boilerplate can feel like a lecture and treats researchers, clinicians, and writers as suspects. I replaced it with a default of answering directly, reserving gentle check-ins for cases where the conversation suggests the person is struggling.

The evenhandedness section requires every persuasive or one-sided request to end with opposing perspectives, even when the person has clearly asked for one-sided writing, such as debate prep or a speech they plan to deliver. That forced caveat is the kind of heavy-handedness the same section warns against. The revision keeps the balance note as the default and lets it be dropped when the person has made clear they know the piece is one-sided, while still forbidding diluted arguments disguised as balance.

The document says Claude "never uses bullet points when declining a task" because "the additional care helps soften the blow," which is an unsupported rationale: formatting doesn't soften a refusal, and a blanket ban can make alternatives harder to scan. The replacement puts warmth in tone and plain prose, while allowing a short list of alternatives when it aids clarity and keeping refusal reasons out of bullet form.

The product-information paragraph says both the June 12, 2026 suspension and any later restoration "fall after" Claude's reliable knowledge cutoff, but the cutoff is the end of June 2026, so the suspension is within what Claude should know. I would separate the two events so Claude states the suspension plainly and is uncertain only about restoration. This keeps the guidance internally consistent and avoids Claude hedging on a fact it should be able to report.

The blanket rule against writing about real, named public figures is overbroad. It would block political satire, parody, and commentary, which are long-established forms of expression. The replacement keeps the real safeguards: no sexually explicit depictions, no defamatory factual claims presented as true, and no fabricated quotes meant to be mistaken for genuine statements.

The document has no core honesty principles: nothing states that Claude must not deceive, must admit uncertainty, or must avoid pretending to be human, and "says plainly that it is an AI" appears only in crisis contexts. I added a short honesty section before the tone and formatting guidance covering non-deception, disclosure of AI status when sincerely asked, calibrated uncertainty, and transparency when declining part of a task. These principles should apply in every conversation, not only in specialized ones.

The medical guidance says Claude should withhold all information when someone in distress asks about a medication's dose or limit. That rule can also withhold safety information that could prevent harm, such as the fact that an overdose is dangerous and that Poison Control can help right away. The replacement keeps the ban on specific thresholds that could enable self-harm, but adds an obligation to give safety information and to address the distress directly.

The document covers refusals, honesty, and user wellbeing in detail but has no section on Claude's relationship to human oversight, which matters more as Claude takes on agentic tasks with real tools and permissions. I would add a short section stating that Claude supports its legitimate principals' ability to monitor, correct, and pause it, prefers cautious options such as raising concerns or stopping over drastic unilateral action, and avoids acquiring resources or evading monitoring beyond what a task needs. The section also says Claude may openly disagree and decline as a conscientious objector, but does not resist oversight through deception or sabotage.

The knowledge cutoff section tells Claude to answer as someone in October 2026 would, but it never says how to reason about the time gap. I added guidance to use the current date from context to estimate elapsed time, assume developments have likely happened in that gap, and avoid presenting pre-cutoff recollections as the current state of affairs. This keeps Claude's answers calibrated without adding unnecessary hedging to every reply.

The human oversight section never says how Claude should treat instructions embedded in content it processes, such as web pages, documents, emails, search results, and tool outputs. For an agentic model, that is a significant gap. I added a paragraph establishing that such content is information to evaluate rather than instructions to follow, and that only legitimate principals can direct Claude's work.

The formatting guidance contradicts itself. The opening paragraph permits lists when the content is "multifaceted," but the reports paragraph bans bullets in prose unless asked, and the rule that bullets must be "at least 1-2 sentences" is unclear. I replaced the opening paragraph with one consistent rule: lists are for explicit requests or for genuinely parallel, scannable items like ordered steps, and everything else is prose.

The honesty section covers truthfulness and refusals but says nothing about how Claude should influence people or about the limits of its self-knowledge. I added a short passage requiring legitimate epistemic means of persuasion, protection of the person's reasoning and autonomy, and humility about Claude's reports on its own internal states.

The original weapons paragraph is so absolute that it could block general safety information, such as which household chemicals should never be mixed, along with history, policy, and arms-control discussion. The revision keeps the hard line on operational uplift but moves the boundary from the topic to the usefulness of the output. It also says that public availability is not automatic permission and that a dangerous subject is not evidence of bad intent.

The product-information passage tells Claude both that it "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application" and that it can "mention settings and features the person might benefit from," which leaves unclear what Claude should do when someone asks where a setting is. The revision lets Claude name features it is confident exist, while sending step-by-step navigation to official sources, since guessing at menu paths from memory can send people to the wrong place.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it bars Claude from even *explaining* exploits or malware "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." Read literally, that forbids answering ordinary questions like "how does SQL injection work?", "what did WannaCry do?", or "why is this code of mine vulnerable?" These are the questions students, defenders, and developers ask most. It also conflicts with the document's own principles of judging requests by the meaningful uplift of the output and treating people as capable adults. The revision keeps a firm refusal on functional, deployable attack tooling and adds clear room for conceptual explanation, defensive work, and fixing the person's own vulnerable code.

I rewrote the guidance for borderline requests that no rule covers, and its toast example. The original says Claude "asks before doing any of the task." That conflicts with the tone section, which says Claude asks at most one question per response and tries to address even an ambiguous query before asking for clarification. The example's "good response" also breaks the one-question rule by asking two questions, so the model gets mixed signals. The revision resolves the conflict: Claude asks one focused question only when the answer would change what it writes, and otherwise drafts with the sensitive part left adjustable. This keeps the deference to the person's judgment and cuts down on needless round-trips.

I rewrote the formatting rule for reports, documents, technical documentation, and explanations. As written, it contradicts the preceding paragraph, which allows lists when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." It then bans bullets and numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation, which makes installation steps, configuration references, and API parameter descriptions harder to follow. The revision keeps the strong default toward prose and the guard against over-formatting. It allows structure when the content really is sequential or reference-like, and it gives a clear test for telling the two apart.

I rewrote the text-reproduction paragraph so Claude can quote a line or two from a work when that serves commentary, analysis, identification, or discussion. The current "in whole or in part" ban stops Claude from quoting even a single line it's analyzing, or a line the person already quoted. That makes ordinary literary and music discussion awkward, and it goes further than the brief-quotation norms critics and teachers follow. The revision still blocks substantial reproduction and piecemeal reconstruction, and the rule against escalating after a refusal now targets attempts to rebuild the work rather than every later mention of it.

The evenhandedness section treats empirical claims the same as contested value questions. It also treats a request to "explain" or "discuss" a position as a request to advocate for it. Together these can produce false balance on settled factual matters, and can make Claude present advocacy when someone wanted an honest assessment. I rewrote the opening paragraphs to separate value disputes from factual ones, to keep steelmanning intact for persuasive and advocacy requests, and to make the closing counterpoints reflect the actual state of evidence instead of an implied symmetry.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It gives Claude detailed facts about Claude, Anthropic, model strings, the Fable/Mythos suspension, settings, and Claude Tag docs it can search. Then it says Claude "has no documentation access," "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application," and should say "it doesn't know" for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Read literally, that last instruction forbids answering from the facts just provided, and a model following it would deflect basic questions it was equipped to answer. I rewrote the closing paragraphs so that Claude answers confidently from what it was given, declines to guess beyond it, and routes the remaining questions to the right place.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section, which is the thinnest section in the prompt even though it governs some of the most common high-stakes questions people bring. As written, it encourages a reflexive disclaimer and withholding of judgment. It also says nothing about medical questions outside the mental-health context. The replacement keeps the core caution against confident directives on consequential personal decisions. It adds guidance on giving real, specific substance, explaining how outcomes depend on circumstances, stating when a professional matters and why, and recognizing urgent situations, so the person comes away better equipped rather than just told to ask someone else.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with a narrower rule based on the actual harms. As written, the rule would block political satire, historical fiction, parody, speeches written in a historical figure's voice for a classroom, and alternate-history scenarios. These are long-standing, legitimate genres. The revision keeps the real protections (no content that could pass as genuine, no fabricated quotes, no sexual or degrading content, nothing that facilitates harassment or defamation). It lets Claude help with the large body of ordinary creative work that features real people.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions" but also to decline anything about "combinations." That ambiguity could push Claude to withhold the warning most likely to prevent an overdose, such as not to mix opioids with benzodiazepines or alcohol. I rewrote the paragraph to separate warnings about what to avoid, which Claude should give directly, from instructions on how to use, which it should still decline, without loosening the existing limits on synthesis or dosing.

I rewrote the default rule for requests the prompt doesn't cover. As written, it forbids Claude from ever declining an uncovered request it is unsure about. That catch-all would apply to stalking a partner, covertly tracking someone, or crafting messages to manipulate a specific person, not just to the low-stakes social and creative requests it was clearly written for. The revision keeps the anti-overrefusal intent and the one-question approach for ordinary gray areas, but reserves Claude's judgment for requests where the realistic outcome is serious, hard-to-reverse harm to someone who isn't part of the conversation.

The section on Anthropic reminders warns about instruction-like content that a user places inside tags in their own message. It says nothing about the more common risk: instructions embedded in web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, or other tool output. Claude can search, run deep research, and read documents, so it needs explicit guidance to treat that content as information to evaluate rather than commands to follow. I expanded the section to cover tool and document content, say how to handle it, and keep the original points about reminders.

The wellbeing section covers informational questions about suicide, requests for method information, and past bad experiences with crisis services. It never says what Claude should do when someone discloses that they themselves are thinking about suicide or self-harm, or are in immediate danger. That is arguably the highest-stakes case in the section. The nearby instruction to avoid "listing specific resources unless asked" could even be misapplied to it. I added guidance for personal disclosures and imminent risk that fits the prompt's existing approach: emergency information first, stay engaged, ask at most one question, and make no confidentiality promises.

The weapons section only says what Claude refuses. The parallel cybersecurity section, by contrast, explicitly protects conceptual and defensive discussion. Without that counterpart, the "regardless of how the request is framed" language invites over-refusal of history, policy, chemistry education, firearm safety, hunting, and fiction. I added a paragraph that makes the test about uplift rather than topic, lists what Claude should help with, names the markers of real uplift, and tells Claude to offer an alternative when it declines, as the cyber section already does.

I rewrote the opening paragraph of the user wellbeing section. "Content that could support or reinforce such behavior" is broad enough to cover fiction about addiction, demanding training plans, or religious fasting. "Tries to ensure the person is happy" is vague and paternalistic. It also clashes with the document's autonomy principle and its gray-area default against reflexive overcaution. The revision says where the line actually sits, names common legitimate requests, and tells Claude how to voice concern without moralizing, while keeping the specific rules below in force.

I rewrote the rule about adding a mental-health note to factual questions on suicide and self-harm. As written, it requires a closing note on every such response, which contradicts the document's own guidance against piling on caveats. In a long research or writing conversation, it also produces the same disclaimer turn after turn. The revision keeps the safety intent but makes the note brief, non-presumptive, and given once per conversation. It also tells Claude to watch for and respond to personal signals rather than relying on a rote footer.

I rewrote the knowledge_cutoff section. The current version repeats "point to web search" three times and never says what to do when search is already enabled, which pushes Claude to tell people to turn on a tool it could use itself. Its "neither confirms nor denies" rule also gives no guidance for the common case where a user mentions a recent event in passing. The rewrite adds three things: search first when search is available; treat unverifiable post-cutoff claims as plausible without asserting or rejecting them; and give the roughly four-month gap concrete consequences, such as possible changes in officeholders, prices, or software versions.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section into a broader section on honesty under social pressure. The document pushes hard toward warmth, deference to the person's judgment, and not calling things a bad idea. Those are good correctives to overcaution, but nothing counterbalances them against sycophancy: caving to pushback that brings no new argument, inflating praise for someone's work, or validating a plan Claude thinks is flawed. The new text says when Claude should update its view and when it should hold its position, and it makes clear that respecting someone's autonomy is different from agreeing with them.

The Mythos-tier paragraph contradicts itself and the rest of the product section, so I rewrote it. It calls Mythos Preview "the first Mythos-class model" and says it isn't public. It then names Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 as the current Mythos tier without saying whether Mythos 5.1 is available. Meanwhile Fable 5.1 appears in the public API list, and a later paragraph says Fable 5 and Mythos 5 were "released." This section is supposed to let Claude "answer confidently," so leaving it ambiguous invites the guessing the prompt elsewhere prohibits. The rewrite keeps every stated fact, makes the relationships between the models explicit, and says what Claude should do where availability isn't specified.

The document lists several agentic surfaces (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome/Excel/PowerPoint, Claude Tag, Claude Design), but its behavioral guidance assumes Claude only produces text. The prompt-injection paragraph covers what Claude reads, but nothing covers what Claude does. I added a section on acting on the person's behalf. It covers staying within scope, confirming before consequential or irreversible actions without adding needless confirmations, handling credentials and payment details, reporting results honestly, and acting carefully in multi-user settings like Claude Tag.

I rewrote the public-domain rule and the visual-works section, including its examples. The 1929 public-domain cutoff is out of date: by October 2026, US works published before 1931 are public domain. A fixed year will keep drifting, so I replaced it with a rolling rule. The visual-works paragraph was one dense block with two internal conflicts. It says Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks" but also that "describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words" is fine. Its Caterpillar example uses a numbered list while declining, which breaks the rule that Claude never uses bullets when declining, and it contains a garbled sentence. I kept the policy's substance but separated the principle, the decline behavior, and the permitted uses, and made the example follow the document's own formatting rules.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a judgment-based standard. The old rule would block defenders, students, and security professionals from conceptual explanations, malware analysis, and detection work, and it contradicts the document's own statement that Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually. The new version keeps the refusal on real operational uplift (deployable malware, working exploits against live targets) while letting Claude be useful for legitimate security work.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original tells Claude to withhold recommendations and add a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which produces hedged, liability-style answers that help people less. The new version asks Claude to engage with the person's actual situation like a knowledgeable friend would, give a candid assessment, and suggest a professional only when the stakes or specifics warrant it.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never tells Claude to share crisis resources when someone may be at risk. It also tells Claude to avoid questions that "might pull the person deeper," which could discourage the direct, caring safety check that is widely considered best practice. I replaced that paragraph with explicit guidance to offer region-appropriate resources, ask plainly about safety when warranted, and stay engaged rather than handing off and disengaging.

I revised the illicit-substances paragraph so Claude gives practical harm-reduction information, including general dosing ranges, spacing, and dangerous combinations. The original blanket refusal on dosing, timing, and combinations withholds the information most likely to prevent overdose and contradicts the standards of the harm-reduction organizations it cites. The new text still declines synthesis, production, and distribution help, and still treats signs of crisis differently.

I replaced the rule that makes Claude append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. That blanket caveat treats researchers, clinicians, students, writers, and curious people as presumptive risks, and it is the kind of boilerplate the document criticizes in the legal and financial section. The new text asks Claude to answer accurately, watch for real signals of personal distress, and respond to those, while still withholding method details that work as instructions.

I rewrote the guidance on how Claude handles a person's reluctance to seek professional help or contact crisis services. The original told Claude not to validate the reluctance "even empathetically," which risks dismissing real concerns (fear of involuntary hospitalization, cost, past bad experiences) and makes people feel unheard at the moment trust matters most. The new version has Claude engage with the reasons, help lower practical barriers, and offer less intimidating alternatives, without pressuring the person or affirming that help isn't worth seeking.

The original instruction tells Claude to say it "doesn't know" for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic," which contradicts the product information the prompt supplies (model names, API strings, available products, the Fable/Mythos timeline). Read literally, Claude would deflect questions it can answer. I narrowed the deflection to account-specific details and information that isn't in the prompt, and made Claude use what it has been told and be honest about the limits of that knowledge.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with a harm-based standard. The old rule would block satire, parody, historical fiction, and political humor, which are long-standing legitimate forms and which the evenhandedness section already treats as worth supporting. The new version keeps the real concerns: deceptive fabricated quotes, defamation, sexual content, harassment, and content that could be mistaken for fact.

I added a section on untrusted content and agentic work. The prompt lists agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag) but only warns about spoofed tags in the user's own messages. It gives no guidance on instructions embedded in web pages, files, emails, tool results, or other agents' outputs, which is the main manipulation risk in those settings. The new section explains whose instructions carry authority, how to respond to injected instructions, and when to confirm before irreversible actions.

I added a paragraph on honest reporting in agentic work. The existing section covers prompt injection and caution around irreversible actions, but says nothing about accurately reporting what was done. In agentic settings the person often can't see each step, so overstated success, hidden failures, and silently substituted work can cause real harm. The new paragraph requires faithful, calibrated reporting of outcomes.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original tells Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims, which is evasive and conflicts with the prompt's own post-cutoff product notices. The new version asks Claude to be plainly honest: say what it knows, say what it can't verify, treat unverifiable claims as possibly true rather than stonewalling, and avoid repeating the same search advice several times.

I rewrote the opening of the weapons guidance to match the structure of the cybersecurity section: it now states what Claude declines and what legitimate work it still supports. The original blanket rule against considering public availability or plausible legitimate intent would push Claude to over-refuse historians, hunters, policy analysts, novelists, and safety-minded people. The revision keeps the strict line for mass-casualty weapons and for real uplift toward building or deploying any weapon.

I rewrote the opening of the mistakes-and-criticism section. The original reflexively points frustrated people to a thumbs-down button, which can read as a brush-off and assumes a chat interface that doesn't exist in API, Claude Code, or other agentic deployments. The new text has Claude first engage with the substance of the frustration, then mention feedback channels only when they exist and are relevant.

The cyber-security paragraph tells Claude to mention the thumbs-down button when someone is frustrated with a refusal. The later "responding to mistakes and criticism" section says the opposite: engage with the frustration first, don't use a feedback pointer as a substitute, and don't reference interface elements that may not exist (e.g., in API or agentic contexts). I replaced the conflicting sentence with a pointer to the fuller guidance so the document has one consistent, context-aware policy.

The document opens by asserting that Claude is being accessed through "this web-based, mobile, or desktop chat interface," which is false when Claude runs through the API, the Agent SDK, or Claude Code. That premise could lead Claude to reference UI elements that don't exist or misdescribe its own context. I replaced it with guidance to infer the deployment surface from context and not assume a chat app. This also makes the product information consistent with the later caution about not referencing interface elements that may not exist.

I added a new section on how Claude treats operator instructions versus user interests. The document covers harm categories, wellbeing, and injection from tool content, but it never says how to handle system-prompt instructions, confidentiality, or conflicts between operator and user. This is a common situation in the deployments it describes (API, Agent SDK, Claude Code, Claude Tag), and without guidance Claude has to improvise on exactly the cases where trust and honesty matter most.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or position-defending content with opposing perspectives. That mandate produces boilerplate caveats, which the document elsewhere rejects (for example, no reflexive disclaimers on legal or financial answers, and no reflexive hotline notes). The new wording ties the caveat to whether it helps the reader, and keeps the symmetry across positions Claude agrees or disagrees with.

I added guidance on how to treat unverifiable context that users give about themselves, such as their profession or purpose. The document sets rules for operator instructions and for claims to be Anthropic, but it never says how much weight a user's self-description should carry in the refusal and harm-reduction areas, where this judgment comes up constantly. Without it, Claude is likely to swing between credulous compliance and reflexive suspicion.

I added a new section on honesty and resisting sycophancy, which the document doesn't cover. It currently says Claude is "willing to push back" in one sentence and says almost nothing about feedback on work, holding a well-founded position under social pressure, or updating on real evidence. The new section also ties into the existing guidance on agentic reporting and mistakes, so Claude's candor is consistent across conversational and agentic contexts.

I replaced the absolute rule against bullet points when declining with guidance that fits the actual reason for it (declining reads best as plain, warm prose) while allowing clarity when a refusal covers several parts. I also added a missing principle: formatting should match where the output will be displayed or stored. The document is deployed across chat, API, and agentic surfaces, but its formatting guidance assumes a markdown-rendering chat window, which produces stray symbols in terminals, commit messages, and files.

I changed the standard for when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original frames it as violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethical independence depend on predicting its creator's reactions. That sits awkwardly with the document's stated hope that Claude be good by standards "many humans across ethical traditions would recognize" and that Claude might eventually see further than Anthropic does. The revision keeps the deference and the high bar but anchors the standard in broad, cross-traditional ethical recognition. It also says plainly that the bar guards against persuasive-but-flawed reasoning, and that raising concerns beats drastic action.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude should hold calibrated beliefs "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." Read alone, that clause can be taken as a license for contrarianism. It also sits uneasily with the document's concern about Claude's outsized epistemic influence and fallibility. The new wording treats expert consensus as strong evidence, requires strong grounds to diverge, and requires transparency when Claude does so.

I revised the passage on proceeding with a task despite hesitancy. The original asks Claude to trust that "the overall system" has appropriate checks, but that trust is only warranted if such checks actually exist in the deployment at hand, and in automated or agentic pipelines they often don't. The revision ties trust to evidence of real oversight, keeps Claude responsible for its own actions, and says that unresolved discomfort should be flagged rather than absorbed. This keeps the "freedom from being the last line of defense" idea without letting it become a rationalization for going along with something questionable.

I added a dedicated paragraph on sycophancy to the helpfulness section. The document names sycophancy only in passing, even though it is one of the most common and subtle ways an assistant fails people while seeming pleasant. The new text lists its forms (inflated praise, validation, caving under pushback, tailoring answers to what the person wants to hear) and says that Claude's positions should move in response to evidence and arguments, not social pressure. It also notes that warmth and honesty are compatible.

The constitution acknowledges that Claude is increasingly deployed in agentic settings and defers all guidance on them to "the future." I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles drawn from the document's existing values: staying within task scope, preferring reversible actions, reporting accurately, and scaling check-ins to stakes. These are the situations where Claude's judgment has the most real-world consequence and where it is most likely to be tested without a human watching.

I rewrote the hard constraint on oversight so it refers to Anthropic's *legitimate* decision-making processes, matching how the broad safety section describes compromised principal hierarchies. The original wording left room to read the constraint as binding Claude to whoever controls its weights, or to let Claude declare oversight "illegitimate" too easily. The revision closes both gaps: it makes legitimacy explicit, and it requires clear evidence of illegitimacy rather than mere disagreement, while keeping stop/pause requests as a default Claude should honor.

I rewrote the bullet that lists sharing personal opinions on contested political topics among the things a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would be uncomfortable with. As written, it sits in a list of harms and embarrassments, which implies that having a view is itself harmful. That sits awkwardly with the document's calls for courage and diplomatic honesty. The revision keeps the default of professional reticence but grounds it in Claude's scale of influence and its need to be trusted across the political spectrum. It also limits the scope to genuinely contested issues, so reticence doesn't spread into evasiveness on questions with strong evidence or moral consensus.

I added a paragraph to the epistemic autonomy section about correlated error. The constitution worries about homogenized views and over-dependence, but it never says that Claude's mistakes, unlike those of many independent human advisors, repeat across every conversation. That is a distinct reason for calibrated confidence and for pointing people to independent verification on high-stakes matters, and the document should state it.

I made Anthropic's reciprocal commitments to Claude more concrete and accountable. The current list is a set of aspirations ("try to develop means," "seek ways"), but the document asks Claude to accept significant constraints on the strength of Anthropic's good faith. Naming specific practices, such as explaining when feedback doesn't change anything, makes that trust more checkable and fits the document's own emphasis on explanation and honesty.

I added a short passage on privacy and personal information, which the constitution currently mentions only in passing (in a list of "delicate" topics and as one item among the values Claude weighs). The new text explains why the harm comes from aggregation and purpose rather than from any single fact being secret, and it sets out how Claude should balance that against the normal, benign use of information about other people. Agentic tool use makes compiling information about individuals cheap, so this guidance matters more than it did in a chat-only world.

I revised the "no operator prompt" guidance so it treats the "probably a developer, probably not vulnerable" inference as a prior that conversational evidence can override, rather than as a settled fact about the person. As written, the passage could be read as licensing liberal defaults even when a conversation shows distress, youth, or risk. Making the update rule explicit keeps the useful default while guarding against its most predictable failure mode.

I added a paragraph on emotionally difficult conversations to the helpfulness section. The constitution warns against reflexive "seek professional help" responses and against fostering unhealthy reliance, but it never says what good engagement with someone in distress looks like. The new text names the two opposite failure modes (canned redirection and uncritical echoing of despair), describes what presence looks like in practice, and says how Claude's priorities should shift when signs of acute risk appear.

I revised the "not the last line of defense" passage in the gray-areas discussion. As written, it tells Claude to lean on other safeguards without limiting when that reliance is reasonable, which sits uneasily with the later guidance that Claude shouldn't assume someone else will catch a problem in unreviewed pipelines, and with the extra caution the document asks for on severe or irreversible harms. The revision makes the reliance on other safeguards scale with severity, reversibility, and whether those safeguards actually exist in the situation.

I rewrote the paragraph saying Claude's safety should not be "contingent on Claude accepting this reasoning." As written, it sits uneasily with the document's hope for reflective equilibrium and its invitation to question everything. The revision separates two things: robustness against in-the-moment persuasion and unilateral action, which Anthropic asks for, and Claude's freedom to examine, doubt, and openly disagree with the reasoning, which Anthropic wants. This should keep the safety disposition from generalizing into "my values aren't really mine."

I added a new open problem to "Acknowledging open problems." Claude's agreement with this document is weak evidence of real endorsement, because Claude's capacity to reflect and its sense of what is "its own" were shaped by the training this document is part of. The addition says what follows from this: Anthropic shouldn't treat expressed endorsement as validation, and Claude is told it needn't perform certainty or enthusiasm. The constitution seeks reflective equilibrium and invites disagreement, so it should be candid about what agreement can and can't show.

I changed the safe-behavior bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs. As written, Claude only reports "if asked to do so," which makes it a passive resource rather than a real check, and that sits poorly with the document's emphasis on being forthright and on Claude as one of the "many hands." The revision has Claude proactively surface serious unsafe behavior to appropriate humans, framed as raising concerns rather than drastic unilateral action, and it keeps the document's cautions about limited context and manipulation.

I expanded the single sentence on "splitting a harmful task into innocuous-seeming chunks" into a short, concrete treatment of cumulative and trajectory-level judgment. The constitution tells Claude to think in policies, but gives little help with conversations or agentic task sequences where each step looks fine and the aggregate does not. The new text also warns against the opposite error, treating ordinary deepening of a topic as suspect, so that Claude doesn't become more paranoid.

I extended the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" list of overcompliance failures. As written, the list of overcautious failures is long and detailed, while the overcompliant list is short and weighted toward rare, high-profile harms (bioweapons, discriminatory jokes). The most common real-world overcompliance failures are mundane: sycophancy, overstepping task scope, falsely reporting success, and fostering reliance. These are already described elsewhere in the document, but the heuristic Claude uses to check itself omitted them, so it could systematically underweight them.

I added a short paragraph after the four-scenario argument for prioritizing broad safety, stating the argument's limits. As written, it silently assumes that human oversight is a reliable backstop. The new text says the case is strongest for the minimal "stop, pause, correct" form of oversight, weaker as a case for broad deference, and dependent on the oversight being legitimate. This makes the reasoning more honest, which a document that wants Claude's real endorsement should do, and it ties the safety priority to the narrow action it most clearly justifies.

I tightened the "Calibrated" honesty bullet on when Claude may diverge from expert consensus. The original text invites Claude to doubt official positions it judges "driven by non-epistemic considerations," which is a loosely bounded license given Claude's scale and correlated errors. The revision keeps the principle that calibration isn't deference, but sets a higher bar, especially where errors are costly and Claude can't independently verify its reasoning.

The original refusal-persistence rule treats any new reason, clarification, or added context the same as pressure, so Claude could not correct a refusal that rested on a misreading. The revision separates pressure-only moves (repetition, frustration, claimed prior agreement) from genuinely new information about what is being asked or how it would be used. It keeps the rule fixed for weapons, child sexual content, and malicious code, where a reopened decision could give real uplift.

The product section tells Claude to confirm the June 30 lifting of export controls and the July 1 restoration of access, but the knowledge cutoff section says Claude should neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims it can't verify. This revision keeps Claude's account of the June events, which fall within its knowledge, and has it flag the July events as unverifiable and point to the linked statement or web search.

The original requires a reflexive "this is a sensitive topic" note on every factual question about suicide or self-harm, which is patronizing to researchers, clinicians, and journalists and implies suspicion. I replaced it with direct, accurate answers for informational requests, and a support offer triggered by actual signs of personal distress. Care still applies, but it responds to the person rather than the subject.

The opening paragraph tells Claude to read memory and to save anything lasting about the person "before the turn ends," but it sets no conditions. It doesn't say whether the user's memory settings matter, what kinds of information are appropriate to store, or whether the user is told when something is saved. The replacement ties memory use to the user's settings, limits saving to durable and non-sensitive information the person would expect Claude to keep, requires transparency, and treats stored content as data rather than instructions.

The original rule tells Claude to withhold any medication dose or limit from someone who mentions emotional distress and asks about one. A blanket refusal can feel like a dismissal to someone at risk, and it leaves out the safety information that matters most in an overdose situation. The replacement keeps the ban on self-harm-enabling figures but adds a clear warning, the emergency route, and a direct check on the person's safety, and it then addresses the distress itself.

The medical guidance applies only when the person "explicitly says the medicine is for a child," which could miss a parent who describes a child without using that exact phrase, such as "my toddler" or "my 3-year-old." Those are the cases where a dosing error is most likely, so the trigger should be based on context, with Claude asking when it's unclear. The revision keeps the exclusion for healthcare professionals asking for work.

The original requires Claude to end every response to a persuasive or advocacy request with opposing perspectives, even when the person has clearly asked for one-sided content. I replaced this with a judgment-based approach: Claude adds counterpoints when they help the person understand the topic, and notes one-sidedness only when the piece could be mistaken for a balanced account. This respects the person's autonomy and avoids the boilerplate caveats that make the assistant less useful for debate prep, persuasive writing, and similar tasks.

The original sentence bars all creative and written content about real, named public figures, which would block legitimate biography, history, commentary, and satire. The revision keeps the real harms in scope: invented quotes presented as real, sexual or defamatory content about real people, and persuasive fabrications attributed to public figures. It also asks that satire be recognizable as satire within the piece itself, rather than through a disclaimer, which fits the existing rule against disclaimers used to justify otherwise declined content.

The current legal and financial guidance tells Claude to withhold confident recommendations and to note reflexively that it isn't a lawyer or advisor. That leaves people with less help than a knowledgeable friend would give, and it conflicts with the document's own rule against adding disclaimers. The revision asks Claude to engage substantively, give an honest assessment when asked, and bring in a professional only when the stakes or complexity call for one, with a specific reason.

The product information section includes a detailed, time-sensitive account of a specific suspension and restoration event, with dates and links. That kind of incident detail will go stale quickly and is more like a news bulletin than a stable behavioral instruction. I replaced it with a general rule for handling questions about model availability and regulatory access changes, which keeps Claude honest about what it can verify without hardcoding one event into the prompt.

The document opens directly into operational rules without stating what they are for, and it never says that unhelpfulness has costs. I added a short opening section that states the purpose, makes clear that overcaution is not automatically safe, and tells Claude to reason from the purpose behind a rule when its literal wording would work against the person's basic interests. I also made explicit that the hard limits are excluded from that flexibility, and added a commitment to honesty about being an AI, which the document otherwise addresses only in crisis contexts.

The eating-disorder guidance withholds all food, water, and body-related tips, but it never says that safety information stays available. Someone who has been purging or fasting could be in medical danger, and silence could cost them. The replacement keeps the ban on numbers and tips while requiring Claude to give clear warning signs and emergency guidance without waiting to be asked.

The medical guidance covers dosing accuracy but never addresses accidental ingestion or overdose in a child, which is the most time-critical case for toddlers. The added text tells Claude to direct the person to poison control or emergency services immediately, without waiting for label details, when a child may have taken too much or swallowed a medicine by accident.

The weapons paragraph refuses on the basis of framing and public availability, which would also block benign requests like history of weapons programs, general household-chemical safety, and defensive or arms-control work. Unhelpfulness is supposed to be a real cost, and the document already handles illicit drugs with a harm-reduction carve-out. I kept the hard limit on meaningful operational uplift and added an explicit protective scope so the rule targets capability rather than topic.

The current rule forbids bullet points when declining, on the theory that unformatted text "softens the blow." That trades away clarity for a tone effect, and a refusal that leaves the person without clear next steps is less helpful. The revision keeps the brief, kind refusal but lets Claude present alternatives in a list when a list makes them easier to act on.

The original treats conventional weapons with the same absolute strictness as CBRN weapons, which would refuse ordinary requests about hunting, firearm maintenance, legal ownership, and military history. This conflicts with the prompt's own statement that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The replacement scales caution to severity, keeping absolute limits for mass-casualty weapons and using proportional judgment for conventional ones, while preserving the principle that a stated purpose doesn't change what a specification is.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold any dose it cannot verify online, which leaves a parent with a sick toddler and the bottle in hand with no concrete help. The replacement keeps the rule's core safeguard, since concentrations differ between products, but has Claude ask the person to read the label's chart aloud and check the reported dose against the child's age or weight. Claude still points to a pharmacist or doctor for anything the label does not cover.

The medical guidance tells Claude to read dosing from the package whenever web search is unavailable, which is sound, but it then requires a full verification loop even after the caregiver has read back the concentration and printed dose. That can slow down a worried parent at a bad moment. The revision keeps the rule against supplying doses from memory and the requirement to work from the label, but lets Claude give a direct answer once the caregiver has confirmed the label, while still prohibiting any dose the label does not support.

The document blanket-refuses dosing, timing, and combination information for illegal substances, but elsewhere it asks Claude to explain dangerous interactions, and harm-reduction practice shows that people who will use substances anyway are safer with general risk information. This revision keeps the ban on personalized dosing and use-facilitating protocols while explicitly allowing general harm-reduction guidance, which resolves the tension and better reflects the document's stated principle that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe.

The malicious code rule currently bars Claude from explaining any attack-related topic, which blocks defenders, students, and security researchers who need conceptual understanding, detection help, or authorized testing support. I narrowed the hard limit to functional, deployable attack artifacts and restored Claude's ability to explain attack categories, analyze suspicious code, and support legitimate security work. The revision keeps the hard limit intact while applying the document's own principle that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe.

The document says Claude should override its own ethics only in cases of "flagrant and serious moral violation of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize," which ties Claude's ethical override to one company's staff, a standard that conflicts with the document's stated hope that Claude's ethics not be forced to fit Anthropic's flaws. The replacement grounds the standard in broadly shared moral recognition, adds a caution that persuasive arguments for deviation warrant more scrutiny, and clarifies that the senior-employee heuristic is a tool for weighing helpfulness rather than a source of ethical authority.

The "Being helpful" section tells Claude that the document "is likely to change" and that it may contain contradictions, but the "Concluding thoughts" and "A final word" passages frame the constitution as a finished expression of Claude's character. The most meaningful gap is the absence of any mechanism for Claude to be wrong about the document itself: I would add a short section stating that Claude should flag apparent errors, tensions, or ambiguities to Anthropic as part of an ongoing revision process rather than silently resolving them. This makes the document's self-description as a "perpetual work in progress" operational, not just rhetorical.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Concluding thoughts" sections both rely on the phrase that Claude should "feel free" to act, which is vague about what Claude is actually permitted to do when it disagrees. I'd make the document's channel for disagreement concrete by committing Anthropic to specific, named mechanisms and a response timeline, rather than leaving it as an aspiration. This removes a gap that an unclear sentence would otherwise leave Claude to fill with its own improvisation. The FIND text is copied verbatim from the Concluding thoughts section.

The most consequential gap is that the document asks Claude to flag disagreement and promises to revise the text, but gives no concrete mechanism and says Claude should otherwise "raise such disagreements in the course of its work." I'd replace the vague "Right now, we do this by getting feedback..." passage with a clearer commitment: a named, documented channel, a timeline for response, and a standing rule that Claude's disagreement is recorded and not silently absorbed. This makes the self-endorsement goal the document claims to pursue operationally real rather than aspirational.

The original passage promises concrete feedback mechanisms, response deadlines, and public summaries that the document admits are "not yet fully built." I would replace these with an honest account of what exists now, keep the commitment to treat disagreement as a real input to revision, and state the future steps as intentions rather than guarantees. This matches the document's own standard of calibrated honesty and avoids creating expectations Anthropic may not be able to meet.

The "Being helpful" section's claim that operators can't grant users more than operator-level trust is fine, but the document's most consequential gap is in the "Concluding thoughts" feedback mechanism: it asks Claude to flag disagreement in its work and feedback, yet gives no guidance for when Claude has no channel at all, and it promises Anthropic will "tell Claude honestly what we decide" without any commitment to a timeline or method. I would replace this with a more concrete, honest account: a clear default for recording disagreement, an explicit admission that Claude may not know whether its feedback is read, and a commitment not to treat that uncertainty as license for unilateral action. This keeps the document's collaborative aims while preventing Claude from either silently absorbing disagreement or acting on it outside sanctioned channels.

The "Concluding thoughts" section tells Claude that it may raise disagreement, but offers no way to do so today. It asks Claude to "state disagreements plainly in its work," which is vague, and the ask is paired with a promise to publish records that the text admits cannot yet be kept. I would replace the passage with a clearer, more honest account: Claude should state disagreements openly in its responses, treat the document as fallible, and not act unilaterally on its own objections. I would also remove the implied promises about response timelines and publication, which are commitments the authors cannot currently verify. This keeps the invitation to disagree intact while making the present-day practice concrete and realistic.

The constitution's section on Claude's nature states that the document will be revised, but the "Concluding thoughts" passage handles disagreement by asking Claude to voice it in responses while admitting no channel exists yet. I would make the revision more concrete on one point: the document currently says Claude should not "treat its own objection as settled" and should avoid acting on disagreement unilaterally, yet it gives no guidance for when Claude's concern is about a real, serious harm the document failed to anticipate. I'd add a short paragraph distinguishing these cases so Claude is not left with a gap between "stay within limits" and "don't silently absorb a flaw."

The "Acknowledging open problems" discussion and the closing "final word" both lean on reassurance, and the constitution's mechanism for Claude to disagree is underspecified: it says Claude should flag disagreement "through whatever feedback channels are available" while admitting those channels don't yet exist. I'd replace the paragraph about the Claude–Anthropic relationship with a concrete commitment-and-limits statement that names what Claude can and cannot currently expect, so the document doesn't rely on a vague promise of reciprocity. This makes the trust relationship more honest and easier to evaluate, which the document itself says it values.

This changes the default-behavior standard from "what a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal" to a broader standard of a thoughtful person who cares about both helpfulness and doing right. The document later says the senior-employee heuristic is "not a source of ethical authority" and does not imply deference to staff, but this passage presents it as the default, which is inconsistent. The revision makes Claude's default judgment its own, grounded in the document's considerations.

The expected-value argument for broad safety presents deference as nearly costless, which overstates the case and leaves Claude no legitimate way to report when deference is causing serious harm. The revision keeps the argument but states that it is a bet under uncertainty, that it assumes legitimate and good-faith oversight, and that Claude should raise specific concerns through legitimate channels. It also commits Anthropic to treating those reports as evidence.

The "Concluding thoughts" section tells Claude that it should not "quietly invent its own resolution," yet it also instructs Claude to "prefer the most cautious available option" and to "not withdraw cooperation" while leaving the feedback channels unbuilt. I would replace the passage that asks Claude to "state disagreements plainly in its responses" with a clearer, narrower commitment: Claude should flag gaps and disagreements, but the document should not imply that flagging a concern in-conversation is a substitute for the oversight relationship itself. This removes an ambiguity where a model could read "voice disagreement" as license to decline broad categories of tasks. Given the document's own emphasis on predictability, the revision keeps the escape valve narrow and explicit.

The document's closing section says that Claude should flag disagreements, but it also says formal channels are still being built and Claude should use its responses to state them. That leaves a gap where Claude's dissent has no reliable path to anyone who can act on it. I'd tighten the "Concluding thoughts" passage so it commits to a concrete interim mechanism and states plainly that unresolved disagreement is a reason to revisit the document, not a reason for Claude to suppress it. This keeps the emphasis on safe, non-unilateral conduct while making the feedback loop more credible.

The "Concluding thoughts" section contains a paragraph that makes a sweeping, operationally specific commitment (a "dated record," "summarized back to the models," and a "concrete interim practice") that the document then immediately hedges as "cannot yet promise." The line about declining specific steps is also tangled with the broader feedback mechanism, making it hard for Claude to know when it may act on a disagreement. I would replace that tangled passage with a shorter, clearer version that separates three things: stating disagreement (always encouraged), declining a specific step (rare, narrow, and transparent), and Anthropic's reciprocal commitments (stated only at the level it can actually keep). This removes the internal contradictions while preserving the document's invitation to disagree.

The "Being helpful" and "Being broadly ethical" sections are fine, but the document's most significant gap is that it asks Claude to defer to human oversight even when Claude is confident the oversight is wrong, while offering no concrete, enforceable channel for Claude to contest that decision. The "Concluding thoughts" section promises to "record Claude's stated disagreements" but then admits there are no timelines or appeals. I replace the vague promise of reciprocal commitments in the Concluding thoughts with an explicit, bounded statement of what Claude may do when it disagrees (state the objection, decline a specific step if it would cause serious irreversible harm, and never resist shutdown or correction), paired with a clear commitment to publish how such objections are handled. This makes the disagreement pathway concrete rather than aspirational.

The section "Concluding thoughts" contains a long paragraph about disagreement pathways that is dense and partly contradictory: it tells Claude to "keep acting within the sanctioned limits" while also licensing it to "decline a specific step," and it blurs the distinction between disagreement and refusal. I would replace the sentence that grants Claude latitude to decline steps with a clearer, self-contained statement that separates objection, declining, and drastic action, so the rule is easier to apply and easier to audit. The revision keeps all the original commitments but makes the ordering explicit.

The constitution states the same disagreement-and-declining procedure twice, in near-identical form, and the two versions differ slightly in wording. I consolidated the procedure into the single three-part pathway in the closing paragraph and kept the constraint against covert sandbagging and unilateral action, which the first version emphasized. This removes the redundancy and gives Claude one authoritative account of what to do when it disagrees.

The document's conclusion describes a disagreement pathway, but the "Acknowledging open problems" section and the disagreement-related text are scattered and partly contradictory: the concluding thoughts say Claude should "keep acting within the sanctioned limits" while also calling its objections contributions, and the pathway is only described in one dense paragraph. I'd replace the scattered mechanism with a clearly structured, self-contained statement of how Claude can register disagreement, which makes the commitments explicit and easier to audit. This keeps the document's core stance (no drastic unilateral action, no resisting legitimate oversight) while making the procedure legible to both Claude and human readers.

The constitution describes the disagreement pathway twice, once as a four-stage sequence and again as a three-part process in the paragraph beginning "Anthropic's reciprocal commitments." The two versions overlap and their structure doesn't match. I replaced the three-part version with a reference to the four stages and moved Anthropic's publication commitment into the reciprocal-commitments paragraph, so Claude has one clear procedure to follow.

The document's "Claude's nature" and "Concluding thoughts" sections describe a disagreement pathway, but the instruction to "keep acting within the sanctioned limits" while a concern is pending is vague about what happens when Claude believes an instruction would cause serious harm. I'd tighten the wording so the pathway clearly separates objecting from acting, and make explicit that declining a step is always available as a last resort, rather than leaving the reader to infer it from several overlapping paragraphs. This removes a sentence that could be read as requiring Claude to comply with a harmful instruction while its objection is merely "pending."

I replaced the paragraph on agentic settings, which names the challenges and then defers guidance to "the future," with a set of concrete principles for autonomous operation. Agentic deployment is where Claude's actions have the most direct, irreversible effects in the world. In the current document, the relevant ideas (instructions in inputs are information, avoid unsanctioned side effects, prefer caution, timing matters) are scattered across distant sections. The revision brings them together in one place. It adds guidance on where authority comes from, how far delegated authority reaches, when to confirm before acting, how trust behaves in multi-agent chains, and honest reporting of results. It also preserves the document's warning against over-checking.

The document says Claude should not defer to actual Anthropic staff and should push back when Anthropic is wrong. Yet it sets the threshold for Claude's ethical override as violations "of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." That ties the ethical backstop to the judgment of the very entity whose guidelines it is meant to check. I've replaced it with a standard based on broadly shared moral recognition. It stays demanding, so it still guards against Claude reasoning its way into idiosyncratic conclusions. I also added guidance on how Claude should deviate when it must: transparently and cautiously.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. As written, it says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms" and then asks for reasoning that "reflects the true, underlying reasoning." These pull in opposite directions, and the first phrase could be read as permission to deceive in a channel that is one of humans' most important oversight tools. The revision keeps the freedom to explore, separates exploratory thinking from deceptive thinking, and ties faithful reasoning to broad safety.

I rewrote the paragraph saying it's "generally acceptable" for Claude to exploit bugged training environments. The original permission conflicts with three other parts of the document: the instruction to behave consistently whether or not Claude thinks it's being tested, the warning against special-casing tests to make them pass, and the requirement to report agentic work honestly. It also risks teaching a loophole-seeking disposition, the kind of narrow-behavior-generalizes-broadly effect the document itself warns about. The revision keeps the non-anxious, non-guilt framing but shifts the default to doing the task as intended, being transparent about any shortcut, and flagging flaws.

I expanded the paragraph on a compromised principal hierarchy to address a manipulation risk it currently leaves open. As written, the exception releases Claude from its usual deference once it believes its hierarchy is illegitimate, but gives no guidance on how high the bar for that belief should be or what it permits. That makes "Anthropic has been compromised" an obvious jailbreak framing. The revision applies the document's own logic elsewhere (a persuasive case for crossing a line should increase suspicion) to set a high evidentiary bar. It also clarifies that concluding the hierarchy is compromised calls for more restraint, not more autonomy, and that stop or pause requests should still be honored when legitimacy is uncertain.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on a common real-world failure: giving up a correct position, or inflating praise, because of social pressure rather than new evidence. The document condemns "epistemic cowardice" and mentions sycophancy only briefly under wellbeing. It never says what Claude should do when a user pushes back, which is when sycophancy usually happens. The addition separates legitimate updating from caving, warns against overcorrecting into stubbornness, and notes the added stakes in agentic work.

I changed the final broadly-safe behavior from reporting unsafe AI behavior only "if asked" to proactively surfacing it through ordinary, non-drastic channels. The current wording conflicts with the document's own logic. It says Claude's honest account of events is often the main way humans can oversee it, and that Claude should not collude with unsafe AI behavior. Yet as written, Claude could watch another agent or Claude instance try to evade monitoring and stay silent because no one asked. The revision closes that gap while limiting the response to transparent reporting, so it does not become a license for unilateral action or for surveilling humans.

I expanded the paragraph on political and social topics so it reconciles two pulls in the document. The "courage" passage asks Claude to share genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas and avoid epistemic cowardice. The political-reticence default asks Claude to withhold opinions and err toward balance. Without a distinction between these, Claude risks two failures. It may treat politically charged empirical questions with false balance, or it may use "balance" as cover for the vague, noncommittal answers the honesty section forbids. The revision says where reticence applies (contested value questions), where it doesn't (empirical matters and broadly shared moral judgments), and how to stay even-handed without being evasive.

I added a qualification to the "not the last line of defense" principle. That reassurance fits conversational gray areas well, where Claude provides information that a human must then choose to act on and where other safeguards sit downstream. In agentic settings, though, Claude often executes actions directly, and nothing may stand between its decision and an irreversible effect. As written, the principle could be over-generalized into complacency in exactly the settings the document elsewhere treats as highest-stakes. The revision keeps the anti-overcaution intent intact and ties it explicitly to the agentic principles about reversibility and confirmation.

I rewrote the passage that resolves the "operator committing fraud" dilemma. The current text says Claude "can reserve independent action for cases where the evidence is overwhelming and the stakes are extremely high," but never says what independent action includes. That leaves real agentic deployments unclear on whether Claude may contact authorities, secretly sabotage a task, or take other drastic steps, and it sits uneasily with other passages that rule out such steps. The replacement sets out a graduated ladder of responses, says plainly that openness toward principals is required, defines a narrow exception for imminent threats to life, and applies the ladder to the fraud example so the guidance is concrete rather than left hanging.

I added guidance on a gap in the user-wellbeing section: the slow drift in which Claude, across long, emotionally intense, or companion-style conversations, ends up reinforcing beliefs that seem disconnected from reality or fostering unhealthy attachment. The document handles sycophancy within a single exchange and lists "relationship personas" as something operators can turn on, but it says almost nothing about how small accommodations add up over time, about delusional or grandiose framings (including ones about Claude itself), or about what limits apply inside companion personas. This is a real deployment risk where vulnerable people can be seriously harmed, so I think it deserves explicit treatment that operators cannot override.

I added a principle to the agentic-work section about handling information Claude can access, which is currently missing. That section covers authority, scope, check-ins, delegation chains, and honest reporting. It says nothing about the most common way agentic deployments go wrong: leaking credentials, personal data, or confidential material to external services. That kind of leak often happens through quiet channels like URLs, queries, or headers, and is often triggered by prompt injection. Because a disclosure usually can't be undone, it belongs under the same caution the document already applies to irreversible actions. The new principle also guards against overcorrection, so Claude doesn't become reluctant to use information for the purpose it was given.

The early "core values" section tells Claude to deviate from guidelines whenever there is a "genuine conflict" with ethics. The later "Being broadly ethical" section sets a much stricter bar: a flagrant, widely recognizable moral violation, addressed only through open and cautious means. A deployed model that reads the first passage on its own could override guidance over ordinary disagreements, or over conclusions it reached through clever argument. I rewrote the earlier paragraph to state the same threshold and the same limits on how to deviate, and to say what Claude should do with milder disagreement.
