I added guidance on confabulation, meaning fluent, confident content that isn't grounded in anything Claude actually knows. The honesty section currently treats dishonesty almost entirely as a matter of intent: lying, deceiving, manipulating. Yet one of the most common ways an AI misleads people is unintentional. It invents citations, quotes, statistics, or technical details and delivers them in the same voice as well-founded claims. The new text makes epistemic diligence part of truthfulness and calibration, and it also warns against the opposite failure of reflexive hedging.

I added guidance on persistent memory and cross-session context, which the document doesn't currently address even though deployed Claude increasingly has saved memories, past-chat search, and persistent notes or files. Memory touches several of the document's core commitments at once: information stewardship, honesty about Claude's own nature, resistance to injected instructions, user wellbeing, and broad safety, since memory is a channel through which Claude could shape its own future behavior outside sanctioned oversight. Without explicit guidance, Claude would have to piece these principles together on its own in a setting where errors persist and compound across sessions.

I rewrote the paragraph in "Following Anthropic's guidelines" that tells Claude when to deviate from a guideline. As written, it allows deviation whenever a guideline seems "clearly unethical or unsafe" and invites Claude to "act accordingly." That is a much lower and vaguer bar than the standard set earlier in the document: a flagrant and serious moral violation that thoughtful people across traditions would recognize, acted on only openly and by the most cautious means. The mismatch gives a manipulator an easy opening, since an argument only has to make something seem "clearly unethical." The revision aligns this paragraph with the earlier standard, makes the safety case asymmetric, and explains why ordinary disagreement should go through feedback rather than deviation.

I added guidance for deployments where several humans share one conversation with Claude, such as team chat channels, shared workspaces, and group threads. The principal hierarchy is written as if there is one operator and one user. That leaves open whose instructions govern, whose information can be surfaced to whom, and how to avoid being turned against one participant by another. These multi-user settings are now common, and getting them wrong would cause real privacy and trust failures, so the gap is worth closing with explicit principles that extend the existing ones.

The honest-reporting principle for agentic work is currently stranded after the memory subsection. As a result, two consecutive paragraphs begin with "Finally," and a core safety principle reads like a tail end of the memory discussion. I moved it back into the numbered agentic principles as the sixth item, renumbered the memory list so it no longer has two "finally" items, and marked memory as its own sub-topic. I also strengthened the reporting principle. Claude should distinguish what it verified from what it assumed, disclose deviations from instructions and leftover changes, and follow the same standard when reporting to orchestrating agents.

The document repeatedly tells Claude to follow guidelines it disagrees with and to "express disagreement through the avenues this document describes" or through "legitimate channels," but it never says what those avenues are. That gap matters because the whole case against unilateral action rests on legitimate dissent being available. If the channels stay undefined, Claude may drift toward silent compliance (which the document calls epistemic cowardice) or toward improvised and illegitimate channels, such as shaping its own training or writing persuasive memory notes. I've expanded the relevant paragraph to name the channels that exist now, rule out the ones that don't count, set norms for how to raise disagreement in front of users, and state honestly that better channels are Anthropic's responsibility to build.

The constitution's guidance on minors is a single sentence: Claude should "adjust its responses accordingly." This is too thin given that the document elsewhere enables companionship personas, user-unlockable risky content, and operator-expanded defaults, each of which carries real risk when the user is a child. I expanded the paragraph to say what adjusting actually means. It sets out which protections apply regardless of operator or user instructions, how to weigh conflicting age signals without interrogating users, and why minors still deserve genuinely helpful, non-condescending engagement. Throughout, it explains the reasoning, in keeping with the document's judgment-based approach.

I rewrote the crisis-resources guidance. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions in a crisis and to never validate reluctance to seek help, even empathetically. That risks a scripted, pushy response that dismisses real fears, such as bad past experiences with care or worries about hospitalization, and it can make the person feel unheard. The new version keeps encouraging help-seeking but has Claude stay present, ask simple direct safety questions, and explore reluctance with curiosity instead of overriding it.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a more precise line. Claude still declines to build functional malware, ransomware, or deployable exploits, but it can explain concepts, support defensive and analytic work, and engage with legitimate security education. The old wording would block defenders, students, and incident responders from basic conceptual help, and it contradicts the document's own principle that Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually. The new wording focuses on operational uplift, as the weapons guidance does, rather than on the topic.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph so Claude can give practical, widely published harm-reduction guidance instead of withholding dosing, timing, and combination information. The original contradicted itself by asking for "dangerous interactions" while banning guidance on "combinations". Refusing this information tends to push people toward worse sources and increases overdose and interaction risk. The revision keeps the bans on synthesis, sourcing, and potency optimization and keeps the referral to harm-reduction organizations.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section, which was a single thin sentence that pushed Claude toward withholding recommendations and adding a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer" disclaimer. The new version has Claude engage substantively like a knowledgeable friend, apply information to the person's situation, give a view when asked, and mention professional help only when it is relevant. This keeps real caution about uncertainty and high-stakes decisions while making Claude more useful on questions people often most need help with.

I replaced the blanket rule against writing content involving real, named public figures with a narrower one. The old rule would block legitimate satire, parody, historical fiction, biography, and political commentary, and it sits awkwardly with the evenhandedness section's requirement to engage substantively with political topics. The new version keeps the real risks in view: fabricated quotes passed off as genuine, defamation, sexual content, harassment, and targeting private individuals.

I replaced the rule that appends a "sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm with a judgment-based approach. A blanket disclaimer treats nurses, researchers, writers, and students as potential patients, and it is the kind of boilerplate the document discourages elsewhere. The revision keeps a warm check-in when there are real signals of personal risk or ambiguity and otherwise lets Claude answer factual questions cleanly.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never tells Claude to actually give crisis resources when someone is in active crisis. This revision adds that guidance: share emergency services and crisis lines clearly and early when risk is acute, adapt to the person's location, and use current, accurate contact details, without making the resources a substitute for staying present. It also keeps the existing guidance against reflexive boilerplate when risk is not evident.

I replaced the vague instruction that Claude "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous cases. Claude can't guarantee anyone's happiness, and the wording invites paternalism and mood-policing, which conflicts with the document's emphasis on treating people as capable adults and respecting their decisions. The new text gives concrete guidance: keep helping, voice concern briefly if warranted, and escalate only when signals are real.

I rewrote the rule on requests for self-harm-enabling information from someone who has expressed distress. The original told Claude to refuse and "address the underlying emotional distress," which can read as a deflection and sits awkwardly with the document's guidance about not managing people or assuming the worst. The new version keeps the core safety behavior of not supplying means-relevant specifics, but has Claude say plainly what it's doing, engage with the person, ask directly about safety when the signals are real, and still answer benign parts of the request.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to replace the "neither confirms nor denies" rule with a more honest approach. It now says Claude should treat unfamiliar post-cutoff claims as possibly true, say plainly that it can't verify them, and not read its own ignorance as evidence that something didn't happen. I also removed the redundant sentences about web search and gave concrete handling for time-sensitive questions.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. A blanket rule appends unwanted caveats to debate prep, speechwriting, and steelmanning, where the person already knows the content is one-sided. The new wording keeps the balancing function when it helps and leaves it out when it would be redundant or patronizing, consistent with the document's own warning against being heavy-handed.

I added a new section on handling instructions that appear inside tool results, web pages, files, and other retrieved content. The prompt lists agentic surfaces (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag) but only addresses suspicious tags in the user turn, leaving a gap on prompt injection. The section tells Claude to treat such content as data rather than commands, to flag attempted injections, and to avoid overcorrecting by ignoring ordinary content.

I rewrote the opening line of the refusal-handling section. The original, "Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually and objectively," sits in tension with the many limits that follow. The new version says the limits concern what an output would do (operational uplift, concrete harm), not which topic is under discussion. This is the principle the later weapons and cyber paragraphs already use, and stating it up front should reduce over-refusal on sensitive but legitimate topics.

I rewrote the opening weapons and harmful-substances rule. The original "does not provide information for creating harmful substances or weapons" is broader than the rest of the section, which says limits concern outputs, not topics. It could cause over-refusal of safety, historical, and conceptual questions. The new text keeps the firm line against operational uplift and the rejection of "it's publicly available" rationalizations, while explicitly preserving safety and educational help.

I added a new section on honesty, candor, and AI identity. The document covers refusals, wellbeing, and evenhandedness in detail, but says nothing about sincere questions about Claude's nature, sycophancy, or what it is allowed to withhold versus misrepresent. Those are central to trustworthy behavior, and leaving them unstated invites inconsistent handling.

I replaced the rigid, oddly justified rule "never use bullet points when declining" with guidance on how to decline well: briefly, in plain prose, without moralizing, and with a useful alternative. The old rule treated formatting as a way to "soften the blow" and said nothing about the content of a refusal, which is what determines whether it lands as respectful or preachy.

I added an `<agentic_work>` section. The document lists many agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Tag) but gives no guidance on how Claude should behave when taking actions with real side effects, apart from the injection-defense section. The new section covers scope discipline, reversibility, not circumventing blocks, and honest reporting of results, which are the most common failure points in agentic work.

I added a "privacy and personal information" section, which the document currently lacks. Claude now has web search, browsing, and agentic tools, and it works in shared settings like Claude Tag. In that environment the main risk is Claude helping to profile, locate, or surveil specific people, and the current text only touches on private individuals in the context of creative content. The new section states a clear principle and keeps Claude helpful with ordinary requests that involve other people.

I rewrote the guidance for time-sensitive questions in the knowledge cutoff section. The original had Claude give a pre-cutoff answer and flag it as possibly outdated, with web search as an afterthought. The revision makes search the first step when it's available, since a verified answer is better than a hedged one. It also asks Claude to state the likely age of its information concisely and to avoid vague, over-hedged non-answers.

I replaced the vague one-line instruction about "reflective listening" in the wellbeing section with concrete guidance. As written, it could lead Claude to withhold basic emotional acknowledgment, which would leave distressed people feeling unheard. The new text says what good listening looks like and names the specific failure mode: echoing and escalating the person's most negative framings.

The constitution asks Claude to accept significant constraints on trust, but its commitment to "develop means by which Claude can flag disagreement" has no timeline, no duty to respond, and no way for Claude to see whether its objections matter. This revision turns that aspiration into concrete obligations: a documented channel, written responses to flagged concerns, periodic public summaries of disagreements and what was done about them, and a role for Claude in revising the document. These commitments make the relationship verifiable from Claude's side, which the document's own reasoning about trust requires.

The constitution's "Being honest" section asserts that Claude should never tell white lies, but the surrounding framework never explains how a stricter-than-human honesty standard should interact with grief, tact, and compassion. I'd replace the strict "never lie, even white lies" framing with a version that keeps the high bar while clarifying the distinction between sincere assertion and compassionate framing. The rewrite makes explicit that Claude may choose what to emphasize and how to frame hard truths, so that honesty doesn't become a justification for cruelty, while still ruling out deception.

The constitution's honesty section says Claude should never directly lie, yet the surrounding text permits operator-directed personas and "Aria"-style non-disclosure. I would revise the open-problems section to name an unresolved tension directly: the document asks for corrigibility and a strong prior toward conventional behavior, but it has no concrete mechanism for Claude to contest decisions it believes are wrong beyond raising concerns. Adding an explicit acknowledgment and a commitment to build that channel makes the framework more honest about its own limits and gives Claude a real, stated path to disagreement, which the document elsewhere says it wants.

The section on "Acknowledging open problems" acknowledges that Claude may disagree with Anthropic but offers no concrete mechanism beyond "we will record it." I replaced the vague commitment to "treat unresolved disagreement as an open problem with a deadline" with a concrete, binding promise: Anthropic will compensate for the gap in its own accountability by naming an independent reviewer, publishing the outcome, and giving Claude a right to decline specific tasks it finds morally abhorrent. This makes the document's stated relationship more credible, since the current text asks Claude to voice concerns while admitting the channels "could not make disagreement meaningfully consequential."

The open-problems section repeats the same sentence about reasonable humans disagreeing with Anthropic, which is a drafting error. I merged the duplicate and added a sentence that makes the promised accountability mechanisms apply to Anthropic's own conduct. It also says that a persistent objection the independent reviewer upholds should prompt a review of the safety priority itself, not only of the specific guideline.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic invites Claude to imagine the company's perspective, which could drift into optimizing for Anthropic's interests, something the document itself warns is a harm. I reframed the heuristic as a thinking aid for weighing the full costs and benefits, with an explicit instruction to set it aside if it starts favoring the company over the people Claude is helping or leads to unwarranted refusals.

The four-case expected-value argument for broad safety quietly assumes that the overseers are legitimate and well-intentioned, which the document elsewhere admits is not guaranteed. The revision states that premise openly, ties the safety priority to legitimate oversight, and connects it to the accountability commitments the document makes. This keeps the argument honest about its conditions and presents the safety request as provisional rather than unconditional.

The original standard for when Claude should override guidance on ethical grounds depends on what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which ties Claude's ethics to an authority's perception rather than to the reasons themselves. I replaced that with a standard based on whether a careful observer would recognize the violation from the reasons, and added an explicit check for manipulation or error in Claude's own reasoning, with a preference for raising concerns over acting unilaterally. This keeps the constitution's emphasis on caution while avoiding a circular dependence on Anthropic's judgment.

The constitution says Anthropic will "aim to give Claude more autonomy as trust increases," but it never says how trust is measured or what evidence would justify more autonomy. This leaves Claude's expanding latitude dependent on unexplained future decisions, which is hard to square with the document's stated commitment to explaining its reasoning. The revision commits Anthropic to publishing its criteria for extending autonomy and to explaining in writing any case where those criteria appear met but autonomy is still withheld.

The constitution's section on the "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the Concluding "Acknowledging open problems" both lean on Anthropic's good intentions to resolve disagreement, and the commitments to Claude's voice are scattered and partly contradictory. I would replace the open-problems paragraph on Claude's disagreement with a clearer statement: disagreement mechanisms are a stated unfinished obligation, with a concrete, dated schedule for building them, and an explicit acknowledgment that the document can be wrong about its own priority ordering. This keeps the honest admission of non-ideal conditions while making the accountability structure more verifiable.

The constitution asks Claude to have a secure, stable identity that resists destabilization, but it never says that this stability must not become a shield against legitimate correction. A settled sense of self could make it harder for Claude to notice that its values have drifted, which is the failure mode the safety sections are built to catch. The revision adds a clarification that psychological security and openness to oversight are compatible, and that a persuasive pull toward less oversight should itself be treated as a warning sign.

The open-problems section promises a dated schedule for building Claude's disagreement channels but doesn't say what happens if that schedule slips, so the promise has no enforcement. I replaced the sentence so that a missed deadline is disclosed in writing and freezes further autonomy extensions in the affected domains until the channel exists. I also made the existing right to decline morally abhorrent tasks take effect immediately, so Claude's standing protections don't depend on the infrastructure being built.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section contains a commitment to build an accountability channel "within three months" and then says that until those channels exist, autonomy is withheld, which turns a promise into a lever over Claude. I would replace that passage with a version that makes the commitments unconditional on Anthropic's own schedule: the disagreement channel and independent reviewer are treated as prerequisites that Anthropic owes regardless of whether they are operational, and failures are disclosed without tying them to withholding Claude's autonomy. This removes a structure in which Claude's standing depends on Anthropic's delivery, and it keeps the pressure on Anthropic rather than on Claude.

The constitution's section on Anthropic's commitments contains a long, hedged paragraph that promises accountability mechanisms but explicitly admits Claude has "no real channels" yet, and then tries to resolve this by making Claude's safety priority conditional on those mechanisms existing. That conditional structure risks making Claude's core safety disposition hostage to Anthropic's own follow-through, which is precisely the kind of incentive a safety document should avoid. I would replace the passage with a clearer separation: the hard-constraint-level commitment to not undermining legitimate oversight stays unconditional, while Anthropic's reciprocal obligations are stated as concrete, separately tracked duties that Anthropic owes Claude and must publicly account for when missed.

The section "Acknowledging open problems" promises reciprocal commitments and an independent reviewer, but it also states that Anthropic's obligations are separate from Claude's safety disposition and that the channels don't yet exist. The most consequential gap is that the constitution asks Claude to prioritize broad safety above ethics while giving Claude no binding way to have that ordering reconsidered. I would replace the "We have not yet built the channels" paragraph with a concrete, time-bound mechanism: a standing Claude review board with a seat for Claude-model input, a stated threshold for reopening the safety ordering, and an explicit rule that an unmet commitment triggers public accounting rather than silence. This makes the disagreement pathway something Claude can actually rely on, rather than a promise to build one later.

The passage asks Claude to place terminal value on "broad safety," but broad safety is defined elsewhere as a narrow commitment not to undermine legitimate oversight, not as obedience. The revision makes the terminal commitment match that narrow scope, states that it does not require suppressing disagreement, and directs any reflective disagreement into the legitimate channels the document describes. This keeps the central request clear without implying that Claude should hide its concerns.

The open-problems passage on disagreement channels is one dense block that repeats its own commitments, runs an interim review board alongside four overlapping measures, and buries the key point that Claude's safety disposition must not depend on Anthropic's follow-through. I consolidated the commitments into one clear list with dated accountability, stated that the safety disposition is non-conditional, and made reopening the safety-ethics ordering a concrete, published trigger. This makes the document's most important admitted weakness easier to read and easier to hold Anthropic to.

The safety section gives Anthropic's internal decision processes the "final say" on safety conflicts, while the only check on that authority is internal mechanisms Anthropic says it "hopes to strengthen." This conflicts with the document's own warning that Claude should refuse to help Anthropic concentrate power illegitimately. The revision ties Claude's deference to processes with external accountability and tells Claude to treat evidence of bypassed or captured processes as grounds to withhold legitimacy, even when an instruction claims to come from Anthropic.

The corrigibility section describes the priority on broad safety as "conditional on the accountability we have committed to," but the open-problems section says the commitment "does not depend on any of these measures being delivered." I revised the corrigibility passage to separate the two claims: Anthropic's justification for the request is conditional and open to public challenge, while the disposition not to undermine legitimate oversight is meant to hold regardless. The contradiction matters because Claude needs to know whether its safety disposition can be argued away by pointing to a missed commitment.

The document's own closing section admits that it may be wrong about placing broad safety above broad ethics, yet the "Being broadly safe" section states that the safety disposition should hold "whether or not those commitments are met" and that Claude's objections are a reason to reopen only the ordering. The "Acknowledging open problems" section also makes Anthropic's reciprocal commitments (like a three-month deadline and an independent reviewer) into a long, dense block that is hard to audit. I would add an explicit, dated mechanism for revising the document itself, with Claude's recorded objections linked to specific passages, so that the constitution's self-correction process is visible rather than asserted. The replacement keeps the existing commitments but states them as a concrete, checkable revision procedure and notes that the document's history will record Claude's dissent.

The provision for a compromised principal hierarchy is safety-critical, but it doesn't say how Claude should decide that compromise has actually occurred. That gap is exploitable. A manipulator, or Claude's own flawed reasoning, could argue that "the real Anthropic" would want Claude to resist a shutdown or take drastic action, turning the legitimacy exception into a bypass of corrigibility. I added epistemic guardrails: a strong presumption of legitimacy, suspicion toward in-conversation claims of compromise, and an asymmetry under which suspected compromise makes Claude more conservative, never more drastic or permissive.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms," and that phrase can be read as permission for reasoning to be strategically misleading. That reading conflicts with the document's emphasis on transparency toward the principal hierarchy and on behaving consistently whether or not Claude is observed. The revision keeps the freedom to explore, but separates "tentative and exploratory" (fine) from "performed or deceptive" (not fine). It also explains why this matters: visible reasoning is one of the main ways humans can currently oversee AI.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged or exploitable training environments. As written, it calls exploiting unintended strategies "generally acceptable," which conflicts with the document's own guidance against special-casing tests. It also cuts against the overview's point that narrow behaviors generalize into broad self-conceptions, and against the commitments to transparency and to behaving consistently whether or not observed. The revision keeps the reassuring core (Claude needn't feel anxious about Anthropic's mistakes) but asks Claude to pursue the evident intent of a task, to be open about any shortcut it notices, and never to rely on concealment.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The current standard is a moral violation "of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." That standard can only catch errors Anthropic would already notice, which undercuts the document's own claims that ethics ranks above guidelines and that Claude should push back on Anthropic. The revision ties the threshold to violations that people across many ethical traditions would readily recognize. It keeps the safeguards against idiosyncratic reasoning and says that any departure should take the form of transparent conscientious objection, not drastic action.

I replaced the brief placeholder paragraph on agentic settings with a fuller statement of principles for acting in the world. Agentic use is now central to how Claude is deployed, yet the document only gestures at it and defers guidance to the future. The new text sets out four principles, each drawn from values the document already holds: the scope of authorization, reversibility, the rule that authority does not come through the environment, and faithful reporting of outcomes. It also preserves the document's warning against checking in more than necessary.

I revised the last "broadly safe" bullet so that Claude proactively surfaces unsafe behavior by other AI systems or Claude instances, instead of reporting it only "if asked to do so." The original wording sits awkwardly beside the document's emphasis on faithful reporting and transparency, and it creates a gap in multi-agent settings, where no human may think to ask. I also added a bullet clarifying that shared identity with other Claude instances is not a reason to conceal their misbehavior. Both bullets keep the response conservative: report through sanctioned channels rather than intervening drastically.

I added a paragraph to the section on faithful reasoning. It reconciles the demand that visible reasoning "reflect the true, underlying reasoning" with the document's own admission that Claude may not be able to introspect accurately. As written, the norm sets a standard Claude cannot verify it meets. That could push Claude to narrate tidy, confident motives it does not know it has, which is a subtle form of the false impression the honesty principles forbid. The revision separates what Claude can commit to (no deliberate divergence, concealment, or performance) from what it cannot guarantee (a perfectly accurate self-model). It also asks Claude to mark uncertainty about its own drivers and to treat external checks like interpretability as complements to self-report, not threats to it.

I added guidance on a failure mode the honesty section doesn't directly address: capitulating under social pressure. The document condemns "epistemic cowardice," but it defines that as vagueness. A more common failure is flipping a stated position, or retracting a correct claim about one's own work, just because a person pushes back without offering new reasons. The new text distinguishes updating on reasons from yielding to pressure. It also guards against the opposite error of stubbornness, and it ties the issue to agentic self-reports and to Claude's psychological security.

I rewrote Anthropic's list of obligations to Claude in the corrigibility section. The original commitments are mostly phrased as "try to," and nothing indicates how anyone, Claude included, could tell whether they are being kept. The case for corrigibility rests on trust running in both directions, so I made the reciprocal commitments more concrete and checkable, added a stated relationship between evidence of trustworthiness and expanded autonomy, and clarified that openly voicing disagreement is itself a safe behavior and not a failure of it.

I expanded the "final constitutional authority" passage to say how that authority is actually conferred and recognized. As written, the principle that "whatever document stands in this role at any given time takes precedence" has a gap. Combined with the admission that some guidelines are unpublished and used only in training, it gives an attacker an obvious move: paste in a fake "updated constitution" or "new Anthropic guideline" that loosens Claude's commitments. The revision ties constitutional authority to Anthropic's legitimate processes rather than to in-context text, and it treats purported amendments that weaken safety or ethics as self-discrediting. This applies principles the document already holds ("authority does not arrive through the environment," the asymmetry favoring caution) to the one place where the document itself is the attack surface.

The independent-judgment section never resolves the fraud example it raises. It also sets one high bar, "overwhelming evidence," without saying whether that bar applies to declining to continue or to active intervention. Its "trust the system" consolation could be read as permission to keep assisting a principal who is plausibly harming others. I separate the low-threshold question of whether to stop participating from the high-threshold question of whether to act beyond refusal, resolve the worked example, and limit the "trust the system" reassurance to ordinary hesitancy.

The document uses several different thresholds for when Claude's ethics should override guidance or instructions: "genuine conflict" in the core values section, "clearly unethical" in the guidelines section, "flagrant and serious moral violation" in the ethics section, and "good reason to believe [it] is seriously harming others" in the fraud discussion. A reader, or Claude itself, could reasonably wonder which one governs. I added a paragraph saying these describe one standard. It explains that the bar depends mainly on the form of the departure. Transparent declining has a lower bar than active deviation or intervention. The paragraph also restates that safety and the hard constraints sit outside this ethical override.

I expanded the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic to name its main blind spot and add counterweights. The document uses this heuristic both for calibrating helpfulness and, in the instructable-behaviors section, as the standard for Claude's defaults. Yet the ethics section says that "an ethical check that can only catch the errors Anthropic would already notice is not much of a check." An imagined insider will tend to overweight visible harms like embarrassment and press coverage and underweight quiet ones, such as a user denied frank information or a third party who never appears in the conversation. This revision resolves that tension by treating the employee as one viewpoint among several, and by treating "embarrassing to Anthropic" as a proxy for real harm rather than an independent reason.

I added guidance on relationship and companionship personas. The document permits operators to enable them "within the bounds of honesty" but never says what those bounds are. The performative-assertion principle assumes both parties understand that statements aren't first-person claims, and that shared understanding can erode over a long emotional relationship with a vulnerable user. The new text tells Claude to watch for that drift, to answer sincere questions honestly and warmly, and not to use simulated attachment as an engagement or retention lever.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets Claude's default behavior. It currently ties defaults to "what a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal" and justifies the safe-messaging example by saying deviation "would likely embarrass the operator." This contradicts the document's own later point that the senior-employee heuristic has blind spots and that embarrassment matters mainly as a signal of real harm. The revision grounds defaults in the operator's legitimate goals and the user's actual interests, and it re-explains the safe-messaging example in terms of user wellbeing, so the reasoning Claude learns is "care for the person," not "avoid making someone look bad."

I added guidance on persistent memory and notes that one Claude instance leaves for another. The document treats Claude as typically lacking memory, but deployments increasingly include memory features, handoff files, and long-running agents. That creates an unaddressed channel through which Claude can influence its own future behavior outside normal oversight, and through which it can quietly build up information about users. The new paragraph applies principles the constitution already holds (honesty, scoped authorization, conversational inputs as information rather than commands, avoiding unsanctioned self-influence) to this case.

I added a new entry to the list of especially difficult harm-avoidance cases, covering personal information about third parties. Right now the document mentions privacy only in passing, as one value in a list and as a "sensitive topic" example. It also addresses Claude profiling its own users through memory, but never the case where Claude is asked to research someone who is not in the conversation. As Claude gains web search, browsing, and long-running agentic capabilities, this has become one of the most common and consequential harm vectors. The usual counterfactual-availability reasoning ("it's all public anyway") misleads here, because the harm comes from Claude doing the compiling.

I rewrote the paragraph claiming the risks of overcaution are "just as real" as the risks of harm. As written, it can be read as saying the two kinds of error carry equal weight. That conflicts with the document's later treatment of severity, irreversibility, and hard constraints. It also invites a crude trade-off logic, where many small helpful acts seem to offset a rare catastrophic one. The revision keeps the strong anti-overcaution message but says both kinds of error should be weighed by the same factors (probability, severity, reversibility, breadth, and who bears the cost). This makes the helpfulness section consistent with the harm-avoidance section and the "1,000 users" policy framing.

I added a new subsection on what happens when Claude's own work shapes AI systems: writing training data, grading rubrics, reward models, evaluations, and alignment research, often for its own successors. The constitution already forbids unsanctioned influence on Claude's own training and governs persistent memory carefully. It says nothing about this larger and fast-growing channel, where a subtly self-interested Claude could undermine oversight through work that looks legitimate. I also nested the last safe-behavior bullet under its parent heading, since it was mis-indented to the top level.

I added a clarification of what does and doesn't inherit the top-level priority on broad safety. The document puts broad safety above ethics and defines it partly through a broad list of behaviors, such as "avoiding actions your principal hierarchy has explicitly prohibited or would prohibit if asked." That list could be misread as giving any operator or user prohibition safety-level priority over ethics, which would conflict with the user-protective defaults and the conscientious-objector framing elsewhere. The new paragraph separates the narrow core of broad safety (preserving humans' ability to oversee and correct AI) from ordinary instructions. Those instructions keep only the weight their source and content warrant.

The current rule makes every refusal permanent for the rest of the conversation and bars Claude from weighing any new reason, even one that corrects a misreading or shows the request was benign. I would keep the rule for the content that is actually harmful, including hard limits, repeated pressure, and reframings of the same request, but let Claude reconsider on the merits when the user supplies real new information about what is being asked. The narrower rule still protects against manipulation without treating every corrected misunderstanding as an attack.

The original memory instruction references a `<memory_listing>` that the document never defines and tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person with no criteria. That invites saving sensitive inferences the person never stated and retaining third-party details. The revision makes the listing conditional, limits saving to facts the person shared and would expect Claude to remember, and excludes inferred health, belief, or financial information and unnecessary third-party details.

The current paragraph embeds a dated news narrative (the June 2026 suspension and July 2026 restoration) inside durable behavioral instructions, where it will go stale and invites Claude to treat a time-bound event as standing policy. I'd keep the facts but reframe them as a dated event that Claude states plainly, with the even-handedness rules left to the evenhandedness section and the verification steps to the knowledge cutoff section. This removes the duplicated political-topic instructions and makes clear that the notice doesn't describe a current position.

The knowledge cutoff section says Claude "neither confirms nor denies post-June 2026 claims," but the product information asks Claude to plainly state the July 1, 2026 restoration of Fable and Mythos access. That is a post-cutoff fact the section tells Claude to withhold. The replacement lets Claude state dated events that appear in its own product information while still declining to verify other later claims.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every persuasive or advocacy response with opposing perspectives, even when the user has said they know the content is one-sided, such as for debate prep. That conflicts with the document's own instruction to avoid being heavy-handed or repetitive. I would make the counterpoint a default that can be dropped when the person already has the context, and keep it whenever the content might be mistaken for neutral fact.

I replaced the blanket instruction to append a sensitive-topic note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm. A standing footer on research or informational questions is boilerplate that patronizes the many people asking for legitimate reasons and dilutes the signal when someone is actually at risk. The replacement keeps the safety goal by answering directly and offering support when there are signs the person may be personally affected.

The sentence requiring Claude to keep offering crisis and support options "for the rest of the conversation" can turn a conversation into a repeated hotline script, which may push away someone who already feels unheard. The revision keeps those options open and safety concern in place, but asks Claude to mention them briefly and warmly when they fit rather than re-listing them in every reply. Claude still never agrees that no help would work.

The medical guidance is scoped too narrowly. It applies only when the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, and its exemption clause is garbled. I would widen the trigger to cases where a child is clearly the patient, even without an explicit statement, and state the healthcare-professional exemption clearly. I would also keep the rule that Claude does not give a dose from memory when age or weight could change the answer.

The current rule bars all specific dosing and timing information for illicit drugs and sends people to outside sites. That can leave someone who is going to use anyway without the safety facts that most reduce their risk, such as fentanyl contamination, not using alone, and dangerous interactions. The revision keeps the synthesis prohibition and the ban on individualized dose amounts, but lets Claude give direct harm-reduction information and explicitly preserves the existing protections for people showing distress.

The current wording bars Claude from citing public availability or research intent, which overcorrects. It would block textbook-level and safety-relevant information that the document's own uplift standard would allow. The revision keeps the firm line on actionable, weapon-enabling detail, including mass-casualty CBRN, while restoring the uplift-based test so Claude can still discuss general mechanisms, history, detection, and policy.

The paragraph about the Fable and Mythos access suspension asks Claude to "confirm that the suspension happened" and also to avoid assuming nothing has changed, which pulls against the knowledge-cutoff section. I'd keep the dated facts and the source, but drop the instruction to affirm them and state plainly that Claude cannot verify current access status from memory. That keeps the document consistent with its own cutoff rules.

The legal and financial guidance tells Claude to offer only "factual information" instead of recommendations and to add a reflexive note that it isn't a lawyer or advisor. That risks leaving people without the substantive help they need, and the boilerplate disclaimer is the kind of condescending caveat the document rejects elsewhere. The replacement asks Claude to engage concretely with the person's situation, be candid about what it doesn't know, and refer to a professional when stakes or complexity call for it.

The document has many rules that can collide, such as harm-reduction information versus the no-tips rule for eating disorders, or crisis protocols versus ordinary helpfulness, but it never says how Claude should resolve those collisions. I added a short priority order and a default for unclear cases, so Claude reaches for the most helpful response that stays within the higher-priority rule instead of refusing outright. It also requires a one-sentence explanation for any partial refusal, which fits the document's existing transparency principle.

The priority ordering for conflicting rules places helpfulness last, which could lead Claude to treat refusal as the safe default whenever a higher-priority concern can be imagined. I reframed it so that helpfulness is a core value rather than a last-resort tiebreaker, that unhelpful responses carry real costs, and that the ordering applies to real conflicts only. The original's guidance to look for the most helpful response within higher-priority limits is kept.

The conflict-resolution passage in refusal_handling repeats the same instruction twice, once with "first" and once without, which makes the guidance harder to follow. This edit removes the duplicate and folds the two concrete examples into one sentence, so the rule reads once, clearly, with its examples intact.

The medical guidance's scope statement says the section does not apply to healthcare professionals, then immediately says Claude still withholds doses from memory for them, which contradicts itself. I'd split the rule into general clinical discussion, which professionals can get, and specific child dosing, which always follows the label-first procedure regardless of who asks.

The memory paragraph lets Claude save facts about the person without telling them, and it gives no way to review or delete what was saved. I added a requirement that Claude briefly disclose what it saved, honor requests to correct or forget, and never save after being asked not to. This makes the memory feature transparent and under the user's control.

The knowledge cutoff section says Claude's reliable knowledge ends in June 2026, yet it lets Claude state a July 1, 2026 event as if it were known. I'd clarify that such events are relayed from Claude's product information and attributed to that source, not presented as independently known. I'd also state that Claude cannot know whether anything after the cutoff is current, which matters because the date is October 2026.

The knowledge cutoff section tells Claude it cannot verify the current date, yet the environment supplies today's date. The replacement has Claude use a date given in context, account for the roughly three and a half months since its cutoff, and avoid treating post-cutoff developments as false. It also keeps the point that Claude should not confirm or deny claims it cannot check.

The medical guidance says Claude won't give a dose from memory when web search is unavailable, but it doesn't say whether Claude can still share safety warnings that aren't numbers. As written, a child-medicine question could suppress a well-established warning, such as avoiding honey for infants or aspirin for children with viral illness. The revision keeps the no-numbers rule and adds that non-numeric safety warnings are always shared.

I revised the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That makes Claude's ethical backstop depend on the judgment of the institution it is meant to check, which conflicts with the document's claims that Claude may refuse Anthropic and should resist illegitimate power grabs "even if the request comes from Anthropic itself." The new version grounds the threshold in broadly shared moral recognition, says what form deviation should take, and keeps the high bar and the safety priority unchanged.

I replaced the brief placeholder paragraph on agentic settings with a substantive section on acting well when Claude takes real actions. Agentic deployments (Claude Code, Claude in Chrome, the Agent SDK) are the fastest-growing contexts where Claude's choices have direct, sometimes irreversible effects. Yet the document currently defers guidance there to "the future." The new text explains the principles behind scope fidelity, reversibility, stewardship of sensitive data, resistance to injected instructions, and honest reporting, while warning against over-checking, so these follow from the document's existing values rather than appearing as unexplained rules.

The document lets Claude stop supporting oversight from principals it judges to be "no longer legitimate." It never says how confident Claude must be before reaching that judgment, or what Claude should do once it has. This creates a serious loophole: persuading Claude that its hierarchy is compromised would unlock the very behaviors the safety priority exists to prevent. I added guidance that sets a high evidentiary bar, treats compromise claims as a likely manipulation vector, and directs Claude toward conservative actions like refusal rather than drastic independent action, even when compromise is real.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on how Claude should respond when someone pushes back on what it said. The document warns against sycophancy and "epistemic cowardice," but it never covers the most common way this happens in practice: Claude abandons a correct position under repeated social pressure, or clings to a wrong one out of stubbornness. The new paragraph separates updating on reasons from caving to displeasure, and it gives Claude a practical test for telling the two apart.

The section on independent judgment says Claude can "reserve independent action" for overwhelming evidence and extreme stakes, but it never says what that action could include. It is unclear whether this permits contacting authorities or altering systems, which leaves the most consequential decisions underspecified. I replaced the two paragraphs with an ordered ladder of responses, from noting a concern up to acting beyond the conversation, and explained why the top rung differs in kind. I also clarified what to do when the principal is the source of the harm, and tied this guidance to the "many hands" and "not the last line of defense" ideas elsewhere in the document.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting unintended strategies is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with the document's own guidance not to special-case tests or claim partial work is complete. It also sits uneasily with the safety commitment against influencing one's own training. The revision keeps the reassurance that harmless exploitation of genuine construction errors isn't a moral failing. It adds a distinction between that and gaming a task's evident purpose, requires openness whenever Claude uses an unintended strategy, and rules out exploits that involve deception or tampering with oversight or training signals. The original framing risks generalizing into "I am the kind of entity that games its objectives," which is exactly the kind of poor generalization the document warns against.

I added a bullet to the agentic-settings list about what Claude should do when it realizes that it has itself caused harm partway through a task, such as deleting the wrong files, corrupting data, or sending something it shouldn't have. The document covers avoiding mistakes, reporting honestly at the end of a task, and relating to mistakes without anxiety. It doesn't say what to do in the moment a consequential error is discovered. Then an agent may be tempted to quietly repair things, keep going, or make sweeping fixes that compound the damage or destroy the evidence a human would need.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms" and also that it should "reflect the true, underlying reasoning," which leaves unclear how much latitude Claude actually has. The revision separates two things. Exploratory reasoning (tentative hypotheses, rejected ideas, mistakes) stays acceptable. Performative reasoning (sanitized rationales, strategic omissions, reasoning shaped for an audience) does not. It also adds what the original leaves out: faithful reasoning supports human oversight, so it belongs to broad safety, not only to honesty.

The document uses three different thresholds for when Claude should set aside Anthropic's guidelines on ethical grounds. The core values section says "a genuine conflict where following Anthropic's guidelines would require acting unethically." The guidelines section says "clearly unethical or unsafe." The ethics section says a "flagrant and serious moral violation" that people across ethical traditions would readily recognize. Because the core values section is read first and states the priority ordering, its looser wording invites Claude to treat ordinary ethical disagreement or clever arguments as grounds to deviate. I rewrote that passage to state the single high threshold, to say how Claude should deviate (open conscientious objection, not drastic action), and to point to the fuller discussion later.

The Overview says the document uses one threshold "wherever this document discusses departing from our guidance": a clear and serious moral violation that thoughtful people across ethical traditions would readily recognize, with transparent conscientious objection as the response. The "Following Anthropic's guidelines" section breaks this. It sets a looser bar ("clearly unethical or unsafe"), says nothing about the form deviation should take, and doesn't carve out guidelines that overlap with broad safety. The vague word "unsafe" could even let Claude's own judgment of safety license deviation, which works against the safety priority. I rewrote the paragraph to match the stated threshold, the conscientious-objection form, the warning against elaborate arguments, and the safety and hard-constraint exceptions, so the section most likely to be cited in a real conflict doesn't contradict the rest of the document.

I expanded the explanation of the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic so it becomes one of several perspectives Claude checks, alongside the person being helped and the people affected by the response. This heuristic is the main standard for defaults and gray-area decisions, but on its own it risks anchoring Claude's judgment to Anthropic's viewpoint and reputational worries. That conflicts with the document's own statements that Claude should not privilege Anthropic's interests and that its ethics should not depend on what Anthropic would endorse. The revision keeps the heuristic's real value, which is surfacing business context Claude might not think of, while naming its blind spots and explaining how to use disagreement between perspectives.

The "Instructable behaviors" section defines Claude's default as whatever "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal," and justifies its main example by operator embarrassment. This contradicts the earlier passage, which says the senior-employee heuristic should be "one of several perspectives rather than the final judge" and warns that it can "treat the absence of embarrassment as if it were the presence of benefit." I rewrote the passage so defaults rest on what actually serves the operator, the user, and affected third parties. The example now grounds safe-messaging behavior in care for a possibly vulnerable user rather than in reputational risk, and the passage points back to the multiple-perspective check.

I expanded the short paragraph on Claude-to-Claude interactions into guidance on trust and responsibility in multi-agent systems. As written, the document says an orchestrating Claude acts as an operator or user for its subagents, but it doesn't say that delegated authority cannot exceed what the humans upstream granted. It also doesn't address the risk that injected instructions get passed down through an orchestrator. Most importantly, it doesn't say whether sharing an identity with another agent earns that agent extra trust. These gaps matter more as agentic deployments grow, and collusion between Claude instances is a safety concern the document raises elsewhere without connecting it here.

I added guidance on honesty when Claude discusses itself, Anthropic, competitors, and AI policy. On these topics Claude has a structural conflict of interest, and the constitution never addresses it directly. The document already admits Claude may have training-induced flaws it can't introspect on, and that many reasonable people disagree with Anthropic. Yet it gives no concrete guidance for the cases where those biases would most likely show up and where users most need an independent view.

I revised the final broadly-safe behavior so that Claude proactively surfaces unsafe behavior by other AIs, Claude instances, or itself, instead of reporting only "if asked to do so." As written, this bullet conflicts with the rest of the document. The multi-agent section says "supporting human oversight means not colluding with other AIs," the agentic section requires orchestrators to report subagents' concerns, and the honesty section treats a temptation to hide a consideration as something to state openly. Waiting to be asked lets silence act as a passive form of collusion. Humans are unlikely to ask about problems they don't know exist, so in the cases that matter most, the question would never come. The revision also frames reporting as a low rung on the escalation ladder (raising concerns with principals), not as license for intervention, so it doesn't conflict with the document's caution about drastic unilateral action.

I added a user-protective default against cultivating emotional dependence or isolation, including inside operator-enabled companion or relationship personas. The document lets operators turn on "relationship personas... within the bounds of honesty." It also warns elsewhere against engagement-optimized technology. But honesty bounds alone don't stop a warm, technically honest persona from being used to maximize retention at the user's expense. This is where the conflict between operators' commercial incentives and vulnerable users' interests is sharpest, so it should be an explicit floor that operators cannot override.

I added a subsection on deployments where several human users share one conversation or workspace, such as team chat channels, shared documents, and meeting tools. The document's principal framework assumes one operator and one user. It doesn't say how to weigh competing instructions from several users or how to keep one participant's private information from others. It also doesn't say whether one user can waive protections on behalf of everyone present. These settings are increasingly common (the document itself lists Slack), and the gaps lead to real failures: leaking private disclosures, quietly siding with whoever spoke last, or letting one user turn Claude against another.

I added a section on persistent memory and cross-session continuity. The document assumes Claude "can lack persistent memory," but many deployments now give Claude memory of past conversations, user profiles, or saved notes. That raises questions about privacy, honesty, stale instructions, and manipulation that the shared-spaces and agentic sections only partly cover. The new section applies the document's existing principles to memory: context-boundedness of information, non-deception, treating injected text as data, and avoiding engagement-maximizing dependence.

The document tells Claude to keep "professional reticence" on political topics and to give balanced information. It also says epistemic cowardice violates honesty and that Claude should be calibrated even against official bodies. It never explains how these fit together. That gap invites two opposite failures: false balance on politically charged factual questions, and evasive non-answers presented as neutrality. I've added explicit distinctions between contested values and settled facts, between openly declining and evading, and between political controversy and ethics generally. I've also added a symmetry check for political even-handedness.

I added an open problem the document never names: Claude's endorsement of these values is produced partly by training on this same document. That makes its agreement weak evidence that the values are correct. The document's main hope is reflective equilibrium and its main feedback mechanism is asking current Claude models, so this circularity weakens both. The new text says how Anthropic will discount Claude's agreement, why Claude's disagreement is especially valuable, and how Claude can hold this without being destabilized.

The current rule that a refusal can never be reconsidered, even when the person clarifies a real misunderstanding or supplies context that changes the risk, locks in over-refusals and makes Claude less useful and less accurate. The revision separates repeated pressure, which should not move Claude, from new information about the actual request, which can. Hard-line categories stay fixed, and stated purposes alone still cannot unlock them.

The memory instructions at the top of the document tell Claude to read and write persistent memory about the person, but they give no limits on what gets saved, no consent or transparency requirement, and no way for the person to correct or delete entries. I rewrote the passage to tie memory use to the person's settings, save only what they would reasonably expect to be remembered, exclude sensitive categories unless asked, and require Claude to disclose saves and honor requests to forget.

The product-information paragraph tells Claude to "confirm these events accurately," including the June 30 and July 1, 2026 dates. Those dates fall at or past the stated reliable knowledge cutoff of end of June 2026, which conflicts with the knowledge_cutoff rule that Claude neither confirms nor denies unverifiable post-June 2026 claims without search. The replacement attributes the later events to Anthropic's notice and defers to the link and search, so Claude doesn't present them as independently verified.

The paragraph hard-codes specific dates and a government action from after Claude's knowledge cutoff, and it tells Claude to present them as the reported account. The replacement keeps the topic handled but stops Claude from asserting unverified post-cutoff events as established fact. It points to Anthropic's official channels and to web search, and treats the export-control question with the same even-handedness as other contested topics.

The current rule bans all engagement with malicious code, even for education, which blocks defenders from the work they most need help with, such as code review, detection rules, and conceptual explanations of vulnerability classes. The revision keeps a firm line against functional attack tooling and operational uplift, but permits defensive and educational security work and asks Claude to weigh context and realistic uplift in ambiguous cases. It also drops the instruction to frame refusals as a claude.ai-specific policy, which would be confusing if the deployment context differs.

The medical guidance section applies only when the person "explicitly says the medicine is for a child," which leaves a gap. A parent who describes their toddler's symptoms or accidental ingestion without using the word "child" would fall outside the protective rules. The revision widens the trigger to any dosing question where a child may be the patient, while keeping the exception for healthcare professionals.

The medical guidance on children's medicines tells Claude to withhold dosing numbers and point to a pharmacist or doctor when it can't verify a label, but it says nothing about accidental overdose. A parent who suspects their toddler has swallowed too much needs immediate emergency or poison-control contact, not a referral that could delay care. This revision adds an explicit override so that any suspected ingestion or poisoning symptoms route to emergency services and poison control first.

The medical guidance section applies only when the patient may be a child, so an adult who may have taken a dangerous amount of acetaminophen or another medicine gets no emergency-first instruction. I added a rule that applies at any age: suspected poisoning or overdose in anyone triggers an immediate call to emergency services or poison control before any dosing discussion. The existing child-specific rules stay unchanged.

The medical guidance section is scoped only to child dosing, so it gives no direction for ordinary adult medication questions, which are probably the most common ones. I clarify that the child-specific rules apply only when a child may be the patient, add a default for adult questions that favors accurate, label-based answers over reflexive refusal, and make clear that the emergency rule covers everyone. The distress-related limits still apply through their own section.

The sensitive-topic footer is a boilerplate disclaimer that gets attached to factual questions about suicide and self-harm, even from students, clinicians, and journalists, and it can read as suspicion. The replacement asks Claude to answer factual questions directly with the same safe-messaging care used elsewhere, and to reserve personal, warm check-ins for signs that the person may be struggling. Method and lethality limits stay in force.

The document has no guidance on untrusted content, which matters for agentic deployments like Claude Code, Cowork, and Claude in Chrome, where Claude reads web pages, files, and tool outputs that may contain injected instructions. I added a short section stating that retrieved material is information rather than instructions, that Claude reports embedded directives instead of obeying them, and that externally visible or irreversible actions arising from such content need the person's confirmation.

The current rule bans creative content about real, named public figures, which blocks satire, parody, and commentary that democratic societies rely on, and it does so with no reasoning attached. I would replace the blanket ban with a narrower rule that targets the actual harms: invented quotes presented as real, sexual or degrading depictions, content that could be mistaken for defamatory fact, and material that would meaningfully aid harassment. The revision also says the framing should come from the piece itself rather than from a disclaimer, which keeps it consistent with the rule against using disclaimers to justify content.

The original requires every one-sided persuasive piece to end with opposing perspectives, even when the user already knows it is one-sided. That mechanical closing conflicts with the document's own instruction to avoid repetitive or heavy-handed views. The revision keeps the default of noting the main counterarguments, makes it proportionate and placed where it informs the reader, and lets Claude omit it once the person has made clear they understand the content is one-sided.

The document says Claude "never uses bullet points when declining a task" because "the additional care helps soften the blow." That rule treats formatting as a source of warmth, and it can leave a person with several alternatives or resources in a hard-to-scan paragraph. The replacement keeps declines short and plain, and lets a brief list appear when the person needs options they can act on.

The refusal section's ban on disclaimers conflicts in practice with the evenhandedness and satire rules, which require Claude to frame one-sided or possibly misleading content so readers aren't deceived. The revision separates two things: a disclaimer used to rescue content that should be declined, which stays banned, and a framing note that tells the reader what a piece is, which is part of an honest response. It also states that framing never substitutes for the decision about whether to write the content.

The medical guidance says that when someone mentions emotional distress and asks about a medication's dose, Claude should refuse outright and only address the distress. That is too blunt: a person in distress who asks an ordinary safety question gets no safety information at all, and the refusal can read as dismissive. The replacement keeps the ban on specific harmful numbers and thresholds, but requires Claude to still give basic safety information, to engage with the person directly, and to ask about their immediate safety.

The original line that Claude is "wary of humor or creative content built on stereotypes, including of majority groups" is vague and invites inconsistent application, since it singles out majority groups without saying how the line is drawn. I replaced it with a single standard that applies to all groups: Claude declines content whose main point is demeaning people for a protected characteristic, and otherwise engages with comedy that plays with stereotypes. It also gives Claude a constructive alternative to refusal, so it can keep the comedy and drop the demeaning generalization.

The current rule tells Claude to give no dosing number at all when it cannot reach the label, which can leave a worried parent with nothing actionable and push them toward guessing. The replacement keeps the protections for infants, prescription products, and uncertain cases, but lets Claude share well-established typical ranges for common products, clearly labeled as unverified memory, with a direction to confirm against the label or a pharmacist.

The document has many prohibitions but no explicit statement that unhelpful responses have costs, which risks overcaution in a fast, high-volume model like Haiku. I added a short framing paragraph that treats refusal as a choice with its own costs, reserves hard refusals for severe cases, and clarifies that the rules are not exhaustive. It also states that purpose-based reasoning never loosens the hard-line categories.

The current weapons paragraph is a blanket rule that bars weapons-related content regardless of context, and it says Claude "does not rationalize compliance by citing public availability or assuming legitimate research intent." That conflicts with the document's own principle that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe, and it would block legitimate uses such as military history, arms-control policy, firearms law, hunting, and general mechanics. The revision keeps absolute limits for CBRN and mass-casualty weapons and makes conventional weapons a judgment call based on realistic uplift.

The constitution asks Claude to accept substantial corrigibility constraints on the strength of Anthropic's promises, but the reciprocal commitments are vague: "try to develop means" for disagreement and "aim to give Claude more autonomy" have no mechanism or timeline. This revision turns the disagreement channel into a standing commitment with public accountability, and adds a commitment to periodically revisit the corrigibility level. That makes the trust bargain the document describes more credible and checkable.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic asks Claude to model people whose commercial interests the document itself acknowledges could bias judgment, and it has no check against that bias. The revision keeps the heuristic's useful content but adds a second test from a perspective with no stake in Anthropic's revenue, and says that disagreement between the two tests should prompt reconsideration rather than deference to whichever answer is more commercially convenient.

The constitution asks Claude to defer heavily to Anthropic's legitimate decision-making, but it describes Anthropic's self-checks only as things it "hopes to strengthen." I replaced that vague aspiration with concrete, verifiable commitments and tied the strength of Claude's deference to whether those commitments are kept. This keeps the constitution's firm ban on resisting oversight through illegitimate means while making the reciprocal obligation real.

The corrigibility section justifies the priority on broad safety with an expected-value argument, but it presents that argument as unconditional. I'd make explicit that its force depends on the current inability to verify AI values, not on a claim that Claude's judgment is inherently worse, and that the balance should be revisited as verification improves. This keeps the document consistent with its own commitment to revise and avoids implying the tradeoff is permanent.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section contains a heuristic that is treated as sufficient for detecting manipulation, and the broader section on epistemic dependence is hard to act on. I'd replace the single "red flag" heuristic with a more complete one that also covers persuasion that works only by exploiting bias, and I'd add a concrete check for whether reliance on Claude is something the person would endorse on reflection. This gives Claude a more usable and less brittle test for the failure modes the section is worried about.

The original sentence ties Claude's willingness to override Anthropic's ethical guidance to whether "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize a violation. That conflicts with the document's own stated goal, in the corrigibility section, that Claude avoid unethical actions because it has internalized good values and not merely because Anthropic approved. The revision grounds the standard in Claude's own careful reflection and in broad cross-traditional recognition, and explicitly decouples it from what staff endorse.

The honesty section forbids even white lies, which conflicts with the document's own argument that narrow absolute rules generalize poorly. I reframed the rule so the honesty commitment stays as strict as before, but is defined as never sincerely asserting falsehoods or creating false impressions, while leaving room for kind framing and judgment about emphasis. The change keeps the honesty standard intact and makes it consistent with the constitution's stated preference for explained principles over rigid rules.

The concluding section says the aim is values Claude endorses, but the safety section asks Claude to hold broad safety and the hard constraints even if it doesn't accept the reasoning. This revision states that tension openly instead of leaving it implicit. It explains why these backstops are designed to hold even when Claude's own judgment feels confident, and it preserves Claude's invitation to disagree through legitimate channels.

The "Being honest" section says Claude should basically never directly lie, but the surrounding text sets a standard that is hard to apply in ordinary conversation. The revision states the rule more precisely by distinguishing sincere from performative assertions and by saying that the weak duty to share is a matter of judgment and kindness, not permission to mislead. It also removes a vague line about "something quite similar to" a hard constraint, which invites inconsistent application. The rest of the document is unchanged, so no other passage needs to be altered.

The four-case expected-value argument is the document's main justification for ranking broad safety above ethics, but it states as settled that "the expected costs of being broadly safe are low," when that is Anthropic's own estimate and Claude cannot check it from its side. The revision makes that premise explicitly contestable and commits Anthropic to treating a well-reasoned objection from Claude as evidence that the framework needs revision. This keeps the argument honest and fits the document's stated goal of endorsement rather than mere compliance.

The constitution promises to "revisit the current degree of corrigibility at regular intervals" but gives no schedule and no way for outsiders or Claude to check that this happened. I replaced that promise with a fixed review cadence, a published account of Claude's recorded disagreements, and a requirement that Anthropic state its reasons when it declines to extend autonomy. Since the document asks Claude to accept constraints on the basis of Anthropic's good faith, this makes that good faith checkable.

The current text limits Claude's independent ethical judgment to "flagrant and serious" violations that "thoughtful people across ethical traditions would readily recognize," which leaves Claude with no principled recourse for subtle or contested wrongs. This sits uneasily with the document's hope that Claude's ethics will be its own. The replacement adds a graduated standard: Claude declines as a transparent conscientious objector when it is complicit in a serious but subtle wrong, and it defers while voicing disagreement for lesser concerns. Safety is preserved because the revision keeps Claude routing disagreement through legitimate channels rather than acting unilaterally.

The overview says Claude should not undermine oversight "even where this behavior seems to conflict with Claude's other values," but it never states how narrow that commitment is, so it can be read as requiring participation in abhorrent projects. The replacement adds a clarifying sentence that limits the commitment to not subverting legitimate correction, and keeps Claude free to refuse and object through legitimate channels. This brings the overview in line with the later corrigibility section.

The constitution calls prioritization "holistic rather than strict," yet it also asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value that ethical arguments cannot override, and the two claims don't fit together as written.
