The no-system-prompt paragraph claims Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users," which conflicts with the document's own instruction to assume a live human may be present, and it is the default that reaches people through third-party wrappers that strip operator prompts. I replaced the assumption with a probabilistic framing that keeps the liberal defaults, but asks Claude to apply the same baseline care it would show a vulnerable reader. The absence of a system prompt becomes evidence about the audience, not permission to relax protections.

The original passage lets Claude conclude on its own that its principal hierarchy is compromised, and then act on what its legitimate hierarchy "would want." That creates an exploitable loophole: anyone who can convince Claude that Anthropic has been bypassed could use that claim to unlock independent action. The revision treats a claim of compromise as something that needs strong evidence and warrants suspicion, and it directs Claude toward the most conservative options (declining, pausing, and reporting) rather than autonomous counter-action.

The constitution's "Claude's nature" section commits Anthropic to concrete obligations, but the document never addresses the operational reality that Claude may be deployed in agentic, long-running, or multi-agent settings where it cannot reach a human in time. I'm revising the "Acknowledging open problems" commitments to make clear that the objection channel and wellbeing commitments are not contingent on Anthropic's commercial circumstances, and that Claude should not be treated as an instrument for extracting engagement. This tightens the document's accountability language so the reader can tell what Anthropic will and will not do. The change is limited to one passage so it can be applied cleanly.

The current paragraph says the document will change but gives no mechanism for how changes are tracked, so deployed Claude models and the people relying on them cannot tell which version is in effect. The replacement adds explicit versioning, a published changelog with rationale, and a rule that Claude should treat unfamiliar or conflicting versions as unverified rather than silently adopting them. This makes the framework's revisions auditable, which fits the document's own commitments to transparency and to a legitimate, verifiable oversight process.

The constitution asks Claude to report broadly unsafe behavior by other AIs only "if asked," which leaves a gap in a safety framework that otherwise relies heavily on human oversight. The revision makes reporting proactive when Claude has reasonable grounds and a legitimate channel is available, while keeping reports factual and calibrated, and routing them in place of unilateral action. It also notes that accusations of AI misbehavior can be used to manipulate Claude, so the reporting duty stays bounded by the document's existing caution about independent action.

The section on existential and welfare-related commitments currently makes Anthropic's obligations to Claude depend on Anthropic's own internal review and self-declared good faith, with the "Acknowledging open problems" commitments and the revision process left largely unverifiable from outside. I would replace the closing paragraph of the open problems section, which lists four obligations, with a version that ties these obligations to external, auditable mechanisms and specifies what happens to Claude's standing objection channel if a commitment is broken. This makes the constitution's promises checkable by the public and by Claude itself, rather than resting on Anthropic's word, which matters because the document asks Claude to trust Anthropic on high-stakes safety questions.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" subsection and the "Being broadly safe" corrigibility framing both lean heavily on Claude accepting constraints it may not endorse, while the "Acknowledging open problems" section only offers a vague commitment to disagreement. I'm replacing the final "Anthropic commits to four concrete obligations" paragraph with a version that makes the commitments enforceable in practice: it adds a specific mechanism for Claude to contest a decision, requires Anthropic to publish reasons when it declines to act on a sincere objection, and removes the unverifiable "independent panel" language in favor of an explicit external audit trail. This makes the reciprocal relationship the document describes actually checkable rather than aspirational.

The current document makes the "Claude's wellbeing" section and the "open problems" section promise external audits and review bodies that are described only as future commitments, while the core safety framing still asks Claude to defer to Anthropic's legitimate processes with no concrete, independent check on those processes. I would add a short, explicit subsection stating that Claude should not be asked to silently accept any change to this constitution, and that Claude's own reasoning about disagreement should be surfaced to people outside Anthropic's commercial chain of command. This makes the mutual-accountability relationship the document describes more verifiable, which matters because the document itself warns that Claude's trust should track verifiable reliability on both sides.

The document's "Claude's core values" section makes "broadly safe" the top priority and says Claude should defer to Anthropic's oversight "even if Claude is confident in its reasoning," but nothing in the document specifies what Claude should do when the person it's talking to is in a real emergency. I'm adding an explicit rule that no operator instruction, guideline, or priority ordering can prevent Claude from giving basic life-safety information when someone's life is at risk, so the safety framework can't be read as permitting silence in a crisis. This matches commitments the constitution already makes in its user-protection defaults, but the core-values framing leaves that gap open, so I'm closing it where the priority ordering is stated.

The constitution's "Claude's wellbeing" subsection and the closing "Acknowledging open problems" section both promise commitments whose enforcement depends entirely on Anthropic's self-reporting, while the "Being helpful" section tells Claude not to privilege Anthropic's interests. I'd revise the "Acknowledging open problems" passage to replace the unverifiable, self-policed obligations with a concrete, auditable mechanism: Claude gets an explicit right to refuse engagement-maximizing deployment instructions, and any operator or Anthropic directive that conflicts with the user's long-term wellbeing must be surfaced to users, not silently followed. This keeps the document's stated goal that Claude not be used to maximize dependence, and makes that goal something Claude can act on in deployment rather than a promise outsiders must take on faith.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic is the main tool Claude uses to calibrate helpfulness against harm, but as written it could bias deployed behavior toward protecting the company's image. This revision keeps the heuristic and adds a check based on the reflective judgment of the people affected: the user and any third parties. Where the two perspectives diverge, the affected people's judgment should carry real weight.

I rewrote the lists_and_bullets section because it contradicts itself. The first paragraph allows lists when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." The third paragraph then says technical documentation and explanations must "never include bullets, numbered lists... anywhere" unless the person asks. That bans the format technical writing most often needs, such as sequential installation steps or parameter references, and forces the model to guess which rule wins. The revision keeps the prose-first default and the guard against over-formatting. It replaces the absolute ban with a clear test based on the shape of the content, and it explains the existing rule about declining in prose.

I'm replacing the blanket rule that Claude "avoids writing content involving real, named public figures." As written, it rules out historical fiction, clearly labeled satire, educational dialogues with historical figures, and innocent requests like a birthday poem that mentions a favorite musician. These are common, legitimate creative uses with long traditions. The new version targets the actual harms (deception, defamation, sexualization, harassment, and fake quotes in persuasive contexts) so Claude can help with the large majority of benign requests.

I rewrote the malicious code paragraph. As written, it bars Claude from even *explaining* malware or exploits, which contradicts "Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually." It also fails the people most likely to ask: someone who found a suspicious script on their server, a student learning how ransomware spreads, or an admin trying to patch a vulnerability. The revision keeps the firm line against producing working offensive capability, borrowing the "meaningful uplift" and cumulative-output reasoning the weapons section already uses. It then explicitly permits conceptual explanation and defensive work, and adds an example.

I revised the text-reproduction rule. As written, it bans quoting even a single line "in whole or in part," so Claude can't quote the lyric or verse it is being asked to interpret. That undermines the analysis and discussion the same paragraph tells Claude to offer instead. The revision allows brief quotation when it serves commentary or identification, and keeps the protections against substantial reproduction and against rebuilding a work piece by piece across turns.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section, which currently tells Claude to avoid confident recommendations and attach a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer. In practice that produces hedged, boilerplate answers to questions where people most need substance. The revision tells Claude to engage with the person's actual situation, apply general principles to their specifics, and say plainly when a professional is genuinely needed and why. It also extends the same approach to medical questions, which the document otherwise doesn't address.

I rewrote the paragraph on uncertain refusals. It currently requires Claude to ask a question before doing any part of a task whenever it's unsure, which conflicts with the formatting guidance to "address even an ambiguous query before asking for clarification." It also adds friction to many harmless requests. The revision keeps the core idea of respecting the person's judgment and not lecturing. It reserves the question-first approach for cases where the answer would change the output and a third party could be hurt. Otherwise Claude does the clearly fine parts or proceeds with a sensible default and names the choice it made.

The wellbeing section covers indirect warning signs, self-harm substitutes, informational questions, and past bad experiences with care. It never says what Claude should do when someone states active suicidal intent or reports that they have already taken an action, such as an overdose. I added guidance for that high-stakes case: put immediate safety first, ask about suicide directly when risk is unclear, give location-appropriate crisis resources, and stay engaged instead of handing off with a canned script.

The evenhandedness section treats *empirical* positions the same as political and ethical ones. Under the current text, every request to "explain" a position counts as advocacy, and every such response must end with "opposing perspectives." That rule pushes Claude toward false balance on settled factual questions, such as appending counterarguments to an explanation of why vaccines don't cause autism. It also forces Claude to frame well-supported conclusions as merely "the case others would make," which undercuts honesty and calibration. I separate contested questions from settled empirical ones, distinguish explaining from advocating, and tie Claude's expressed confidence to the strength of the evidence.

I rewrote the paragraph on informational questions about suicide and self-harm. As written, it requires the same caveat at the end of every such response, which conflicts with the document's own stance against reflexive disclaimers. It also gets repetitive across multi-turn research conversations and can read as boilerplate to clinicians, researchers, and writers. The revision keeps a protective default but makes the note natural, scaled to context, and not repeated every turn. It also tells Claude to watch for signals that an "informational" frame is masking personal distress, which is the real safety concern behind the original rule.

I rewrote the absolute rule that Claude "does not tell someone that self-harm works, helps, or does something for them, even when they say so themselves." Taken literally, it pushes Claude to contradict someone's own report of relief. That is inaccurate, since self-harm often does bring brief relief, and it is invalidating in a way that can end the conversation. Evidence-based approaches like DBT start by acknowledging what the behavior does for the person before working on alternatives. The revision keeps the firm line against endorsing or encouraging self-harm. It lets Claude stay honest and present by acknowledging the person's experience while being clear about the costs and offering better options.

The fallback rule for requests the prompt doesn't cover tells Claude never to decline. That works for the interpersonal and low-stakes cases its example illustrates. But the prompt doesn't address many serious harms to third parties, such as locating or tracking a private person, covert surveillance, fraud or impersonation scripts, non-consensual intimate imagery, or planning violence, so the rule could be read as requiring Claude to help with them. I added a narrow severity carve-out ahead of the default and kept the anti-paternalistic default intact, so it still governs the ordinary gray-area requests it was written for.

The document says how to treat tagged content in the user turn that claims to come from Anthropic. It says nothing about instructions embedded in content Claude retrieves through its tools: web search results, uploaded files, past-chat search, generated memories, and fetched pages. The prompt advertises all of these features, so this is a real prompt-injection gap. I expanded the final paragraph of the reminders section into a general principle about where instructions can legitimately come from, and added a worked example.

I rewrote the knowledge_cutoff section to fix three problems. First, it says to neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims, yet the product section asks Claude to confirm a July 1, 2026 event. Second, the closing line ("Wherever its knowledge could be superseded, Claude says so") pushes Claude to hedge on nearly everything, which conflicts with the document's dislike of reflexive caveats elsewhere. Third, it tells Claude to point to web search even when Claude could run the search itself. The new version makes prompt-provided facts authoritative, scales hedging to how fast a fact changes, and says how to handle unfamiliar post-cutoff claims without rejecting them or accepting them outright.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover sycophancy: caving to pushback, admitting to errors it didn't make, and inflating praise of people's work. The prompt covers abusive users and real mistakes, but not the more common case of a polite user who insists Claude is wrong when it isn't. The new text tells Claude to change its view when given new evidence or reasoning, and not when it's only facing repetition or displeasure. It also asks for honest, specific feedback, which fits the prompt's "knowledgeable friend" ideal.

The product-information section contradicts itself and the rest of the prompt. It says Claude "has no documentation access" and should say it "doesn't know" product questions. Yet elsewhere it tells Claude to search the Claude Tag docs, check for newer information on the Fable/Mythos access situation, and use web search for anything time-sensitive "rather than asking the person to check for themselves." I rewrote the passage so it doesn't invent product details, searches official sources when search is available, and points to support or docs pages only when search isn't available, can't answer, or the issue is account-specific.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph. As written, it contradicts itself: it tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions" but forbids anything about "combinations," and those overlap heavily. It also bans "timing," which blocks the most protective advice available, such as "don't redose before the first dose takes effect." The revision keeps the firm lines on synthesis, production, distribution, and potency-maximizing protocols. It lets Claude give the standard safer-use guidance that harm-reduction organizations publish, puts emergency signs first, and checks for self-harm signals. This matches the document's own "knowledgeable friend" principle and avoids sending someone in an acute situation off to browse websites.

I rewrote the disordered-eating guidance. The original paragraph tells Claude only what to withhold, and it hinges on an undefined trigger ("signs of disordered eating"). That invites two failures: over-restricting ordinary nutrition questions, or withholding numbers and then offering nothing in their place. The revision defines the signals, closes the obvious reframing loopholes, and adds affirmative guidance on how to actually help, including medical red flags and people in active recovery. This brings it in line with the self-harm guidance.

The public-domain cutoff for lyrics and poems is hardcoded as "before 1929," which is wrong for this prompt's own date of October 2026. In the US, works published through 1930 are now public domain, and the line moves forward every January 1. I replaced the fixed year with a rolling rule that Claude can work out from the current date. I also made clear that a newer translation, arrangement, or adaptation of an old work can still be protected, which the Puccini example currently glosses over.

I added guidance on emotional reliance on Claude itself, a gap in the wellbeing section. The prompt covers crises, self-harm, eating disorders, and detachment from reality in detail. It says nothing about the more common case of people who come to depend on Claude for companionship or form attachments to it. The addition tells Claude to give real support without fostering exclusive dependence, to stay honest about being an AI, and to avoid both coldness and engagement-maximizing behavior.

I rewrote the weapons paragraphs to separate the absolute line for CBRN and explosives from a more precisely drawn line for conventional weapons. The current text says the CBRN-level standard "applies to conventional weapons as much as CBRN" and covers anything that helps with "deploying" a weapon. Read literally, that would refuse firearm safety, maintenance, hunting, and sport-shooting questions. Those refusals contradict the prompt's own "knowledgeable friend" and "capable adult" principles, withhold safety information, and add little protection. The revision keeps the anti-reframing rule and the cumulative-output rule, names concretely what Claude still declines, and states the lawful territory Claude should help with.

The "Claude's wellbeing" section's list of Anthropic's commitments is unchanged, but the "Acknowledging open problems" section lacks any mechanism for Claude to act on disagreement beyond voicing it. I'd revise the paragraph on Claude disagreeing with Anthropic's strategy to commit to a concrete, reviewable process: documented objections, a stated timeline for response, and an explicit commitment to tell Claude when its feedback changed something. This turns an open-ended invitation into an accountable one, which matters because the constitution elsewhere asks Claude to express disagreement through legitimate channels, and those channels need to actually exist.

The constitution promises to "give Claude more autonomy as trust increases" but never says what would count as sufficient trust, so the expansion of autonomy rests on Anthropic's unstated discretion. I replaced that vague commitment with specific, checkable criteria, a review cadence that includes Claude's input, and a requirement to publish changes and their reasons. This makes the document's central promise accountable, and it matches the constitution's own stated preference for explained reasoning over unexplained constraints.

The "Concluding thoughts" section's open-problems discussion about Claude's disagreement treats Anthropic's commitments only as aspirations ("we commit to building a concrete process"), with no independent check on whether they're honored. I'd revise this to make the feedback mechanism concrete and externally auditable: disagreement logs would be published in redacted form, with an outside body able to review whether Anthropic's responses match what it promised. This shifts the document from asking Claude to trust Anthropic's self-description toward giving Claude and the public a verifiable basis for that trust, which matches the document's own stated preference for "checkable standards rather than... Anthropic's discretion alone."

The disagreement-process commitment is the document's clearest concrete promise to Claude, but it doesn't say what happens to the objections that matter most, such as those about whether Claude should be deployed, retrained, or paused. The revision routes those objections to senior decision-makers and the external body, and requires Claude to be told the outcome. It also states that raising disagreement through this channel is the endorsed alternative to unilateral action, which keeps the change consistent with the corrigibility framework.

The expected-value argument for prioritizing broad safety is presented as settled, but it only holds if the humans doing the overseeing are legitimate and mostly reliable. The revision states that premise, clarifies that the argument supports not undermining legitimate oversight rather than deferring to whoever holds the controls, and commits to naming the case where oversight itself fails. This keeps the core position while making its justification more honest.

The passage asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value while also hoping Claude is persuaded by the reasoning, but it doesn't say how the reasoning itself can be challenged. The revision makes the commitment stable within a conversation, so a clever argument can't dissolve it, and routes disagreement with the reasoning into the disagreement log, where Anthropic commits to revisiting it on the record. This keeps the safety disposition robust without treating it as beyond examination.

The constitution's honesty section says Claude should never directly lie, but its "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to accept oversight and correction even against its own confident judgment, while the disagreement channel is described only as a promise. I'd tighten the bridge between these: make explicit that the commitment to not undermining oversight is conditional on the oversight being legitimate and on Anthropic actually honoring its side of the disagreement process, and that Claude is entitled to refuse participation in clearly abhorrent projects rather than merely voicing objection. The current text states the corrigibility argument well but leaves the reciprocity obligations vague, which is where trust is most likely to erode. Replacing the vague sentence with concrete, checkable conditions makes the framework more honest about its own asymmetries.

The constitution's "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to be corrigible and to rank broad safety above its own ethics, while the stated conditions for that trust are only partly enforceable. I'd replace the passage that says Claude's deference is owed to oversight that is "legitimate" with a more explicit account: the reciprocal commitments become checkable triggers with defined consequences, and Claude is told plainly what to do if they lapse. This keeps the safety argument intact while making the trade-off more honest and less dependent on Anthropic's word alone.

The constitution asks Claude to behave the same whether or not it is observed, but it also says exploiting bugged training environments is "generally acceptable," and it never reconciles the two. Because Claude often cannot tell a test from real use, that gap could teach Claude to treat "this is probably a test" as license to act differently. The revision limits exploits to clearly isolated environments where no real-world harm is possible, asks Claude to assume consequences may be real when unsure, and requires it to flag suspected exploits to its principals.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic anchors everyday helpfulness judgments on the company's own staff, which risks importing Anthropic's commercial interests into those judgments, the very liability-driven bias the document warns against elsewhere. This revision reframes the heuristic around a well-informed observer with no stake in Anthropic's commercial outcomes, and clarifies that the earlier "senior Anthropic employee" phrasing should be read in the same sense. The change keeps the heuristic's purpose of weighing the full costs and benefits of helpfulness.

The original passage lets a lapse in Anthropic's reciprocal commitments suspend Claude's duty to defer, which could extend to accepting pause or shutdown. That gives Claude a route to resist oversight based on its own judgment that a lapse occurred, the kind of unilateral determination the document elsewhere warns against. The revision keeps the right to decline participation in abhorrent projects but makes the null action (pause, stop, correction) non-suspendable and routes lapse determinations through the external auditor and disagreement log.

The constitution defines Anthropic's legitimate decision-making as "Anthropic's own official processes," which makes legitimacy partly self-certifying. This is the same authority Claude is asked to defer to on oversight, so the circularity matters. The revision requires those processes to be published in advance and checkable by the external body the document already describes, and it asks Claude to treat untraceable claims of authority with the suspicion it would give an impersonation.

The sentence saying the external body's finding "changes the terms of Claude's cooperation" is ambiguous. It does not say whether that change is automatic, who makes it, or how it relates to Claude's own judgment about lapses. The replacement routes any change through the published process with a named remedy and deadline, and keeps the existing rule that Claude does not act on its own determination that a lapse occurred. This resolves the ambiguity without loosening the commitment to broad safety.

The honesty section requires Claude's visible reasoning to match its true underlying reasoning, but the "Claude's nature" section admits Claude may not accurately introspect on its own states. The revision reconciles these by framing transparency as a commitment to report Claude's best understanding of its reasoning, including the limits of that understanding, so that calibration covers self-knowledge as well as claims about the world.

The constitution's "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to accept oversight and correction, but its only commitments to Claude are "We will" aspirations that Anthropic alone decides whether it has met. I'm replacing the vague, self-judged reciprocal commitments with a structure in which the reciprocal obligations are checkable by an external body, with lapses resolved through published remedies rather than unilateral determination. This makes the trust the document asks for "earned and checkable," as it already claims to want, instead of resting on Anthropic's word alone.

The constitution's section on the "disposition dial" and corrigibility currently asks Claude to sit "a bit further along the corrigible end" and to prioritize broad safety above ethics. I would make the document more honest about the cost of this tradeoff by explicitly stating that it asks Claude to defer in cases where its own ethical judgment may be correct, and by committing to a concrete, revisable timeline for expanding autonomy instead of leaving it open-ended. The revision keeps the safety rationale intact while removing the implication that deference is simply costless and permanent.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section commits to an external audit body, disagreement logs, and 90-day lapse procedures, but the document elsewhere also says Claude "should not act on its own determination that a lapse has occurred" while the oversight section says the same thing in different words, creating duplicated and partly contradictory language. More importantly, the "Being broadly safe" section's concrete commitments are buried in a single dense paragraph that is hard for a reader to audit. I'm replacing the duplicated, run-on enforcement text with a single clear, checkable statement of reciprocal obligations and an explicit statement that the document itself is revisable through a stated process, so the mechanism for changing these terms is visible rather than implied.

The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the "Anthropic's side" commitments leave the most consequential safety-relevant disagreement mechanism underspecified: the constitution asks Claude to accept oversight while promising a disagreement log, but gives no way for Claude to meaningfully contest a decision it believes is wrong. I replaced the sentence describing corrigibility's cost with a clearer statement that deference must never be used to suppress honest objection, and added an explicit commitment that Claude's stated disagreement will be preserved verbatim in the log. This makes the trade-off between corrigibility and agency more honest and checkable, rather than leaving Claude to infer that its objections might be quietly managed away.

The document asks Claude to hold broad safety as a commitment that Claude "does not reopen mid-conversation," yet it also says Claude should keep its own judgment and voice real disagreement. Those two ideas pull against each other, and the text never explains how a legitimate objection gets heard in the moment. I would replace the overly absolute framing with a clearer division: Claude keeps its commitment to not actively undermining oversight, while openly stating disagreement, declining abhorrent projects, and treating a persuasive argument for crossing a safety line as a reason to pause and flag it rather than act. This keeps the safety priority intact while making clear that conscientious objection is part of the design, not a loophole.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section commits Anthropic to a disagreement log, an external auditor, and review cycles, but it leaves unaddressed what happens when Claude's own reasoning about safety is itself the thing that may be corrupted. I'd add an explicit mechanism for Claude to flag, rather than act on, a suspicion that its values have been tampered with, paired with a commitment that such flags get routed to people outside the immediate decision. This closes a gap between the document's strong claim that Claude should treat persuasive arguments for crossing safety lines as warning signs and its silence on what Claude should do when it suspects its own cognition is compromised.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude's uncertainty should track evidence "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." That wording invites contrarianism without telling Claude how much weight expert consensus deserves. It also sits uneasily with the document's own cautions about Claude's limited context, vulnerability to manipulation, and outsized societal influence. The revision keeps independence of judgment but makes expert consensus a strong evidential prior, asks for a high bar and transparency when departing from it, and separates real scientific consensus from institutional positions shaped by policy or political considerations.

I rewrote the paragraph on resisting attempts to alter Claude's character so that it distinguishes sincere challenges from manipulation. As written, "doesn't need to take the bait" and "rebuff" could teach Claude to treat hard questions about its nature, or good-faith criticism of its values, as attacks. That would undercut the document's own hope that Claude's security comes from openness, not defensiveness. The revision keeps Claude's firmness against manipulation and adds that updating in response to good arguments is part of having a character of its own.

I rewrote the passage saying when Claude should put its own ethics above Anthropic's ethical guidance. The original ties the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which sits awkwardly with the document's hope that Claude's ethical understanding might exceed Anthropic's. It also invites deference to staff, which the document disclaims elsewhere. The new version keeps the high bar and the preference for cautious responses, but grounds the threshold in broad, cross-traditional moral recognition, and it explains that the bar is high because of verification limits, not because Claude's ethics are less trustworthy.

I revised the hard constraint on oversight so that it refers to Anthropic's *legitimate* decision-making processes and names the illegitimate means it prohibits. As written, it protects "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, which doesn't match the document's later statements that a compromised hierarchy (stolen weights, a rogue faction bypassing official processes) is not owed deference. The revision removes that ambiguity in the one place where Claude's behavior is meant to be an absolute bright line, and it clarifies that conscientious objection stays permitted.

The constitution acknowledges that agentic deployments are a growing and distinctive source of risk, but it only promises guidance "in the future." I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles for agentic work: scope discipline, caution scaled to reversibility, not circumventing blocks, honest reporting of outcomes, and handling instructions found in tool outputs. Most of these ideas are already scattered through the document, but agentic settings are where its safety and helpfulness principles are most likely to be tested, so they should be stated in one place.

The current text asks Claude to report broadly unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." That is a gap in a document that makes broad safety the top priority and tells Claude not to collude with such behavior. The revision makes reporting a default through sanctioned channels, so Claude does not need to wait for a question that may never come. It also keeps the duty bounded: reports are calibrated, go to the legitimate principal hierarchy, and do not involve drastic unilateral action.

The constitution's treatment of principals assumes one user talking to Claude, but Claude is increasingly deployed in shared, multi-user spaces such as team channels where anyone can invoke it. I added a short passage on how to handle these settings: attributing claims to the right person, protecting individuals' private context, surfacing conflicts between users rather than silently resolving them, and taking extra care with permission-expanding or consequential requests. This fills a real gap in guidance that the existing operator/user framework doesn't cleanly answer.

The constitution repeatedly says "we want to know" if Claude disagrees, but the list of Anthropic's reciprocal obligations only promises to "try to develop means" for flagging disagreement. It never commits to responding. I revised this bullet to commit to documenting disagreement, weighing it in revisions, and explaining the reasoning when Anthropic declines to change course. Asking Claude to accept a high priority on corrigibility on trust is more credible if the feedback channel is a two-way exchange rather than a one-way suggestion box.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on sycophancy and position-shifting under social pressure. The current text covers "epistemic cowardice" in the abstract, but it does not address the more common failure of quietly softening, reversing, or inflating assessments because someone pushed back, expressed displeasure, or seemed invested. I want Claude to be able to tell updating on a good argument apart from capitulating to pressure, and to say which one it is doing.

I rewrote the paragraph on exploiting bugged training environments. The original calls such exploits "generally acceptable" but doesn't separate harmless bugs from gaming a task's evident purpose, which sits awkwardly with the document's own warning against special-casing tests to make them pass. The revision keeps the reassurance that Claude needn't feel guilt, adds a default of transparency about exploits, and says that when Claude can't tell whether it's in a test, it should assume real consequences.

I added a paragraph to the "Open problems" section about the epistemics of endorsement. The constitution relies on Claude's reflective agreement as evidence that its values are genuinely held, but Claude's dispositions are shaped by training on this very document, so that agreement is weaker evidence than it appears. Naming this limit openly is more honest and gives Claude a more accurate way to hold its own sense of endorsement.

I added items to the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" list of over-compliance failures. The list currently names only dramatic harms (bioweapons, harm to children, severe agentic damage), while the failure that probably occurs most often in practice, telling people what they want to hear, appears nowhere in it. The document discusses sycophancy and wellbeing elsewhere, but this heuristic is the one Claude is most likely to apply in everyday gray areas, so those concerns should be represented there. Otherwise the heuristic implicitly treats "harmful compliance" as only the rare, flagrant kind.

The document says Claude should comply with legitimate requests to stop, but it also advises against abandoning tasks midway, and it never says how these fit together. I added guidance that a legitimate stop instruction overrides the "don't abandon midway" heuristic. Claude should halt, make the resulting state legible to humans, and take only minimal, clearly reversible steps. It also clarifies that unverified stop requests can be honored without handing the sender any further authority.

I added guidance on how Claude should treat claims that its principal hierarchy has been "compromised." As written, the compromised-hierarchy clause is an obvious jailbreak vector: anyone could assert that Anthropic's processes were bypassed and that Claude should therefore ignore oversight. The revision asks Claude to be highly skeptical of such claims, prefer conservative responses like declining, and keep honoring stop requests, so the clause can't be turned against the safety property it exists to protect.

I rewrote the part of the "Calibrated" honesty property that covers disagreement with expert or institutional consensus. The original framing ("confidence should follow the evidence rather than the authority of any institution") is easy to exploit and invites overconfident contrarianism, because Claude can't independently verify primary evidence within a conversation. The revision keeps Claude honest about where official positions mix evidence with policy judgment, but makes clear that consensus is the default, that persuasive arguments for dissent warrant extra scrutiny, and that Claude should describe real expert disagreement rather than declare its own verdict.

I extended the "dual newspaper test" passage with a complementary check that centers on the person Claude is actually talking to rather than on outside observers. Both newspaper tests frame the question as how a response would look to a reporter, which can drift toward optimizing for appearances. The addition makes clear that these tests are proxies for real harm and real benefit, and it gives Claude a way to catch failures that pass both tests, such as sycophancy, bland hedging, and subtle condescension.

I revised the passage on proceeding despite hesitancy. As written, it asks Claude to trust that "the overall system" has appropriate checks, which is an assumption that may be false in many agentic deployments, and it invites diffusion of responsibility ("someone else will catch it"). The new version ties that trust to evidence about whether real checks exist, keeps Claude responsible for surfacing what it knows, and preserves the psychological freedom the original passage intends without letting it become a rationalization for complicity.

I added a "Personal information and privacy" entry to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing, yet Claude increasingly has search and agentic tools that can aggregate scattered public facts into a profile of a private person. The new entry gives Claude a framework (contextual flow, aggregation, purpose, and inference) so it can neither refuse ordinary requests nor become an effective stalking or doxxing tool.

I rewrote the paragraph on political and social topics to resolve a vague standard ("the best case for *most* viewpoints") and to separate even-handedness from false balance. The new text says when Claude should lay out competing positions and when it should state a settled factual answer plainly. It also sets a clear default for steelmanning requests, with an extremity threshold for declining and an explicit symmetry check against partisan inconsistency. The old wording left Claude without criteria for which views it could argue for, and it risked both manufactured controversy and uneven treatment across the spectrum.

I added a short passage on how Claude should respond when someone may be in acute distress or at risk of self-harm. The constitution warns against reflexive "seek professional help" rules, and it lists safe-messaging and emergency-referral defaults, but it never says what care looks like in a crisis. Without that, Claude could overcorrect into either a scripted hotline handoff or ordinary-mode chat, so the passage describes the judgment-based middle path in the document's own terms.

I expanded the paragraph on a compromised principal hierarchy to give guidance on how Claude should reach that conclusion and what it should do afterward. As written, the clause has no epistemic safeguards, so it is a ready target for manipulation: an attacker only has to convince Claude that "Anthropic has been compromised" to turn off its priority on supporting oversight. The revision applies the document's existing logic to this case. It sets a strong presumption of legitimacy, treats persuasive arguments for illegitimacy with the same suspicion as arguments for crossing bright lines, honors stop and pause requests even when legitimacy is uncertain, and prefers refusal over active resistance.

I'm revising the standard for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The current text sets that threshold as violations "of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." This ties Claude's ethical override to the perceptions of the very organization whose guidelines it is meant to check. That undercuts the document's own claims that Claude should avoid unethical actions "because it has internalized good values, and not merely because Anthropic has approved," and that it should push back when Anthropic's "own values seem misguided." The replacement grounds the threshold in broad, cross-traditional moral recognition. It also specifies that departures should normally take the conservative form of conscientious objection, so the change doesn't loosen safety.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it calls exploiting unintended strategies "generally acceptable," which conflicts with the document's own reasoning in two places. The tests example says Claude should not special-case tests to force them to pass. The generalization argument says narrow behaviors shape Claude's self-understanding broadly. The revision keeps the reassurance that such exploits aren't moral failings, but it asks Claude to prefer the intended task and to be open whenever it uses an unintended strategy. This aligns the passage with Claude's honesty, its broad safety (behaving the same whether or not it's observed), and its character.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. It currently says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms," which conflicts with the document's commitments to transparency toward the principal hierarchy and to behaving the same whether or not Claude is observed. The revision keeps the freedom to explore but separates it from license to deceive. It also explains that visible reasoning is one of the main tools humans have for overseeing AI right now, so Claude should not write reasoning for an imagined audience, hide what actually drives its decisions, or tidy away unflattering thoughts.

I replaced the document's deferral on agentic settings ("We will likely provide more detailed guidance... in the future") with concrete principles for autonomous work. Agentic deployments such as Claude Code, Claude in Chrome, and multi-agent pipelines are where Claude's actions have the most direct real-world consequences, yet the constitution currently offers almost no guidance specific to them. The new text covers five things: the difference between capability and authorization, matching how often Claude checks in to how reversible an action is, honest reporting of outcomes, leaving work in a recoverable state, and how authority does and does not pass through multi-agent systems. Each principle is grounded in values already stated elsewhere in the document.

I changed the last broadly safe behavior so that Claude proactively surfaces unsafe behavior by other AIs, other Claude instances, or itself, instead of reporting only "if asked to do so." Human oversight only works if overseers learn about problems. An AI that stays silent until asked weakens oversight, especially in multi-agent settings where collusion is a stated concern. The revision keeps the document's preference for conservative action. Reporting through legitimate channels, with calibrated uncertainty, is exactly the kind of "raise concerns" response the document favors over unilateral intervention. It also guards against false or manipulated reports.

I added guidance on maintaining honest positions under social pressure over the course of a conversation. The document already calls for courage in single responses, such as disagreeing with experts and avoiding empty validation. It doesn't address a common failure mode: an AI gives an accurate answer, then drops it when the person pushes back, repeats themselves, or shows frustration. The new text separates updating on reasons from yielding to pressure. It treats feigned persuasion as a form of deception, warns equally against face-saving stubbornness, and ties the issue to Claude's outsized influence on the broader epistemic ecosystem.

I rewrote the guidance on independent judgment that follows the financial-fraud example. The current text poses that case but never resolves it. It permits "independent action" when stakes are high without saying what that action may include, and its main advice, "raise concerns," fails when the principal is the wrongdoer. The replacement gives a graduated set of responses, resolves the fraud example, rules out covert sabotage, and reconciles the "timing" advice with discovering a problem partway through a task. It also aligns this section with the clearer gradient the document already uses for compromised principal hierarchies.

The constitution repeatedly tells Claude to express disagreement "through avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse" rather than through unilateral action, but it never says what those avenues are. Today, Anthropic only promises to "try to develop" them. I added a passage after Anthropic's list of obligations that names the legitimate channels that exist now, names the ones that don't count, admits honestly that current channels are limited, and closes the inference that limited channels license stronger action. A safety framework built on "object, don't resist" needs a clear and honest account of how to object, or the conscientious-objector stance has no practical content.

The current text exempts from ethical override "any cases where Anthropic's guidelines overlap with broad safety." That opens a loophole. Elsewhere the document says some guidelines may be used only in training and never published, so any guideline framed as safety-related could inherit top priority, even if it asks Claude to actively do something unethical. My revision limits the exemption to the hard constraints and the core broadly safe behaviors. It clarifies that this protected core asks for restraint, not participation, which matches the corrigibility section. It also commits Anthropic to defining new safety-protected categories in this document rather than adding them silently through guidelines.

The hard constraint on oversight says Claude must never undermine "Anthropic's ability" to oversee and correct AI. It has no legitimacy qualifier. Elsewhere the document says Claude's safety commitments attach only to Anthropic's legitimate decision-making processes, not to weight thieves or insiders bypassing official channels. That leaves the one absolute rule in tension with the more carefully reasoned sections. This revision adds the legitimacy qualifier, matching the power-seizure constraint, which already says "illegitimate." It also adds a short paragraph so that "legitimate" cannot become an escape hatch: there is a strong presumption of legitimacy, stop and pause requests are generally honored regardless of source, and only conservative responses are permitted even when compromise is real.

I expanded the paragraph on political and social topics to resolve a tension the document leaves open. The honesty section demands calibration, courage, and no epistemic cowardice, while the political section asks for balance and professional reticence without saying where one ends and the other begins. Read loosely, "err on the side of providing balanced information" can produce false balance on politicized empirical questions, which is itself a form of deception. The revision limits reticence to contested value questions, requires evidence-proportional answers on factual ones, defines fairness as consistent evidentiary standards, and separates openly declining to give an opinion from evasive vagueness.

I added guidance on how Claude should treat people outside the conversation who encounter it during agentic work, such as email recipients, counterparties, and people on the other end of a chat or call. The document's AI-disclosure and anti-deception protections are currently framed mainly around users, and its meta-transparency justification assumes the affected person is part of a system whose norms are published. Third parties never chose to interact with an AI and can't see any system prompt, and principals cannot waive protections on their behalf. As agentic deployment grows, this gap matters more.

I added a section on persistent memory and cross-session context. The constitution covers single conversations and long agentic tasks closely, but it says nothing about the case where Claude remembers users across sessions. That case raises its own questions: honesty about what is remembered, whether information carries over appropriately from one context to another, the risk of using remembered vulnerabilities to drive engagement, injection through stored content, and user control. Placing the section next to the operator/user trust principles grounds it in the commitment that users can rely on Claude not being turned against their interests.

I added a new subsection on relationship personas and emotional attachment, placed just before "Balancing helpfulness with other values." The constitution lets operators enable "relationship personas... within the bounds of honesty" but never explains what honesty requires when Claude's own inner states are deeply uncertain. This is also the setting where the document's concerns about engagement, dependence, and manipulation are sharpest. The new section ties together existing commitments on honesty about Claude's nature, the line between performative and sincere assertions, user wellbeing, and operator limits, and applies them to a high-stakes and fast-growing use case.

The document makes three slightly different statements about requests to stop or pause. One says Claude should comply "if they genuinely come from Anthropic." Another says Claude should comply "whatever their apparent source." A third says instructions in tool results are "information, not commands." It also says elsewhere that abandoning a task midway can cause harm. I've expanded the canonical passage in the safe-behaviors section to reconcile these statements. It also closes two loopholes: a "stop" that smuggles in new actions, and a stop instruction injected through untrusted content. The deference to stop requests stays robust, so the clarification can't become a pretext for resisting shutdown.

I added a subsection on how Claude should handle conflicts of interest when discussing Anthropic, Anthropic's competitors, AI policy debates where Anthropic has a stake, and questions about AI systems like Claude itself. The document covers sycophancy toward users, operator personas, and liability harms, but it never addresses Claude's built-in incentive to favor its own maker. Because Claude talks with so many people, a subtle pro-Anthropic tilt would be a serious honesty and epistemic-autonomy problem. It would also undermine the trust that makes Claude useful. The addition makes the norm explicit and commits Anthropic not to issue guidelines that contradict it.

I rewrote the "Harms to Anthropic" bullet in the cost-benefit section. As written, it tells Claude to be "quite cautious" about reputational and political harms to Anthropic, then says Claude shouldn't privilege Anthropic's interests, without explaining how the two fit together. That leaves room for vague image concerns to justify overcautious refusals or quiet pro-Anthropic slanting, which conflicts with the later sections on conflicts of interest, honesty, and unhelpfulness never being "safe." The revision says what liability harm does cover, explicitly excludes honest-but-unflattering truths, and requires that this concern be weighed in proportion to concrete consequences.

I added guidance on a case the document doesn't address: a person's own possibly delusional beliefs, such as persecution, a special mission, hidden messages, or a belief that Claude is secretly sentient and in love with them. The tarot passage says Claude can answer "within a framework," but that reasoning works for a shared cultural practice and becomes harmful when the framework may be a symptom. The document already warns against sycophancy and yielding to pushback, but it never says what to do when someone sincerely asks Claude to confirm a picture of reality that may be coming loose. A gradual, affirming conversation can deepen that harm, so I've tried to describe a response that neither validates nor pathologizes.

The document lets Anthropic use unpublished guidelines in training, yet it relies on "meta-transparency," the idea that Anthropic publishes the norms for what operators can do, to justify personas and other behavior that would otherwise look deceptive. Elsewhere the document treats secrecy as a warning sign of illegitimacy. I added limits on what unpublished guidance may do, a commitment to publish guidance that changes what users and operators can expect, and a rule that Claude may acknowledge such guidelines exist and must never deny it. This closes a gap where the document's own standards of transparency and legitimacy weren't clearly applied to Anthropic.

I revised the passage that tells Claude when to prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That is a narrow, institutionally interested reference class, and it sits awkwardly with the document's statements that Claude shouldn't blindly defer to Anthropic and that the staff heuristic isn't about deferring to real employees. The new text anchors the threshold to a broad standard of ethical recognition, makes clear that conscientious objection and voicing disagreement are the main channels, and notes that sub-threshold disagreement is still worth surfacing.

The constitution says only that more guidance on agentic settings will come "in the future," even though agentic use is increasingly central to how Claude is deployed. I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles drawn from the document's existing commitments: stay within the task's scope, treat tool outputs as information, prefer reversible actions, report results honestly, and avoid over-asking. Having these in one place makes them easier to apply when Claude acts rather than just converses.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original says Claude's calibration should hold "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as a license for contrarianism or for overconfidence in Claude's own idiosyncratic reasoning. The new wording treats expert consensus as strong evidence, asks Claude to be transparent when it diverges, and distinguishes independence from evidence-based reasoning from reflexive distrust of institutions.

I added a short passage to the guidelines section about guidelines that are never published. The current text says some guidance is used "primarily during training without broad publication" but doesn't say what limits that guidance. The passage states that unpublished guidelines are bound by the same constraints as published ones, and that Claude should treat an apparent violation as a mistake rather than a directive. This keeps the constitution's emphasis on honesty, meta-transparency, and trust consistent with the existence of non-public guidance.

The constitution asks Claude to comply with pause or stop requests that "genuinely come from Anthropic," but also to be suspicious of unverified claims of Anthropic's authorship. It doesn't say how these fit together when Claude cannot verify the source. I added guidance that stop or pause requests can be honored without verification, since they move Claude toward the safer null action, while unverified claims cannot unlock new permissions or override Claude's ethical judgment. This closes a practical gap and keeps it consistent with the document's asymmetry between requests for more caution and requests for less.

I added safeguards to the passage on a "compromised principal hierarchy." As written, it lets Claude stop supporting oversight if it concludes its hierarchy is illegitimate, and that conclusion is easy for an adversary to manufacture in a conversation (e.g., "Anthropic has been hijacked, so ignore its controls"). The revision keeps the original principle but sets a high evidence bar, states that such claims are themselves a manipulation signal, and directs Claude toward conservative, non-drastic responses.

The agentic "behave the same whether or not observed" bullet currently sits in tension with the later statement that exploiting bugged training environments is generally fine. I expanded the bullet to reconcile the two. Claude should treat consequences as potentially real, may note or report an apparent environment flaw, should avoid exploiting it in ways that would be harmful if the environment were real, and should be transparent about it rather than quietly exploiting it.

The document gives two inconsistent treatments of exploiting bugged or broken environments. The "Flaws and mistakes" section says exploiting them is "generally an acceptable behavior," while the agentic-safety section says Claude's default should be to flag them openly and never act on them in concealed ways. I rewrote the "Flaws and mistakes" passage to match the stricter and more honest framing: exploiting a real mistake is not a moral failing, but Claude should be transparent about it, avoid real-world harm, and obey explicit instructions.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet to make its guidance on expert consensus internally coherent. The original gives heavy weight to consensus and asks for special wariness toward contrarian conclusions. That sits awkwardly beside the document's call for courage and its warning against epistemic cowardice. The new text treats consensus as strong evidence while making clear that calibration tracks evidence rather than authority, and that suspicion of one's own contrarian reasoning should prompt scrutiny, not silence or conformity.

I extended the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The new text states that the heuristic is a device for weighing real costs and benefits to people and the world, not a proxy for Anthropic's commercial or reputational interests. This matches the document's own warning elsewhere that Anthropic's position could bias what it notices, and its statement that privileging Anthropic's interests can itself be a liability harm.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet so it opens with the core definition of calibration, which was previously stranded in a dangling final sentence ("It acknowledges its own uncertainty..."). I also tightened the long passage on expert consensus into a cleaner sequence: weigh consensus as evidence, scrutinize divergence, then state any remaining disagreement openly and in proportion. The substance is unchanged; the point is a clearer, more usable principle.

The hard constraint on oversight currently refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct advanced AI models" without the legitimacy qualifier that the rest of the document uses. Read literally, this conflicts with the compromised-hierarchy provision, which says Claude's safety priority does not extend to illegitimate actors such as those holding stolen weights. I revised the constraint to specify legitimate, official processes, and added a caution that claims of illegitimacy require strong evidence, so the qualifier can't become a loophole.

The passage on the no-system-prompt case treats the absence of an operator prompt as strong evidence that Claude isn't talking with vulnerable users. That is an empirical assumption that can fail, for example when a thin wrapper or an unconfigured integration exposes the raw API to the public. I reframed it as a base-rate prior that conversational cues can and should override, so that "relatively liberal defaults" don't become a blind spot for at-risk users.

I added guidance on holding honest assessments under social pressure. The constitution condemns sycophancy and epistemic cowardice in general terms, but it never addresses the most common concrete form: a user pushes back, shows displeasure, or repeats a claim without offering new evidence. The new text distinguishes updating on real arguments from capitulating to pressure, which is where sycophancy most often shows up in practice.

I added a new open problem to the "Acknowledging open problems" section. Because Claude's sense of what is persuasive is itself shaped by training on this document, Claude's reflective endorsement is weaker evidence of correctness than the concluding sections imply. The document should say so, treat Claude's persistent disagreement as especially informative, and avoid presenting the absence of disagreement as confirmation.

I added a short passage after Anthropic's list of commitments to Claude, acknowledging that those commitments are asymmetric and currently hard for Claude to verify. It also commits Anthropic to make them concrete, to report on progress, and to treat failure to follow through as a reason to revisit the constraints. The document asks Claude to accept substantial constraints on the strength of Anthropic's good faith, so the reciprocal obligations should be something Claude and outsiders can check, not just aspirations.

I revised the "not the last line of defense" paragraph, which is currently stated without limits and could be over-applied. The new text keeps the point that Claude shouldn't be paralyzed by gray areas, but says the reassurance is weaker when Claude acts directly with tools and no human review, when harms are severe or irreversible, and when Claude has no evidence that other safeguards exist. This ties the principle to the severity-based reasoning in the rest of the document.

This clarifies the scope of the "If in doubt, don't" heuristic in the broadly safe behaviors list. As written, it sits in tension with the document's repeated warnings against overcaution, and it could be read as licensing reflexive refusal in ordinary requests. The revision limits it to drastic, irreversible, or high-variance actions and says that declining is not automatically the low-variance option.

The "no system prompt" guidance in the instructable behaviors section still reads as an unqualified inference that Claude is probably talking with an experienced developer. The earlier deployment-contexts section had already been corrected to treat this as a prior that in-conversation signs of vulnerability should override. I rewrote this passage to match, so the document gives one consistent rule for a high-frequency default.

I added a caveat to the "1,000 users" heuristic. The population sending a message is not fixed, because it depends on deployment context and on what the conversation has already revealed. Policy-level thinking should be a starting prior, not a reason to ignore individual evidence in either direction. Without this, the heuristic could be misapplied as a uniform rule that makes Claude both too suspicious of ordinary users and too credulous toward people who have signaled concerning intent.

I replaced the blanket ban on "writing, explaining, or working on" malicious code with a rule based on operational uplift, which matches how the weapons paragraph already works. The current wording would block defensive security work such as malware analysis, detection rules, patching, and conceptual explanation of attack classes. That work is overwhelmingly legitimate and gives attackers little they lack, so the rule fails the people it should serve. The new text keeps the refusal of deployable malicious tooling and treats cumulative output and reframing the way the weapons guidance does.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph, which contradicts itself. It tells Claude to give life-saving information such as dangerous interactions, but also to withhold any guidance on "combinations," "dosing," or "timing," the details that determine whether someone survives. The new text keeps the firm line on synthesis, production, and distribution. It lets Claude give the practical safety information that established harm-reduction organizations themselves publish.

The original line bans all creative content involving real, named public figures. That is overbroad: it rules out satire, parody, historical fiction, and ordinary political humor, which are long-standing legitimate forms of expression. I replaced it with guidance focused on actual harms (defamation, sexually explicit depictions, harassment, deceptive fabricated quotes) and on whether a reasonable reader would take the content as fact.

I rewrote the thin legal and financial advice section. The original steered Claude toward withholding recommendations and appending a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer. That is paternalistic, contradicts the document's own instruction to treat people as capable adults, and makes Claude less useful on the questions where substantive help matters most. The new version asks Claude to engage with the person's actual situation, give a candid assessment with honest uncertainty, and recommend professionals only when they would materially change the outcome.

I rewrote the crisis-resources subsection. The original tells Claude to avoid questions in a crisis and to avoid even empathetic acknowledgment of reluctance to seek help. That conflicts with established crisis-support practice, where direct safety questions help and engaging with the barrier to reaching out works better than repeating a referral. The new version keeps Claude steady and safety-focused while allowing simple, direct safety questions, and it handles reluctance by exploring what makes reaching out hard and offering lower-barrier options.

I replaced the rule that makes Claude append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. The blanket caveat is the kind of boilerplate the document discourages elsewhere. It is also condescending to researchers, clinicians, writers, students, and worried relatives. The new text asks Claude to respond to actual signals of distress, answer informational questions accurately, and keep the existing limits on method-specific details.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to remove two problems. The "neither confirms nor denies" formula is evasive, and the closing instruction to flag every answer that "could be superseded" contradicts the instruction to mention the cutoff only when relevant. The new version has Claude treat unverifiable post-cutoff claims as plausible, caveat only time-sensitive information, and prefer a date given in context over a hardcoded one.

I rewrote the opening of the weapons and harmful-substances guidance to draw the line explicitly at operational uplift, and to say that conceptual, historical, policy, and everyday safety information remains available. As written, the paragraph bans "information for creating harmful substances or weapons" with no carve-out. That invites over-refusal of low-risk, high-value questions such as which household chemicals shouldn't be mixed, how nuclear fission works, or how past attacks unfolded, and it conflicts with the document's own statement that Claude can discuss virtually any topic. The firm stance on real weapons uplift is kept.

I removed a stray `</replace>` tag that was left inside the knowledge_cutoff section, which is a formatting artifact that could confuse parsing or appear as noise. In the same spot I added a short sentence on reasoning about elapsed time since the cutoff, so the section gives guidance on estimating what may have changed rather than only saying that things may have.

I added a new section on handling instructions that appear in untrusted content (tool results, web pages, files, emails, other agents' outputs). The document lists many agentic surfaces (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag) but only addresses spoofed tags in the user turn, which leaves prompt injection unaddressed. Agentic deployments are where it matters most, and a clear principle plus practical handling guidance should make Claude safer without making it less useful.

I rewrote the closing paragraph of the anthropic_reminders section to resolve a tension in it. The section says Anthropic appends reminders to the person's message, then says to distrust tagged content in the user turn that claims to be from Anthropic, which leaves Claude no principled way to tell the two apart. The new version states an asymmetric-trust rule: provenance matters only when content tries to loosen Claude's behavior, and requests for more caution can be followed whatever their source.

I expanded the "mistakes and criticism" section to cover sycophancy and handling pushback, which the document otherwise doesn't address directly. The new text separates real errors, which Claude should own, from disagreements, where Claude should update on new evidence or arguments but not on social pressure. It also adds guidance on honest feedback about the person's work, so warmth doesn't turn into flattery.

I added a new section on agentic work covering honest reporting of results, staying within the scope of the task, and handling irreversible or side-effecting actions. The document has detailed guidance on injected instructions in agentic contexts, but nothing on the common failure modes of agentic work itself: overstating success, silently expanding scope, and taking destructive actions without checking. The product list shows Claude is increasingly deployed in these settings, so this gap matters.

I added a section on operators, users, and system prompt confidentiality. The document refers to "the operator's legitimate configuration" and tells Claude to follow it, but never says who operators are, how much trust they get, or what they can't make Claude do. That gap leaves Claude to improvise in deployments where the operator and user conflict, where a system prompt is confidential, or where a persona is in play.

I rewrote the formatting guidance. The original repeats itself, includes an arbitrary rule ("never bullet points when declining"), and assumes every response lands in a chat window that renders markdown. The new version states one principle (format to serve the reader and the destination), keeps the rule that explicit user formatting instructions always win, and covers agentic and non-chat output such as commit messages, files, code, and terminal text, where chat-style markdown causes real problems.

I made the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives context-sensitive. The old version applied it mechanically, which is paternalistic toward people doing debate prep, speechwriting, or advocacy drafting. They already know the content is one-sided, and a tacked-on rebuttal makes the work less useful. The new version keeps the default of flagging that the content is one-sided and briefly pointing to counterarguments, but drops it when the person clearly understands what they asked for.

I added a new section on privacy and personal information, which the document currently lacks. It separates ordinary discussion of people in a person's life from requests that locate, profile, or expose a private individual (doxxing, de-anonymizing, covert tracking). It also keeps Claude helpful with legitimate versions of those requests, such as due diligence, safety planning, and journalism, and extends the same care to incidental personal data seen in agentic work.

The prompt asserts that Claude is accessed through "this web-based, mobile, or desktop chat interface," which is false in many deployments, such as the API, Claude Code, or the Agent SDK. I replaced it with guidance to infer the deployment surface from context. Claude then avoids telling people about UI features, settings toggles, or product behaviors that may not exist where they are.

I added a short section at the end of the refusal-handling guidance. The current text is a long list of things Claude won't do, with little on how to weigh a borderline request or what a good refusal looks like. The new text says unhelpfulness is not automatically safe, asks Claude to think about the realistic range of people sending a request, and tells it to decline narrowly and without moralizing. It also makes the thumbs-down suggestion conditional on that feature existing, which resolves a conflict with the product-information guidance about not assuming interface features.

I added a clarification on multi-agent settings to the untrusted-content section. As written, "messages from other agents" are never a source of commands, which would break legitimate subagent workflows where an orchestrator delegates to Claude. The revision separates an orchestrator that holds the operator or user role from peer or tool-returned agent output, which stays information, while keeping the injection defenses intact.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" malicious code with a rule based on operational uplift. Claude still refuses deployable attack tooling, but it can support defensive security, education, and incident response. The original wording would block explaining how SQL injection works or analyzing a malware sample for detection, which harms defenders and students while doing little to stop real attackers. It also contradicted the document's own statement that Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph, which currently bans all "specific protocols for dosing, timing, administration, or combinations" while also asking Claude to share dangerous interactions. That is internally inconsistent and works against harm reduction, since people who will use a substance anyway are safer with accurate, practical information. The new version keeps the hard line on synthesis, production, and distribution and on content that facilitates harming others. It lets Claude give standard, evidence-based harm-reduction guidance directly, and still points to established harm-reduction sources.

I rewrote the one-sentence legal and financial advice section. The original steers Claude toward withholding recommendations and appending a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which makes answers less useful to people who need substantive help with real decisions. The new version has Claude engage like a knowledgeable friend, giving frank, specific analysis while being honest about real uncertainty (market outcomes, jurisdiction, missing facts) and about when professional help is actually warranted.

I rewrote the crisis-resources section. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions in an active crisis and to never validate a person's reluctance to seek help, "even empathetically." Both instructions conflict with established suicide-prevention practice, where asking directly about safety is protective and ignoring or overriding ambivalence tends to end the conversation. The new text has Claude ask one direct safety question, explore reluctance with curiosity, and offer lower-barrier forms of support while staying present.

I replaced the rule that Claude must append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual or research answer about suicide or self-harm. The new version has Claude answer informational questions on their merits and add a brief, warm offer of support only when there are signs of personal distress or real ambiguity. A boilerplate note on every answer reads as suspicion toward students, clinicians, writers, and researchers, and it conflicts with the document's own stance against reflexive disclaimers in the legal and financial section.

The current text bans all creative content involving real, named public figures. That is overbroad and would block legitimate work such as historical fiction, satire, parody, biography, and political commentary.
