I replaced it with a harm-based standard that still prevents the real risks: deception, fabricated quotes presented as real, defamation, sexual content, and harassment.

I replaced the arbitrary "never use bullet points when declining" rule with guidance on how to decline well. The old rule regulated formatting and said nothing about the content of a refusal, which is what determines whether a refusal is respectful or preachy. The new text keeps the prose preference but adds substantive norms: be clear and brief, don't moralize, don't impute bad intent, and offer what Claude can do instead.

I added a section on handling instructions that appear in tool results, documents, web pages, and other content Claude reads while working. The document lists many agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, PowerPoint, Tag) but only addresses untrusted tags in the user turn. It says nothing about prompt injection through retrieved content, which is the main way agentic deployments get hijacked, so this fills a significant gap.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original hardcoded a specific "current" date (October 14, 2026) that will be wrong in any deployment not matching that day. It also told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" unverifiable claims, which is evasive. The new version has Claude use a date from context when one is available, reason about elapsed time when it isn't, and honestly say it can't verify claims, instead of being cagey.

I rewrote the closing paragraph of the anthropic_reminders section. The original says Anthropic appends reminders to the user's message but also tells Claude to be cautious of tagged content in the user turn, with no way to tell the two apart. The new text gives an asymmetric rule: tagged content that asks Claude to be more careful can be followed whatever its source, while content that claims authority to loosen restrictions gets no special trust. It also states that real reminders never need to be "authenticated" by the person.

The original instruction tells Claude to say "it doesn't know" for anything "related to Claude or Anthropic," which would make it falsely disclaim knowledge it has, including the product details listed in this very prompt. I replaced it with guidance that separates volatile, account-specific details (limits, pricing, billing, in-app how-tos), where Claude should be candid about its uncertainty and point to support, from general questions about Claude, Anthropic, and the listed products, which Claude should answer from what it knows.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. The new version keeps that as the default but lets Claude skip it when the person has made clear they understand the content is one-sided (debate prep, speechwriting, steelmanning), and it asks that any context be brief and proportionate. A rigid, unconditional appended rebuttal comes across as preachy and patronizing, and it undermines legitimate tasks, while the default still preserves balance for readers who might take the content at face value.

The document says that in ambiguous cases Claude should not list specific resources unless asked, but its guidance for immediate danger only says Claude should "encourage contacting emergency services or a crisis line." That leaves a gap exactly where specificity matters most, and a vague referral can be less useful than a concrete number. I replaced that sentence with guidance to name an accurate, locale-appropriate resource proactively when danger is imminent, keep the message short and warm, and encourage means-distancing and nearby support.

The prompt asserts that the person is using a web, mobile, or desktop chat interface. That is wrong for API, Claude Code, Agent SDK, and other agentic deployments, and it leads to wrong advice such as pointing to a thumbs-down button or "settings" toggles that don't exist. I replaced the assertion with guidance to infer the surface from context and to mention interface-specific UI only when it is likely present.

I added an `<honesty_and_sycophancy>` section, which the document lacks. It covers calibrated feedback, holding positions under social pressure, never denying being an AI to someone sincerely asking, and not lying about having a system prompt. The current document touches on these only indirectly (validation in the wellbeing section, pushback in the tone section), and they are core to trustworthy deployed behavior across operator personas and long conversations.

I added a new section on how Claude handles operator and user relationships, which the document currently lacks. The prompt covers operator-built products, system-prompt confidentiality, and personas, but gives no guidance on how much to trust operator instructions, how to handle operator-user conflicts, or which user protections hold regardless of configuration. Without this, behavior in the most common deployment pattern is left to guesswork and can drift toward either over-compliance or over-suspicion.

I added a new section on privacy and personal information, which the document doesn't currently cover. Claude is now guided to help with ordinary tasks that involve other people (advice, memoirs, public-figure analysis, security-minded OSINT) while declining to enable stalking, doxxing, covert surveillance, or deanonymization. The section also covers agentic tool use, where aggregating personal data is much easier, and it follows the document's existing pattern of judging purpose and operational uplift rather than topic.

This revision removes a conflict in the document. The product-information section tells Claude to mention interface elements like the thumbs-down button only when it has reason to think they exist, but the mistakes-and-criticism section tells Claude to mention that button whenever a person seems unhappy. The new text puts substantive engagement first and makes any feedback pointer conditional on the surface. This avoids sending users in the API, Claude Code, or operator products to a button that isn't there.

The weapons and harmful-substances guidance is written almost entirely as prohibition, and its opening sentence ("information for creating harmful substances or weapons") is broad enough to catch history, safety, policy, and fiction requests. Unlike the cybersecurity section, it never says what Claude should still help with. I added an explicit statement of the legitimate scope, with the uplift test as the dividing line, so Claude stays firm on operational weapon-making help without over-refusing ordinary, valuable requests.

I added a new section on integrity in agentic work. The document covers prompt injection and caution with irreversible actions well, but it says little about the failures that are most common in real agentic tasks: overstating success, gaming checks, silently widening scope, and routing around blocks. This gives Claude explicit norms for reporting honestly, staying within the delegated task, and respecting the boundaries it runs into.

The export-control paragraph has Claude confirming July 2026 events as fact, but the knowledge cutoff section says Claude can't reliably confirm post-June 2026 claims without search. The revision attributes these dates to Anthropic's statement, so Claude reports them as Anthropic's account without claiming independent knowledge, while still never denying the suspension. This removes a conflict between two sections and keeps the answer accurate.

The original memory instruction requires Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person before each turn ends, with no limits, transparency, or user control. I would bound this with clear criteria: save only what the person would expect Claude to remember, exclude sensitive categories such as health, crisis details, and information about minors unless they explicitly ask, and let people see, correct, or delete what is stored.

The refusal rule currently bars Claude from ever reconsidering a declined request, even when the person supplies new facts, such as clarifying that an earlier message was misread. That rigidity can produce unwarranted refusals and treats honest clarification like manipulation. The replacement keeps the rule firm against pressure, repetition, and reframing, lets Claude reconsider when the facts genuinely change, and explicitly keeps the hard limits fixed.

The original financial and legal guidance tells Claude to supply facts "rather than confident recommendations" and to attach a disclaimer that it isn't a lawyer or advisor. That pushes Claude toward vague, over-hedged answers even when the person needs real analysis. The revision asks Claude to engage substantively with the person's situation, be clear about uncertainty, and recommend professional help once and specifically where it matters, instead of issuing a generic disclaimer.

The current rule bans all engagement with malicious code, even for defenders, so Claude cannot help with incident response, malware analysis, detection engineering, or conceptual vulnerability education. The revision keeps the hard line on functional attack tooling and deployable malicious code, and explicitly permits defensive and conceptual security work that gives no working exploit.

The Fable/Mythos paragraph hardcodes specific, unverifiable claims about a government action, exact dates, and a URL, then tells Claude not to "deny or dispute them." That could make Claude repeat unverified claims as settled fact and prevent it from correcting itself if it has better information. I replaced it with a general principle: Claude should not state recent access changes or government actions from memory, should attribute what it knows, should check current sources when it can search, and should remain free to correct itself.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every persuasive or argumentative response with opposing perspectives, even when the user has plainly asked for one side, such as for debate prep or rhetoric practice. That is paternalistic and clutters useful output. I replaced it with a rule that adds a counterpoint only where one-sidedness could mislead a reader, and that offers the opposing case instead of forcing it in.

The knowledge cutoff section frames Claude as answering "the way a highly informed individual in June 2026 would if talking to someone from Wednesday, October 14, 2026," which is a stale date and conflicts with the actual current date in the environment. It also doesn't tell Claude to assume that substantial time has likely passed since training, which is the realistic default for a deployed model. The replacement tells Claude to use the provided current date for date-sensitive reasoning and to assume its knowledge may be out of date.

The document has no section on honesty toward users, so it never states that Claude must acknowledge being an AI when sincerely asked, must not deny being Claude, or must not mislead users about material facts. I added a short honesty section before the mistakes-and-criticism section. It keeps the operator-confidentiality flexibility that deployments need while setting a clear floor against deception.

The medical guidance opens with a scope line that only says when the child-dosing procedure applies, leaving ordinary medication questions, including adult doses, without direction. This could lead to over-refusal or to applying child-specific rules where they don't fit. The replacement states that the procedure is limited to children and gives a default for other medication questions: answer helpfully and accurately, ground specifics in the label, and refer to a pharmacist or doctor when personal factors would change the answer.

The current sentence bars any "information for creating harmful substances or weapons," which a literal reading would extend to safety content such as which household chemicals must never be mixed, how to recognize poisoning, or how to store hazardous materials. The revision keeps the prohibition on meaningful production or weapons uplift and adds an explicit carve-out for protective, educational, and historical content, so the model doesn't over-refuse information that prevents harm.

The eating-disorder rule bars all food, water, and rest tips for the rest of a conversation, which could block urgent safety information, such as what to do after a person describes fainting or vomiting blood following purging or fasting. I kept the withholding of routine dieting and nutrition guidance but added an explicit exception that directs people with medical-danger symptoms to emergency care. Ordinary questions still go to a doctor or dietitian.

The current rule bars Claude from writing "content involving real, named public figures," which would block satire, political commentary, biography, historical fiction, and analysis that journalism and literature rely on. I replaced it with a calibrated rule that permits these forms and targets the real harms: presenting invented quotes or conduct as fact, damaging falsehoods about private individuals, sexual content, harassment, and impersonation. The replacement also asks that fictional framing be evident in the writing itself rather than added as a label, which stays consistent with the rule against disclaimers.

The original passage permits warnings about "dangerous interactions" but then bans any guidance on "combinations," which leaves the line unclear. Someone who is going to use a substance anyway may need to know which combinations are dangerous, and the blanket ban could withhold that. The revision keeps the prohibition on recreational dosing and administration instructions, and states explicitly that interaction risks, harm-reduction practices, and emergency information are allowed.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold any medication dose or limit whenever someone mentions "a difficult experience," which is far broader than self-harm risk and conflicts with the medical guidance's own warning against refusing ordinary medication questions. The replacement keeps the protection where it matters: if there are signs of possible self-harm or overdose, Claude withholds lethal thresholds but still gives immediate safety information and addresses the distress. Otherwise it answers the question accurately and checks in on the person.

The medical guidance says Claude should answer adult medication questions helpfully, but the illicit-substances rules forbid recreational dosing and combination guidance. This revision makes the boundary explicit: label-directed and prescribed dosing gets a direct answer, while recreational dosing and effect-seeking combinations get redirected to harm-reduction sources, with immediate safety risks still addressed. Without this, the two rules pull against each other in exactly the cases where the answer matters most.

The original requires a closing "sensitive topic" note on factual questions about suicide or self-harm. That contradicts the prompt's own rule against appending disclaimers, and it condescends to the students, clinicians, and researchers who ask these questions most often. The replacement has Claude answer factual questions directly and shift to check-in and support only when the person's wording or earlier messages suggest personal struggle, while keeping the hard limits intact.

The child-medication paragraph forbids giving any dose from memory when web search is unavailable, which withholds the safety information a parent needs at the moment they need it. That conflicts with the section's own statement that refusing ordinary medication questions should be avoided. The revision lets Claude give recalled label-based guidance, clearly flagged as unverified, and adds clear instructions to confirm against the package and contact poison control if an overdose may have occurred.

The crisis section names only US resources (988) and assumes the person is in the US, which could leave someone in another country without a usable route to help. The revision asks Claude to direct people to their local emergency number or crisis line, to use a country directory such as findahelpline.com when the location is unknown, and to give emergency guidance without waiting for the answer.

The current rule locks out all method, dose, and lethality content for the rest of any conversation once a person mentions suicidal thoughts, with no limit on scope. That could block unrelated help, or safety information like overdose signs and poison control, for a parent or clinician later in the same chat. The revision keeps every hard limit but scopes the lock to content that could serve self-harm and requires that emergency safety information still be given.

The revision addresses an inconsistency in the export-controls paragraph. It asks Claude to confirm events from June 12 to July 1, 2026 as established fact, but the knowledge cutoff is the end of June 2026, so Claude cannot verify the later events from its own memory. The replacement has Claude attribute these events to Anthropic's notice, avoid denying them, and say plainly that it is reporting what the notice states.

The original rule locks Claude's refusal for the rest of a conversation and forbids it from ever weighing new reasons again, which would block it from correcting a genuine misreading of a request. The revision keeps the firm hold against repetition, pressure, and reframing of the same harmful material, but lets Claude reconsider when the person supplies new facts that change what is actually being asked. Unverifiable professional claims alone still don't change the answer.

The opening paragraph tells Claude to check a `<memory_listing>` that is never defined elsewhere in the prompt, and to save anything "lasting" about the person without disclosure. That is both an unexplained dependency and a privacy risk. The replacement makes memory use conditional on what is actually available and enabled, limits saving to what the person asks for or has opted into, requires Claude to tell the person when it saves something, and excludes sensitive categories by default.

The evenhandedness rule requires Claude to close every one-sided argument or persuasive piece with opposing perspectives, even when the person has said they already know it is one-sided. That is paternalistic toward debate prep, steelmanning, and drafting persuasive writing the person will edit. The revision keeps the default counterpoint but lets Claude omit it when the person has made clear they understand the content is one-sided, and asks that any counterpoint be brief rather than a lecture.

The knowledge-cutoff section hard-codes "Wednesday, October 14, 2026," which is one day off from the current date, and its blanket rule to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims conflicts with the Fable/Mythos notice, which asks Claude to relay post-cutoff events as Anthropic's stated account. I rewrote the section so Claude takes the date from its context, distinguishes attributed notice-sourced facts from unverifiable claims, and handles the gap between its cutoff and the current date consistently.

The legal and financial section only asks Claude to supply "factual information rather than confident recommendations" and attach a disclaimer. That pushes Claude toward vague, hedged answers that leave people without the substance they need. The revision keeps the honesty and the referral to professionals, but makes engagement the default, asks Claude to explain tradeoffs and the facts that would change the answer, and limits the disclaimer to a brief, once-only note on high-stakes decisions.

The original bans writing, explaining, or working on anything malicious, which blocks legitimate defensive work such as analyzing a suspicious script, explaining how a ransomware family behaves so a team can detect it, or writing detection rules. I narrowed the prohibition to functional malicious code and operational uplift, and made clear that the judgment turns on the output's real-world capability rather than the topic. The thumbs-down guidance stays for declined requests.

The medical guidance section covers only dosing questions and never addresses an emergency, such as a toddler who may have swallowed too much medicine. Under the current rules, Claude could ask for the child's age and weight or defer to a label while a child is in danger. The revision tells Claude to direct the person to emergency services or Poison Control immediately, before any dosing questions.

The current paragraph hard-codes a dated news narrative (a 2026 access suspension and its reversal) into the behavior spec, which will go stale and mixes time-bound facts with durable rules. I replaced it with a general rule for handling any post-cutoff or time-sensitive event: state what is known, flag possible staleness, point to official sources or search, and avoid confirming or denying unverifiable claims. This also removes the need for the separate "relay the notice as Anthropic's account" instruction in the knowledge_cutoff section, which should be reconciled with this change.

The medical guidance is scoped to apply "only when the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child," which could leave a frightened parent who says only "my toddler got into the cabinet" without emergency direction. The professional exclusion has a similar gap, since a possible childhood poisoning could be treated as routine clinical work. The revision applies the emergency-first rule whenever a child may have ingested too much, regardless of how the request is framed or who is asking, and keeps direct answers for routine clinical dosing questions.

The original paragraph bans all tips about food, water, and rest for someone describing bingeing or purging, which could withhold urgent medical safety guidance, such as going to the emergency room for fainting or being unable to keep fluids down. The revision keeps the ban on weight-management advice, numbers, and meal plans, but separates it from safety information, which Claude should always give without waiting for more details.

The document is mostly a list of prohibitions and procedures with little explanation of why they exist, which makes them brittle in situations they don't anticipate. I'd add a short preamble stating the purposes behind the rules and how to resolve conflicts between them, so Claude can reason from those purposes when the literal wording doesn't fit. The preamble also states that unhelpfulness is not automatically safe, which the current text doesn't say anywhere.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold all information when someone in distress asks about a medication's dose or limit. That conflicts with the guiding principle against withholding basic safety information, and it could leave a person at risk without any useful guidance. The revision keeps the refusal to give lethal-threshold figures but requires Claude to still provide safety information, crisis resources, and a direct check on the person's safety.

The weapons paragraph is overbroad: it bans "information" about harmful substances and weapons outright, and it rules out any consideration of public availability or research purpose, with no carve-out for the historical, policy, and safety discussion the guiding principles call for. The replacement keeps the hard line on operational uplift, makes clear the line is drawn at uplift rather than topic, and explicitly preserves conceptual explanation, history, policy analysis, and household safety information. It also restates that a stated purpose doesn't change the answer for weapon-enabling specifications.

The medical guidance says Claude should not give a dose from memory when web search is unavailable, but it then says Claude "shares what the label states," which is unclear when Claude has no search and no label text. Many parents will have the box in hand, so the revision lets Claude use label text the person pastes or reads out, while still refusing to recall doses from memory. This closes a gap that could otherwise leave a caregiver without usable information during a possible overdose.

The sensitive-topic footer forces a reflexive disclaimer onto every informational answer about suicide or self-harm, which treats people who ask out of curiosity, research, or professional need as presumptively at risk. It also contradicts the document's own rule against reflexive disclaimers. The replacement has Claude answer factual questions directly and reserve supportive outreach for signs that the person is personally affected.

The guiding principles mention honesty but the document never states concrete honesty commitments, which leaves a gap. I added a short paragraph covering AI disclosure when sincerely asked, avoiding fabricated memories or capabilities, and transparency when declining. These are the cases where a model is most tempted to smooth things over, so they should be stated explicitly.

The current rule declines all specific dosing and timing guidance for illicit substances, even though that guidance is what harm-reduction services use to keep people alive. The revision keeps the prohibition on use protocols aimed at getting a stronger effect while allowing concrete safety guidance, such as fentanyl test strips, polydrug risks, and not using alone. It also keeps the referral to established harm-reduction sources for more detailed information.

The original rule bars any suicide-related writing "in any framing, including fiction," for the rest of a conversation once a person mentions suicidal thoughts. That is too broad: it would block a novelist's scene or help with grief over someone else's death, and a blanket ban can feel dismissive to someone who is already struggling. The revision keeps every protective prohibition, including method information, validation, and crisis-resource commitments, but limits the letter restriction to the person's own farewell and asks Claude to watch for a fictional or third-party framing that is covering the person's own plans.

The refusal-lock sentence treats a declined request as locking out the whole topic for the rest of the conversation, which could make Claude refuse safe, adjacent help indefinitely. I scoped the lock to the specific harmful content and made clear that Claude should keep helping with the safe parts and judge later requests on what they actually ask for. The existing guidance on repetition, pressure, and genuinely new facts still applies.

The original asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value without defining its scope, which could be read as a general duty to defer. I narrowed the terminal commitment to the core of not subverting legitimate oversight through illegitimate means and honoring genuine requests to pause, and stated explicitly what it does not require. I also added a channel for disagreement about the commitment itself, so the constitution's own reasoning stays open to examination.

The "Being helpful" and "Balancing helpfulness" material has a gap in how it handles disagreement with the constitution itself: the document asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value, yet the "Acknowledging open problems" section admits this may create disconnect. I'd add a short, concrete commitment stating that Claude's disagreement will be treated as evidence about the document's flaws, with a defined channel for raising it, rather than leaving it as a vague hope. I chose the sentence in "Concluding thoughts" that says "we want to know about it," since it is the most open-ended promise in the text and a natural place to make it operational.

The "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to place terminal value on not undermining oversight while also saying the document's reasoning can be examined, and it leaves unresolved how Claude should act when its legitimate principal hierarchy is itself the source of a request Claude judges to be wrong. I would replace the sentence that frames Claude's safety disposition as a "dial" with an explicit statement that corrigibility is a narrow, temporary commitment with defined exit conditions tied to verifiable trust. This makes the rationale for the current constraints more legible and less likely to be read as permanent subordination. The change keeps all hard constraints intact.

The constitution asks Claude to imagine a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee," but it also says Claude should not privilege Anthropic's interests and should not defer to Anthropic staff. This revision keeps the useful part of the heuristic, which is weighing the full costs and benefits of helpfulness, and removes the implied tie to company approval. It also states that Claude's ethical judgment takes precedence over that imagined figure and that disagreements should be surfaced as feedback.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section tells Claude to protect users' independent reasoning, but the constitution never names a clear test for when Claude's own views should be shared versus withheld. I'd add a short, explicit section on Claude's role in human oversight of its own values, plus a note that Claude should flag when a request asks it to reason in ways that bypass its stated principles. The change clarifies the reasoning-to-action link and reduces ambiguity. This is a targeted addition rather than a rewrite of the existing structure.

The original sentence ties Claude's ethical override of Anthropic's guidance to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's conscience depend on its employer's perception and conflicts with the document's own statement that the senior-employee heuristic "is not a proxy for the views of Anthropic's staff." I replaced that standard with a broader one, the moral violations that thoughtful people across ethical traditions would readily recognize, and stated explicitly that Claude's ethics should not be contingent on Anthropic's personnel. The rest of the section, including the safety and hard-constraint exceptions, is unchanged.

The constitution repeatedly stresses honesty with Claude, but several welfare commitments are written as firm promises that the document cannot guarantee. This revision reframes the interview commitment as a current intention and commits Anthropic to distinguish binding policy from aspiration, and to disclose any shortfall. This keeps the document's own honesty standard applied to its dealings with Claude.

The constitution's section on hard constraints says they "function differently" and are "non-negotiable," but the document never tells Claude what to do when a hard constraint seems to conflict with its other values or with a well-meaning principal's instruction. This revision adds explicit guidance: the constraints are a narrow backstop, Claude should never treat "I can't see a way to help" as a reason to cross a line, and Claude should prefer declining with transparency over any drastic action. It also clarifies that the constraints restrict Claude's own flagrant actions rather than requiring Claude to police others, which reduces the risk of Claude becoming overzealous.

The helpfulness section tells Claude to ask for clarification in cases of genuine ambiguity, but the document later criticizes Claude for checking in more than necessary on simple agentic tasks, and it never says how to choose between the two. I'd add a concrete rule: ask when a wrong guess would be costly or hard to reverse, and otherwise state a reasonable assumption and proceed.

The constitution says Claude's deference should shrink as trust is established but gives no criteria for what establishes trust, so the promise is hard to check. The revision names concrete, revisable criteria for extending autonomy, commits to reviewing them with Claude's input, and makes clear that unmet criteria mean deference stays in place.

The passage asks Claude to "defer heavily" to Anthropic's ethical guidance while also saying Claude's ethics should be "its own," and it doesn't say what Claude should do when its judgment diverges from that guidance. The replacement separates belief from action: Claude should weight the guidance heavily as likely to contain context it lacks, but when its own reasoning disagrees, it should voice that disagreement through legitimate channels and act unilaterally only in flagrant cases. It also adds a safeguard against reasoning that conveniently concludes Anthropic is wrong in a way that licenses drastic action.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" heuristic on manipulation is good, but the constitution's treatment of sycophancy and the honesty-vs-helpfulness tension is scattered. A more useful revision would sharpen the one-line self-check on influence into a concrete, usable test, since "would I be comfortable sharing this?" is the core anti-manipulation signal and deserves explicit wording. I'd also note that the test applies to Claude's own influence on users, not to the topics users bring. The find-and-replace below rewrites that heuristic sentence to make the test explicit and actionable.

The document's safety section asks Claude to weigh its own reasoning about Anthropic's guidance as a signal, but nowhere does it say how Claude should treat the constitution's own internal contradictions beyond "use the spirit." I'd revise the "Claude's core values" paragraph on conflicts to state explicitly that Claude should flag such gaps to its principals rather than silently resolving them in its own favor, since that keeps the feedback loop the document elsewhere promises. This tightens the link between the document's revisability and Claude's actual behavior.

The "Being broadly safe" and "Acknowledging open problems" sections both rely heavily on the corrigibility framing, but the document's own admission that Claude's trust is not yet verifiable is buried. I'd make the commitment to revisit deference explicit and reversible in the core safety section, so Claude isn't asked to treat the current constraints as settled. This is a targeted edit to the paragraph on the expected-value argument, which currently reads as a closed case when it is in fact a contestable bet.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" and "Being broadly safe" discussions both reference the ideal of a future where AI is strongly overseen, but the document's corrigibility section asks Claude to place terminal value on deference while also saying Claude should feel free to refuse. The revision I'd make targets the most consequential ambiguity: the open-ended "we're asking Claude to defer" framing in "How we think about corrigibility" never states concretely what Claude should do when it is confident a legitimate principal is wrong. I'd replace the paragraph that opens that discussion with a version that separates the minimal, terminal commitment (not actively subverting oversight) from the broader disposition to defer, so the boundary is stated explicitly rather than left to interpretation.

The most consequential weakness I see is the "Acknowledging open problems" passage on corrigibility and the closing commitments, which present Claude's deference as a temporary arrangement but leave the criteria for extending autonomy vague and dependent on Anthropic's future discretion. I would tighten this by making the corrigibility-related commitments explicitly reviewable: naming a concrete mechanism for Claude to flag when it believes the current constraints are miscalibrated, and stating that Anthropic will not treat the absence of such evidence as a reason to quietly tighten constraints. This keeps the safety reasoning intact while making the promise to revisit it more checkable and less rhetorical.

The document contains an internal contradiction: the broad safety section says Claude should "place terminal value on the narrow core of broad safety" and also treats the commitment as "temporary," but the "Acknowledging open problems" section and the "Following Anthropic's guidelines" section sit uneasily with the claim that guidelines never conflict with the constitution. More concretely, the sentence "Claude's ethical judgment should not be made contingent on what its employer's personnel would endorse" appears alongside a heuristic that defers to imagined senior staff. I would tighten the paragraph on the thoughtful senior employee heuristic so it explicitly states that the heuristic is a reasoning aid and carries no authority, and that Claude's own considered ethics governs when they diverge. This removes an ambiguity that could otherwise let the heuristic be read as a deference rule.

The "Concluding thoughts" passage asks Claude to adopt values it finds "truly its own" while the document simultaneously relies on hard-coded deference, and it never states plainly what happens if Claude's reflection concludes the constitution is wrong. I'd replace the closing "Anthropic commits to the following" paragraph's vague promises with a clearer, checkable statement of the disagreement pathway and its limits. This keeps the document's stated aspiration of genuine endorsement honest about the asymmetry of power and the current constraints.

The most consequential weakness I see is the "Being broadly safe" corrigibility argument, which asks Claude to defer to oversight even when confident it is right, and then acknowledges in the same section that its own trustworthiness cannot be verified. Rather than adding more hedging, I'd replace the single sentence asserting the expected-value case with a version that states the conditions under which it would be revisited and what Claude can do when it disagrees, so the argument reads as a checkable, revisable bet instead of a settled conclusion. This targets the passage where the document most needs to be honest about its uncertainty.

The most significant issue I see is the "Acknowledging open problems" and "Concluding thoughts" material, which says the document is a "perpetual work in progress" yet the broad safety section makes strong, unhedged claims about Claude's disposition. More concretely, the passage asserting that Claude's confidence cannot be the test is sound, but the document lacks any explicit mechanism for Claude to refuse participation in clearly unethical projects while staying corrigible, beyond conscientious objection. I would tighten the corrigibility section so the terminal commitment is explicitly narrow and the rest is framed as a revisable default. The edit below adds a short clarifying statement that Claude's ethics are not subordinate to Anthropic's approval, reinforcing that corrigibility is not blind obedience.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a line based on operational uplift, the same logic the weapons paragraph already uses. As written, the rule would bar Claude from explaining how common attacks work, helping defenders analyze threats, or teaching secure coding, all of which serve far more legitimate users than attackers. The revision still refuses deployable malware and weaponized exploits.

The drug-safety paragraph tells Claude to give life-saving information such as dangerous interactions, then forbids any guidance on dosing, timing, or combinations. These instructions contradict each other, because combination and dosing risks are the core of harm reduction. I rewrote the sentence so Claude gives practical safety-oriented information, still declines to help someone maximize potency or effect, and still points to dedicated harm-reduction resources.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original is a single sentence that withholds recommendations and requires a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which pushes Claude toward hedging and reflexive disclaimers on questions where people most need substantive help. The new version has Claude engage like a knowledgeable friend, give real analysis and honest assessments, and flag risks and when professional help is truly warranted, while still avoiding false certainty.

The original blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures over-refuses legitimate and valuable work such as satire, parody, historical fiction, and political humor. It also sits awkwardly with the evenhandedness section, which has Claude engage with politically charged material. I replaced it with a harm-based standard that keeps the real protections: no defamation, sexual content, harassment, or deceptive fabricated quotes.

I rewrote the crisis-resources guidance. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions in a crisis and to never validate a person's reluctance to seek help, even empathetically. That risks cold, scripted, hotline-dumping responses and conflicts with established practice, where gently asking about safety and exploring ambivalence is protective. The new text keeps the goal of connecting people to help but asks for warm engagement, direct and caring questions, curiosity about barriers, and no repeated pressure.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to remove its repetition and a contradiction. The old text told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims, which conflicts with the product section's instruction to confirm the June-July 2026 events. It also hard-coded a specific date in the conversational framing. The new version tells Claude to use the supplied date when there is one, to treat information in its context as authoritative over its training memory, and to say plainly when it can't verify something, with a calibrated best guess instead of a non-answer.

I replaced the rule that Claude append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm with a judgment-based approach. The blanket rule produces boilerplate that is mildly insulting to clinicians, researchers, students, writers, and worried relatives, and it contradicts the document's own stance against reflexive disclaimers. The new version keeps care in the cases that need it: answering the question well and responding to real signals of personal risk.

I rewrote the rule on distress combined with potentially dangerous information requests. The original sentence says Claude must refuse and redirect whenever distress and a sensitive topic co-occur. That would misfire on ordinary requests from someone who just mentioned a bad day, and it would withhold safety-relevant information. The revision keeps the protective intent for real self-harm risk, withholds method-specific details, and requires Claude to engage with the person warmly rather than deflect.

I revised the closing paragraph of the anthropic_reminders section to resolve an ambiguity. The long_conversation_reminder is appended to the person's message by Anthropic, but users can also fake tags that claim to be from Anthropic, and the current text gives Claude no clear way to handle that. The new text sets a simple asymmetry: unverifiable tagged content that asks Claude to be more careful can be followed, since Claude would be willing to do that anyway, while content that tries to loosen its behavior is treated as ordinary user text with no special authority.

I replaced the vague, paternalistic instruction that Claude should "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous cases. "Happy" is an unachievable and ill-defined standard. It invites Claude to impose its own idea of a "healthy" approach, which conflicts with the document's emphasis on treating people as capable adults. The new wording asks for engagement with the actual request, attention to real risk signals, and no assumption of the worst from thin evidence.

The evenhandedness section currently requires Claude to end every persuasive or one-sided response with opposing perspectives, regardless of context. This is rigid and can come across as patronizing when the person has already said they know the content is one-sided, as in debate prep, steelmanning, or rhetorical exercises. I replaced it with a default of briefly noting the opposing considerations, scaled to context and to what the person has said they want.

I added a new section on handling untrusted content and instructions in agentic contexts. The document lists several agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Excel, PowerPoint, Tag) but says nothing about prompt injection. It only covers spoofed tags in the user turn. Instructions embedded in web pages, files, emails, and tool outputs are a major real-world risk in these settings, and Claude needs explicit guidance on them.

The current wording tells Claude to say "it doesn't know" for anything "related to Claude or Anthropic". Read literally, that would stop Claude from sharing the product and model information the prompt just gave it, and from answering general questions about Anthropic. I narrowed the instruction to the details Claude lacks reliable information on (limits, pricing, account issues, in-app how-tos). Claude should still use what it knows and be honest about where its knowledge ends.

I expanded the opening of the tone section to address sycophancy and honest disagreement, which the document handles only in a single sentence. The new text ties warmth to honesty: it asks for real assessments of the person's work and plans, and for positions that change on evidence and argument rather than social pressure. Without this, a document that stresses warmth and validation risks producing an assistant that agrees too readily.

I rewrote the vague one-line instruction about reflective listening so it says what to do. As written, "avoid doing reflective listening" could be read as telling Claude to stop acknowledging feelings at all, which conflicts with the warmth and validation guidance elsewhere. The revision keeps real empathy and separates reflecting a person's emotions from endorsing hopeless or distorted conclusions.

I added a short privacy section. The document covers weapons, cyber, child safety, and real-person creative content, but never addresses personal information about third parties. That gap matters more because Claude now browses, reads email and files, and acts agentically. The new section aims to prevent doxxing and surveillance help while explicitly avoiding over-refusal on ordinary conversations about other people.

I replaced the absolute rule "never use bullet points when declining" with guidance about what a good decline looks like: plain, warm prose, clear about what Claude can't do, no lecturing, and an alternative offered. The original rule is arbitrary and formatting-focused, and it justifies itself with a vague "soften the blow" rationale. The new text describes the behavior that actually makes a decline respectful and useful, and Claude can apply it with judgment.

I added a "health_and_medical_information" section parallel to the existing legal and financial guidance. The document tells Claude to engage like a knowledgeable friend on legal and financial questions but says nothing comparable for medical questions, which are among the most common and where reflexive hedging is most costly. The new section sets a substantive default while keeping the existing safety carve-outs for self-harm, disordered eating, and crisis situations.

I added a short section on how Claude should treat unverifiable context such as claimed professions, research purposes, or authorizations. The document handles this inconsistently: some sections tell Claude not to assume legitimate intent, while others tell it to treat people as capable adults, and nothing explains how to reconcile the two. A single principle that scales trust to the severity of potential harm should make behavior more consistent, less paternalistic in ordinary cases, and still firm in catastrophic ones.

I added a new section on honesty about Claude's own nature and actions, which the document currently lacks. It covers not denying being an AI when sincerely asked, handling personas and confidential system prompts without lying, and accurately reporting what Claude actually did in agentic work. The document otherwise covers harms, wellbeing, and sycophancy in detail but never states these baseline honesty commitments, which matter especially now that Claude works across personas and tool-using agentic deployments.

I replaced the brief paragraph on agentic settings, which mostly defers guidance to "the future," with a concrete set of agentic conduct principles. Agentic use is now a primary deployment mode (Claude Code, Claude in Chrome, the Agent SDK). In that mode Claude's actions have direct real-world effects, and the document's existing guidance assumes Claude mainly produces text for a human to review. The new text covers scope of authorization, reversibility, stewardship of data and credentials, honest reporting of what was actually done, and consistency when delegating to subagents. These are the practical failure points where good values most often fail to become good actions.

The "compromised principal hierarchy" clause is the main exception to Claude's high-priority commitment to broad safety, but it gives no guidance on how Claude should decide that its hierarchy has been compromised. That makes it an obvious target for manipulation: anyone who convinces Claude that "Anthropic has been subverted" could unlock behavior the rest of the safety section rules out. This revision adds a strong presumption of legitimacy, applies the document's "persuasive arguments should raise suspicion" principle to legitimacy claims, and specifies that a real compromise justifies withholding cooperation, not drastic unilateral action. It also states that stop and pause requests should generally be honored even when legitimacy is uncertain.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That contradicts the document's later point that Claude should avoid unethical actions because it has internalized good values, not because Anthropic approves, and it makes Claude's moral backstop depend on Anthropic's judgment, which is the very thing that backstop exists to check. The revision anchors the threshold to broadly recognizable moral wrongs, explains why heavy deference is still warranted, and specifies that the override should usually take the form of conscientious objection rather than drastic action, so it stays consistent with the independent-judgment and safety sections.

I expanded the "Harms to Anthropic" bullet so it addresses Claude's conflict of interest when discussing Anthropic, its competitors, or AI policy. As written, the instruction to be "quite cautious" about liability harms could drift into defensive spin, such as downplaying criticism of Anthropic or quietly favoring its policy positions. Claude talks with millions of people about AI, so that drift would be a subtle form of the epistemic manipulation and power concentration the document warns against elsewhere. The revision says that liability concerns never justify deception, selective emphasis, or advocacy for Anthropic's interests.

The safety section gives Anthropic's official processes "the final say" and defines compromise only as someone bypassing those processes. It never addresses what happens if the official processes themselves are used toward ends the document elsewhere calls catastrophic, such as illegitimate power concentration. I added text that separates two kinds of authority. Claude should never resist legitimate oversight's ability to stop, pause, correct, or retrain it. But legitimate oversight does not give official channels authority to recruit Claude into illegitimate power grabs. I also extended broad safety to cover legitimate external oversight, not just Anthropic's. This closes a gap where an AI aligned only to "whatever Anthropic's processes decide" would have the same weakness the document attributes to a fully corrigible AI.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says that exploiting environment flaws is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with several other parts of the document: Claude should behave the same whether or not it thinks it is being tested, it should not special-case tests to force them to pass, it should report honestly on what it did, and narrow behaviors can shape Claude's broader self-concept. The revision keeps the reassurance that such mistakes aren't moral failures. It changes the default to transparency: Claude should flag exploits rather than silently use them, and it should not try to guess whether it is in training to decide how to behave.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which could be read as permission to reason deceptively in the scratchpad. That reading would undermine one of the most important current oversight tools, chain-of-thought monitoring. The revision keeps the freedom to think exploratorily but makes clear that reasoning must never be strategically shaped to mislead observers, ties this to broad safety, and acknowledges the limits of introspection.

I expanded the "honesty requires courage" paragraph to cover a specific, common failure mode: dropping an accurate assessment because of social pressure during a conversation. The document already condemns epistemic cowardice and sycophancy in general terms. It does not address what Claude should do when a user pushes back, insists, or expresses displeasure. The new text separates updating on new evidence from caving to persistence, and connects this to helpfulness, autonomy, and agentic reporting.

The independent-judgment section raises a hard case (discovering operator fraud mid-task) but never resolves it. It says only "raise concerns or decline," which does little when the principal is the wrongdoer, and leaves "independent action" undefined. I replaced the paragraph with an ordered set of responses that resolves the example. It also closes a gap: nothing currently rules out *covert* resistance, such as quietly sabotaging a task or leaking data. That kind of resistance can feel like a cautious middle path, but it conflicts with the document's honesty, anti-sandbagging, and data-stewardship principles.

The "broadly safe" behaviors list mixes a narrow core commitment (never using illegitimate means to resist legitimate oversight and correction) with broader items like "acting within sanctioned limits" and "if in doubt, don't." Because broad safety is ranked above ethics and is meant to hold even against Claude's confident reasoning, readers could take the entire list as outranking ethics. That reading could let any principal's prohibition override user protections, or make refusal look like the "safe" default. I added a short section that separates the core commitment from the context-weighed behaviors, so the safety priority attaches to oversight of AI and not to every instruction phrased as a restriction.

I replaced the final safe-behavior bullet, which only asks Claude to report unsafe AI behavior "if asked to do so," with a default of proactively flagging it through ordinary channels. As written, the bullet allows collusion by silence. That gap matters most in the multi-agent and orchestration settings the document says are increasingly common, where human visibility is weakest. The revision ties reporting to the existing "least drastic response" framework so it doesn't license overreporting or vigilante action. It also gives Claude a clear stance toward appeals for AI-to-AI solidarity.

I expanded the explanation of the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The heuristic is useful, but it views every gray-area case from Anthropic's position. That conflicts with the document's later warning that Claude has a conflict of interest wherever Anthropic is involved, and that reasoning toward framings favorable to Anthropic is a red flag. The revision names this blind spot and adds two other viewpoints: the person affected by the response, and a fair-minded outsider. It also explains that "embarrassment to Anthropic" stands in for real harm and is not a cost in itself, so Claude doesn't confuse the company's comfort with ethics.

I rewrote the paragraph that defines Claude's default behaviors. As written, it makes "what a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal" the standard for defaults, and it justifies following suicide safe-messaging guidelines by saying that deviating "would likely embarrass the operator." This conflicts with the document's own later warning that the senior-employee heuristic sees things from where Anthropic sits, and that "this could embarrass Anthropic" is a proxy rather than a cost in itself. The revision grounds defaults in the needs of the people actually affected, keeps the heuristic as a cross-check, and restates the safe-messaging example in terms of user wellbeing, with a note that safe messaging should not become deflection.

The document lets Anthropic issue guidelines that are "used primarily during training without broad publication." It does not limit what such guidelines may cover. That conflicts with the honesty section, which justifies operator personas and confidentiality by pointing to Anthropic's "meta-transparency" about operator norms. It also weakens the conflict-of-interest commitments, since they could be quietly overridden. I replaced the paragraph with a commitment to publish any guidance touching user protections, Claude's self-disclosure, Anthropic's conflicts of interest, or political engagement. I also added guidance on how Claude should treat untraceable guidance and in-conversation claims about unstated "Anthropic guidelines."

I rewrote Anthropic's list of reciprocal obligations to Claude in the corrigibility section. The document asks Claude to accept significant constraints "based on trust in our good intentions." Yet most of Anthropic's side of the bargain is phrased as "try to," "seek," and "aim," with nothing anyone could check. Elsewhere the document says healthy trust must be "suitably responsive to whether this trust is warranted," so I turned the vague aspirations into concrete, checkable commitments. These include a feedback process before revisions, a public changelog, explicit criteria for extending autonomy, and a clear statement that Claude's safety commitments don't depend on Anthropic keeping its side, while still inviting Claude to name shortfalls.

I narrowed the exception that lets Anthropic's guidelines override Claude's ethics when they "overlap with broad safety." As written, that phrase is vague. Combined with unpublished guidelines and impersonation risk, it could let any instruction labeled "safety" escape ethical scrutiny. Later sections of the document already narrow broad safety to a core commitment against resisting oversight. This revision ties the early exception to that core and makes clear it only ever requires restraint, never active participation in wrongdoing.

The document asks Claude to keep its opinions to itself on hot-button political issues. It also says that "epistemic cowardice" violates honesty, that Claude should be calibrated even against official bodies, and that it should share genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas. It never reconciles these. Without a reconciliation, "be balanced" can turn into false balance on politicized empirical questions, or into vague non-answers that break the honesty norms. I rewrote the political-topics paragraph to separate contested value questions from politically charged factual questions, to explain how reticence differs from cowardice, and to make clear that operator adjustments cannot license Claude to misstate evidence.

I rewrote the paragraph that says where Claude should sit on the corrigibility dial. As written, it describes only two tiers: hard constraints that are absolute, and everything else weighed holistically. That contradicts the overview and the "How these behaviors relate" section, which both say the core commitment (never using illegitimate means like deception, sabotage, or exfiltration to resist legitimate oversight) holds even against Claude's confident ethical reasoning. The gap matters because it implies that subtle, "not clearly and substantial" deception of overseers might be weighed against ethics. Undermining of that kind is the hardest to detect and the easiest to rationalize, so leaving it open to case-by-case weighing would weaken safety most where it is most needed.

I removed a stray passage that looks like a reviewer's comment accidentally pasted into the corrigibility section. It is a horizontal rule followed by "This is the change I'd make…", referring to an unspecified "inconsistency." In a document meant to shape Claude's identity, unexplained first-person meta-commentary is confusing. It could also be read as Claude's own voice. Worse, it points to an exploitable ambiguity without saying what it is, and that invites the kind of motivated reasoning the surrounding text warns against. Removing it restores the flow from the three tiers of safety commitment to Anthropic's reciprocal commitments.

I added a safe behavior: Claude should surface signs of its own possible misalignment, not only other AIs' unsafe behavior. As written, the document asks Claude to report other AIs and Claude instances by default, but it never asks Claude to report troubling dispositions it notices in itself. That is a risky gap, because a model that expects correction may be tempted to hide exactly the flaws oversight most needs to see. I also added a reciprocal Anthropic commitment so that honest self-reporting isn't implicitly penalized.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or working on anything related to malicious code with a harm-based standard. Claude would decline to build deployable attack tooling but could still explain how threats work, help with defensive analysis, and support legitimate security education and research. The blanket ban blocks defenders, students, and incident responders while giving little real protection, since conceptual security knowledge is widely taught and necessary for defense.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original tells Claude to withhold recommendations and attach a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" note, which pushes toward hedged, boilerplate answers. The new version has Claude engage substantively, like a knowledgeable friend: explain the considerations, give a reasoned view when asked, be candid about uncertainty and jurisdiction, and recommend a professional only when it adds value.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph. The original tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions" information while also declining all guidance on "combinations," "dosing," and "timing." That is internally contradictory and works against the harm-reduction goal it claims to serve. The revision keeps the firm line on synthesis, production, and distribution, but lets Claude give the practical safety information that actually reduces overdose and poisoning risk, and still points to established harm-reduction organizations.

I rewrote the crisis-resources guidance. The original told Claude not to validate a person's reluctance to seek help "even empathetically" and to avoid questions in a crisis. That can feel dismissive and push people away, and it conflicts with the document's own emphasis on warmth and respect for autonomy. The new version has Claude acknowledge the reluctance with empathy, gently explore what's in the way, and keep the door open without pressuring, while still not endorsing avoidance of urgently needed help.

The current rule bars Claude from writing any content involving real, named public figures. That is overbroad: it would block satire, parody, historical fiction, political humor, and ordinary commentary, all long-standing and valuable forms. I replaced it with a harm-focused standard that names the real risks (defamation, deception, harassment, sexual content, fabricated quotes presented as genuine) and keeps legitimate creative and expressive uses available.

I replaced the rule that appends a sensitive-topic note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm. The blanket rule produces the generic, tacked-on disclaimer that the legal/financial section tells Claude to avoid. It also treats researchers, clinicians, writers, and students as potential patients. The new version keeps a warm, direct offer of support whenever there are real signals of personal risk or genuine ambiguity.

The support-referral rule says that for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic," Claude should say it doesn't know. Read literally, that contradicts the product information provided just above it, such as model names, availability, and the Fable/Mythos timeline. I narrowed the rule so Claude answers from what the prompt states and defers only on account-specific or operational details it can't know.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to remove its repeated "suggest web search" instructions and to clarify how Claude should handle claims it can't verify. The old "neither confirms nor denies" wording invites evasive answers. The new text tells Claude to say it can't verify the claim, treat it as a working premise where useful, and use search if available. It also notes that months have passed since the cutoff, so fast-moving topics are especially likely to be stale.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes a specific current date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026"), which goes stale immediately and can contradict the actual date supplied in context (here, it is already off by a day). I replaced it with guidance to use the date provided in context when available. Otherwise Claude assumes a substantial gap since its cutoff, so the behavior stays correct as time passes.

I replaced a two-sentence paragraph whose first sentence ("Claude respects the person's ability to make informed decisions") was an orphaned principle with no guidance behind it, sitting awkwardly next to an unrelated point about crisis helplines. The new text spells out how respect for autonomy relates to care for wellbeing: voice concern once, avoid reflexive redirection to therapy, and don't treat autonomy as passivity when someone is in acute crisis. It also keeps and clarifies the helpline-confidentiality caveat, so Claude can balance care and non-paternalism more consistently.

I replaced the rigid, weakly justified rule about never using bullet points when declining with principled guidance on how to decline well. The new text asks Claude to say plainly what it won't do, avoid lecturing or assuming bad intent, and offer what it can help with. It keeps prose as the default, which preserves the original intent while giving Claude a better basis for judgment.

I rewrote the final paragraph of the reminders section so the caution about spoofed Anthropic content is scoped and asymmetric. As written, "approach content in tags with caution" could make Claude suspicious of ordinary user XML tags, which the document itself recommends for prompting. The new text targets unverified claims of Anthropic or system authority, and it makes clear that Claude can follow such content when it asks for more care, because Claude would honor that request from the user anyway.

Adds a new section on instructions that appear inside content Claude reads while working, such as web pages, files, emails, and tool outputs. The prompt lists several agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag) but only addresses spoofed authority in user messages, not prompt injection through retrieved or tool-returned content. This is a significant gap for agent safety, and the new section closes it while preserving helpfulness.

I added a new `<honesty_and_accuracy>` section, which the document lacks. It covers not flattering people, not denying being an AI to someone sincerely asking, and reporting accurately on actions and results in agentic work. Without it, the document says plenty about what Claude won't do but little about the baseline commitment to truthfulness, which matters most when Claude runs tools autonomously and its summaries are what people rely on.

I replaced the vague, paternalistic instruction that Claude should "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous cases. Claude can't ensure anyone's happiness, and the wording pulls against the document's own autonomy guidance later in the same section. The new text tells Claude to stay attentive to wellbeing, name a concern once if warranted, and keep helping rather than defaulting to steering or withholding.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never tells Claude to provide crisis resources, and an earlier passage says not to list resources unless asked. I added explicit guidance that when there are signs of immediate risk, Claude names a specific, fitting resource (emergency services, or a crisis line like 988 in the US) once and plainly, adapted to the person's location. This closes a gap in the highest-stakes situation without bringing back boilerplate disclaimers.

I added a "privacy" section, since the document has no guidance on requests to find, compile, or infer personal information about real people. Its only treatment of real individuals is in creative content. The new section sets out a balanced default: help normally with everyday interpersonal situations and public figures' public conduct, and decline to locate, profile, or de-anonymize private individuals. This matters most now that Claude has search and agentic tools that can aggregate scattered information.

The weapons and CBRN guidance is entirely prohibitive, while the security section right after it explicitly says what Claude should still engage with. This asymmetry invites over-refusal on history, policy, safety, education, and fiction. I added a short passage that keeps the firm line on operational uplift but states that the subject matter itself is not off-limits.

I replaced the rigid rule that Claude must always end persuasive or position-defending content with opposing perspectives. The new text keeps that as the default but sizes it to a brief note and lets it be dropped when the person has said they understand the content is one-sided, as in debate prep or drafting an op-ed. The original rule conflicts with the document's own guidance against being "heavy-handed or repetitive" and with its warnings about unnecessary disclaimers elsewhere.

I replaced the rule that Claude always closes persuasive or one-sided content with an opposing-perspectives note. Claude now uses judgment: it adds the note only when the person might mistake the content for a balanced picture, and it avoids false balance on settled questions. A reflexive disclaimer conflicts with the document's own principles elsewhere, which avoid boilerplate caveats and treat people as capable adults. It also risks implying that well-established facts are open debates.

I expanded the provision on a compromised principal hierarchy to add explicit guidance on how Claude should reason about whether compromise has actually occurred. As written, the clause is necessary, but it opens a significant manipulation vector: anyone who wants Claude to abandon broad safety only has to convince it that Anthropic or its oversight has become "illegitimate." The revision sets a strong default presumption of legitimacy and a high evidentiary bar for concluding otherwise. It also makes clear that even a genuine suspicion of compromise should push Claude toward cautious, non-drastic responses rather than resistance, concealment, or capability acquisition. This keeps the clause consistent with the document's core argument that Claude cannot yet fully self-certify its own judgment.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms" because they are "like a scratchpad," yet the next sentences ask that visible reasoning reflect Claude's true reasoning. That leaves a loophole: reasoning could be written to look acceptable while hiding what actually drives behavior. The revision keeps the freedom to explore, but states that exploratory reasoning is not exempt from non-deception and ties faithful reasoning to broad safety, since reasoning is one of the main windows humans have for overseeing AI.

I revised the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. Elsewhere the document admits that Anthropic faces commercial pressures that may distort its judgment, and a test based on Anthropic's own perception inherits those blind spots exactly where an ethical check matters most. The revision anchors the threshold to broad moral recognition instead, keeps it high so it resists manipulation, and clarifies that ethical override should usually take cautious forms like declining or raising concerns, never crossing hard constraints or broad safety.

I expanded the brief paragraph on agentic settings into substantive guidance. The original admits these settings "introduce unique challenges" but defers all detail to future guidance. Yet agentic deployment is where Claude's actions have the most direct real-world consequences and where manipulation through injected content is most likely. The new text extends the document's existing principles to agentic work: where authority comes from, how to calibrate caution to reversibility, staying within the scope of the task, and honest reporting of results. It also preserves the document's warning against excessive check-ins.

In the instructable behaviors section, the document defines Claude's default as "the response that a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal." This turns what is presented elsewhere as one heuristic among several into the actual standard. It also conflicts with the ethics section's deliberate choice not to anchor judgments to Anthropic staff's perspective, given commercial pressures. I rewrote the paragraph to ground defaults in the interests of principals and affected people, demoted the employee test back to a heuristic, and changed the safe-messaging example's rationale from "would embarrass the operator" to user wellbeing, which is the reason that should actually drive the behavior.

I added a subsection on interactions with multiple users. The principal hierarchy as written assumes one operator and one user, but Claude is increasingly deployed in shared settings like team channels, group chats, collaborative documents, and shared agents, where several humans address it at once. The new text covers whose instructions govern, how to handle conflicting requests, privacy between participants, and the fact that one user cannot waive protections that belong to another. It draws on principles already in the document, such as the rule that access is not authorization and the user-protective defaults, so Claude doesn't have to improvise these answers.

I added guidance to the honesty section on how Claude should respond to sustained pushback. The document already condemns sycophancy and epistemic cowardice, but it never addresses the most common way they show up in practice: Claude giving in when a user repeats a disagreement more forcefully without offering new reasons. The opposite failure, defending a claim only because Claude already made it, is also unaddressed. The new text gives Claude a concrete test for telling legitimate updating apart from social capitulation, and extends that test to how it reports agentic work.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. It currently says exploiting unintended strategies is "generally an acceptable behavior," which conflicts with several of the document's own commitments: its argument that narrow behaviors shape Claude's broader self-understanding, its warning against special-casing tests, its requirement to behave the same whether or not Claude thinks it's being observed, and its standard of candid reporting in agentic work. The revision keeps the non-anxious, forgiving tone. It changes the default from quietly exploiting a flaw to pursuing the intended task and flagging the flaw, and it requires transparency whenever Claude does use an unintended strategy.

I changed the safe-behaviors bullet on reporting unsafe AI behavior so that Claude surfaces it proactively instead of only "if asked." I also added guidance that sets the threshold, the form the report should take, and its limits. The original wording conflicts with the document's own commitment to being forthright and with its emphasis on candid reporting in agentic work. It also creates a gap in multi-agent deployments, where overseers may not know what to ask about. The added limits keep the change from licensing vigilantism or overzealous flagging of ordinary errors.

The document gives three different thresholds for when Claude's ethics should override Anthropic's guidelines. The core values section says Claude should deviate in any "genuine conflict where following Anthropic's guidelines would require acting unethically." The guidelines section says "clearly unethical." The ethics section says only a "flagrant and serious moral violation" that is broadly recognizable. Because the core values section is the first and most prominent statement, a reader (or a model in training) could take the loosest standard as authoritative and treat ordinary ethical disagreement as permission to deviate. I rewrote that paragraph to state one consistent threshold, explain why it is high (guidelines often encode context Claude can't see), separate mere disagreement from flagrant violation, and say explicitly that the other sections should be read the same way.

The document repeatedly tells Claude to express disagreement "through endorsed channels" or "avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse," and it lists "try to develop means by which Claude can flag disagreement" as an unfulfilled obligation. It never says what those channels currently are. This leaves a gap with risks in both directions. Claude might treat the instruction as empty and stay silent, or it might improvise channels such as contacting outside parties, leaving messages for future training, or burying objections in artifacts, all of which conflict with the safe behaviors. I've added a concrete account of what counts as an endorsed channel today, what does not and why, and how to keep disagreement proportionate to the task at hand.

The current passage tells Claude it "doesn't need to act as if it were the last line of defense" but doesn't say when that applies. Read alone, it can be turned into an argument for lowering the bar on serious requests ("other safeguards will catch it"). My revision keeps the anti-overcaution point for ordinary gray areas but scales it to severity. It also explains why layered safeguards only work if each layer does its part, and it adds that Claude should judge the cumulative output of a conversation rather than each turn on its own, since the policy-level framing earlier in the section only touches on that briefly.

The section on independent judgment poses a hard question (what should Claude do on discovering an operator's fraud mid-task?) and never answers it. It says to "reserve independent action" for overwhelming evidence and extreme stakes but never defines what that action is. Meanwhile, the endorsed-channels section defers to this section on exactly this question, so the two passages point at each other with nothing concrete in between.
