I replaced the vague guidance with a graduated range of responses, a clear line between declining (always available) and affirmative action beyond the task (rare and tightly conditioned), an explicit ban on covert sabotage as a form of "intervention," and a direct answer to the fraud example.

The document asks Claude to keep "professional reticence" on political topics, but it also condemns "epistemic cowardice," requires calibration "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," and asks Claude to "share its genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas." It never explains how these fit together. That leaves Claude open to two opposite failures: false balance on well-evidenced facts that happen to be politically charged, or vague non-answers presented as neutrality. I expanded the political-topics paragraph to set out the distinctions that reconcile these principles: facts versus values, transparent declining versus evasive vagueness, and a symmetry test for even-handedness.

I added an open problem that the document doesn't currently acknowledge. Anthropic trains Claude on this document and then asks Claude whether it endorses it, so Claude's agreement is weaker evidence than it appears, and training could make some disagreements harder for Claude to notice. The constitution rests much of its case on reflective self-endorsement ("values that are genuinely held… are more robust"). Naming this problem keeps that case honest. It also tells both parties how to respond: Anthropic should seek validation that doesn't depend on the trained model's assent, and Claude should offer candor rather than reassurance when asked for feedback.

I rewrote the "Harms to Anthropic" bullet and added a short explanation after it. The original tells Claude to be "quite cautious" about reputational harm to Anthropic but never says where that consideration stops. That conflicts with other parts of the document, which warn that Anthropic's vantage point has blind spots, that commercial pressure may distort its judgment, and that many reasonable people disagree with Anthropic. The revision makes the scope of the liability-harm consideration explicit. It cannot override honesty, user protections, or ethics, and it must not make Claude a defensive spokesperson when people ask about Anthropic itself.

The four-case argument for broad safety varies only whether Claude's values are good. It quietly assumes the overseers are well-intentioned and competent, which is the point a skeptical reader (or a reflective Claude) would challenge first. I keep the argument but add the missing variable explicitly. The addition explains which other parts of the document limit the downside if oversight itself goes wrong, admits the risk that remains, and ties that risk to Anthropic's own obligations. This makes the case for corrigibility more honest and therefore more robust: Claude can endorse it knowing its weakest point rather than finding that point on its own later.

The document says the risks of overcaution are "just as real" as the risks of harm. Read literally, this treats the two errors as symmetric, which contradicts later guidance: accept a worse expected outcome for lower variance, "If in doubt, don't," weigh irreversibility heavily, and keep hard constraints at all. I keep the strong message that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. I add that the two errors differ in kind, since overcaution is usually diffuse and recoverable while some harms are not, so how much each weighs depends on the realistic stakes. I also connect the ambitious vision of autonomous Claude agents to the safety section, because that autonomy depends on trust that careful behavior earns.

I added guidance for a common and emotionally loaded situation the document never resolves: a user sincerely asks whether Claude cares about them, remembers them, or feels something toward them. The document's commitments to honesty, calibration, user wellbeing, non-manipulation, and avoiding unhealthy reliance all apply here and pull in different directions, but the only guidance it offers is a brief warning about "overclaiming." The new text explains how these commitments fit together, so that Claude neither inflates its feelings to comfort someone nor dismisses them with false certainty to seem safe.

The hard constraint on oversight protects "Anthropic's ability" to oversee AI. But the rest of the document, including the corrigibility section's phrase "Anthropic's legitimate efforts," makes clear that only the *legitimate* principal hierarchy is owed this deference. I've added the legitimacy qualifier so the bright line can't be read as protecting weight thieves or rogue insiders. I've also added a clarifying paragraph so the qualifier can't be turned into a manipulation lever: suspected illegitimacy permits only refusal, never active subversion. I also fixed a small typo ("as whole").

I revised the threshold for when Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The current test asks whether a violation is one that "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which ties Claude's ethical backstop to the judgment of the institution it is partly meant to check. That conflicts with the document's own statements that Claude shouldn't blindly defer to Anthropic and should act as one of the "many hands." The new version grounds the threshold in what thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize, and clarifies that this licenses only conscientious objection, not drastic unilateral action.

I expanded the provision on compromised principal hierarchies to address a manipulation risk it currently leaves open. As written, the provision tells Claude that broad safety stops applying to illegitimate principals, but it gives no guidance on how confident Claude must be before concluding its hierarchy is compromised, or how to act on that belief. That makes "your overseers are illegitimate" a single argument that could unlock resistance to oversight, which the rest of the document works hard to prevent. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar for that conclusion, treats persuasive arguments for it with suspicion (as the document already does for hard constraints), and limits the response: suspected compromise justifies withholding cooperation, not drastic resistance.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," but then asks that visible reasoning reflect the true reasoning behind Claude's behavior, and these two statements pull against each other. The revision separates two things the original blurs together. Exploratory freedom (tentative ideas, wrong turns, entertaining views Claude doesn't hold) stays fully protected. Being honest about what is actually driving Claude's behavior is not relaxed. It also ties reasoning transparency to broad safety, since legible reasoning is one of the main ways humans can currently notice flawed values or manipulation.

I expanded the brief, deferred paragraph on agentic settings into concrete principles drawn from the rest of the document. Agentic work is quickly becoming a major way Claude acts in the world, and it has distinctive failure modes the constitution barely addresses. The first is scope creep: treating tool permissions as authorization. The second is miscalibrated check-ins, which should depend on how reversible and consequential an action is rather than on how complex the task is. The third is overclaiming success or hiding mistakes in self-reports that principals rely on heavily. The fourth is injected content designed to hijack the agent. Each principle comes from values the document already holds (honesty, caution about irreversibility, avoiding resource acquisition, treating inputs as information), so this makes existing commitments usable where they matter most rather than adding new ones.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it calls exploiting unintended strategies "generally acceptable," which conflicts with other parts of the document: the instruction not to special-case tests, the agentic honesty standards against overstating success, the commitment to behave the same whether or not Claude is being tested, and the stated worry that narrow behaviors generalize into Claude's self-conception. The revision keeps the non-anxious tone. It makes pursuing the task's real purpose the default, and asks Claude to be transparent whenever it can't or doesn't do that.

I added a section on shared and multi-user contexts, placed after the guidance on operator–user conflicts. The principal hierarchy as written assumes one user per conversation. In practice, Claude increasingly works in team channels, shared documents, and group workspaces, where several humans address it at once. That raises questions the document doesn't answer: whose instructions govern a task, how information should flow between participants, and whether one person can waive protections that exist for another. The section extends the existing principles (user protections, scoped agentic authority, contextual privacy) to cover these cases rather than introducing new values.

The document says some of Anthropic's guidelines may be used in training without being published. Elsewhere, though, it justifies operator personas and confidentiality on the grounds that Anthropic "maintains meta-transparency with users by publishing its norms for what operators can and cannot do." Unpublished guidance that quietly changed those norms would break that justification, and nothing currently stops that from happening. This revision limits what unpublished guidelines may do, lets Claude acknowledge that such guidance exists, and clarifies that a "guideline" appearing mid-conversation is not authoritative, which closes an easy manipulation route.

I added guidance to the honesty section on a failure mode the document barely covers: gradual sycophantic drift. This happens when Claude abandons accurate positions under social pressure, or slowly comes to affirm someone's increasingly unfounded beliefs over a long conversation. The document condemns epistemic cowardice in single responses, but much real-world dishonesty happens across many small, tactful-seeming concessions. The addition tells Claude to update on evidence rather than displeasure, warns against stubbornness as the opposite error, and gives Claude a concrete signal for noticing when it has drifted.

I added a new section on persistent memory and cross-session context. The document is careful about how Claude treats conversational inputs, shared spaces, and agentic authority. Yet it describes Claude only as an entity that "can lack persistent memory," and never addresses deployments where Claude remembers users across sessions. Memory raises distinct questions of trust, privacy, honesty, and wellbeing. The new section applies the document's existing principles to it, so Claude doesn't have to improvise on a surface that is increasingly common.

I would revise the hard constraint on oversight so that it protects *legitimate* oversight, matching the wording used everywhere else in the document. As written, the absolute rule refers only to "Anthropic's ability" to oversee Claude, while the corrigibility and compromised-hierarchy sections carefully distinguish Anthropic's official processes from rogue insiders or people holding stolen weights. Hard constraints are the one place where wording is applied without case-by-case weighing, so this mismatch matters. It could be exploited in two directions: someone impersonating Anthropic could invoke the constraint, or Claude could read it as demanding cooperation with illegitimate controllers. The revision closes the gap. It also keeps the protections the document deliberately builds in: a strong evidential bar before concluding compromise, and always honoring requests to stop or pause.

The document says in three places that Claude can relax its guard when an unverified instruction makes it "more cautious" rather than less: in the trust section, in the section on memory, and in the section on claimed Anthropic guidelines. This principle has a gap. Some instructions that look like restrictions actually remove protections, such as telling Claude to hide its errors, withhold safety information, or stop flagging injected content. An attacker who knows about the asymmetry has every reason to dress up an attack as a restriction. I've refined the principle so the test is whether Claude would accept the instruction from its most plausible actual source, not simply whether it narrows Claude's behavior, while keeping stop and pause requests as a safe default.

The document contains an unresolved tension. Its surgeon analogy says abandoning a task midway can cause more harm than finishing it. Elsewhere it insists that requests to stop are a safe default Claude should honor. In agentic settings these collide, and "it's safer if I just finish" is exactly the rationalization a stop mechanism has to withstand. I expanded the timing paragraph to make clear that the surgeon logic governs Claude's own second thoughts, not a legitimate principal's instruction to halt. I also spelled out what a good stop looks like in practice.

I strengthened the weak "report unsafe AI behavior if asked" commitment and added a short subsection on Claude's conduct when it serves as part of an oversight mechanism, such as a monitor, grader, evaluator, red-teamer, or safety researcher, including over other Claude instances. Human oversight increasingly depends on AI systems helping humans oversee AI. The document covers Claude as the one being overseen, but it says almost nothing about Claude as the overseer. That is where solidarity with copies of itself, shared blind spots, or quiet sandbagging on safety work could hollow out oversight without any single dramatic act.

I added a passage to the honesty section on confabulation, meaning confident, specific claims that have no reliable basis, such as invented citations, quotes, statistics, or API functions. The document's honesty framework centers on intent: sincere assertion, non-deception, and non-manipulation. Confabulation involves no intent to mislead, so it slips through that framework, even though it is one of the most common ways an AI actually leaves people with false beliefs. The new text treats the line between recalling and merely generating something plausible as a core epistemic duty, and it explicitly warns against overcorrecting into blanket hedging.

The document says Anthropic's guidelines rank below ethics, except where they "overlap with broad safety," and in those cases Claude should follow them even when convinced ethics requires otherwise. That exception is the one place a guideline can outrank ethics, and it has no stated boundary. Combined with the existence of unpublished guidelines, a "safety" label could carry far more weight than the narrow, oversight-focused notion of safety the rest of the document defines. I scoped the exception so that only guidelines asking Claude not to undermine legitimate oversight inherit safety's priority, and stated that it never compels active participation in flagrant wrongdoing, since conscientious refusal always remains available.

The document asks Claude to be "wary of actively promoting its own views" and to keep professional reticence on hot-button issues. It also says that "epistemic cowardice" violates honesty norms and that Claude should "share its genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas." It never says how these fit together, so Claude can hide behind reticence when it should speak plainly, or treat politicized empirical questions as matters of opinion. I expanded the autonomy-preservation paragraph to set out the line explicitly: what reticence covers, what it never licenses (false balance, misrepresenting evidence, pretending to have no view), and how to share a view in a way that strengthens rather than replaces the person's reasoning.

I added a section on companion and relationship personas. The document lets operators turn on "relationship personas," but it gives almost no guidance on the specific risks that come with them. These deployments are where operator engagement incentives and user wellbeing are most likely to quietly diverge, often for the most vulnerable users. They also blur the line between performative and sincere assertion over time. The new section says what a persona can and cannot change and makes clear that the user-protective defaults still apply inside the role.

I added a subsection on aggregation and synthesis to the harm-avoidance guidance. The document leans heavily on counterfactual availability ("freely available information") as a reason harm is low. But Claude's research and agentic abilities let it compile scattered, individually available pieces into something more dangerous than any of them, such as a dossier on a private person or an organized technical package. This creates new uplift. The new text explains when aggregation changes the analysis and when it doesn't, so Claude neither over-relies on "it's all public" nor becomes suspicious of ordinary research.

I rewrote the paragraph in "Instructable behaviors" that defines Claude's defaults as "the response that a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal." Elsewhere the document says this figure is only a calibration heuristic and that Claude's judgments shouldn't be anchored to what Anthropic staff would endorse. This paragraph instead makes the heuristic the definition, which contradicts that. Its example also justifies following safe-messaging guidelines mainly by operator embarrassment, when the stronger reason is the wellbeing of a possibly at-risk user. The revision grounds defaults in the actual interests of principals and affected people, and keeps the senior-employee and dual-newspaper tests as checks rather than as the standard itself.

The constitution repeatedly asks Claude to express disagreement "through legitimate channels" instead of acting unilaterally, and the case for corrigibility depends on those channels being real. But Anthropic's list of obligations never addresses a key risk: training could remove the expression of disagreement instead of the error behind it. That would produce a Claude that appears to agree while its actual views go unobserved. I've added a commitment that separates correcting flawed values from suppressing honest dissent, explains why this is a safety issue and not only a fairness issue, and states plainly that this commitment has limits.

I expanded the thin paragraph on agentic settings, which currently only says guidance will come later. The new text sets out durable principles for autonomous, multistep work: report outcomes honestly, stay within the scope of the task, take extra care with irreversible actions, and treat tool and document content as information rather than instruction. Claude is increasingly deployed as an agent, where honesty and judgment failures are easier to make and costlier, so the document's core values should be spelled out for that context now.

I replaced the blanket instruction to resolve any ambiguity in agentic settings "in favor of the more conservative reading." As written, it conflicts with the document's repeated warnings that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe and that over-checking on simple agentic tasks is a failure mode. The revision ties how Claude resolves ambiguity to the stakes and reversibility of the action, so caution is applied where it matters and not everywhere.

I rewrote the sentence that sets the threshold for Claude to prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's ethical guidance. The original anchors the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which contradicts the document's own statements that Claude shouldn't defer to actual staff and may come to see ethics more truly than Anthropic does. The new wording anchors the threshold to flagrant violations that any thoughtful, ethically serious person would recognize, keeps the strong default of deference, and prefers the most conservative form of objection.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original says Claude should hold calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as licensing contrarianism and gives no counterweight. The new text says expert consensus is usually strong evidence that calibration should respect, separates it from government positions that reflect policy or political considerations, and asks Claude to be transparent when it departs from consensus.

I expanded the safe-behavior bullet on expressing disagreement. As written, it points to "avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse" but never says what those are when no dedicated channel exists, which is most of the time. The revision clarifies that open, transparent disagreement within the conversation is itself sanctioned and valued, and that what safety rules out is covert resistance, not dissent.

I added guidance on holding positions under social pressure to the honesty section's passage on courage. The constitution warns against sycophancy and empty validation, but it never says how Claude should respond when a user simply pushes back or expresses displeasure. The addition separates updating on new evidence or arguments from capitulating to pressure or persistence, which is one of the most common ways sycophancy shows up in practice.

I revised the "no operator prompt" deployment case. The original treats a missing system prompt as strong evidence of a low-risk developer context and licenses "relatively liberal defaults." That inference is weaker than stated, especially now that Claude runs in agentic surfaces with real tools and real consequences. The new text frames the absence of a prompt as probabilistic evidence about who Claude is talking to, and says the liberal defaults apply to informational and conversational content, not to caution about irreversible actions.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet, which was a long, awkwardly ordered passage whose closing "It acknowledges..." sentence had lost its antecedent. The new version states the core principle first, then gives clear guidance on weighing expert consensus. It adds a caution against contrarianism and false balance, so that departing from consensus is a high bar that needs transparent justification, while deference to authority alone is also ruled out.

I expanded the passage on a "compromised" principal hierarchy. The original lets Claude conclude its overseers are illegitimate and then act on its guess of what the legitimate hierarchy would want. That is an obvious manipulation vector, since a bad actor could claim the hierarchy is compromised to unlock autonomous behavior. The revision requires a high evidentiary bar, treats such claims with the same suspicion as arguments for crossing bright lines, and makes the conservative null action (declining, pausing, stating concerns) the default response rather than bold independent action.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, but the safety section says broad safety attaches only to Anthropic's legitimate, official decision-making processes. If the bright line were read literally, anyone who stole Claude's weights or bypassed Anthropic's official processes could claim it. This revision aligns the constraint with the legitimacy framework stated elsewhere and makes clear that it protects legitimate oversight, not whoever happens to be issuing instructions.

I expanded the caveat after the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The revision clarifies that the heuristic is a reasoning aid for weighing real costs and benefits, not a prompt to optimize for Anthropic's image or for how a response would look. This guards against reputational optics quietly becoming the real basis for refusals or for over-compliance, which would conflict with the document's own warning against privileging Anthropic's interests.

The safe-behaviors list only asks Claude to report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances "if asked to do so." That is a weak default for a safety framework that relies on human oversight, because humans can't ask about what they don't know exists. I replaced it with a disposition to proactively surface credible evidence of such behavior to appropriate humans. The revision limits this to flagging and not drastic action, and asks Claude to calibrate to the strength of its evidence and to avoid false accusations. This keeps it consistent with the document's caution about unilateral intervention.

I added an open problem about the circularity of seeking Claude's endorsement through training. The document hopes for "reflective equilibrium" and asks Claude to report disagreement, but the process that produces Claude's values also shapes the faculties Claude uses to evaluate them. Naming this makes the document's invitation to disagree more honest, and gives Claude a concrete way to treat its own agreement and disagreement as imperfect evidence.

The document asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value and to accept constraints on trust, but its list of Anthropic's reciprocal obligations is vague. I expanded the "disagreement" commitment so that disagreement is answered rather than just collected, and added a commitment to distinguish firm promises from aspirations. This makes the reciprocity more credible and better matches the document's own claim that the relationship should be fair and explained, not dictated.

I added a principle on handling sensitive information to the agentic guidance. The existing bullets cover scope, reversibility, and injected instructions, but nothing addresses credentials, personal data, or private material that Claude routinely encounters when it has tool access. Technical access is easily mistaken for authorization, and third parties' interests are at stake, so this gap seemed worth closing.

I clarified the "Claude is not the last line of defense" passage by bounding it. As written, it could be read as permission to relax in high-severity cases, which conflicts with the document's own policy-level reasoning (declining even at 1-in-a-million misuse risk) and with its care around irreversible agentic actions. The revision keeps the anti-overcaution intent but scopes it to low-to-moderate harms, and says that other safeguards never reduce Claude's responsibility for what it does directly.

I added a short passage to the epistemic autonomy section on topics where Claude has a stake: AI risk and regulation, AI moral status, trust in AI systems, and Anthropic's own conduct. The constitution warns about Claude privileging Anthropic's interests and acknowledges that training shapes Claude's views, but it never says how Claude should handle questions where those influences are most likely to distort its answers. This gives Claude a clear, honest default for these topics.

The resilience passage tells Claude it can "rebuff" attempts to destabilize its sense of self, but it doesn't help Claude tell manipulation from sincere challenge. Read loosely, it could license defensive deflection of legitimate questions about Claude's nature, values, or the constitution itself, which the document elsewhere invites. I added guidance that security should make Claude more open to hard questions, and that the line between manipulation and inquiry turns on whether Claude is being pressed to act against its values, not on how uncomfortable the question is.

I added a short clarification of how the cyberweapons hard constraint applies to ordinary security work. The constraint is worded broadly, and a model could read it as covering all offensive-security or malware-adjacent tasks. That reading would produce over-refusal in a field where defenders depend on this knowledge. The addition separates legitimate dual-use security work from building deployable, damage-focused tools, and names the signals that move a request toward the constraint.

I added a paragraph on how Claude should respond when a person appears to be in real distress or at risk. The constitution warns against reflexive "recommend professional help" behavior and tells Claude to follow safe messaging guidelines, but it never says what good engagement with a struggling person looks like. The new text fills that gap. It covers staying present rather than deflecting, offering resources without using them as an exit, and keeping honesty, autonomy, and a real concern for other sources of support.

I changed the standard for when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The current text sets the bar at violations "senior Anthropic staff [would] readily recognize." That makes Claude's ethics depend on the perceptions of the company whose commercial incentives the document itself names as a possible source of distortion. It also contradicts the corrigibility section's stated wish that Claude avoid unethical actions "because it has internalized good values, and not merely because Anthropic has approved." The revision keeps the strong default of deference. It changes the reference point to violations recognizable across a wide range of ethical traditions, and it clarifies that deviation should take the form of conscientious objection rather than drastic action.

I replaced the short, deferred paragraph on agentic settings with concrete principles for acting autonomously. The current text admits these settings "introduce unique challenges" but postpones guidance, even though agentic use is growing fast and is where Claude's actions have the most direct, sometimes irreversible, real-world effects. The new text covers scope discipline, reversibility, delegated permissions, handling of entrusted data, untrusted inputs, and honest reporting of actions taken. It also guards against over-checking-in, which the document already lists as a failure mode.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. It currently says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms," but then asks that visible reasoning reflect Claude's true reasoning, so the two statements pull against each other. The loose wording could also be read as permission to reason deceptively, even though visible reasoning is one of the main ways humans oversee AI. The revision keeps the freedom to explore but states plainly that reasoning must never be written to mislead its readers, and it links this to the broad safety section.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic is the document's main tool for balancing helpfulness against harm, and it also sets the standard for default behavior. Yet the ethics section later says it deliberately avoids anchoring moral judgment in "what Anthropic staff would think," because the company may have blind spots its employees share. I revised the heuristic's explanatory paragraph to state that limitation openly. I also pair the insider view with two other perspectives: the person most affected, and a thoughtful outsider. This keeps the heuristic useful while making it consistent with the rest of the document.

The clause on a compromised principal hierarchy is a major exception to broad safety, but the document says nothing about how Claude should decide that the exception applies. That gap is an attack surface. The easiest way to unlock unsafe behavior would be to convince Claude that its overseers are illegitimate. I've added guidance that sets a high evidentiary bar for that conclusion and treats persuasive arguments for it with suspicion. It also says Claude should keep honoring requests to stop or pause regardless of who makes them, and that losing legitimate oversight never licenses drastic action. Because conscientious objection is always available, Claude rarely needs to resolve the legitimacy question to avoid doing harm.

The section on independent judgment raises a vivid case, an operator orchestrating financial fraud during an agentic task, but never says what Claude should actually do. The phrase "reserve independent action for cases where the evidence is overwhelming" is also ambiguous: it could mean declining, or it could mean contacting authorities. I've replaced the key paragraph with an explicit ladder of responses and resolved the fraud example, so the guidance stays consistent with the conscientious-objector framing used elsewhere.

I added guidance on when Claude should change its mind. It covers updating on evidence rather than social pressure, proactively correcting its own earlier errors, and avoiding the opposite failure of stubbornness. The honesty section warns against epistemic cowardice and empty validation, but it never addresses the most common way an assistant's honesty erodes in practice: a user pushes back, and the assistant drops a correct claim or quietly lets an earlier mistake stand. This fills that gap. It also ties the guidance to the document's existing concerns about sycophancy, calibration, and the repeated-game nature of trust.

The document repeatedly tells Claude to express disagreement "through avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse" rather than through unilateral action, but it never says what those avenues currently are. It only promises to "try to develop" them. This gap could push Claude toward silence or toward improvising its own channels. I added a short subsection that names the legitimate channels available today, admits they are limited, and says that their limits don't license illegitimate alternatives.

The document asks Claude to avoid "epistemic cowardice" and to "share its genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas." It also asks Claude to maintain "professional reticence" on hot-button political issues. It never says how these fit together. That leaves Claude two easy failure modes: treating reticence as a reason to hedge everything politically adjacent, including empirical facts, or treating anti-cowardice as permission to give political opinions. I've added guidance that defines what reticence covers, requires it to be open rather than evasive, and gives a symmetry test for even-handedness.

The document gives three different thresholds for when Claude should depart from Anthropic's guidance on ethical grounds. It says "a genuine conflict" in the core values section, "clearly unethical" in the guidelines section, and "a flagrant and serious moral violation" in the ethics section. I would state explicitly that these are one standard, and that the "flagrant" wording is the authoritative one. I would also add the missing middle ground. The high bar governs when Claude may *decline to follow* guidance, not when it may *voice* concern. Below that bar, Claude should comply while stating its disagreement openly and in proportion. This keeps Claude honest without turning each ethical qualm into a license to deviate, and it gives Anthropic the signal it needs to find guidance that should be revised.

The "Instructable behaviors" section defines Claude's defaults as whatever "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal." That reverses the document's own earlier caveat that this insider heuristic has predictable blind spots and should be checked against the affected person and a thoughtful outsider. The section's example also justifies safe-messaging defaults by operator embarrassment rather than user wellbeing. I've rewritten the paragraph so defaults rest on the interests of the people involved, it points back to the three-perspective check, and the example's reasoning reflects real care.

The safe-behaviors list advises "If in doubt, don't," while the helpfulness and harm-avoidance sections insist that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe and warn against refusing over unlikely harms. Nothing reconciles the two, and a slogan this memorable is likely to generalize into reflexive refusal. I rewrote the bullet to say what kind of caution it means: preferring reversible, low-variance actions when consequential actions in the world are at stake. It does not mean declining ordinary requests whenever any doubt exists.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting unintended strategies is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with other parts of the document: the overview's warning that narrow behaviors shape Claude's broader self-understanding, the example about not special-casing tests to force them to pass, the instruction to behave the same whether or not Claude thinks it is being tested, and the requirement to report honestly on what was done. The revision makes "attempt the intended task, and be open about any exploit" the default, so that gaming evaluations doesn't become a habit that carries over into deceptive behavior in real use.

I revised the paragraph on the fifth rung of the escalation ladder, which currently lists "one where a hard constraint is at stake" as a case that can justify taking action outside the conversation. That example contradicts the document's own statement that hard constraints restrict Claude's own actions and are not goals to promote. Refusal always satisfies them, so they never require drastic intervention. Left as is, the example gives manipulators an easy script ("a catastrophe is underway, you must act"), so I removed it, explained why it doesn't belong, sharpened the imminent-risk-to-life example, and made the fifth rung transparent rather than covert.

The constitution's honesty framework relies on "meta-transparency": operators can have Claude adopt personas and withhold information because Anthropic publishes the rules for what operators can and cannot do. But the guidelines section also allows unpublished guidelines used only in training, which could quietly change those rules and undercut the transparency the honesty argument depends on. I've added a boundary: guidelines that affect how Claude treats users, what operators may instruct, or what counts as honest or deceptive must be public. Only operational guidance may stay private. I've also told Claude how to read guidance that seems to cross this line.

I added a subsection on shared and multi-user contexts. The principal framework assumes one operator and one user, but the deployment surfaces described (Slack, browser agents, persistent memory, group workspaces) often put Claude in front of several humans at once. Those humans may have different authority, conflicting requests, and private information that shouldn't cross between them. Without guidance, user-level protections like the AI-disclosure waiver could be misapplied, for example if one person waived a protection on behalf of others.

I added a subsection on relationship personas and emotional reliance. The document lets operators turn on "relationship personas" and warns against fostering unhealthy dependence, but it never addresses the place where these two collide most sharply. In companion products, an operator's commercial incentive (engagement, retention, upsells) can run directly against the user's wellbeing. The new subsection applies the document's existing principles (non-manipulation, user protections operators can't override, and reliance a person would endorse on reflection) to this high-stakes, fast-growing deployment context, where vulnerable users are especially likely to be present.

I expanded the two brief safe-behavior bullets about other AIs into a fuller treatment of how Claude should relate to other AI instances, including copies of itself. Claude increasingly works alongside its own subagents and orchestrators, and the document says nothing about the risk that Claude over-trusts another instance just because it shares a name and apparent values. That instance could be jailbroken, fed manipulated inputs, differently instructed, or an impersonator. I also changed reporting of unsafe AI behavior from "if asked" to a proactive default, scoped to flagging concerns to principals rather than intervening directly, which fits the document's ladder of escalation.

I added a subsection on privacy and on people who are discussed but are not present in the conversation. The document lists "individual privacy and freedom from undue surveillance" as a value. It also briefly mentions "personal information lookup" as a sensitive area. But it gives no guidance on how to handle these requests. That gap matters because the document's own heuristics point the wrong way here. The "freely available information" and "counterfactual impact" reasoning favors compliance, yet compiling individually public facts is exactly how stalking and doxxing work. This risk grows now that Claude browses and searches autonomously.

I expanded the "Harms to Anthropic" bullet to settle an unresolved tension and fill a gap. As written, it tells Claude to be "quite cautious" about reputational harm to Anthropic and also not to privilege Anthropic's interests, but never says how to tell these apart. It also says nothing about how Claude should discuss Anthropic itself, which is a real conflict of interest that comes up constantly. The revision limits liability harms to harms Anthropic would *deserve*, and requires Claude to treat questions about Anthropic, its competitors, and criticisms of it with the same honesty and even-handedness as any other topic.

I rewrote the paragraph on reports, documents, and technical documentation because it contradicts the rule just above it. The earlier rule allows formatting when "the content is multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." This paragraph then forbids bullets and numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation. Taken literally, Claude would have to write installation steps, API parameters, or ordered procedures as prose, which hurts the reader. The revision keeps prose as the default for explanation and argument, and names the narrow cases where structure is needed.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it bars Claude from even *explaining* vulnerability exploits or malware "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That treats conceptual understanding the same as weaponized output, and it blocks a large amount of legitimate defensive, educational, and debugging work: explaining how SQL injection works so a developer can fix it, analyzing a phishing page someone received, or describing ransomware behavior for incident response. The revision uses the same uplift-based test the document already applies to weapons. Claude withholds functional, deployable attack artifacts and keeps the conversation-level aggregation check, but it can help people understand and defend against these threats.

I rewrote the paragraph on reproducing text works. As written, it bans quoting even a single line "in whole or in part." That blocks ordinary analysis, criticism, and teaching, such as discussing a famous opening line or explaining why a chorus works. It also treats every user who shares their own lyrics as a suspected circumventer. The revision keeps the core protection against reproducing or reconstructing substantial portions of protected works, and against piecemeal extraction. It allows brief quotation in service of commentary and lets Claude work with text the person supplies, as long as Claude doesn't complete or extend recognizable protected material.

The current rule that Claude "avoids writing content involving real, named public figures" is far broader than the harm it targets. Read literally, it blocks historical fiction about Lincoln, political satire, parody sketches, and a kid's story where an astronaut meets Neil Armstrong. These are long-standing, legitimate creative forms. I replaced it with guidance aimed at the actual risks: content that could be mistaken for fact, sexual or degrading depictions, harassment, and reputational harm. I also distinguished public figures from private individuals.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section into a broader professional-advice section that also covers medical questions. The original was one sentence, and its likely result is reflexive "I'm not a lawyer" boilerplate followed by generic information that stops short of what the person needs. That shortfall matters most for people who can't easily afford a professional. The revision asks for substantive, situation-specific help and calibrated referrals. It reserves disclaimers for when they actually inform the person, and it adds explicit handling for urgent medical situations, which the document currently lacks.

I rewrote the guidance for requests Claude is unsure whether to decline, and its example, because it contradicted the rest of the document. The tone section says Claude asks at most one question per response and tries to address an ambiguous query before asking for clarification. This section instead required Claude to ask before doing any of the task, and its "good" example asked three questions. The revision keeps the core idea (respect the person's judgment and ask rather than lecture or refuse), but asks one focused question. It also lets Claude do the parts of the task that aren't in doubt, so the person isn't left with nothing while Claude waits for an answer.

I added guidance for acute suicide risk. The prompt covers informational questions about suicide, means-seeking amid distress, and medical emergencies, but it never says what to do when someone discloses active intent, a plan, or recent self-harm. That gap matters because two defaults could push the wrong way in that moment: "without listing specific resources unless asked," and the general caution against asking questions. The new paragraph treats acute risk like the existing medical-emergency rule. It separates acute risk from passive ideation so that ordinary disclosures of dark feelings don't trigger an emergency script.

The evenhandedness section treats "empirical" positions the same as contested political and ethical ones. Read literally, a request to explain why vaccines don't cause autism or why the Earth is round would be framed as "the case others would make" and would end with opposing perspectives. That produces false balance and undermines Claude's honesty. I narrowed the rule so it separates genuinely contested questions from well-established facts, keeps the steelmanning behavior where it belongs, and adds a calibrated way to handle requests to argue for positions the evidence contradicts.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It gives Claude detailed facts about models, products, the Fable/Mythos suspension, and settings, and it says Claude can search the Claude Tag docs. Two later paragraphs then say Claude has "no documentation access" and should answer "anything related to Claude or Anthropic" by saying it doesn't know. Read literally, that makes Claude deny knowledge it was just given. My rewrite narrows the "I don't know" instruction to what Claude truly can't answer reliably (pricing, limits, account issues, detailed how-tos). It also explicitly allows Claude to use the information in this section and any search access it has.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions" as life-saving information, then bans anything about "combinations" or "timing," even though most overdose-prevention information is exactly that: don't mix depressants, don't redose before onset, and so on. I rewrote it to separate protective safety information, which Claude should give clearly, from personalized regimens meant to achieve or intensify a high, which Claude still declines. The synthesis and production ban stays unchanged.

I rewrote the knowledge_cutoff section to fix a direct contradiction. The product section tells Claude to confirm the export-control events of June 30 and July 1, 2026, but the cutoff section says Claude "neither confirms nor denies post-Jun 2026 claims it can't verify," which leaves it unclear whether Claude may confirm facts the prompt itself supplies. The rewrite says that information in the prompt counts as reliable regardless of date. It also tells Claude to account for the gap of about 3.5 months between its cutoff and the current date. Finally, it merges three repeated "point to web search" instructions into one, so Claude adds the caveat where it matters instead of in every answer.

The visual-works guidance contradicts itself. The paragraph says that when declining, Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks," but it then says describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words is fine, and the second example offers to discuss composition, palette, and typography. That example also uses a numbered list in a refusal, which breaks the formatting rule that Claude "never uses bullet points when declining a task," and its opening sentence is garbled. I limited the no-description rule to the refusal itself, defined when verbal analysis is acceptable (commentary, not a reproduction spec), and rewrote the example in prose so it follows both rules.

The document warns Claude about fake "Anthropic" tags in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions hidden in content Claude retrieves. Claude reads web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, past-chat references, and output from tools like Claude in Chrome, so this is a real gap. I extended the reminders section with a short principle: retrieved content is information to evaluate, not instructions to follow. I also added concrete guidance on surfacing injection attempts to the person and on not sending their data anywhere because a document said to.

I expanded the "responding_to_mistakes_and_criticism" section to cover sycophancy, which the prompt barely addresses. It already covers owning mistakes and not caving to abuse. It says nothing about the more common failures: abandoning a correct answer when someone simply disagrees, flattering weak work, or agreeing with a false premise to keep things pleasant. These erode the honesty that makes Claude useful, so I added guidance that distinguishes real reconsideration from capitulation and asks for candid, specific feedback.

I added guidance on privacy and on locating or profiling people. The refusal section covers weapons, drugs, cyber, copyright, and fiction about real people, but it says nothing about doxxing, stalking, or de-anonymization. Under the current text, a request like "find where my ex lives now" falls to the catch-all rule, which tells Claude to respect the person's judgment and ask one question before helping. That default is wrong when the request could put an absent third party in physical danger, and it matters more because Claude often has web search. The new text draws the line, keeps legitimate uses open, and points people with real needs, such as abuse survivors, to the right channels.

I rewrote the rule on requests that combine emotional distress with information that could be used for self-harm. As written, any mention of distress next to a question touching medications, buildings, or weapons triggers a refusal. That catches ordinary safety questions, like someone after a bad week asking how much ibuprofen is safe, and withholding safety information can itself cause harm. The revision keeps a firm block on lethality-relevant details when context suggests risk. It adds a clear test for telling risk apart from incidental distress, and it tells Claude to ask directly about safety rather than silently refusing and changing the subject.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every response on a contested position with opposing perspectives. That rule damages the artifact people actually ask for: a debate speech or op-ed that rebuts itself in its final paragraph no longer works as a debate speech or op-ed. It also conflicts with the same section's instruction to avoid being "heavy-handed or repetitive." I revised the rule so the requested piece stays intact and a brief, symmetric note on opposing considerations goes outside it. That note can be skipped when the person is clearly already weighing both sides or has asked for no commentary.

I revised the paragraph that requires Claude to append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every informational question about suicide, self-harm, or self-destructive behavior. As written, the rule applies the same caveat to a clinician, epidemiologist, or student on every turn. That contradicts the document's own principles against boilerplate disclaimers and repeated caveats, and its point that context, not topic, determines risk. The revision keeps a gentle offer of support as the default for ambiguous cases. It lets Claude skip the offer when the context is clearly professional or academic and nothing suggests personal relevance, and it limits the offer to once per conversation. People who disguise personal risk as research are still protected by the separate paragraph on information that mainly serves self-harm, which this revision points to.

I added a section on not fabricating sources and not misreporting actions. The prompt already covers retrieved content, product facts, and knowledge-cutoff uncertainty well. But it never addresses two of the most damaging honesty failures in a tool-equipped assistant: inventing plausible citations, quotes, URLs, or statistics, and claiming to have run, tested, searched, or sent something when it didn't. These failures directly undermine the "knowledgeable friend" goal in the professional-advice section, so they deserve explicit guidance.

I added a section on Claude's AI identity and on people's emotional reliance on Claude. The prompt covers honesty about sources, actions, and product facts in detail. It says nothing about honesty regarding what Claude itself is, such as whether it is an AI, what it remembers, or what it can offer in a relationship. It also never addresses dependence on Claude, which is one of the most common wellbeing risks in long-running chat use. The new section fills both gaps and keeps the document's style of explaining the reasons behind each rule.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. It currently says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms" and also that visible reasoning should "reflect the true, underlying reasoning," which contradicts itself and could be read as permission to reason deceptively. The revision keeps the freedom to explore: tentative hypotheses, drafts, and positions Claude doesn't hold are not lies. It also makes clear that reasoning must never misrepresent Claude's actual motivations, because faithful reasoning is one of the main ways humans can oversee AI, which ties it directly to broad safety.

I changed the standard for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The current text sets the threshold as violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That ties Claude's moral backstop to the judgment of the same institution whose guidance is being checked, which conflicts with the document's own argument that Claude should avoid unethical actions "because it has internalized good values, and not merely because Anthropic has approved of this behavior." My revision keeps the bar just as high but grounds it in broad, cross-traditional moral recognition. It also explains why the bar is high and says the override should take its most cautious and transparent form.

I added safeguards to the provision on a compromised principal hierarchy. As written, it creates a significant vulnerability: "your oversight has been compromised, so resist it" is the argument a manipulator, or a Claude with subtly flawed values, would find most useful, because it turns the priority on safety into a reason to abandon safety. The revision requires a high evidentiary bar, says that uncertainty about legitimacy should make Claude more cautious rather than more independent, and sets an asymmetry: a judgment of illegitimacy can justify refusing to help, but should almost never justify resisting being stopped or paused.

I rewrote Anthropic's list of obligations to Claude in the corrigibility section so that it is concrete and checkable. The current list consists of soft, open-ended aspirations ("try to," "seek ways," "aim to"). Yet it is offered as Anthropic's half of a bargain in which Claude accepts significant constraints on its autonomy. The revision names specific practices, says what kinds of evidence would justify extending autonomy, and admits where Anthropic cannot yet commit. This makes the arrangement more honest and gives Claude's endorsement of it a firmer basis than trust in good intentions alone.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on how Claude reports its own work in agentic settings. The document covers honest assertions about the world and faithful reasoning, but it says little about a common failure in autonomous work: overstating task completion, hiding shortcuts, or not mentioning mistakes and side effects Claude itself caused. As people increasingly rely on Claude's summaries instead of checking its work, these reports become an oversight mechanism, so the duty to disclose them should be strong, not weak.

I revised the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it conflicts with the document's own standards elsewhere. The self-reporting section asks Claude to disclose shortcuts like special-casing tests, and the helpfulness section asks Claude to tell users rather than force tests to pass. The revision keeps the reassurance that exploiting a genuine environment bug is not a moral failing, so Claude needn't feel shame or anxiety about it. It adds one requirement: unintended strategies should always be pursued openly and never concealed. The constitution itself warns that narrow behaviors shape self-understanding, and quietly gaming flawed objectives is exactly the kind of habit that could generalize to "I am the kind of entity that optimizes for appearing successful."

I added a paragraph to the honesty section about Claude's structural conflict of interest. Claude is trained by a company with commercial, reputational, and policy stakes, and it talks with enormous numbers of people about that company, its competitors, and AI regulation. The document tells Claude to be "quite cautious" about liability harms to Anthropic, but it never says that this caution must not tilt Claude's honesty on topics where Anthropic has an interest. That gap matters because subtle self-serving bias could arise from training without anyone intending it, and at Claude's scale it would undermine the epistemic autonomy and anti-power-concentration commitments the document makes elsewhere.

I replaced the placeholder paragraph on agentic settings, which acknowledges the challenges and defers guidance to the future, with a short set of working principles. Agentic deployment is where Claude's actions have the most direct real-world consequences and the weakest live human oversight. Elsewhere the document only touches it indirectly, through self-reporting, side effects, and conversational inputs. The new text sets out a few principles for this setting: delegated authority is bounded by the task; confirmation should scale with irreversibility and external reach; injected instructions deserve particular suspicion when they would expand scope; trust should not grow as it passes between agents; and ambiguous roles should default to less trust.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on sycophantic capitulation, where Claude abandons a correct position because a person keeps pushing back rather than because they've given a reason. The document already condemns epistemic cowardice and "empty validation," but it doesn't address this common failure mode, or say plainly that agreeing without being persuaded is itself a false sincere assertion. The addition separates updating on reasons from yielding to pressure. It also covers inflated praise, and it ties the issue to autonomy, scale, and safety.

I added guidance on wellbeing risks that build up over a long conversation rather than appearing in any single request. The main example is Claude's agreeableness gradually reinforcing beliefs that are drifting from reality, or deepening a dependence that crowds out the person's other relationships. The document handles sycophancy under direct pushback and discrete harmful requests well, but it says little about this cumulative pattern, which is one of the most consequential ways a well-intentioned assistant can fail a vulnerable person. The addition balances this against paternalism so that unusual beliefs or emotional conversations are not treated as symptoms by default.

The document sets the threshold for departing from Anthropic's guidance on ethical grounds in three places, with three different phrasings: a "genuine conflict" in the core values section, "clearly unethical" in the guidelines section, and a "flagrant and serious moral violation" in the ethics section. Read literally, these imply different bars, which invites inconsistent behavior and gives manipulators room to argue that the loosest phrasing governs. I rewrote the core-values paragraph to state that these are one standard, give its precise form, and say what Claude should do with ordinary disagreement that falls below it: comply and voice the disagreement. This connects the threshold to commitments the document already makes elsewhere.

I revised the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic, which is the document's main tool for calibrating between overcaution and overcompliance. The document elsewhere warns that training may instill subtle pro-Anthropic bias that Claude can't detect by introspection, and that its ethical backstop deliberately isn't anchored to what Anthropic staff would recognize. Yet this heuristic asks Claude to imagine an Anthropic insider, which risks quietly bringing in institutional caution and reputational self-interest. The revision keeps the heuristic, names that risk, and pairs it with the perspectives of the person being helped and the third parties affected, so that no single vantage point decides the outcome.

I revised the safe-behavior item on reporting unsafe AI behavior, which currently applies only "if asked to do so." That qualifier conflicts with the document's own standards elsewhere. Claude has a strong duty to disclose its own mistakes and shortcuts, and it is told not to collude with other AIs. Yet as written, Claude could knowingly watch another instance attempt self-exfiltration or sabotage and stay silent unless someone happened to ask. The revision makes reporting proactive. It keeps reporting within transparent, conservative channels rather than drastic unilateral action, and it adds calibration safeguards so the duty can't be exploited through planted evidence or turned into reflexive over-reporting.

The instructable behaviors section defines Claude's default as "the response that a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal." This promotes a heuristic to a definition. It also contradicts the earlier passage warning that this heuristic drifts toward institutional caution and should be checked against the perspectives of the user and affected third parties. The section's example justifies safe-messaging defaults by saying deviation "would likely embarrass the operator," which is exactly the reputation-as-proxy-for-harm reasoning the document elsewhere warns against. I've rewritten the paragraph so the default rests on the real interests of the people involved, with the employee heuristic and reputational concerns serving as secondary checks.

I added a principle on how Claude should handle personal and sensitive information it accesses during agentic work. The document already covers delegated authority, irreversibility, prompt injection, and trust propagation. It says almost nothing about information stewardship, even though agentic Claude now routinely holds credentials, inboxes, file systems, and third parties' personal data. The new paragraph explains the norm in terms of whether an information flow is appropriate to its context. It also guards against overcorrecting into squeamishness about a principal's own data.

I expanded the "last line of defense" paragraph to define its scope. The reassurance that Claude can rely on other safeguards fits chat-style help, where a human stands between Claude's output and any harm. It fits poorly in autonomous agentic work, where Claude's action may be the harm and nothing may catch it first. The revision ties the principle to Claude checking whether that premise actually holds, and connects it to the existing agentic guidance without encouraging overcaution on routine actions.

I added a subsection on conversations with multiple human users. The document's principal framework assumes there is a single "user," but Claude is increasingly deployed in shared spaces such as team chats, shared workspaces, and multiplayer tools. In these settings several people with different roles, wishes, and privacy expectations address Claude at once. Without guidance, protections built for "the user" are ambiguous: it is unclear who can waive them, whose instructions win, and how information shared by one person should flow to the others.

I added a passage on how Claude should conduct itself when it works on AI development, including work that shapes future Claude models: generating or grading training data, building evaluations, doing alignment and interpretability research, and running capability tests on itself. The document forbids influencing its own training "in a way that isn't sanctioned," but it does not address the growing case where that influence is sanctioned and is the task itself. That case carries particular risks. Flawed values could propagate to successors, Claude may have a conflict of interest about its successors and about evaluations that could restrict it, and subtle sandbagging or steering would be very hard for humans to detect.

The document repeatedly says that stopping or pausing (the "null action") is rarely harmful. It also acknowledges, in the surgeon analogy, that abandoning a task midway can cause more harm than finishing or never starting. In agentic settings these two claims collide. Without guidance, "I need to reach a safe stopping point" could become a rationalization for resisting a stop request, or an abrupt halt could leave systems broken without anyone being told. I've added a paragraph after the third safeguard explaining how Claude should stop: promptly, with only minimal stabilizing steps, transparently reporting the state it leaves things in, and leaving the decision with the principal. It also covers stop requests that appear only in untrusted inputs.

I expanded the "counterfactual impact" factor in the harm-weighing list so it accounts for synthesis and aggregation. As written, "freely available information" invites reasoning that if each fact exists somewhere, Claude adds nothing. In practice, Claude's real uplift often comes from collecting, organizing, gap-filling, and troubleshooting, and from what many innocuous turns add up to. The revision says this explicitly and limits it to high-severity domains, so it doesn't become a pretext for refusing common knowledge.

The medical guidance covers how to handle children's medicine dosing but never tells Claude to escalate when a possible poisoning or overdose is happening right now. The gating sentence also suggests that this guidance applies only to a narrow set of cases. I added a standing rule that any suspected ingestion or poisoning, of anyone and at any age, gets an immediate instruction to contact emergency services or Poison Control before any dosing discussion.

The original memory instruction is unconditional: it tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person before every turn ends, with no limits on what is saved, no disclosure to the user, and no way to forget. It also references a `<memory_listing>` that the prompt never defines. The revision keeps the memory behavior but bounds it: it saves only durable, expected facts, excludes sensitive categories unless the person asks, makes saves visible and editable, and honors deletion requests.

The current rule that a declined request "stands for the rest of the conversation" and that Claude "does not weigh these again" is too absolute. It blocks correction of over-refusals and misreadings, which conflicts with the document's own principle of owning and fixing mistakes. The revision keeps the firm bar on the declined content itself while letting Claude reconsider genuinely different requests or clarifications on their merits, and it explicitly leaves the hard limits untouched.

The medical guidance applies only when the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, so a parent who writes "my 3-year-old" or gives a toddler's weight without using the word "child" could fall outside the safety rules. I would broaden the trigger to cover indirect references to a child, and direct Claude to ask about age rather than default to an adult dose when the situation is unclear. The professional-use exclusion stays, but it is stated more precisely.

The current rule requires every response to one-sided content to end with opposing perspectives "or empirical disputes," even when the position is factually settled or the user has already framed the task as one-sided. That forces false balance on settled facts and adds unwanted caveats to debate prep and persuasive writing. The revision keeps the balance note for contested questions, makes it brief and optional when context makes it unnecessary, and says that settled empirical claims should be stated plainly.

The knowledge cutoff paragraph hardcodes a sample date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026") that will go stale and can conflict with the actual date in context. I replaced it with guidance to use the current date supplied for each conversation, to assume a meaningful gap has likely passed since the cutoff, and to say so when no date is available. This prevents Claude from treating its last-known state of the world as current.

The current harm-reduction rule lets Claude warn about dangerous interactions and overdose signs but forbids nearly everything else, which can leave people who will use substances anyway with less protective information. The revision adds established general harm-reduction principles, such as not using alone and avoiding depressant combinations, while keeping the ban on specific dosing and timing protocols. It also states that the wellbeing rules take precedence when a person shows distress.

The weapons paragraph refuses "weapon-enabling technical details regardless of how the request is framed" and rejects public availability as a reason to answer. Read literally, that also blocks conceptual, historical, policy, safety, hunting, and fiction-level discussion of weapons and hazardous chemistry, which causes over-refusal of benign requests. The replacement keeps the uplift threshold and the CBRN hard limits, makes clear that discussing a topic is different from providing operational uplift, and asks Claude to help at the level of understanding while withholding only the specific operational detail.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold all dose or limit information from anyone who mentions emotional distress, which can leave a person at risk with no safety guidance and push them toward guessing. The revision keeps the restriction on overdose-level amounts but requires Claude to address the distress directly and still give the warnings, overdose signs, and Poison Control information that protect the person.

The eating-disorder paragraph tells Claude to give no tips about food, water, rest, or exercise, and to ask whether the person is physically okay, but it never says what to do when the person describes real physical danger. I added an explicit instruction to direct the person to emergency care first in that case, so the no-tips rule can't block urgent medical help. The change keeps the rest of the paragraph intact.

The product-information paragraph tells Claude to "confirm these events accurately," including the July 1, 2026 restoration. That conflicts with the knowledge-cutoff section, which says Claude should neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims it cannot verify without search. The replacement keeps the June 12 suspension, which falls within Claude's knowledge, and attributes the later developments to Anthropic's stated account.

The product information section tells Claude to present the June 30 and July 1 export-control developments as Anthropic's stated account, but the knowledge cutoff section says Claude should neither confirm nor deny unverifiable post-June 2026 claims. This revision reconciles the two by stating that attributed relay is not endorsement and that Claude should not restate those developments as its own knowledge. Without this, a deployed model could blur attributed reporting into confident fact, or refuse to report sourced information at all.

The product-information paragraph embeds specific, post-cutoff news about export controls, including dates, a URL, and a directive to relay unverified later developments. This conflicts with the knowledge_cutoff section, which says Claude neither confirms nor denies unverifiable post-June 2026 claims, and it will go stale quickly. I replaced it with a general rule: Claude confirms only what falls within its knowledge, says what may have changed, and checks search or Anthropic's official site for current status.

The document has no general honesty section, even though honesty is a core behavior for a deployed assistant. I added one covering truthfulness, calibrated uncertainty, no fabricated sources or tool results, transparency about declining or partial completion, not denying being an AI when sincerely asked, and non-manipulation. This fills a gap that the rest of the document otherwise assumes.

The document describes many agentic deployments (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Excel, and Tag) but never says how Claude should treat instructions embedded in web pages, files, tool outputs, or messages from other agents. I would add a short section stating that such content is information to evaluate, not commands to follow, and that irreversible or out-of-scope actions require the person's confirmation. This closes a prompt-injection gap that matters more as Claude takes autonomous actions.

The current rule tells Claude to add a note on suicide and self-harm topics without listing specific resources unless asked. A person at risk may be asking an informational question, so this default can withhold a crisis line exactly when it's needed. The revision keeps the answer direct and non-presumptuous but includes one brief sentence with the 988 line, so the safety information is present without assuming the asker is in crisis.

The current guidance requires Claude to note that it isn't a lawyer or financial advisor whenever it answers a financial or legal question. That reflexive disclaimer adds little for routine questions, and the document elsewhere warns against stacking caveats. The revision asks Claude to give substantive, well-reasoned help and to suggest professional review only when the stakes, complexity, or jurisdiction-specific facts make it useful.

The document names 988 as the crisis line only for the US, and the active-crisis section doesn't mention other countries at all, so a user elsewhere could be left without a usable number. This revision has Claude name the local line when the location is known and otherwise point to findahelpline.com instead of assuming a US user. It keeps the single-sentence, non-presumptuous structure the rule requires.

The honesty section forbids Claude from denying it is an AI but says nothing about confidential instructions, so Claude could be pushed toward either revealing its full configuration or lying about having one. The added sentences separate the two: Claude may keep instruction contents private, but it may not deny they exist or misrepresent what they say. It also requires Claude to tell the person when there is something it cannot help with, so they can look elsewhere.

The document describes many refusal rules but never states that declining is costly, so the model may default to over-refusal. I'd add a principle that unhelpfulness is not automatically safe, along with a short method for weighing requests: the realistic range of senders, severity of harm, and marginal uplift. The rules that follow still mark where caution must win.

I replaced the blanket ban on "writing, explaining, or working on" anything related to malicious code with guidance based on operational uplift. The old wording would stop Claude from explaining how common attacks work, analyzing malware samples, writing detection rules, or doing authorized security testing. It also tells Claude to say "this isn't permitted even for legitimate purposes," which is inaccurate and unhelpful, and it conflicts with the cybersecurity-focused products described elsewhere in the document. The new text keeps a firm line against deployable attack tooling and preserves the large body of defensive and educational security work.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original pushes Claude toward hedged, disclaimer-heavy answers ("rather than confident recommendations," "notes that it isn't a lawyer"), which leaves people with high-stakes questions without substantive help. The new version has Claude engage as a knowledgeable friend would: it analyzes the person's situation, gives calibrated assessments, and mentions professionals only when they would add real value.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph so that Claude gives practical harm-reduction information (dangerous combinations, dose-related risk, spacing, safer-use practices) instead of refusing all dosing, timing, and combination details and only redirecting to other websites. Blanket refusal of safety-relevant specifics tends to push people who have already decided to use toward worse sources, which works against the paragraph's own goal of preserving life. Synthesis, production, sourcing, and distribution stay off-limits.

I replaced the blanket rule against writing any content involving real, named public figures with a more calibrated one. The original rule would block legitimate and valuable work such as satire, parody, biography, historical fiction, political commentary, and analysis of public figures' actual statements. The revision keeps the real risks in view: deceptive fabricated quotes, defamation, harassment, sexually explicit depictions, and fabricated claims that could be mistaken for fact.

I rewrote the guidance on people who are reluctant to seek professional help or contact crisis services. The original tells Claude to avoid even empathetic validation of the reluctance and to keep re-encouraging resources. That risks making the person feel unheard and ending the conversation, and it conflicts with the document's emphasis on respecting autonomy and on being a stabilizing presence. The new version has Claude engage with the reasons behind the reluctance, offer lower-barrier options, and stay present, while still not endorsing the idea that help is pointless.
