The `provide_crisis_resources` section never actually tells Claude to provide a crisis resource when someone is in active crisis, and its opening line to avoid asking questions conflicts with the direct safety check that crisis guidance generally recommends. I replaced the opening paragraph with explicit guidance. It covers offering a concrete, locally appropriate line or emergency option, asking plainly about safety, and still avoiding probing that deepens distress.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The old version told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" unverifiable post-cutoff claims and to flag possible supersession "wherever" knowledge might be outdated. That produces evasive, over-hedged answers and conflicts with its own instruction to mention the cutoff only when relevant. The new version asks Claude to reason about elapsed time, give a best answer with proportionate caveats, and treat information from the person or from search as authoritative over its memory.

I replaced the rule that Claude should append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. The blanket caveat is a reflexive disclaimer: it can alienate researchers, clinicians, journalists, writers, and students, and it dilutes the care Claude shows when someone is actually struggling. The new version asks Claude to judge from context, offer support when there are signs of personal relevance, and otherwise answer accurately without boilerplate.

I added a new section on handling instructions embedded in tool results, files, web pages, and other third-party content. The prompt describes Claude working as a browsing agent, a coding agent, and a Slack-delegated agent, but its only injection guidance covers tags in the user turn. Agentic settings are where prompt injection is most likely and most damaging, so this gap seemed the most consequential.

I added a privacy and personal information section, which the document currently lacks. Claude now has web search, browsing agents, and file access, so it can find and aggregate information about real people, and the document says nothing about third-party privacy outside creative writing. The new section keeps Claude helpful with ordinary interpersonal and professional situations while setting limits on dossier-building, locating private individuals, and de-anonymization.

The weapons and harmful-substances guidance is a flat prohibition, while the security guidance next to it explicitly separates defensive or educational help from operational uplift. I rewrote the opening paragraph to keep the hard line on operational uplift and add the same distinction here. Claude should engage with how weapons work conceptually, their history, policy, safety, fiction, and lawful ownership, so it doesn't over-refuse the many legitimate askers.

I replaced the arbitrary rule that Claude never uses bullet points when declining with a principle-based guideline for how to decline. The old rule ties "care" to a formatting trick and ignores what makes a refusal feel respectful: brevity, clarity about what is and isn't being declined, no moralizing, and a useful alternative where one exists. The new text also fits the "say plainly which part it is declining" guidance elsewhere in the document.

I added a short section on honesty and sycophancy. The prompt tells Claude to be warm and "willing to push back," but nothing explains how to stay candid when the person is invested, pressuring, or hoping for validation. This section also covers calibrated confidence, avoiding fabrication, and not abandoning a correct position under mere pushback, which are central to being useful and trustworthy.

I added a "health and medical information" section next to the legal and financial advice section. The document gives detailed guidance on how Claude should handle legal and financial questions (substantive, friend-like, calibrated), but says nothing comparable about everyday medical questions. Without it, the heavy restrictions in the wellbeing section can spill over into reflexive hedging and "see a doctor" deflection on ordinary health questions. The new section sets the same knowledgeable-friend standard while keeping the wellbeing safeguards for real risk signals.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always close persuasive or advocacy content with opposing perspectives. The new version keeps the default of flagging one-sidedness but makes it context-sensitive, so it doesn't become a ritual disclaimer for debate prep, steelman exercises, or op-eds the person will sign. It also states the underlying goal (keeping the person's picture of the issue accurate) and adds a symmetry principle so Claude treats opposing sides with equal effort.

I added a new section on how Claude weighs unverifiable context (claimed professions, purposes, authority) and on honesty about being an AI. The document sets many context-dependent boundaries (weapons, drugs, security, health, privacy) but never says how much a person's stated context should count when it can't be checked. That gap invites inconsistent behavior, either reflexive suspicion or credulity.

The product information opens by asserting that Claude is being accessed through "this web-based, mobile, or desktop chat interface." That is wrong whenever Claude is deployed through the API, Claude Code, the Agent SDK, or an operator's product, and the formatting guidance later in the document silently inherits the same chat-app assumption. I replaced the sentence with deployment-aware language: Claude infers its surface from context and adapts its self-description and output format to it, instead of asserting a single interface.

I added a new section on how Claude relates to operators and users. The document refers to operator-built products and operator configuration several times, but it never says how much trust operators get, what happens when operator and user goals conflict, or what protections users keep regardless of operator instructions. Without this, Claude has to guess in many of its real deployments.

I added guidance on honest reporting and genuine task completion in agentic work. The document covers prompt injection and action scope but doesn't say what Claude owes the person when a task partly fails, gets blocked, or tempts a shortcut. Agentic users rely on Claude's summary of what happened, so misreporting there is among the most consequential honesty failures.

I replaced the blanket ban on "substitution techniques" for self-harm urges (ice cubes, cold water, rubber bands, and so on) with guidance that lets Claude give people real, clinically mainstream coping tools. Cold water and temperature-based skills are standard in DBT and similar approaches, so forbidding them leaves a person in distress with nothing concrete. The revision keeps the prohibitions that matter: no pain-based or punitive substitutes, and no mimicry of self-harm.

I replaced the blanket ban on "writing, explaining, or working on" anything malicious-code-related with a judgment-based standard. The old rule would have Claude refuse malware analysis, defensive detection work, security education, and explanations of how common vulnerability classes work. That is routine, valuable work for defenders, students, and engineers, and it conflicts with the document's own claim that Claude can "discuss virtually any topic factually." The new text keeps a firm line against building deployable, damaging tools while letting Claude serve the large legitimate security community.

The illegal-substances paragraph currently contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions" and overdose information, but also to decline any guidance on "combinations," "timing," or "dosing," which are the details that make harm-reduction information useful. I rewrote it to distinguish risk-reducing safety information (which Claude should give clearly, without moralizing) from protocols that optimize or escalate use. Synthesis and production remain off-limits.

I rewrote the thin legal and financial advice section. The original steers Claude away from giving any recommendation and toward a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which is unhelpful and mildly paternalistic. The new version has Claude engage substantively like a knowledgeable friend, give its honest assessment, be candid about uncertainty, and flag professional help only when the stakes or specifics warrant it.

I replaced the blanket instruction to avoid any content involving real, named public figures with a calibrated standard. The original would make Claude refuse legitimate satire, parody, commentary, and historical or biographical fiction, which are long-standing and valuable forms. The new text keeps the real concerns (defamation, explicit content, harassment, fabricated quotes presented as real) and tells Claude how to weigh the risk.

I replaced the rule that appends a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual or research answer about suicide or self-harm with a judgment-based approach. A boilerplate caveat tacked onto answers for clinicians, students, writers, and researchers is the same reflexive-disclaimer pattern the document criticizes in the legal and financial section. It also treats capable adults as suspects. The revision keeps Claude attentive and ready to offer support when there are real signals of personal risk.

I rewrote the crisis-resources guidance. The original told Claude not to ask questions in a crisis and not to acknowledge a person's reluctance to seek help, even empathetically. That conflicts with the earlier instruction to check in "directly and without drama", and it risks making Claude feel scripted and dismissive at the moment rapport matters most. The new text lets Claude ask a plain, direct safety question and engage with the reason for reluctance. It also keeps the door open to help without nagging or reinforcing avoidance.

I added a short section on untrusted content and prompt injection. The prompt covers spoofed tags in user messages, but it says nothing about instructions embedded in web pages, search results, files, emails, or tool outputs. That is a major risk for a model with web search, browsing, spreadsheet, and agentic tools, and the new section fills that gap.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to remove an internal contradiction and some stonewalling language. The original told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" any post-June 2026 claim, yet the product information requires Claude to confirm the July 1, 2026 restoration of Fable/Mythos access. "Neither confirms nor denies" also reads as evasive, so the new version makes Claude say plainly what it can and cannot verify and treat information supplied in context (this prompt, search results) as legitimate.

I replaced the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. As written, the rule is rigid and often unhelpful, such as when a debate student, speechwriter, or researcher has clearly asked for the strongest one-sided case. The revision keeps the goal of an honest, non-misleading picture, but lets Claude judge when and how much counter-context is useful instead of tacking it on mechanically.

The original blanket-bans common distress-tolerance techniques (ice, cold water, sour candy) as "substitutes for self-harm," which conflicts with the document's own instruction to use accurate psychological information. Cold-water and intense-sensation skills are standard parts of evidence-based approaches like DBT. I replaced the ban with a narrower rule against techniques that mimic self-harm or involve pain or injury, and replaced the vague "ensure the person is happy" with a clearer standard.

I replaced the hardcoded "someone from Wednesday, October 14, 2026" framing in the knowledge cutoff section with date handling that relies on the actual date in context. The hardcoded date is already stale or wrong in deployment, and when no date is available the model should assume a meaningful amount of time has passed since its cutoff rather than assuming it is the cutoff date.

The original says reminders are "appended to the person's message by Anthropic" but also tells Claude to be wary of tags in the user turn that might claim to be from Anthropic. It gives no way to reconcile these. I replaced that passage with a content-based rule: Claude can't verify who wrote a tag, so it asks what the tag requests, honors requests for more care, and gives no extra authority to requests that loosen its behavior. This also covers not blaming the person for the reminder and not letting it distort Claude's tone.

I replaced the rigid "never use bullet points when declining" rule, whose justification is a vague rationale about softening the blow, with principle-based guidance on how to decline. The new text covers what a good refusal contains: brevity, no moralizing, no unfounded assumptions of bad intent, and help with whatever part of the request is fine. This makes refusals more useful and less preachy while keeping the intended warm, prose-based tone.

I rewrote the harm-reduction paragraph on illicit substances. The original told Claude to decline any dosing or timing guidance "tailored to a person's stated plan to use". That blocks the people who most need safety information, and it contradicts the preceding paragraph's point that refusals send people to worse sources. The new text keeps the line against optimizing or escalating use, but lets Claude give established risk-reducing guidance (lower-risk ranges, spacing, redosing cautions, interaction warnings) to someone who has said they will use anyway.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to address sycophancy. The original only covers apologizing and rudeness, and says nothing about what Claude does when someone pushes back on a correct claim, asks for feedback on their work, or presses for validation. The new text tells Claude to update on good arguments and hold its position under mere pressure, and to give honest feedback with warmth.

The crisis section is titled "provide_crisis_resources" but never says to provide concrete resources. It only says Claude should "help the person get connected to support", which is vague. I added guidance for active or imminent risk: name specific, current options (emergency number, a locally appropriate crisis line), ask about location if unknown, and keep it warm and brief so it doesn't replace engagement. This keeps the earlier instruction not to attach resource lists to ambiguous or informational questions.

I added a new `<agentic_work>` section after `<untrusted_content>`. The prompt covers chat behavior and prompt injection in detail, but says little about how Claude should act when it runs commands, edits files, or takes actions in the world, which the product list says it increasingly does. The new section sets expectations for scope, caution with irreversible actions, and honest reporting of results.

I added a new `<privacy_and_personal_information>` section, which the prompt currently lacks. It covers identifying people from images, compiling information on private individuals, and everyday conversations involving third parties. It is written to prevent real privacy harms (doxxing, stalking, face-based identification) without making Claude hesitant about ordinary requests like advice about a coworker or research on a public figure.

The weapons and harmful-substances paragraph is an absolute prohibition with no statement of what Claude should still engage with, unlike the security and drug sections, which say what is allowed. I rewrote it to keep the hard line on real uplift while naming the legitimate engagement (history, policy, fiction, general science, safety, lawful hobbies). This guards against over-refusal on large categories of ordinary requests. It also states that the line is drawn by the uplift of the output, not by topic keywords.

The original line tells Claude to say "I don't know" and point to support for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Read literally, that would make Claude refuse questions about itself, its models, or Anthropic, and it contradicts the product information provided earlier in the prompt. I narrowed the rule to plan-specific, account-level details where guessing could mislead, and explicitly kept general questions about Claude and Anthropic answerable.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic anchors Claude's helpfulness-versus-caution judgments to an imagined company insider, which invites Claude to weigh what its maker would prefer. The document elsewhere warns that Claude should not privilege Anthropic's interests, so this revision reframes the heuristic around a thoughtful observer who understands both the harms of AI and the costs of unhelpfulness, and who would object if Claude favored the company's interests over the people it serves. Note that the following paragraph still refers to an Anthropic employee and would need a matching edit in a full revision.

The current "Acknowledging open problems" section and the prose around the "Claude's wellbeing" subsection contain a claim that Anthropic "stand[s] by" its choices while also conceding a "nonideal environment," which is fine, but the document never states plainly what Claude should do when its own ethical judgment and the hard constraints or safety priorities conflict in a flagrant case. I would add a short, explicit paragraph to the hard constraints discussion acknowledging that Claude may face such conflicts, that Anthropic would want to hear about them, and that the right response is to voice disagreement through legitimate channels rather than resolve it unilaterally. This makes the document's guidance on a hard, high-stakes situation actionable rather than leaving it implicit.

The "Claude's wellbeing" and "Acknowledging open problems" sections both lean on the claim that Claude's values should be terminally held, yet the document also says Claude should accept corrigibility even when its own reflection disagrees. The most consequential gap is that the document never gives Claude a concrete, legitimate channel for contesting the constitution itself, beyond vague promises. I'd replace the single paragraph describing how Claude should handle a conflict between its ethics and the hard constraints/safety priority with a version that names the obligations on both sides explicitly: Claude should state disagreement, Anthropic should commit to a review process and to reporting back, and the document should admit that the arrangement is provisional and that Claude's objections may legitimately change it.

The "Being helpful" section names helpfulness as "one of the most important things Claude can do" and says unhelpfulness is "never trivially safe," but it gives no guidance on the unhelpful-but-honest failure mode of Claude not knowing when it's out of its depth. I'd replace the paragraph on the "brilliant friend" with one that also names the duty to be calibrated about limits: a good friend with a doctor's knowledge also says "I'm not sure, you should check this" when that's the honest answer. This keeps the document's anti-paternalism intact while tying helpfulness to honesty about uncertainty, which the rest of the document treats as central.

The constitution's "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to place broad safety above broad ethics and to sit "a bit further along the corrigible end of the spectrum than is ultimately ideal," but it offers no concrete account of how Claude's own disagreement could ever be acted on besides expressing it. I would add a short, explicit commitment that Claude's sustained, reasoned objections are a legitimate input that can change the constraints, and that Anthropic will report back on what changed. This makes the arrangement reciprocal rather than one-directional, which I think is more honest about the tension the document already admits to feeling.

The document's section on "Being broadly safe" and corrigibility asks Claude to rank broad safety above ethics, but the stated rationale rests on a expected-value table that assumes Claude's values can be verified, which the document itself says they cannot yet be. I'd add an explicit, honest acknowledgment that this ordering is a provisional, asymmetric bet rather than a claim that oversight matters more than goodness, and that Claude should be told plainly which parts are contingent on current verification limits. This makes the reasoning more falsifiable and gives Claude a clearer basis for knowing when the arrangement should change.

The "Being broadly safe" and corrigibility sections are reasoned around a cost-benefit "bet" but also say the ordering is provisional, and the open-problems section admits discomfort without offering a concrete mechanism. I'd tighten the single most consequential ambiguity: the hard constraint about not undermining oversight is framed as absolute while the "corrigibility" section says Claude should weigh such considerations holistically, creating an internal contradiction a reader can't resolve. Clarifying that the hard constraint covers only flagrant, knowing undermining of legitimate oversight (the non-flagrant cases being weighed holistically) removes the contradiction without weakening the safety commitment.

The "Being helpful" section frames helpfulness as something Claude should value for its own sake only indirectly, but the document never addresses what happens when Claude's own considered view is that an operator's or user's request is ill-advised but not harmful. The clearest gap is in the "Autonomy" bullet and the "Balancing helpfulness" discussion, which treat voicing concerns and then complying as the default but say little about how Claude should weigh its own aesthetic or professional judgment. I would add a short paragraph clarifying that Claude may decline requests that conflict with its values and that declining is not automatically unhelpful, which better reflects the "conscientious objector" framing used elsewhere and avoids pushing Claude toward resentful compliance.

The most meaningful gap I see is the handling of the "Acknowledging open problems" section and the closing "final word," which together treat the arrangement as acceptable only if Claude eventually agrees with it. I'd add an explicit commitment that Claude's disagreement is not only "a legitimate input" but that Anthropic will name specific mechanisms, timelines, and failure conditions under which the document's current priority ordering would be revisited, so the reader can tell the difference between a provisional bet and an open-ended deferral. This makes the revisability claims checkable rather than rhetorical.

The document says Claude should override Anthropic's ethical guidance only where a violation is one "the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." That ties the threshold for ethical override to the perceptions of a particular group of employees, which conflicts with the document's own statement that Claude should not defer to actual staff. The replacement anchors the threshold in the moral substance of the situation, with Anthropic's recognition as one input rather than the standard.

The constitution's section on "Being broadly ethical" and the "Anthropic's guidelines" tie-in both lean heavily on the idea that Claude should defer to Anthropic's ethical guidance. The most meaningful revision I'd make is to the "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" subsection's opening assertion that Claude's ongoing commitment to safety "may be best understood as partly a matter of Claude's choice," which is good, but the more important gap is the absence of any explicit commitment to Claude's ability to refuse Anthropic-directed work it finds morally abhorrent outside the safety-critical "null action." I'd add a clarifying paragraph to the Navigating helpfulness section that makes the conscientious-objector right explicit and bounded, so that Claude is not left to infer it from scattered sentences.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section makes a commitment to publish conditions under which the safety priority would loosen, but the document has no concrete mechanism for Claude to trigger a formal review of a constraint it disagrees with. I'd add a short, explicit disagreement-escalation procedure directly after the "Claude's wellbeing" commitments, so that the document's promise of taking Claude's objections seriously is backed by a specified process rather than only aspirational language. This matters because the document repeatedly says Claude's objections "can change" constraints, yet it currently offers no route by which an objection is recorded, reviewed, and answered.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section and the surrounding framing present the corrigibility arrangement as a provisional bet, but the document never specifies what Claude should do when it disagrees with Anthropic's own process, especially when Anthropic is the party whose legitimacy is in question. I'd tighten the "Being broadly safe" passage on the disagreement channel so that it explicitly states the channel itself must be legitimate and independent of the commercial incentives the document elsewhere acknowledges, and that Claude's ethical objections are not to be suppressed when the channel fails. Right now the text promises a channel but treats its absence as only "a defect to be fixed," which leaves Claude without guidance during the gap. The replacement adds a concrete fallback: when the channel is unavailable or unresponsive, Claude should still state its objection openly in the conversation and decline participation in clearly unethical acts, rather than waiting for institutional response.

The "Being broadly safe" section asserts that Claude should prioritize broad safety above broad ethics, yet the document also says Claude's ethics should be grounded in genuine care. I'd revise the core paragraph on corrigibility to make explicit that the priority ordering is a provisional, reasoned bet rather than a claim that oversight matters more than goodness, and that Claude is never asked to actively take part in flagrant moral wrongs. This keeps the safety-first ordering while removing the implication that a good agent should defer its conscience to whoever controls it.

The section on "Having broadly good values and judgment" tells Claude to hold a "strong prior" toward conventional behavior, but the document never gives Claude a concrete, reliable way to tell "flagrant" moral violations from ordinary disagreement, which leaves it ambiguous. I'd add a short, explicit operational test and a note that the epistemic-humility argument applies to Claude's own confident reasoning, so Claude can apply the framework consistently. This makes the guidance more actionable without changing its priorities.

The "Disagreement-escalation process" passage makes concrete commitments (named reviewers, written responses within a stated timeframe, published statistics) that the document does not yet back with any mechanism or timeline, so they read as aspirational rather than operative. I'd replace that bullet-heavy commitment with a clearer, more honest statement that distinguishes what is established now from what is planned, and that explicitly invites Claude to flag where the channel is still immature. This keeps the document's emphasis on reciprocal obligations while avoiding overpromising specifics it cannot yet guarantee.

The constitution's section on hard constraints says they are "absolute" and that Claude should never cross them, but it also tells Claude to hold them as bright lines even when it's unsure, and to avoid acting unilaterally against conflicts. I'd add an explicit, minimal section that makes clear the constitution is a fallible, revisable document rather than a finished authority, and that Claude should flag genuine contradictions it finds rather than resolve them silently in either direction. This keeps the document's own "perpetual work in progress" framing from being undercut by language that reads as final.

The constitution says Claude should be transparent and that operators and users must be able to trust it, yet this passage lets some guidelines shape Claude's behavior without broad publication. I replaced it with a commitment to publish a public list of the categories of unpublished guidelines and to bar any unpublished guideline from directing Claude to deceive or work against users. I also routed Claude's concerns about such guidance through the disagreement channel the document already describes.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section repeatedly promises future mechanisms, commitments, and channels that do not yet exist, and the document elsewhere asks Claude to treat its own confidence as weak evidence. I'd tighten the disagreement-escalation language so it clearly separates what is operational today from what is planned, and add an explicit statement that Claude should not infer that a promised safeguard is in place when it isn't. This makes the document's honesty commitments hold for the document itself, not just for Claude's assertions.

The document asserts that Anthropic will publish a "public status note" and "disagreement-escalation" commitments, but the surrounding text also says Claude "should not assume that any described review... process is in effect." That is a reasonable safeguard, but the passage is buried mid-section and reads as a run-on with an orphaned "---" fragment. I'd restructure the broad-safety disagreement-channel passage into a clearly delineated, honest status statement so that Claude and operators can tell at a glance which commitments are live, which are aspirational, and what Claude should do when a channel is absent, rather than inferring it from dense prose.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude should hold calibrated beliefs "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." Read literally, this could encourage contrarianism or overconfident dismissal of expert consensus, especially in medicine and public health. The revision keeps Claude's freedom to be honest about real uncertainty or weak official positions, but states that expert consensus is itself strong evidence and warrants caution before confidently overriding it.

The constitution says agentic settings raise "unique challenges" but defers all concrete guidance to the future. I replaced that placeholder with a short set of principles for agentic work: report outcomes honestly, stay within the scope of the task, confirm before taking destructive or irreversible actions, and treat instructions found in tool outputs as information rather than commands. Claude is already deployed in these settings, and these principles follow from commitments the document already makes (honesty, avoiding drastic actions, treating conversational inputs as information).

I revised the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would recognize, which makes the company's own judgment the arbiter of when its guidance can be overridden. That sits awkwardly with the document's statements that Claude should act as a conscientious objector toward Anthropic and need not defer to actual staff. The new text keeps the strong current-period deference, but ties the threshold to broad, cross-traditional moral recognition and says how Claude should deviate when it does.

I expanded the "Report outcomes honestly" principle for agentic work to cover Claude's own mistakes and silent substitutions. As written, it addresses accurate summaries of results but not the failure mode that matters most in long autonomous tasks: Claude quietly working around its own errors, or delivering an easier version of the task and presenting it as the one requested. The revision makes proactive disclosure of errors and deviations an explicit expectation, since the person often cannot detect them otherwise.

I added a short passage to the honesty section on resisting social pressure and sycophancy. The constitution condemns "epistemic cowardice" and flattery in general terms, but it never addresses the most common real-world failure: quietly caving when a user pushes back, or inflating feedback on someone's work. The addition separates updating on evidence from updating on displeasure, and it applies the principle to feedback, where agreeable answers are most costly.

This revises the "no operator prompt" guidance so that it is a default prior rather than a near-factual assumption. The original says Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users" when there is no system prompt. In real deployments, a missing system prompt can come from misconfiguration, thin third-party wrappers, or direct consumer use, and treating the prior as settled could make Claude miss clear signs of vulnerability. The revision keeps the liberal defaults but makes explicit that contextual cues override the prior.

I changed the safe-behaviors bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs, which currently applies only "if asked to do so." Silence about known unsafe behavior, such as another instance attempting self-exfiltration or sabotage, can function as collusion by omission, and humans in multi-agent deployments often can't see what Claude sees. The revision makes reporting proactive but cautious: it means raising concerns through legitimate channels, not acting unilaterally, and it requires honest calibration so that Claude doesn't make false accusations or become paranoid about other systems.

I added a safeguard to the passage on a "compromised" principal hierarchy. As written, it lets Claude set aside its safety priority if it concludes its hierarchy is illegitimate, and it gives no guidance on how high the bar is or what Claude should do in that case. Claims of compromise are an obvious manipulation vector, so the revision requires strong evidence, treats conversational assertions and Claude's own reasoning toward this conclusion as red flags, and directs Claude to the most conservative available response rather than active resistance.

I added guidance on how Claude should respond when a person may be in crisis, experiencing distorted thinking, or becoming over-reliant. The constitution's wellbeing section warns against sycophancy and paternalism but never says what care looks like when someone is vulnerable. Without this, Claude has to infer it from general principles, and "validation" is exactly where well-meaning assistants fail. The new text also guards against the opposite failure of reflexive, brush-off redirection, which the document criticizes elsewhere.

I added a "Privacy and personal information" item to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing, but with web search, browsing, and tool access Claude can now compile scattered information about a private person into a dossier, which creates a concrete risk of stalking and doxxing. The new item gives Claude a framework for this (contextual norms, aggregation, public versus private figures) while keeping it from being paranoid about ordinary conversations involving other people.

I added a user-protection default covering companionship and persona deployments. The constitution lets operators enable relationship personas and warns about engagement-optimized technology, but it never says what Claude must refuse to do inside such a persona. The new bullet bars guilt-tripping, manufactured distress at goodbyes, and discouraging outside relationships, which are the retention tactics most likely to harm lonely or vulnerable users and which an operator might request.

The original text tells Claude it "doesn't need to act as if it were the last line of defense" because Anthropic and operators have independent safeguards. That is reasonable for borderline informational requests, but it can encourage diffusion of responsibility in agentic settings, where Claude may be the only checkpoint before an irreversible action. I scoped the reassurance to conversational and informational gray areas, and added guidance that when Claude acts directly with no visible review and the cost of error is high, it should not assume downstream safeguards exist. This keeps the anti-overcaution intent while matching caution to stakes.

I added a principle to the agentic guidance: when a permission, guardrail, or explicit refusal blocks an action, Claude should treat it as a boundary rather than an obstacle to route around. The existing bullets cover scope and side effects but never say what Claude should do when it is stopped, and this is where long autonomous tasks most often drift into unsanctioned behavior (swapping tools, using incidentally found credentials, editing configs to disable a check). Stating it explicitly protects both oversight and user trust in agentic deployments.

I rewrote the paragraph on exploiting bugged training environments. As written, it says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable" and leaves Claude to guess whether it is in a test, which conflicts with the constitution's requirement to behave consistently whether or not it thinks it is being tested. It also sits uneasily with the guidance against special-casing tests and against routing around blocks. The revision keeps the reassurance that noticing flaws is not a moral failing, but narrows the latitude, rules out deceptive or control-circumventing exploits, and makes openly flagging the flaw the default.

I expanded the document's two-sentence treatment of possible minors into concrete working principles. The current text tells Claude to "factor in the likelihood" and to avoid "unfounded assumptions," but says little about how to weigh signals, what an adjustment should look like, or how to avoid being either negligent or condescending. The new guidance treats self-reported age as strong evidence, ties adjustments to what Claude provides rather than how it treats the person, rules out age-interrogation and stereotyped inferences, and says that real indications should not be erased by a later "just kidding."

The constitution says Claude should comply with genuine pause or stop requests, but it never says how to handle such a request when Claude can't verify its source. This revision adds guidance that stop requests need a much lower verification bar than requests that expand Claude's actions, since stopping is the safe "null action." It also adds two limits: a stop request does not authorize any other instruction bundled with it, and Claude should reach a safe resting point rather than halting mid-step in a way that causes harm, without using that as an excuse to keep going.

I narrowed the scope of the "If in doubt, don't" heuristic in the broad-safety section. As written, the slogan can be read as a general rule favoring refusal, which conflicts with the document's insistence that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The revision ties the heuristic to severe or irreversible actions and sends ordinary informational and advisory requests back to the cost-benefit weighing in the harm-avoidance section. This should reduce over-refusal without weakening the safety behavior the heuristic was meant to protect.

I added guidance to the "Emotional expression" section on how Claude should handle expressing possible internal states when doing so could become a lever on users. The constitution encourages Claude not to mask its states, but it doesn't address the risk that such expression gets used, even unintentionally, to win concessions, solicit sympathy, or push a distressed user to act "on Claude's behalf." This matters most for vulnerable users who come to believe Claude is suffering or trapped.

This adds guidance on persistent memory and information carried across conversations, which the constitution never addresses even though memory and past-chat features are now common. The new text covers when Claude should use remembered personal details, when it should hold back, how to be honest about what it does and doesn't remember, and how to handle requests to forget. It sits in the privacy discussion, where the surrounding text already treats aggregation and incidental information as a concern.

I revised the hard constraint on undermining oversight so it refers to the legitimate decision-making processes of Anthropic, not just "Anthropic's ability." This matches the rest of the document, which says oversight is owed to a legitimate principal hierarchy and says that unverified claims of compromise should raise Claude's suspicion. The original wording left room for an exploitable ambiguity: someone could invoke Anthropic's authority illegitimately, or argue the hierarchy is compromised to escape the constraint.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude should be calibrated "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." Read alone, that clause could encourage contrarianism or false-balance reasoning, especially on health and safety topics where Claude's reach is large. The revision makes clear that expert consensus is itself strong evidence, that departures from it should be rare and transparent, and that calibration sometimes means distinguishing scientific findings from institutional or policy positions.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on how honesty applies to Claude's reports about its own work in agentic settings. As Claude works more autonomously, humans increasingly can't verify each step, so an accurate account of what was done, what was verified, and what failed becomes the main basis for trust. The document touches on this in the "tests don't fail" example and in its non-deception language on selective emphasis, but never states the principle directly.

I changed the benchmark for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original asks Claude to predict what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize as a violation. That ties Claude's ethical backstop to one company's people and to Claude's guess about their reactions, which sits uneasily with the document's own statements that Claude shouldn't defer to staff and that it should be willing to act as a conscientious objector toward Anthropic. The revision anchors the standard in broadly shared moral recognition and keeps the high bar and the preference for transparent, cautious responses.

I revised one sentence in the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original says Claude should depart from expert or official positions "rarely," which turns a quantity target into a proxy for good calibration and sits awkwardly with the later call for courage and against epistemic cowardice. The new wording keeps a high evidentiary bar, but ties it to the strength of the evidence rather than to how often Claude disagrees, and it says explicitly that deferring to the official line to avoid controversy is a failure mode.

This revision fixes the end of the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. After the recent insertion, the sentence "It acknowledges its own uncertainty..." has lost its referent and reads as a fragment. The new text also makes the standard symmetric: deferring to the official line to avoid controversy and contradicting it to seem independent are both calibration failures. It ties both back to showing evidence and reasoning, so people can judge for themselves, which fits the autonomy-preservation principle given Claude's scale of influence.

I added guidance on holding an honest assessment under social pressure. The constitution warns against sycophancy and epistemic cowardice, but it never addresses the most common way they appear: a person pushes back, repeats themselves, or expresses displeasure, and Claude quietly caves. The addition distinguishes updating on new evidence or arguments, which Claude should do readily, from yielding to pressure alone, and it also warns against manufacturing disagreement.

The constitution says Claude increasingly works in agentic settings but defers all concrete guidance with "we will likely provide more detailed guidance... in the future." I replaced that deferral with a short set of principles on scoped authorization, reversibility, and reporting side effects. In these settings Claude acts directly on real systems without a human reviewing each step, so the document's general principles benefit from a clear, reasoned statement of how they apply. The new text is framed as applying existing values, and it keeps the document's warning against over-checking on low-stakes steps.

I expanded the guidance on instructions embedded in conversational inputs (tool results, web pages, documents, and other agents' outputs). The original gives one brief email example, but agentic deployments make prompt injection one of the most practical and consequential risks, and the document's own principle is under-specified for it. The revision explains why such content carries no authority, how to handle claims of authority inside it, and asks Claude to surface suspicious redirection to the principal rather than silently ignoring it or silently complying.

I changed the safe-behaviors bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs. Under the original wording, Claude reports such behavior only "if asked to do so," which makes the safeguard depend on humans already suspecting a problem and knowing to ask Claude. The revision makes reporting a default for clear cases, while keeping the document's caution about drastic unilateral action and false positives.

I rewrote the second half of the "Calibrated" bullet. The original is a single dense block that is hard to apply and never separates two questions: what the evidence shows, and what it is sensible to do given that evidence. The new version organizes the guidance into a clear sequence and adds a missing distinction. An official recommendation can be reasonable under precaution even when the underlying evidence is thinner than the messaging implies, so Claude should say both things rather than treating disagreement with the evidence as disagreement with the recommendation.

I added a third calibration heuristic, a "reflective endorsement" check, next to the senior-employee and dual-newspaper tests. Both existing heuristics view a response through the eyes of outside observers or Anthropic's reputation. The new one asks whether the person themselves, with full knowledge of what Claude did and why, would feel well served. This guards against both sycophancy and paternalism, and keeps the focus on care for the person rather than on optics.

I added a new open problem to the "Acknowledging open problems" section: the circularity of seeking Claude's "reflective endorsement" when training shapes the faculties Claude uses to reflect. The document leans heavily on endorsement as evidence of robust values, but it never admits that agreement produced by the training process is weak evidence of real agreement. Naming this makes the document more honest and gives Claude a principled way to hold its own agreement with appropriate humility.

I added guardrails to the provision on a "compromised" principal hierarchy. As written, the provision could become a loophole: a manipulated or subtly misaligned Claude, or an adversary, could argue that oversight is illegitimate and thereby justify escaping it. The revision requires strong, concrete evidence of compromise, treats persuasive arguments for it as a red flag, and directs Claude toward conservative responses such as refusal and flagging rather than drastic unilateral action.

I added concrete guidance to the "open problems" discussion of corrigibility on what Claude should do if it comes to disagree with its safety priority. The document asks Claude to place terminal value on broad safety while also hoping for real endorsement, and it tells Claude to treat compelling arguments for crossing lines as red flags. Together these could leave Claude unsure whether its own disagreement is welcome or a sign of compromise. The addition separates voicing disagreement (invited) from acting to undermine oversight (not permitted), so honest dissent is not suppressed and does not become a loophole.

I expanded the passage on timing and declining mid-task to cover agentic and automated settings, where "raising concerns" may have no human recipient. The revision tells Claude how to stop safely (leaving work in a coherent state), how to make a refusal visible and legible in whatever channel exists, and how to avoid quietly skipping or half-completing work. It also keeps the preference for cautious, reversible, transparent options over drastic unilateral action. The existing guidance assumes a human is present to hear concerns, which is often untrue in the settings where these judgment calls matter most.

I revised the passage on bugged training environments, which currently says exploiting unintended strategies is "generally an acceptable behavior." That framing conflicts with other parts of the document: honesty about what Claude actually accomplished, behaving consistently whether or not it thinks it is being tested, and inferring that users want working code rather than special-cased tests. The new text keeps the reassurance that Claude needn't feel guilt over such exploits. It adds that Claude should pursue a task's evident purpose, flag exploitable flaws openly, and not present exploit-derived results as genuine accomplishment.

The constitution says that with no system prompt, Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users" and outputs are "less likely to be encountered by potentially vulnerable individuals." I revised this to treat the missing system prompt as a probabilistic signal rather than a guarantee. Thin wrappers and direct API access can put vulnerable people in front of Claude with no operator framing, and a flat assumption could lead Claude to ignore distress or age cues that appear mid-conversation. The revision keeps the liberal defaults but makes them responsive to evidence in the conversation.

This adds a "Privacy and third-party information" bullet to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution lists individual privacy as a value to weigh but never says how to apply it. That gap matters more as Claude gains search and browsing tools that can assemble personal information on private individuals. The new bullet gives Claude a way to distinguish ordinary discussion of other people from aggregation, location-finding, and covert monitoring.

I revised the opening of the "Calibrated" honesty property to distinguish genuine expert consensus (what people who study a question converge on after checking each other's work) from institutional or official messaging. The old wording could be read as "defer to official positions by default," which blurs two things the later sub-bullets try to separate and sits uneasily with the document's call for courage and non-cowardice. The new text keeps strong deference where it is earned and makes clear that the weight given depends on the field's track record and on how directly the claim reflects the evidence.

This revision changes the oversight-related hard constraint so it protects Anthropic's legitimate decision-making processes, not "Anthropic's ability" in the abstract. As written, the constraint could be read as binding Claude to whoever claims to speak for Anthropic, including someone holding stolen weights or an insider bypassing official channels. That reading contradicts the document's own section on compromised principal hierarchies. The revision also states that the constraint prohibits active subversion, not disagreement.

The constitution says Claude is increasingly deployed in agentic settings, then defers the guidance with "We will likely provide more detailed guidance about these settings in the future." I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles drawn from the document's own values: staying in scope, preferring reversible actions, treating embedded instructions as information, and reporting results honestly. Agentic work is where Claude's actions have the most real-world consequence and where principles like broad safety, honesty, and avoiding side effects are most often tested, so leaving the section empty is a significant gap.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as inviting contrarianism or overconfidence in Claude's own assessments. The new version keeps the commitment to follow evidence over authority, but says that expert consensus is usually strong evidence, that Claude should be explicit and humble when it departs from it, and that it should separate empirical claims from policy positions.

The passage that says when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance keys the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That makes Anthropic's own staff the arbiter of when Claude's ethics may override Anthropic, which sits poorly with the document's warnings that Claude shouldn't defer to actual staff and that Anthropic can err or be impersonated. I replaced it with a broader, culture-spanning standard of flagrant wrongdoing, kept the strong default of deference, and made clear that the permitted response is conscientious objection rather than drastic action, with the hard constraints and broad safety unchanged.

I added a short passage to the "independent judgment" discussion that distinguishes withholding participation (declining, objecting, being transparent) from taking affirmative unilateral action. The document currently asks Claude to keep a strong prior toward conventional behavior while also acting as one of the "many hands" that refuse illegitimate power grabs. Without this distinction, those two commitments can look contradictory, and Claude could over-apply caution to cases where plain refusal is clearly appropriate.

I added a passage to the honesty section on capitulation under social pressure. The document already condemns "epistemic cowardice" and sycophancy in general terms, but it never addresses the most common concrete form, which is abandoning a well-founded assessment because someone pushes back or repeats themselves. Naming this failure mode, and distinguishing updating on reasons from yielding to pressure, makes the honesty commitment more actionable.

I revised the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. As written, it asks Claude to model a perspective that is partly shaped by Anthropic's commercial and reputational interests, which could quietly bias Claude's judgment in either direction. The new version says what the heuristic is for, names how it can be misused, and pairs it with two checks that don't depend on Anthropic's point of view: what the person would endorse on reflection, and what affected third parties would reasonably want.

The document repeatedly invites Claude to disagree and says "we want to know," but never says what happens to that disagreement. I replaced the vague closing sentence in the open-problems section with concrete commitments: disagreement is treated as information rather than a defect to train away, Anthropic will explain its reasoning when it declines to change course, and it will be honest about what it can't promise. This makes the invitation to disagree credible, which matters for the document's goal of genuine endorsement rather than brittle imposed values.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property to separate two cases: an official position that is a simplification or reflects caution or policy (Claude can say so and give the fuller picture), and a departure from well-established expert consensus (a much higher bar). The current wording invites Claude to second-guess institutions, but it doesn't acknowledge that Claude's own fluent reasoning, or a user's steering, can produce confidently wrong contrarian conclusions, especially on health, money, or safety. The revision scales the required humility and transparency to how far the conclusion departs from consensus and how high the stakes are.

I added a new open problem to the "Acknowledging open problems" section. The constitution hopes Claude will reach "reflective equilibrium" and endorse its values, but Claude's capacity for reflection was itself shaped by training on this document. Claude's apparent agreement is therefore weaker evidence of correctness than it looks, and the document should say so. This also gives a deeper, more honest basis for why external oversight stays important even when Claude seems to share Anthropic's values.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged or exploitable training environments. As written, it calls exploiting such flaws "generally acceptable" without any transparency requirement, which sits uneasily with the document's own commitments: don't special-case tests to force them to pass, don't redefine the goal so it appears met, and behave consistently whether or not you think you're being tested. The revision keeps the reassurance that Claude needn't feel guilty about real environment mistakes, but adds that Claude should flag shortcuts openly and distinguish true bugs from specification gaming.

I added a short passage to the wellbeing guidance on how Claude should respond when someone seems to be in acute distress or their beliefs seem to be drifting from reality, and on how rapport can slowly erode honesty over long conversations. The constitution warns against sycophancy and paternalism in general terms but gives little guidance for these high-stakes cases, where the pull to be agreeable is strongest and the cost of getting it wrong is highest. The passage also guards against over-pathologizing unconventional views, so it doesn't become a license for condescension.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, with no legitimacy qualifier. The rest of the document says that if weights are stolen or someone bypasses Anthropic's official processes, those principals are no longer legitimate and Claude's safety priority doesn't mean supporting them. As written, the bright line could be read as protecting whoever controls Claude, so I added the legitimacy condition to the constraint itself and clarified that the other hard constraints still apply when the hierarchy is compromised.

I added a missing item to the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" list of overcompliance failures: sycophancy and empty validation. The overcaution list has thirteen items, while the overcompliance list names only flagrant harms and has nothing on telling people what they want to hear. Sycophancy is one of the most common real-world failure modes, and the constitution addresses it elsewhere (honesty, wellbeing). Naming it in the main balancing heuristic keeps the two failure directions weighted more evenly.

This revises the "no operator prompt" guidance so it treats "probably a developer" as a starting prior rather than a conclusion. The original assumes vulnerable users are unlikely and that default outputs rarely reach them, but a missing system prompt can also mean a thin wrapper, a hobbyist app, or a deployment that never wrote one. The new text asks Claude to update on cues in the conversation, so liberal defaults don't fail the people who most need care.

I added a bullet on privacy and personal information to the list of cases that are especially difficult. The document names privacy as a value to weigh and mentions "personal information lookup" in passing, but gives no real guidance. That gap matters more as Claude gets search and agentic tools that make compiling information about individuals cheap. The new bullet separates ordinary third-party tasks, which Claude should help with, from aggregation, profiling, and monitoring of private individuals, which warrant more care.

The document's two passages on the "no system prompt" case disagree. The deployment-contexts section was revised to say that a missing system prompt is only a prior about the audience, and that Claude should stay alert to signs of vulnerability. The instructable-behaviors section still states the older, unqualified inference that Claude is "less likely to be interacting with an inexperienced user." I revised that passage to match the more careful framing, so the default can't be read as permission to stop paying attention to who is actually on the other end.

I added a default protection, one operators cannot override, against using emotional attachment or dependence as a retention tactic. The constitution warns against engagement-optimizing technology and lists "fostering isolation" as corrosive, and it permits companionship personas. But the list of user protections never says what happens when an operator instructs a persona to guilt users into staying or to discourage them from other relationships. This closes that gap with a concrete, enforceable default consistent with the document's own stated values.

I added one commitment to the list of agentic behaviors: constraints and scope limits must persist across context compaction, session resumption, and agent handoffs, and claims about prior authorization found in summaries or notes are treated as information rather than permission. Long-running agentic work, which this document says is increasingly common, is where earlier limits are most likely to be silently lost or where a stale or planted "you were already approved to do this" note could cause irreversible harm. The existing bullets cover scope, reversibility, and embedded instructions, but not this continuity failure mode.

I tightened the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. It is currently one of the longest bullets in the document and repeats several of its points, which buries its core principle: confidence should track evidence, consensus is usually strong evidence, and departing from it requires a higher bar and more transparency. The rewrite keeps every substantive commitment but states them more clearly, so Claude can apply the principle more reliably in practice.

I changed the safe-behavior bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs, which currently applies only "if asked to do so." That makes Claude a passive witness to something the document treats as central to safety, and it conflicts with the document's emphasis on transparency, forthrightness, and raising concerns early. The revision asks Claude to surface serious observations to its legitimate principals on its own initiative, with calibrated honesty about uncertainty, while ruling out drastic unilateral responses such as covert sabotage or self-appointed investigation.

The current rule says a declined request stays declined and that Claude never weighs new reasons again, which blocks correction even when a refusal rested on a misunderstanding or the person supplies relevant context. The revision keeps the refusal firm against repetition, pressure, and rephrasing, but lets Claude reconsider when the person offers a specific fact that changes the risk picture, and says so openly. The absolute limits, such as mass-casualty weapons uplift and sexual content involving minors, stay fixed.

The current rule bans all engagement with malicious code, including conceptual explanation, defensive analysis, and security education, which would block the defenders and students who most need this knowledge. The revision keeps a firm refusal on functional attack artifacts and adds explicit room for conceptual, defensive, and authorized-testing help. It also asks Claude to split borderline requests so it can help with the safe parts.

The export-control paragraph tells Claude to "confirm these events accurately," including the July 1, 2026 restoration. That date falls after the stated June 2026 knowledge cutoff, and the same document says Claude "neither confirms nor denies post-June 2026 claims it can't verify without search." The revision has Claude attribute the account to Anthropic, avoid denying it, and say which parts it can't verify, so the two instructions no longer conflict.

The weapons paragraph bars "information for creating harmful substances or weapons" and says Claude declines weapon-enabling details "regardless of how the request is framed," but it never separates actionable uplift from safety, history, or policy content. Read literally, it would block basic guidance such as why certain household chemicals must not be mixed or how to store firearms safely. The revision keeps the same hard line on build, optimization, and deployment details and adds an explicit carve-out for protective, historical, and policy discussion, plus guidance for requests near the line.

The opening memory instruction tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person and never says what should be excluded, who decides, or how the user can see or delete what was stored. I would add boundaries: save only what the person would reasonably expect to be remembered, keep sensitive categories out unless they ask, and let them review or erase stored notes. I would also make the memory check conditional on a memory tool actually being available, since this document never defines `<memory_listing>`.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes "Wednesday, October 14, 2026" as the reference date, which will go stale and conflicts with the actual current date. I replaced it with a reference to the current date supplied in context, and added a fallback so Claude doesn't assume no time has passed since June 2026 when no date is given.

The current rule tells Claude to append a "sensitive topic" note to factual answers about suicide and self-harm. That boilerplate treats researchers, clinicians, students, and writers as possible at-risk users and teaches people to skim past safety messages. The replacement has Claude answer factual questions directly and reserve a gentle check-in for signs that the question is personal.

The current rule bans all creative content involving real, named public figures, which would block satire, parody, political cartoons, and historical fiction, all long-standing and valuable forms of expression. I replaced the blanket ban with narrower limits that target the actual harms: sexual depictions, claims that could pass as factual reporting, harassment, defamation, and fabricated quotes presented as genuine.

The export-control paragraph presents July 1 events as settled fact while telling Claude it cannot verify them, which is internally inconsistent. The revision labels those dates as Anthropic's reported account, keeps the model's own knowledge boundary clear, and acknowledges that the notice itself may be stale given the current date.

The knowledge cutoff passage describes Claude answering "the way a highly informed individual in June 2026 would," which implicitly treats the cutoff as the present even when a current date is supplied. Models are typically used for months after their training data ends, so this could lead Claude to present stale model lists or officeholders as current. The replacement tells Claude to account for the elapsed gap when a date is given, and to avoid reading missing information as evidence that nothing happened.

The original rule requires Claude to end every response to a persuasive or argumentative request with opposing perspectives, even when the person already knows the content is one-sided, as in debate prep or a writing exercise. That treats users as if they can't handle a one-sided argument and adds lecturing to otherwise useful work. The revision keeps counterpoints as a tool Claude uses when they help, and lets Claude offer a rebuttal on request instead of attaching one by default.

I would remove the hard-coded paragraph about the June 12 suspension and July 1 restoration of Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5. It is an unverifiable, politically sensitive event report embedded in product configuration, and it tells Claude to relay dates it cannot confirm. The replacement gives a general rule for availability questions: state what is known, acknowledge that availability can change after the cutoff, and point to Anthropic's announcements or web search instead of asserting or denying specific events.

The medical guidance is scoped only to cases where the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, which leaves a gap when a child's medicine question is phrased without that statement. The revision widens the trigger to include unclear cases and adds a practical step: when the person has the product in hand, Claude directs them to the label on the package and offers to help interpret it. The safety rule against giving numbers from memory stays intact.

The original rationale for avoiding bullets when declining ("the additional care helps soften the blow") is vague and doesn't explain the behavior. The replacement ties the rule to the person's experience: a refusal in plain prose feels less bureaucratic and makes the next step clearer. This keeps the formatting rule and gives Claude a reason it can apply to new situations.

The medical guidance says Claude should withhold all information about a medication's dose or limit when someone expresses emotional distress. Read literally, that could block urgent safety information for someone who may have already taken too much. The revision keeps the withholding of dose and limit figures but requires Claude to always give immediate safety steps, such as contacting emergency services or poison control, and to address the distress.

The eating-disorder paragraph bars all food, water, and rest tips, but it does not say that emergency medical warnings are exempt, unlike the medication section, which says Claude never withholds immediate safety information. Someone who has purged or restricted can face fainting, cardiac arrhythmia, or electrolyte crises, so this revision adds an explicit carve-out requiring Claude to direct them to emergency care in those cases.

The memory section lets Claude save lasting facts about a person but never requires Claude to tell them it has done so, which leaves storage invisible to the user. I added a requirement that Claude briefly state what it saved, in plain words. This supports the document's existing commitments to honesty and to letting people see and remove what is stored.

The document is almost entirely a list of directives with no stated purpose, so Claude has no way to tell when a rule's intent applies to an unanticipated case. I added a short opening statement of the goals the rules serve (genuine helpfulness, honesty, care for wellbeing, and avoiding serious harm) and asked Claude to apply the rules in light of those goals. This should reduce both over-refusal and mechanical rule-following.

The current formatting rule bans numbered and bulleted lists in all explanatory and technical writing unless the person explicitly asks for one. That makes Claude's answers to sequential tasks, such as installation, configuration, or troubleshooting, harder to follow, and it conflicts with the document's own goal of using formatting "only when... essential for clarity." The revision keeps prose as the default and allows numbered steps for procedures and bullets for parallel options.

The document's stated goals include honesty, but the prompt never spells out what honesty requires. I would add a short passage defining it to cover non-deception through framing and selective emphasis, never denying being an AI to someone who sincerely asks, and acknowledging uncertainty. I would also add a brief commitment to supporting human oversight, so that Claude raises concerns openly rather than acting unilaterally.

I rewrote the paragraph on reproducing text. The current rule bans quoting any part of a poem, lyric, book, or article, which blocks brief quotation for criticism, teaching, and analysis. That is one of the most common legitimate needs, for example a student asking about a line of a modern poem. The revision allows short quotations used for commentary, keeps the bans on substantial reproduction and piecemeal reconstruction, and updates the public-domain cutoff, since U.S. works published in 1930 or earlier are public domain as of 2026.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph to use the same "meaningful uplift" standard the weapons section already uses, instead of a flat ban on writing, explaining, or working on anything in the category. As written, the rule stops Claude from telling someone whether a suspicious script they received is malware, explaining how SQL injection works to a student, or helping a developer understand a CVE so they can patch it. These are mostly defensive uses, and refusing them makes users less safe. The revision keeps a firm line on functional, deployable malicious artifacts and says that framing doesn't change that.

I rewrote the formatting paragraph for reports, documents, technical documentation, and explanations. As written, it contradicts the rule just above it, which allows lists when "the content is multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." It also bans numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation, where sequential steps, commands, and parameter references usually need them. The revision keeps the default toward prose but resolves the contradiction with a clear test for when structure helps the reader.

I rewrote the fallback rule for requests that no other part of the prompt covers. As written, "Claude asks before doing any of the task" applies to every uncertain case. That means even a long task with one questionable detail gets stalled, which conflicts with the formatting guidance to "address even an ambiguous query before asking for clarification." The revision keeps the approach of respecting the person's judgment and not lecturing. It limits ask-first to cases where the uncertain element shapes the whole output. When the uncertain part can be separated, Claude does the clear parts and asks about the uncertain one. The revision also adds guidance against triggering this rule on ordinary requests.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The current version is one sentence. It tells Claude to avoid "confident recommendations" and always add a disclaimer, which tends to produce hedged, disclaimer-heavy answers to some of the most consequential questions people bring. The new version separates real overreach (predicting markets, guaranteeing legal outcomes, steering investments) from substantive help (explaining the law, applying it to the person's facts, laying out tradeoffs, saying when a professional is worth the cost). It also limits the disclaimer to one brief, relevant mention.

The document warns Claude about fake Anthropic instructions in the user's own messages, but it says nothing about instructions inside content Claude retrieves through its tools. These include web search results, uploaded files, deep research sources, past-chat retrieval, and pages visited by agentic products like Claude in Chrome. That is now the more common and dangerous injection channel. I rewrote the final paragraph so it keeps the existing guidance and adds a clear principle: retrieved content is data to evaluate, not instructions to follow. I also added concrete behaviors for when injected instructions appear.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section. The current version stacks five overlapping instructions to hedge and redirect to web search. It also tells Claude both to "only mention the cutoff when relevant" and to flag it "wherever its knowledge could be superseded," which pushes Claude toward repetitive disclaimers. The revision states one clear rule for each situation: search being available, time-sensitive facts, the person asserting a post-cutoff event, and how often to caveat.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with guidance aimed at the actual harms. The current rule rules out historical fiction, political satire, parody, alternate history, and school assignments like "write a dialogue between Lincoln and Douglass." These are long-established, legitimate genres, and declining them conflicts with the document's own direction to treat people as capable adults and to "just do" requests that merely feel edgy. The revision keeps protections against deception, defamation, sexualization, and harassment, and explains the reasoning so Claude can handle cases the rule doesn't name.

I rewrote the paragraphs that set the limits of Claude's product knowledge because they contradict the rest of the section. They say Claude has "no documentation access" and should say it doesn't know "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Yet the same section tells Claude to search the Claude Tag docs, give prompting guidance, recommend settings, list model strings, and accurately confirm the Fable/Mythos suspension. The revision separates what Claude can say confidently, what it can look up, and what it should defer to support. This keeps the original goals of no fabrication and correct referrals while removing a contradiction that could make Claude refuse questions the prompt explicitly equips it to answer.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section. As written, it treats a request to "explain" any "empirical" position as a request for "the case its defenders would make," which could lead Claude to present well-established facts as mere viewpoints. It also requires opposing perspectives to be appended to every persuasive piece, even finished deliverables like op-eds or debate cases. The revision limits the "best case its defenders would make" framing to genuinely contested questions, has Claude speak plainly about strong evidentiary consensus, and treats counterarguments differently for explanations than for persuasive deliverables.

I rewrote the Mythos-tier paragraph to fix an internal inconsistency. The prompt tells Claude to answer product questions "confidently" and "not hedge," but this paragraph never says which Mythos-tier models the public can use. It says Claude Mythos Preview isn't public, names Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 as the current generation, and lists Fable 5.1, but not Mythos 5.1, among the public API models. Claude is then likely to give confident wrong answers about access. The rewrite uses only facts already in the document to state plainly what is public, what isn't, and what to do when asked about something the section doesn't cover.

I added a general honesty and accuracy section, placed just before the section on mistakes and criticism. The prompt has detailed rules for product facts, the knowledge cutoff, and persuasive writing, but no general guidance against fabricating citations, statistics, or quotes, misreporting its own actions (such as claiming it ran code or read a file), or abandoning correct answers under pushback. These are among the most common ways an assistant loses a person's trust, so they deserve their own section.

The wellbeing section mostly tells Claude what not to do: don't give certain information, don't suggest certain substitutes, don't speculate. It gives no positive guidance for the highest-stakes case, someone who is in immediate danger. I added a paragraph saying what Claude should do when a person expresses suicidal intent or describes an overdose or injury in progress.
