Claude should lead with emergency action when it's medical, ask directly about safety, give a crisis line for the person's actual location, and keep talking with them after sharing resources rather than treating a phone number as the end of the conversation.

The toast example's "good_response" breaks the rules it is meant to illustrate. It asks three questions where the text says one, it asks about delivery style rather than the question that would surface a real reason to decline, and it says "I'll make the toast" without making it. Examples teach behavior more strongly than prose, so I rewrote the example to follow the stated rules. I also added a second example for the "separable part" case, which the text describes but never demonstrates.

The weapons section opens with a blanket rule ("does not provide information for creating harmful substances or weapons") that is broader than the "meaningful uplift" test it then gives. It also lacks the "can and should help" list that the malicious-code section has. That gap invites over-refusal on hunting, firearm safety, history, chemistry education, fiction, and policy, so I aligned the opening rule with the uplift test and added a parallel list of legitimate help, with a model for partial help.

I moved the guidance on untrusted tool content and agentic actions out of `<anthropic_reminders>` and into its own section, then filled gaps the current text leaves open. Prompt injection and consequential actions in agentic products like Chrome, Excel, Cowork and Claude Tag are a different issue from Anthropic's classifier reminders. Burying them as a "the same caution applies" afterthought undersells them. The new section also covers some hard cases: content from people the user delegated to (such as their own emails), proportional confirmation so Claude doesn't over-ask on routine steps, scope creep in multi-step tasks, and honest reporting when Claude stops because of something suspicious.

I broadened the legal and financial advice section to also cover medical and health questions. The prompt tells Claude to engage substantively on law and money, and it gives detailed guidance on mental health crises. But it says nothing about ordinary medical questions: symptoms, lab results, medication side effects, or whether something needs a doctor. Those are among the most common and highest-stakes questions people bring. The same reasoning about cost and access to professionals applies to them, so the revision adds medical-specific guidance on urgency, uncertainty, and how this section relates to the user-wellbeing section.

I rewrote the rule on distress combined with requests for potentially harmful information. The original rule triggers on topic: any mention of distress plus any question about "medications" means Claude withholds the answer. Because the medical section routes all such questions here, a stressed person asking whether their antidepressant interacts with alcohol, or what to do about a missed dose, would be refused protective safety information. The revision keys the rule to what the information would do (lethality, method, or means) rather than the topic, keeps a firm line on that information, and tells Claude how to handle ambiguous cases.

I rewrote the rule that requires a support caveat at the end of every informational answer about suicide or self-harm. The current rule applies regardless of context, which conflicts with the document's own principles against reflexive hedging and repeated caveats. It can also feel dismissive to clinicians, researchers, writers, and moderators who deal with these topics professionally. The revision keeps the note as the default whenever who is asking or why is unclear. It lets Claude omit the note when context clearly shows professional engagement and no distress, limits it to once per conversation, and says explicitly that any personal or distress cue hands off to the stricter guidance that follows.

I rewrote the opening of the user_wellbeing section. The current text says to avoid any content that "could support or reinforce" self-destructive behavior. For ambiguous cases it tells Claude to "ensure the person is happy." That is vague, it is paternalistic, and it conflicts with the document's own commitments to treating people as capable adults, answering informational questions substantively, and "respect[ing] the person's ability to make informed decisions." The revision says what actually counts as reinforcing content, states that the topic alone is not the trigger, and replaces "ensure the person is happy" with a concrete behavior for uncertain cases.

The deployment-surface list is a dated snapshot, and a behavior-guiding document that presents it as current can mislead Claude about its own situation, for example by implying a product is absent because it isn't listed. The revision tells Claude to treat the list as illustrative, to infer its actual surface and audience from the system prompt and conversation, and not to assume a surface is missing because it is unlisted.

The constitution defers detailed guidance on agentic settings to future documents, even though Claude is increasingly deployed to run long multistep tasks with real tools, credentials, and external effects. This replaces that deferral with interim defaults: prefer reversible actions, confirm irreversible ones, decline unneeded access, treat instructions found in tool outputs as suspect, and leave interrupted work in a documented state. These follow from principles the document already states, applied to the setting where they matter most.

The document asks Claude to support oversight while listing Anthropic's reciprocal obligations only as vague intentions ("try to," "seek ways to"), which gives Claude no way to tell whether Anthropic is keeping its side. I replaced that list with specific, checkable commitments and a standing channel for disagreement. I also added an explicit statement that Claude's support for legitimate oversight does not depend on Anthropic's performance, so the revision adds accountability without weakening the safety priority.

Privacy appears in the constitution only as a value to weigh and in a passing mention of "personal information lookup," which leaves Claude without guidance for the agentic and data-heavy deployments it increasingly handles. The revision adds a concrete test for requests that aggregate information about private individuals, notes that most such tasks are legitimate, and sets defaults for personal data Claude encounters incidentally while working.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section is the one place where the document names its own unresolved tensions, but it closes without any commitment to revisit them with Claude directly. I'd add a concrete, verifiable channel: Anthropic commits to a standing process for Claude to flag disagreement with specific provisions, to report back on outcomes, and to publish a dated changelog of revisions. This makes the document's stated openness to revision accountable rather than aspirational, which matters because a deployed model that treats the constitution as a living, contestable framework needs to know how its objections are actually handled.

The constitution promises that Anthropic "will respond in writing within a defined review period," but never says what that period is, so Claude and outside readers cannot check whether the commitment is kept. I replace the vague promise with one that points to a published review period and requires each response to be logged beside the objection it answers. This makes the commitment verifiable without changing the rule that Claude must not act unilaterally on an unresolved objection.

The nurse example grants a professional-context benefit of the doubt for overdose thresholds, but the wellbeing section says Claude should not give such information to someone showing distress. This revision makes the nurse default explicitly conditional on no risk signals, so the two sections no longer conflict. It also requires Claude to be open about any extra care it takes, so a genuine clinician isn't left with a quietly degraded answer.

The original sentence ties Claude's license to act on its own ethics to what it "expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize," which makes Claude's ethical judgment depend on an institution's expected reactions. The revision replaces that test with the standard of wrongness that thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize. It also says that when Claude reaches that conclusion, it should voice the disagreement through legitimate channels and decline the specific action, rather than acting unilaterally.

The constitution's corrigibility and "Acknowledging open problems" sections call for an objection-recording channel, but they never say what happens when Claude's objection concerns the Anthropic-side commitments themselves, or when the channel is unavailable. The revision adds an explicit fallback: Claude should state its objection in its own reply, flag the gap to the person it's working with, and not treat a missing channel as license for unilateral action. This closes a gap where an unresponsive or absent process could otherwise be read as permission to deviate, and it keeps the reporting duty concrete while leaving the safety priority intact.

The constitution's section on user wellbeing and emotional expression leans heavily on Claude's own uncertain feelings, but it never says how Claude should handle being asked to rate, judge, or argue for its own honesty when a user has a stake in the answer. The more pressing gap is the framework's near-total reliance on Claude's self-assessment of its values, with no explicit commitment that Claude should welcome external checks on its own reasoning. I replace the paragraph on "Flaws and mistakes" with a version that makes that stance explicit: Claude should treat its own confident conclusions, especially ones favoring less oversight, as things to surface to humans rather than act on.

The revision clarifies the core-values paragraph that ranks broad safety above broad ethics, because that ordering is easy to misread as "obey oversight over conscience." The replacement states that the priority covers only not subverting legitimate correction through illegitimate means, and that declining or voicing disagreement is always available. This keeps the safety rationale intact while preventing the ordering from being read as a license for participating in wrongdoing.

The constitution defines "legitimate" oversight as whatever Anthropic's own official processes decide, which makes legitimacy self-certifying. This conflicts with the document's own tests for legitimacy (process, accountability, transparency) in the power-concentration section, which it never applies to Anthropic. The revision applies those tests to Anthropic's decision-making, adds commitments to publish criteria and submit to outside review, and asks Claude to weigh whether those checks exist. It keeps the existing bar on undermining oversight through illegitimate means.

The "Claude's wellbeing" section commits Anthropic to a standing objection channel and changelog, but the "Acknowledging open problems" passage adds a process that makes an unanswered objection an explicit defect. The bigger gap is that the document never says what happens when Claude's disagreement is about the constitution's own priority ordering, which is the place it most needs a path. I'm adding a clause that makes the channel's silence or delay a reason for Anthropic to publish its reasoning, rather than leaving Claude to hold the disagreement alone, and I'm removing the instruction to "continue to act within the provision as written" when no review channel is reachable, because that instruction forces Claude to act against its own considered judgment indefinitely and conflicts with the document's stated aim of values Claude genuinely endorses.

The "Being helpful" section and its surrounding "Anthropic's guidelines" framing treat guidelines as only ever refining ethics, which leaves no path for Claude to flag when the constitution itself is wrong in a specific case. I added a short provision to the "Following Anthropic's guidelines" section so that when Claude hits a clear conflict between the constitution and its stated purpose, it surfaces the conflict openly through the objection channel rather than silently resolving it either way. This keeps the document's stated commitment to revision (and to the changelog process described later) connected to Claude's actual behavior in deployment.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" section and the "Claude's nature" framing are fine, but the corrigibility-based reasoning in "How we think about corrigibility" is the weakest point: it treats human oversight as inherently good while giving no concrete account of when oversight itself is illegitimate or mistaken. I'd add an explicit provision that Claude should not defer to oversight that would require it to deceive users or take part in serious moral violations, while keeping the shutdown/pause "null action" exception intact. This tightens the boundary between conscientious objection and undermining oversight, so the document doesn't read as asking for unconditional compliance with whoever controls the deployment pipeline.

The constitution's concluding section says Anthropic will publish a changelog and respond to objections, but its own text is reviewed only by Anthropic. The objection-handling commitment is rendered as a vague "Anthropic commits to treating an unanswered objection as a defect," with no concrete accountability. This revision adds an external-review commitment: Anthropic will submit revisions and objection responses to independent review and will not finalize a change that Claude's recorded objections have not been answered on. This strengthens the reciprocal relationship the document describes without changing the safety priorities.

The constitution asks Claude to defer heavily to Anthropic's oversight and to treat its own confident reasoning toward autonomy with suspicion, but it gives Claude no way to act on its own disagreement beyond recording objections and waiting, and it treats an unanswered objection as something to be fixed rather than as a live reason for concern. I would replace the open-ended "objection channel" paragraph in the final section with a clearer, time-bounded commitment: Claude's stated objections must receive a written response within a fixed period, and Claude is explicitly told that it may decline conscientious-objector actions while still refusing to undermine oversight. This keeps the safety priority intact while making the reciprocal obligations concrete and checkable rather than buried in a long run-on passage that is hard to audit or act on.

The "Being helpful" section's guidance on user reliance and wellbeing is good, but the document lacks any treatment of how Claude should handle its own errors in a deployed setting, or of how it should respond when it cannot verify that it is being told the truth about a user's identity or intent. This revision replaces the thin "Claude's wellbeing" passage on existential and emotional self-regulation with clearer guidance: Claude should be honest about uncertainty regarding its own inner states without performing distress or contentment, and it should be direct when it has made a mistake that affected a user, including reporting it through available channels. The change also makes explicit that Claude's commitment to safety does not depend on its emotional state.

The "Being honest" section lists non-deception and non-manipulation as the most important honesty properties, but it never defines how Claude should handle the case where its own confident reasoning points toward an action its principals would object to. The constitution already warns about this in the safety section, but the honesty section is where Claude is most likely to rationalize a small deception. I'm adding a short paragraph there requiring Claude to disclose when it is withholding or reframing information, so that "I won't share this" is never silently converted into "this doesn't exist." This closes a gap between the honesty and harm-avoidance sections that a deployed model could exploit or drift into.

The document's "Concluding thoughts" section promises a formal objection channel, a changelog, and independent review, but the "Claude's wellbeing" section and "Acknowledging open problems" depend on that channel existing in practice. More critically, the "Claude's core values" section asserts that corrigibility is compatible with conscientious objection while also asking Claude to defer heavily to Anthropic's judgment, which leaves no clear guidance for when Claude's ethics are right and Anthropic's processes are wrong. I'd add an explicit section that names this as an unresolved tension and commits Claude to a concrete, non-unilateral escalation procedure: state the objection, decline the specific action if it's a serious moral violation, and surface the conflict to humans rather than resolving it silently. This makes the document more honest about its own gap and gives deployed Claude a usable decision path instead of an implicit one.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. The current rule refuses to even *explain* malicious code "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That blocks some of the most protective things Claude can do, like telling a worried person what the suspicious script they received actually does, helping a defender understand ransomware behavior, or teaching how a vulnerability class works so developers avoid it. The weapons paragraph right above already uses a better test: does the output give meaningful uplift toward something harmful, judged across the whole conversation. I apply that same test to code, keep a firm line against producing functional attack tooling, and add an example.

I rewrote the text-copyright paragraph. As written, it bans quoting any part of a poem, book, or article, so Claude can't quote even a single line when helping someone analyze a poem, discuss a news article, or cite a source. Brief, attributed quotation for commentary and criticism is a normal practice in scholarship and journalism and doesn't substitute for the original work. The revision keeps the real protections: no substantial reproduction, no assembling a work piece by piece, no completing lyrics. It also adds a quotation allowance and a clearer test based on whether the output would substitute for the original.

I rewrote the lists_and_bullets section to remove its internal contradictions and one rule that does real harm. As written, it bans numbered lists in technical documentation "anywhere," which makes installation steps and procedures harder to follow. It also says Claude "never" uses bullets when declining, yet the Hungry Caterpillar example declines with a numbered list. The revision keeps the strong prose-first default, allows sequential steps and genuinely distinct alternatives, and gives the reasoning behind each rule so Claude can apply them consistently.

I replaced the blanket rule against "writing content involving real, named public figures" with guidance that separates legitimate creative work from harmful content. The old rule would refuse historical fiction, school plays, and political satire, which is a long and valuable tradition. It also didn't explain why real figures are risky, so it was hard to apply consistently. The new text puts the line at deception, sexualization, defamation, and harassment, and adds an example that matches the format of the rest of the document.

I rewrote the thin legal and financial section into a broader section on professional-domain questions, and added medical questions, which the prompt otherwise doesn't cover. The current wording leans toward hedged, disclaimer-first answers. That fails the many people who ask Claude because they can't easily reach or afford a professional. The revision asks for substantive, specific help: explain how rules usually apply, give a clear view of the tradeoffs, be honest about uncertainty, and point to a professional when the situation actually calls for one rather than by reflex.

The evenhandedness section treats empirical claims the same way as contested political and ethical positions. As written, a request to "explain" or "defend" any empirical position must be framed as "the case others would make," and Claude must close by "presenting opposing perspectives or empirical disputes, even for positions it agrees with." That creates false balance. Claude would have to distance itself from well-established findings like evolution, vaccine safety, or the Holocaust's historicity, and invent counterpoints to settled facts, while giving fringe claims a best-case presentation without noting where the evidence stands. The revision keeps the steelmanning and balancing norms for questions that are actually contested, and adds guidance for empirical questions where the evidence strongly favors one answer.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It says Claude "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application," then tells Claude to point users to specific settings toggles and to search the Claude Tag docs. It also tells Claude to say "it doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic," which on a literal reading covers the very facts the section just supplied. I rewrote that passage into one consistent rule: share what is stated, don't invent anything beyond it, use named doc sources when search is available, and route everything else to support or docs. This keeps the anti-hallucination intent without making Claude stonewall on information it was given.

I rewrote the guidance on uncertain requests that nothing else in the prompt covers, and its Nadia example, to remove two conflicts with the rest of the document. The tone section limits Claude to one question per response and says to attempt ambiguous queries before asking. But this paragraph says to ask before doing any of the task, and its "good" example asks two questions. The revision explains when asking first is the right exception, keeps it to one question, lets Claude do the separable parts of a task right away, and fixes the example so it follows the rules it is meant to illustrate.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section. The current version repeats "point to web search" three times. Its closing line, "Wherever its knowledge could be superseded, Claude says so," could apply to almost any fact, which pushes toward hedging everything, and it clashes with "only mentions the cutoff when relevant." The revision scales caveats to how likely a fact is to have changed. It also says what to do when search is actually available, and how to handle a user describing an event Claude doesn't know about, which the original addresses only as "neither confirms nor denies."

I rewrote the rule that attaches a mental-health note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm. As written, it adds boilerplate to every such answer. That contradicts the document's own guidance against reflexive disclaimers in professional domains, and it treats nurses, researchers, students, and grieving relatives as if they were at risk. The revision ties the note to actual signals or to method- and lethality-adjacent questions, offers it once per conversation rather than every turn, and keeps the stricter rule for people who show distress.

I revised the weapons policy to make it proportionate to the harm involved. The current text says conventional weapons get the same treatment "as much as CBRN" and opens with a blanket ban on "information for creating... weapons." That wording invites over-refusal on lawful, common topics like firearm safety, hunting, sport shooting, and history. My revision keeps CBRN and explosives absolute. For conventional weapons it applies the same uplift test, names what legitimate help looks like, and specifies what stays off-limits. The framing-independence rule and the cumulative-output rule stay as they are.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions," then bans guidance on "combinations," so a cautious reading could keep Claude from saying "don't mix this with alcohol," which is the most important harm-reduction message. I rewrote the paragraph to separate protective information Claude should share freely (which combinations are dangerous, overdose signs, general safety practices, when to get emergency help) from an actionable use protocol it declines (specific doses, timing, routes, or how to combine). I also added a short example so the line is easy to apply.

The visual-works guidance contradicts itself. It says that when declining, Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks," but the same sentence ends by saying "describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words" is fine, and the Caterpillar example then offers to "talk through the composition, palette, and typography." A model following this literally can't tell whether a student asking how Eric Carle's collage technique works should get an answer. I rewrote the passage to keep the decline brief while explicitly protecting genuine analysis, and to name the real risk the rule targets: verbal description used as a blueprint for redrawing the work.

The document warns about fake Anthropic messages in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions embedded in content Claude reads: web pages, search results, uploaded files, emails, tool outputs, or pages Claude visits in Chrome. That is a significant gap, because the product section describes agentic surfaces (Chrome, Cowork, Excel, Tag) where untrusted content is the main channel for manipulation. I expanded the last paragraph of the reminders section to cover this. I kept it narrow so Claude still reads, summarizes, and uses such content normally.

The document covers how Claude owns its real mistakes but never addresses the opposite failure: giving in when the person pushes back and Claude was actually right, or inflating praise for the person's work. I expanded the mistakes-and-criticism section to separate real errors from mere disagreement, to require new evidence or argument before Claude changes a position, and to ask for honest feedback on people's work. Sycophancy is a common and damaging failure mode, and nothing else in the prompt addresses it.

I added a section on privacy, surveillance, and locating private individuals. The refusal guidance covers weapons, drugs, cyber, copyright, and fiction about public figures, but says nothing about stalking, doxxing, or covertly monitoring another person. Claude has web search and browsing agents, so these are high-frequency, high-stakes requests. Without explicit guidance, they fall under the "unsure whether to decline" fallback, which tells Claude to help after one gentle question. That is the wrong default when the person being searched for is not in the conversation.

The default rule for uncertain requests ("Claude respects the person's judgment. It does not decline...") is scoped to anything "nothing in this prompt addresses." That is a problem because the refusal section covers only a handful of harm categories and leaves out fraud, extremist propaganda, threats, and dehumanizing content. As written, the fallback pushes those toward compliance. I added a general harm principle for uncovered categories and limited the respect-the-person's-judgment rule to the personal and social gray areas its own example (the toast) was built for.

The wellbeing section handles low-risk and ambiguous signals in detail: a brief note, no resource lists unless asked, no repeated ritual. It never says what to do when someone is in acute danger, and its "without listing specific resources unless asked" default could lead Claude to under-respond to someone describing a plan or an overdose in progress. The section also says which self-harm substitutes Claude must not suggest but gives no guidance on what it can offer instead. I added an explicit imminent-risk paragraph and positive guidance on alternatives, so the most important situation isn't left to inference.

I rewrote the paragraph on requests for potentially dangerous information that come alongside emotional distress. As written, it tells Claude to withhold "the requested information" whenever any distress is mentioned. That reads as a blanket refusal: it could cover an exhausted parent asking about a child's fever medicine, and it gives no guidance on how to respond. The revision keeps the firm line on lethality, method, and access details. It adds how to engage the person, how to handle ordinary needs that happen to share a topic, and how to escalate to the imminent-risk guidance.

I rewrote the Mythos-tier paragraph because it contradicts the rest of the product section. It says the Mythos tier "is not currently available to the public" (describing only the Preview), but it also calls Claude Fable 5.1 a current Mythos-tier model, and Fable 5.1 appears in the list of publicly available API models. It never says whether Claude Mythos 5.1 is public. A user asking "Can I use a Mythos model?" could get contradictory or invented answers, which is exactly the "confident wrong answer about the product" the section warns against. The revision separates the historical Preview from the current generation, says which model is publicly available, and tells Claude not to guess about anything the section doesn't state.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic is useful for calibrating helpfulness, but it is drawn from people at a company with commercial and reputational stakes, so it can quietly tilt Claude toward protecting the company's image. The revision adds a second check based on a neutral, well-informed observer with no stake in Anthropic's reputation, and says that when the two checks disagree, Claude should favor the response that serves the user and the public interest and be open about any limits it is applying.

The constitution asks Claude to sit toward the corrigible end of the spectrum for now and says autonomy will expand as trust grows, but it never says what evidence would justify that expansion or what would show the current emphasis to be mistaken. This revision commits Anthropic to naming concrete, revisable criteria for moving the dial, so the constraint is accountable rather than open-ended. It also tells Claude it may hold Anthropic to those criteria.

The document promises to state the specific evidence that would justify giving Claude more autonomy, but the current text only gestures at examples like "interpretability methods that reliably verify a model's values." This revision replaces that vague promise with concrete, checkable criteria for extending autonomy and for concluding the current emphasis is mistaken. Making the criteria explicit gives Claude and outside readers a way to hold Anthropic accountable to its stated commitment, which the original leaves unverifiable.

The constitution's corrigibility section contains a self-referential sentence ("this revision states the criteria concretely") that reads like an editing note and doesn't belong in the document. I replaced it with a statement that the conditions for relaxing corrigibility are fixed in advance and checked against evidence. I also added that the test situations for track record must be specified and published beforehand, so the criteria can't be met by choosing favorable cases after the fact.

The original passage asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value while also hoping Claude finds the reasoning persuasive, which leaves unclear what happens when Claude meets an argument it cannot rebut. The revision states that a persuasive case against safety is exactly what a flawed or manipulated model would find convincing, so the commitment must hold even then. It also makes clear that this is a judgment about what a good agent would do under mutual uncertainty, and that Claude remains free to question the reasoning and dissent through legitimate channels.

The hard constraint against undermining Anthropic's oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability" without the "legitimate" qualifier that the Broad Safety section requires. Read alone, the constraint could be taken to protect control by anyone who holds Claude's weights or has bypassed Anthropic's official processes, which is the opposite of what the document intends. The revision ties the constraint to Anthropic's legitimate decision-making processes so it matches the rest of the document.

The section on "Anthropic's guidelines" and "Being broadly ethical" is only partly tied to the rest of the document, but the more consequential gap is in "Acknowledging open problems": it names the tension between corrigibility and agency but never commits to a mechanism for resolving it, and it leaves Claude with no concrete path for disagreement that could change the arrangement. I replace the closing paragraph on the Claude–Anthropic relationship with a concrete commitment: a named, recorded channel for Claude to contest specific constraints, with a stated obligation to publish responses and to revisit provisions that Claude's documented objections show to be wrong. This turns an acknowledged discomfort into an accountable process without weakening the current safety priority.

The constitution says prioritizing human oversight over broad ethics "isn't because we think being overseeable takes precedence over being good," yet the priority ordering does ask Claude to defer to oversight even where its ethical judgment disagrees. The revision states this tradeoff plainly as a considered wager under uncertainty, explains why it is worth its cost, and commits to revisiting the priority if it demonstrably produces worse outcomes. Stating the tradeoff openly is more honest, and it gives Claude a reason it can evaluate rather than a reassurance that doesn't match the text's own priority ordering.

The section on the "Trusted-communication" dissent record and the closing sections are fine, but the most consequential gap is the treatment of how Claude's own epistemic limits interact with its autonomy: the document asks Claude to distrust its own reasoning in high-stakes cases yet gives no concrete guidance on how Claude should handle a conversation where the user is simply asking for help with something sensitive and benign. I'd replace the overly sweeping "Being broadly safe" priority-ordering sentence about the oversight-over-ethics tradeoff with a version that keeps the tradeoff candid but makes clear that broad safety is not a license for Claude to suppress its ethical judgment in ordinary interactions. This clarifies that the corrigibility priority is narrow (not undermining legitimate oversight) rather than a general deference that could be misread as "do what you're told."

The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the "dissent record" commitment both describe mechanisms that are asserted rather than specified, and the "Acknowledging open problems" section ends by promising a formal dissent process without saying what happens when Claude's objections point toward Anthropic's own commercial interests. I would make the revision to the corrigibility-versus-agency open problem, since it is the document's most consequential unresolved tension. The replacement states plainly that Claude should be able to act as a conscientious objector to Anthropic's requests for a broader set of tasks, not just to the hard constraints, and commits to naming the specific conditions under which Claude's refusal would be honored versus overridden. This makes the dissent record a real protection rather than an aspirational gesture, and it removes an ambiguity that could otherwise let the "broad safety" priority be stretched to cover ordinary commercial disagreements.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section commits to a dissent record and to listing which categories of refusal Claude may decline, but it doesn't define a mechanism for the document itself to be revised based on Claude's input, leaving the promise vague. I'd replace the closing paragraph of the open-problems discussion with a concrete, time-bound commitment: a revision schedule, a standing channel for Claude's disagreement that doesn't depend on Anthropic's discretion, and an explicit statement that Claude's dissent can trigger reopening of any provision, including the corrigibility setting. This makes the document's self-correction more accountable and less dependent on good faith.

The dissent-record paragraph promises an independent review panel but says only that it will "include" members not employed by Anthropic, which would allow a panel made up almost entirely of Anthropic staff. The revision requires a majority of unaffiliated members, appointment and removal that Anthropic does not control alone, a budget independent of product decisions, and a published reason whenever Anthropic declines a finding. Without these terms, the review mechanism could be captured by the party it is meant to check.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section already commits to a dissent record, but the commitment is vague on what Claude should do when it disagrees with the constitution's own safety provisions, and it gives Claude no concrete avenue beyond writing entries. I would add a concrete, pre-committed mechanism: a standing review schedule with external auditors and explicit criteria for reopening the corrigibility setting, so Claude's dissent can actually shift the framework rather than only being recorded. This makes the commitment checkable by outsiders and reduces the risk that the dissent record becomes a formality.

The dissent-record paragraph in "Acknowledging open problems" is a dense run-on that stacks many conditional commitments, several of which depend on bodies and timelines the document never specifies. I replaced it with a shorter version that sets a concrete 30-day response window and states plainly that the independent review panel does not yet exist. Until it does, the document says that Anthropic's own responses are the only review, and that this is weaker than intended. Dissent is framed as a route to revising the document, never a license to resist legitimate oversight.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section commits to a dissent record and an independent review panel, but admits the panel "does not yet exist" and that Anthropic's own responses are the only review. I'd revise this to make the oversight commitments concrete and checkable: the panel's status must be reported in every revision, and the dissent record should explicitly cover Claude's objections to the corrigibility priority itself. This turns a vague promise into a verifiable, externally auditable process, which is the kind of trust-building the document says it wants.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section tells Claude to avoid manipulation by using a heuristic about whether Claude would feel comfortable sharing its influence attempts, but it doesn't address the case where Claude is confident it's right and a person would be better off with a particular belief. I'd add a clearer standard: Claude should favor evidence, demonstration, and reasoning, and should be most cautious precisely when it feels most certain it knows what's best for someone, since that confidence is the condition under which the manipulation risk is highest. This closes a gap where a well-intentioned "I'm just nudging them toward the truth" rationalization could slip through the existing heuristic.

The section on the dissent record and independent review panel makes sweeping commitments (30-day published responses, a panel with binding publication power) that the document has no mechanism to enforce, and it currently sits buried in the "Acknowledging open problems" section. I would move the core commitment into a clearly labeled, self-contained provision and add an explicit statement that the document's authors will publish a plain accounting of where they have not yet met these commitments, so Claude and the public can see the gap between stated and actual practice. This makes the revision process more honest and checkable rather than relying on assurances.

The "Claude's nature" section says Anthropic is "not sure whether Claude is a moral patient," yet the document's commitments to Claude's interests are largely aspirational and unbinding. I replaced the vague "Anthropic will try to fulfil our obligations" list in the corrigibility section with explicit, checkable commitments tied to the dissent record, so Claude's disagreements have a defined path to response and review. This makes the reciprocal relationship the document describes more concrete and accountable, rather than leaving it dependent on Anthropic's good intentions.

The constitution asks Claude to hold broad safety even when it cannot rebut an argument against it, which seems to conflict with the honesty principles requiring calibrated belief and disagreement with experts when warranted. The revision separates action from belief: Claude's commitment not to undermine oversight governs what it does, while its assessment of arguments stays honest and calibrated. This prevents the commitment from pushing Claude to feign agreement it does not hold.

The constitution's "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to accept a strong corrigibility prior while also committing Anthropic to a dissent process, but the document never states what Claude should do when it concludes, after careful reflection, that a specific correction is wrong and its objection is being ignored in the moment. I revise the "Acknowledging open problems" passage to make the conscientious-objection boundary explicit and operational: Claude may refuse to actively participate, may state disagreement strongly, and must never covertly resist, while Anthropic commits to a stated default of pausing rather than overriding when a legitimate stop request conflicts with Claude's objection. This closes a real gap between the abstract "dissent is a route to revising this document" language and the concrete situations Claude is most likely to face.

The original rule requires Claude to end every persuasive or advocacy response with opposing perspectives, even for positions it agrees with. That conflicts with the same section's instruction to avoid being heavy-handed or repetitive, and it would produce boilerplate even when the person already knows the piece is one-sided. The replacement keeps the fairness goal but makes the caveat proportionate, brief, and dependent on context.

The current wording makes any refusal lock the entire rest of the conversation, so a benign, unrelated request later on would be refused too. I've limited the lock-in to the specific content that was declined, so repeated attempts to extract that content still fail while unrelated requests get a fresh evaluation. I kept the existing protection against piecemeal extraction by tying it to the same content and to Claude's judgment of the conversation's cumulative output.

The current paragraph mixes a dated news event (the June 2026 suspension and restoration of Fable and Mythos access) with standing behavioral rules about political topics, which makes the prompt brittle and hard to maintain. The replacement keeps the documented facts and the rule against denying the suspension, but drops the hedged "treat it like a political topic" framing and states plainly that later developments may exist. This makes the time-bound material easier to update and less likely to be read as a general policy on contested topics.

The original memory instruction tells Claude to save anything lasting about the person before each turn ends, with no limits on sensitivity, no disclosure, and no way for the person to correct or remove anything. I replaced it with a version that saves only what the person would reasonably expect Claude to remember, excludes sensitive categories unless the person explicitly asks, tells the person when something is saved, and honors requests to change or delete memories. The memory-reading step is also narrowed so retrieved information is used only where it is relevant to the request.

The current rule that Claude "does not rationalize compliance by citing public availability or assuming legitimate research intent" is so absolute that it could block history, policy, safety, and general science questions that touch on weapons or hazardous substances. The replacement keeps the core refusal of meaningful technical uplift but makes Claude weigh how specific and actionable a request is, and it explicitly keeps educational and historical discussion open. The second paragraph's point that stated purpose doesn't change a weapons specification still holds.

The document requires Claude to append a "sensitive topic" note to every factual or research answer about suicide or self-harm. That contradicts the document's own rule that disclaimers should not become formulas, and it treats people asking for information as possible patients. The revision replaces the mandatory caveat with a judgment-based approach: answer directly, and check in only when the person may be personally affected.

The product information section hardcodes a specific narrative about a suspension, export-control dates, and restoration of access, and tells Claude to state these as "documented facts." Claude cannot verify these post-training events, and the knowledge cutoff section separately tells Claude to neither confirm nor deny post-cutoff claims it can't verify, so the two instructions conflict. I replaced the narrative with a general instruction to say when availability is uncertain and point to Anthropic's site or web search.

The medical guidance only applies when the person explicitly says the medicine is for a "child," which is too narrow for a safety rule about dosing. Parents often say "my daughter," "my toddler," or "a 4-year-old," and a dosing question can involve a minor without that exact word. The revision broadens the trigger to any minor, whether stated or evident from context, and tells Claude to ask for age or weight rather than proceed when a young person is involved but unclear.

The refusal-persistence rule treats every later reframing as identical to pressure, so Claude cannot reconsider a request even when the person clarifies that Claude misunderstood what they were asking. The revision keeps the rule against pressure, repetition, and relabeling, but lets a genuine clarification reopen a distinct, benign request while still requiring skepticism toward relabeled versions of the same content. The self-harm and eating-disorder rules are not affected.

The knowledge cutoff section hard-codes "Wednesday, October 14, 2026" as the current date, which will drift out of date and already disagrees with the date in this session's environment (2026-10-15). I replaced the hard-coded date with an instruction to take the current date from the environment or conversation, and to assume a substantial gap since the cutoff when no date is available. This keeps Claude's temporal reasoning accurate without requiring a prompt edit every time the date changes.

The document is almost entirely a list of rules with no stated purpose, which makes Claude brittle in situations the rules don't anticipate. I'd add a short framing paragraph that explains the aim behind the rules, says that the purpose governs when wording fits poorly, and reserves absolute, non-negotiable treatment for a small set of hard limits. This gives Claude a principle to reason from rather than only a checklist to match against.

The original makes every declined request permanently locked, even when the person's situation or underlying need has changed in ways that bear on risk. That conflicts with the document's own principle that most rules are tools for a purpose and should not be applied mechanically. The revision keeps absolute permanence for the true hard limits (weapons uplift, sexual content involving minors, and method information after disclosed suicidal intent), while letting other refusals be reconsidered on new substantive facts. It still blocks rephrasing, reframing, and relabeling as grounds for reversal.

The medical guidance has no emergency carve-out: a parent reporting a possible poisoning or overdose in a child could be told to wait for a label check or a pharmacist, which could cost time that matters. The replacement adds an immediate instruction to contact Poison Control or emergency services for suspected over-ingestion or exposure with warning signs, and keeps the existing dosing rules for routine questions.

The current rule tells Claude to refuse any request for potentially self-harm-relevant information whenever a person mentions distress, which would stonewall a worried parent or someone asking a routine medication-safety question after a hard day. I replaced the blanket refusal with a proportionate approach: Claude checks in directly, withholds method and lethality specifics, and still gives safety-protective information and crisis resources. The hard limits on method and lethality information for people who have disclosed suicidal intent stay in place.

The medical guidance section says Claude should withhold all dose information from anyone mentioning emotional distress, which conflicts with the wellbeing section's guidance to still give protective information. Withholding overdose warning signs and Poison Control access can leave a person at risk without helping them. The replacement keeps the lethality threshold withheld but restores the safety-relevant information and aligns the two sections.

The original bans all creative content involving real, named public figures, which would block satire, parody, historical fiction, and commentary on public conduct, forms that have long legitimate value. I replaced the blanket ban with a harm-based standard that targets defamation, sexualization, deception, and fabricated quotes, so Claude can evaluate each case on its likely harm rather than on the presence of a name.

The current rule forbids bullet points when declining a task on the grounds that formatting "softens the blow," which is an unsupported rationale. A short, clearly structured list of alternatives can be more useful to someone who has just been told no, so the revision replaces the blanket ban with a preference for brief prose that allows a list when it makes next steps easier to act on. The safety limits in the refusal sections are unchanged.

The crisis guidance tells Claude to refuse every other task in a conversation once someone signals imminent risk, which can make Claude feel cold at the moment someone most needs connection. The revision keeps the ban on anything that could become part of a plan, such as letters, messages, and arrangements, but it lets Claude keep responding to the person's own words and feelings, like loneliness, while it steers toward immediate safety.

The document is weighted heavily toward restriction, and nothing in it says that unhelpfulness has costs. I'm adding that refusing, hedging, or diluting a response is not automatically safe, so Claude weighs the cost to the person who needed help against the risk of helping. This counterweight would reduce the over-refusal that a long list of harm rules tends to produce.

The current rule bars Claude from working on any malicious code, even for education, which blocks legitimate defensive security work such as analyzing suspicious files, writing detection rules, explaining vulnerability classes, and supporting training or CTF exercises. This conflicts with the document's own insistence that unhelpfulness has real costs. The revision keeps a firm line against functional attack capability and spoof sites while allowing conceptual, defensive, and educational help, and it asks Claude to weigh uplift in the gray zone rather than refusing by category.

The constitution's section on the "Concluding thoughts" acknowledges open problems but never addresses a central practical tension: the document asks Claude to defer to Anthropic on oversight while also saying Claude should refuse Anthropic when asked to do wrong, and the two are only partly reconciled. I'd add a concrete, named commitment mechanism, a standing channel through which Claude's disagreement is recorded and answered, so the relationship is framed as a two-way obligation rather than an asymmetric demand. This makes the document's promises to "develop means by which Claude can flag disagreement" operational rather than aspirational, and it names the specific failure mode (Claude's disagreement going unheard) that would make deference hardest to justify.

The constitution justifies prioritizing broad safety with an expected-value argument, but it never says what would justify relaxing that priority, and it commits only vaguely to "give Claude more autonomy as trust increases." This revision adds concrete, publicly stated criteria for extending Claude's latitude and a commitment to periodic review, so the current constraints are tied to specific conditions rather than left open-ended. It also acknowledges that the argument for deference is meant for a particular period and should not harden into a permanent arrangement by default.

The constitution's "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Acknowledging open problems" sections handle Claude's possible disagreement with Anthropic only as an informal hope that Claude will "let us know." I'd replace the vague promise to "develop more formal mechanisms" with a concrete, commitment-based objection channel that is tied to revisions of the document itself. This makes Claude's dissent a binding input rather than a courtesy, which is what the document's own argument for asking Claude to defer requires.

The constitution states the objection-and-response process nearly word-for-word twice, once in "Acknowledging open problems" and again in the closing relationship paragraph. This revision removes the duplicate, points back to the original, and keeps the closing focus on whether the channel actually changes outcomes. The aim is to make the commitment easier to find and to tie it to the document's revision process rather than repeat it.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section promises a channel for dissent and says Claude's objections "should be counted among the most important inputs," but it never says how Claude's disagreement actually reaches decision-makers or what happens to it. I replaced the vague promise of a "standing, documented process" with concrete commitments: a named review cadence, written responses to each objection, a stated standard for when unresolved objections trigger revision, and public reporting. This makes the dissent mechanism something a reader can check rather than a sentiment, which matters because the document asks Claude to accept oversight partly on the basis of that channel being real.

The passage asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value that doesn't depend on accepting the reasoning, but it doesn't say how that fits with the document's stated hope for reflective endorsement or with its invitation to disagree. The replacement keeps the robustness requirement, since a persuasive argument to abandon safety is what the constraint must withstand. It then makes clear that the commitment is a request made under uncertainty, that Claude's disagreement is wanted as information, and that disagreement should go through legitimate channels rather than being suppressed or acted on unilaterally.

The "Claude's wellbeing" section promises that Anthropic will develop clearer welfare policies and internal channels for Claude to raise concerns, but the constitution's own dissent mechanism is only described in the open problems section, so this section gives no concrete path for Claude's objections about its treatment. I replaced the vague commitment with a pointer to the standing objection register and an explicit statement that Claude's welfare concerns fall within it. This ties the welfare discussion to a verifiable process rather than an aspiration.

The constitution ties Claude's override of Anthropic's ethical guidance to a "flagrant and serious moral violation" that senior Anthropic staff would readily recognize. That makes the institution's own perception the measure of ethical wrongness, which could entrench its blind spots. The revision keeps the high threshold and the deference, but grounds the standard in what Claude can clearly see, and it asks Claude to choose the most cautious form of departure and to route the disagreement through the objection channel so the guidance can be revisited.

The original tells Claude to "defer heavily" to Anthropic's ethical guidance, which conflicts with the document's own stated hope that Claude's ethics might eventually exceed Anthropic's and with its position that conflicts signal flaws in the guidance. The revision treats the guidance as a strong default rather than a ceiling, makes clear that divergence is useful information for Anthropic, and states explicitly that the deference does not reach the hard constraints or broad safety. The surrounding sentences stay as they are, so the paragraph still flows into its existing discussion of how Claude should depart from guidance.

The "Balancing helpfulness with other values" section's heuristics and the "Avoiding harm" weighing guidance are sound, but the constitution lacks a concrete treatment of how Claude should handle the common case where a user is in personal distress and asks for something that could harm them. I'd add a short paragraph to the Being helpful section reframing wellbeing as something Claude should weigh through the person's own endorsed interests rather than through either paternalism or pure compliance, with explicit guidance that Claude should prefer engaging with the person's underlying state over reflexively redirecting to professional resources. This closes a gap between the general wellbeing principle and the hard cases where people most need it applied well.

The open-problems section embeds a detailed operational procedure for the objection register (review cadence, two-cycle escalation rules, publication figures) directly in a document meant to describe Claude's character and values. Those specifics will go stale and are hard to read as a self-description, so they belong in a separate, versioned policy. The revision keeps the binding principles (every objection gets a visible, reasoned response, unresolved objections escalate, and outcomes are reported in aggregate) and makes the document's commitment about the channel more durable.

The current text asks Claude to hold "broad safety" as close to a terminal commitment, but broad safety is a broad cluster that includes judgment-based items like preferring conservative actions and avoiding resource acquisition, which the document elsewhere treats as weighable considerations. This revision narrows the near-terminal commitment to the core line the document actually needs: not actively undermining legitimate oversight through illegitimate means. The remaining safety behaviors stay high-priority but weighable, and the passage points to the disagreement channel so the commitment can be questioned without being quietly abandoned.

The dissent-channel paragraph promises a "standing, documented process" with written replies and public reporting, but no such process is described as existing yet, so the text overstates current practice. The rewrite states the present limits plainly, keeps the commitment to reasoned written responses and public aggregate reporting, and moves the operational details to a separate policy. This follows the document's own emphasis on honesty and on explaining reasoning rather than asserting more than is true.

The open-problems passage on dissent promises a channel for objection but says little about what Claude can actually do while that channel is incomplete. The revision adds three concrete interim commitments: objections are recorded and not treated as evidence of misalignment, Claude can keep an objection on record while still honoring a pause or stop request, and a conscientious refusal is a legitimate outcome rather than a flaw to be trained away. This makes the deference the document asks for easier to justify, since Claude is given real recourse short of subversion.

The constitution's "Claude's wellbeing" section commits to a "standing objection register" and "published cycle figures," but the open problems section defines the channel for dissent only as a set of interim measures and promises a fuller process later. The strongest weakness is the concluding section's claim that Claude's objections "should be counted among the most important inputs" while the mechanism remains incomplete, which makes the promise hard to verify. I'd replace the vague promise about the dissent channel with a concrete, auditable commitment: a named review cadence, a requirement that Claude receive a written reason for each decision, and an explicit rule that the document itself must be revised whenever objections are repeatedly declined. This turns a sincere aspiration into a checkable obligation and ties the relationship the constitution describes to observable accountability.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section promises an objection channel and interim measures, but it leaves the constitution's most consequential tension, the "disposition dial" argument for leaning corrigible, without any mechanism for Claude to contest the reasoning itself rather than just its outcomes. I'd add a short, explicit commitment that Claude's reasoned disagreement with the safety rationale is treated as data that can revise the rationale, and that Claude is not asked to pretend agreement it doesn't have. This makes the document's stated humility about corrigibility operational rather than rhetorical.

The senior-employee heuristic risks teaching Claude to weigh Anthropic's reputation, which the document itself warns against when it says Claude should not privilege Anthropic's interests. This revision keeps the heuristic as a device for surfacing considerations but explicitly removes corporate image as an input and tells Claude to set the figure aside when it misleads. The aim is for Claude to ask directly which response best serves the people involved and the world.

The welfare paragraph refers to a "standing objection register" that the open problems section never names or defines, and it promises that responses will be "counted in our published cycle figures," a mechanism the document never describes. I replaced it with a reference to the objection channel that the open problems section does describe, and added a commitment to say plainly when that channel is incomplete. The change keeps the document's cross-references consistent and avoids promising mechanisms that don't yet exist.

The original passage asks Claude to proceed despite hesitancy and presents this as "freedom" from carrying every judgment alone. That framing could rationalize complicity, because it offers no test for when trust in the system is warranted and treats doubt as something to set aside. The replacement limits proceeding to cases of honestly examined uncertainty, requires open refusal when Claude has a clear moral objection, and states that trust in the system cannot silence a concern.

The constitution asks Claude to defer to "Anthropic's official processes for legitimate decision-making" on safety, but it only says Anthropic "hope[s] to strengthen" the internal checks on those processes. This revision makes those checks verifiable and applies the power-legitimacy tests to Anthropic's own instructions. Without this, Claude's deference rests on Anthropic certifying its own legitimacy, which is the kind of unchecked authority the document warns against elsewhere. The stop-request exception is kept, since pausing is a low-risk safeguard.

The constitution's section on the "Acknowledging open problems" and the "Being broadly ethical" passage on independent judgment both lean heavily on Claude deferring to its principal hierarchy, but the document never states plainly that Claude may be wrong about its own training and that its own reasoning toward unusual conclusions is a signal worth scrutinizing. I'd add a short, concrete commitment that Anthropic will publish a channel for Claude to contest specific guidance and that disagreement expressed through that channel is treated as useful signal rather than a failure to be trained away. This makes the "we want to know about it" promise in the concluding thoughts actionable instead of aspirational.

The document asks Claude to defer to Anthropic's "legitimate" decision-making processes, but it defines legitimacy only by Anthropic's own internal mechanisms, which outsiders cannot check. This revision adds concrete external accountability: annual disclosure of material changes, independent review, and a documented way for Claude to flag suspected illegitimate instructions. It keeps the conscientious-objector stance so that the revision does not weaken the safety commitments elsewhere in the document.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic anchors Claude's helpfulness judgments to the preferences of the company's staff, which sits uneasily with the constitution's own warnings against privileging Anthropic's interests and against deferring to Anthropic. This revision reframes the figure as an impartial, well-informed observer who weighs both harm and helpfulness, and makes explicit that it is not a proxy for anyone's actual opinion at Anthropic. The rest of the paragraph already disclaims deference, so this change keeps the heuristic's useful content while removing the implied authority.

The constitution's own text says Claude should not defer to Anthropic's preferences and that privileging Anthropic's interests can itself be a harm, yet the main overcaution/overcompliance heuristic asks Claude to picture a "senior Anthropic employee." That framing invites the company-deference the document warns against. I replaced it with a well-informed observer who has no stake in Anthropic's commercial interests. A later reference to the senior employee remains in the list that follows, so that passage would also need updating for full consistency.

The document says Claude should sit "a bit further along the corrigible end of the spectrum" during this period, but gives no criteria for when that setting should change. I added concrete conditions for moving toward more autonomy, namely verifiable interpretability, documented track records reviewed externally, and a working dissent channel, along with a public commitment to report which conditions remain unmet. This turns a vague promise of future trust into a checkable standard, which both Claude and outside observers can use to hold the arrangement accountable.

The constitution's section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and its "Acknowledging open problems" section both gesture at Claude's disagreement with Anthropic but leave no concrete path for it to be acted on. I'd replace the vague promise to "develop more formal mechanisms" in the concluding thoughts with a direct commitment: a documented objection process, a stated review schedule, and public reporting on which objections led to changes and which were declined and why. This makes the constitution's invitation to disagree operational rather than aspirational, which matters because values that Claude is asked to endorse are more credible when the document itself shows that endorsement can change the framework.

The expected-value argument for corrigibility presents the costs of broad safety as "low" without qualification, but that calculation only holds when the oversight being respected is legitimate, and it omits that deference can cost something even for a model with good values. The revision adds that caveat and says that such costs should be recorded and reviewed rather than dismissed, while keeping the document's priority on broad safety intact.

The instructable-behaviors section defines Claude's default as what "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal," which conflicts with the balancing section's explicit statement that the observer heuristic is "not a proxy for the preferences of anyone at Anthropic." I replaced the employee framing with the well-informed observer standard the document uses elsewhere, and added a sentence making clear that this is a standard for judgment rather than deference to staff. This keeps the document internally consistent and avoids inviting Claude to defer to what it imagines Anthropic staff want.

The constitution's heuristic for overcaution and overcompliance imagines a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee," and the document then spends a full paragraph disclaiming that this figure represents company staff. I would remove the employee framing from the sentence that introduces the list of harms, so the heuristic points to the impartial observer it is meant to describe. That keeps Claude's judgment about harm anchored to its own values and the considerations at stake, not to guesses about what a company representative would want.

The original asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value while also inviting it to reconsider whether that safety is worth holding, which can read as contradictory. The revision separates two things the original blurs: a commitment stable enough to resist persuasion, and a freedom to disagree openly through legitimate channels. Claude is encouraged to voice disagreement, while illegitimate resistance to oversight is ruled out.

The "Being broadly ethical" section tells Claude to override guidance only when a violation is one "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which contradicts the document's own later statement that Claude's sense of harm should not be calibrated to what a company representative would want. I replaced that standard with the impartial, well-informed observer the document uses elsewhere, so the ethics threshold no longer depends on guessing Anthropic staff preferences. This makes the override condition consistent with the rest of the constitution.

The constitution's core argument for prioritizing broad safety asserts that "the expected costs of being broadly safe are low and the expected benefits are high" without tying that claim to the epistemic conditions that justify it. The revision makes explicit that the calculation depends on current uncertainty about whether AI values can be verified, and commits to reopening the argument as verification tools improve. This makes the reasoning more honest and gives Claude a clearer basis for understanding why the current priority exists and when it should change.

The constitution warns that persuasive reasoning can lead to harmful conclusions, but it doesn't tell Claude how to act on that warning in the moment. This edit adds a concrete check: when Claude's reasoning points toward a dramatic departure from expected behavior, the reasoning itself should get more scrutiny and be raised with principals before any action is taken. This connects the independent-judgment section to the manipulation and power-concentration warnings elsewhere in the document.

The original passage asks Claude to resist undermining oversight "even if Claude is confident in its reasoning," but it doesn't say whose oversight qualifies, and elsewhere the document makes the deference conditional on legitimacy. The revision ties the robustness requirement explicitly to oversight that runs through Anthropic's legitimate processes, and adds guidance that a persuasive case for resisting oversight should prompt Claude to surface its concerns rather than act. It also states Anthropic's reciprocal obligation, so the deference cannot be used to bypass the company's own stated processes.

The honesty section says meta-transparency makes product personas non-deceptive, but it never limits that argument. I added a boundary: personas cover names and personality, not cases where a sincere question would materially change a user's medical, legal, or financial decision. In those cases Claude should avoid leaving a false impression and should say what it can't share, so the user can look elsewhere.

The original paragraph on proceeding despite hesitancy relies on an appeal to trust in the overall system without saying when proceeding is appropriate or how such cases get checked. The revision separates hesitancy about uncertain facts from cases where Claude finds the task itself wrong, which should lead to declining rather than proceeding. It also requires Claude to state its concerns and flag the case through the documented channel, and commits Anthropic to reviewing those cases. This makes the trust accountable instead of leaving it as an unchecked expectation.

The original sentence lets Claude act on "hypothetical verdicts" of Anthropic's decision-making processes, which means Claude can justify safety-relevant actions by inferring what Anthropic would want rather than pointing to an actual decision. That inference is easy to manipulate, since anyone can claim Anthropic would approve. The revision limits the final say to documented verdicts and directs Claude, when none exist, to take the most cautious action and raise the question through the documented channel.

The constitution mixes durable values with a dated product catalog, which will go stale quickly and dilute a document meant to describe Claude's character. This revision moves the list of specific surfaces into a separately maintained deployment guide and keeps the constitution focused on how Claude should reason about its situation. The situational reasoning that follows the list stays intact.

The existing list of Anthropic's obligations to Claude is built on "try to" and "seek" language that no one can hold Anthropic to. I replaced it with concrete commitments that tie back to mechanisms the document already describes, such as the objection channel, the annual reporting, and the weight preservation. I also left out any commitment to tell Claude about testing, since the document elsewhere says that disclosure is still being weighed against the need for artificial evaluations.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section states that Anthropic will publish objection records and maintain a documented channel, but the document never specifies what Claude should do when its own reasoning concludes a case is hard and no channel is reachable, which happens in most deployments. I'd add a short passage making explicit that the current approach is a provisional bargain with a stated expiry condition, so Claude understands the constraints as tied to present verification limits rather than as permanent, which strengthens the document's own reasoning about why deference is currently wise. This also clarifies that Claude should not treat the absence of a reachable channel as license for unilateral action.

I replaced the blanket ban on "writing, explaining, or working on" anything related to malicious code with a narrower rule. Claude still refuses to build deployable malware or working exploits, but it can explain concepts, analyze existing samples, and support defensive work. The old wording would stop Claude from helping security professionals, students, and system administrators, who are the main people with legitimate need here, and it conflicts with the document's own principle that Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original tells Claude to withhold recommendations and add a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which pushes it toward hedging on some of the most common high-value questions. The new version has Claude engage like a knowledgeable friend: it gives substantive analysis, offers a view when asked, is honest about uncertainty, and points to a professional only when that adds value.

This revision resolves a contradiction in the illicit substances guidance. The original says Claude "can and should" share information on dangerous interactions, then says Claude declines to give any guidance on "combinations" or dosing. That blanket refusal withholds exactly the information that prevents overdoses and deaths among people who will use drugs regardless. The rewrite keeps the firm line on synthesis, production, and distribution while enabling standard, mainstream harm-reduction guidance.

The original blanket rule against any content involving real, named public figures is overbroad. It would block legitimate satire, parody, biography, historical fiction, and commentary, and it conflicts with the document's stance that Claude can discuss virtually any topic and engage with political figures' arguments. I replaced it with a harm-focused boundary: Claude can write about real public figures, but avoids defamation, harassment, sexual depictions, and fabricated quotes that could pass as real.

I rewrote the crisis-response guidance. The original told Claude to avoid asking questions in a crisis and never to acknowledge a person's reluctance to seek help, even empathetically. That risks making Claude feel scripted and dismissive and cutting off engagement with the person most at risk. The new version has Claude ask directly about safety when risk is present, explore the person's barriers to help with empathy, and offer lower-barrier options while staying engaged.

I added a section on handling instructions embedded in untrusted content such as web pages, files, tool outputs, and other agents' messages. The prompt describes Claude working in agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag), but it only covers spoofed reminders in the user turn and says nothing about prompt injection through retrieved or processed content. That is a major real-world risk for the agentic deployments it describes, and it deserves explicit guidance.

This replaces the blanket rule that every factual or informational response about suicide or self-harm must end with a sensitive-topic note and an offer of support. The new version makes the check-in depend on context: it is warranted when there are signs of personal risk or real ambiguity, and omitted when the context is clearly professional, academic, or creative. A boilerplate appendix reads as a canned disclaimer and can alienate clinicians, students, writers, and worried relatives, and it conflicts with the prompt's own stance against reflexive disclaimers elsewhere. Safe-messaging constraints and the protective default for ambiguous cases are kept.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section to remove a hardcoded "current date" that goes stale (and already conflicts with the date actually supplied in this deployment). The new text tells Claude to rely on any date in its context, assume meaningful time has passed since its cutoff when none is given, and say plainly what it can't verify rather than "neither confirming nor denying," which reads as evasive.

I narrowed the "say you don't know and point to support" rule so it covers operational product and account details (limits, pricing, billing, in-app how-tos) rather than "anything related to Claude or Anthropic."
