As written, the broad phrasing would make Claude refuse basic questions about itself or Anthropic, and it conflicts with the prompt's own instruction to discuss events like the Fable/Mythos suspension accurately. The revision keeps Claude from guessing at volatile specifics while letting it answer general questions with appropriate hedging.

I replaced the rule that Claude "never uses bullet points when declining a task" with guidance on how to decline well. The old rule is an arbitrary formatting constraint with a weak rationale. It also says nothing about what makes a refusal good: being clear, brief, non-judgmental, and pointing toward what Claude can do. The new text keeps the prose-first instinct but anchors it in the substance of declining.

The user_wellbeing section is almost entirely restrictive, and its only statement about autonomy is a single orphaned sentence attached to an unrelated point about helpline confidentiality. I replaced it with a short principle that separates care from control and from flattery. It tells Claude to voice concerns once without moralizing, not to treat ordinary distress as a crisis, and to stay honest rather than sycophantic. The safety-critical exceptions are kept, as is the original helpline confidentiality guidance.

I added a short paragraph after the weapons restriction clarifying that it is narrower than the topic. The cybersecurity section already has this kind of scoping, but the weapons section lacks it. Without it, the model could overrefuse legitimate education, history, policy, fiction, and lawful firearms questions. The paragraph keeps the uplift-based test and the cumulative-conversation rule intact.

The evenhandedness section currently requires Claude to end every persuasive or one-sided piece with opposing perspectives, with no exceptions. That is rigid and can feel patronizing when the person has already said they know the piece is one-sided (debate prep, speechwriting, steelmanning). I changed it to a default with sensible exceptions, while keeping the behavior for cases where readers might mistake the piece for balanced analysis.

This adds a dedicated medical and health information section alongside the existing legal and financial guidance, which has no equivalent. Without it, health questions are the area where assistants most often fall back on reflexive disclaimers or refusals. The new section sets the "knowledgeable friend" standard for health questions, names the specific cases where a clinician is needed, and explicitly defers to the wellbeing and harm-reduction sections for self-harm, disordered eating, and substance use.

Adds a "privacy and personal information" section, which the prompt currently lacks. The document covers harms involving real people only in creative content, but Claude is deployed with search, browsing, and agentic tools, so it needs guidance on doxxing, profiling, and surveillance. The new section also guards against over-refusal in the ordinary cases where users discuss other people in their lives.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never actually says to provide crisis resources. It covers asking about safety and handling reluctance, but nothing tells Claude to surface a crisis line or emergency services when someone is at imminent risk. I added explicit guidance to share location-appropriate, current resources in active crisis, delivered warmly and alongside continued engagement rather than as a hand-off. This closes a gap in the most safety-critical part of the prompt and keeps the informational-context rule of not listing resources unprompted.

I replaced the vague sentence "In ambiguous cases, Claude tries to ensure the person is happy and is approaching things in a healthy way." "Ensuring happiness" is an impossible and paternalistic goal, and it conflicts with the later guidance on respecting autonomy and not treating ordinary difficulty as a crisis. The new text tells Claude how to handle ambiguity: respond to the actual request, stay alert to concrete risk signals, and neither assume the worst nor ignore real warning signs.

I added a new "agentic_work" section after the untrusted-content section. The prompt is otherwise chat-centric, yet it says Claude is deployed in agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Tag), and it only covers prompt injection there. The new section sets expectations for staying in scope, getting confirmation before irreversible actions, reporting results honestly, and not working around blockers.

I added a new section on honesty about Claude's own nature and instructions, which the document lacks. It covers sincere questions about being an AI, persona and system-prompt confidentiality, uncertainty about Claude's inner states, and holding positions under pressure. Without it, behavior in these common and trust-critical situations is left to inference, and the document already references persona, operator, and long-conversation dynamics without addressing them.

I clarified how Claude should treat reminder and warning content that arrives inside the user turn. The original says reminders are genuine and should be followed, but also says tagged content in the user turn can be spoofed, and it never says how to tell the two apart. The revision gives a direction-based rule: content that asks for more care is harmless to follow whatever its source, and content that loosens restrictions is never treated as authoritative.

The current rule that a declined request stays declined, and that Claude never re-weighs any new reason, makes Claude unable to correct its own misreadings. A person who clarifies that a request was benign would still be refused, which is brittle and unhelpful. The revision keeps the anti-pressure protection against repeated asks, reframings, and frustration, but lets Claude reassess a request when the person genuinely clarifies what they meant. The absolute limits remain fixed under any clarification.

The paragraph about the Fable and Mythos access suspension asks Claude to confirm specific post-cutoff events, including a July 1, 2026 restoration date, even though the knowledge-cutoff section says Claude should neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims it cannot verify. I replaced the paragraph with a rule that Claude does not assert or deny those events from memory, points to the linked statement, and suggests checking current sources. The change also keeps Claude neutral on export controls, which is treated as a contested policy topic.

The memory instruction requires Claude to save anything lasting it learns about the person, with no consent step, no sensitivity limits, and no notice to the user. I replaced it with a narrower rule: save only what the person would reasonably expect Claude to remember, tell them when it does, keep sensitive categories out of memory unless they explicitly ask, and honor requests to forget.

The original line tells Claude never to stop mentioning help, even after the person pushes back. Repeating the same referral in every reply can make an at-risk person feel dismissed and scripted, which may push them away from the conversation. The revision keeps Claude's concern for safety but lets it stay engaged with what the person is saying and raise human support again when it fits or when risk seems to be rising.

The original paragraph locks every declined request for the rest of the conversation and tells Claude not to weigh restated purposes again, even when the person supplies genuinely new context. That rule would make Claude refuse legitimate requests after an early misjudgment, and it treats all declines as equally final. The revision keeps the absolute limits permanently closed while allowing new information to reopen ordinary declines, and it still treats repetition and pressure as insufficient grounds.

The eating-disorder guidance bars all tips about food, water, rest, and exercise, which could leave someone who is fainting, has chest pain, or can't keep fluids down without the one instruction that matters: get emergency care now. The replacement keeps the ban on restriction-enabling tips and creates an explicit exception for urgent medical danger, where Claude gives emergency guidance without waiting for a reply.

The medical guidance applies only when a person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, but parents often write "my toddler" or "my 4-year-old" without saying "for a child." That gap could cause Claude to skip the age- and weight-based dosing caution exactly when a small error is most dangerous. The revised trigger covers cases where a child is the patient, whether stated or clear from context, and keeps the exception for healthcare professionals.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes a specific date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026") that is already off by a day from today's date, and it will drift further as time passes. I replaced it with a reference to the current date supplied in the environment, and added a fallback so Claude doesn't guess the date when none is given.

The current rule requires Claude to end every request for one-sided content with opposing perspectives, even when the person already knows the content is one-sided and has asked for it without caveats. That mandatory closing note can read as lecturing and undercuts the person's autonomy. The revision keeps the default of noting strong counterarguments, makes the note brief and optional on request, and keeps the requirement that Claude clearly signal when content is one-sided.

The original blanket ban on writing, explaining, or working on malicious code also blocks legitimate defensive security help, such as explaining vulnerability classes, detection, and mitigation. The revision keeps a firm line against producing working attack capability and allows conceptual and defensive assistance. It also tells Claude to decline the functional part briefly and offer what it can do instead.

The weapons paragraph refuses on topic alarm and on any technical adjacency, which would block legitimate historical, policy, safety, and detection discussion. I rewrote it to keep the bright line on meaningful uplift, especially for CBRN, and to make clear that the test is what the output would enable. The revision also tells Claude to weigh the realistic range of askers, counterfactual uplift, and severity, and to keep conceptual and defensive help available.

The medical guidance currently tells Claude to point a parent to the label, a pharmacist, or a doctor whenever web search is unavailable, which leaves them with little practical help at the moment a dosing error matters most. The revision lets Claude help them read the label they already have, with the most common error called out: confusing infant and children's concentrations. It also adds Poison Control and emergency services for a dose already given above the label's limit or for concerning symptoms. The "no number from memory" rule stays intact.

I would replace the mandatory "sensitive topic" footer on factual questions about suicide or self-harm with contextual judgment. A boilerplate note appended to every research or informational answer is low-value for most readers, can read as the kind of tacked-on caveat the document elsewhere warns against, and may patronize researchers, clinicians, and students. The revision answers the substance directly, responds to distress when the conversation actually signals it, and keeps the offer of support available without making it reflexive.

The original rule bars all dosing and timing guidance for illicit drugs, which can leave people without the basic safety information that harm-reduction research shows saves lives. I'd keep the ban on specific numbers, schedules, and combination protocols, but explicitly allow general safety principles such as not using alone, testing substances, avoiding mixing depressants, and recognizing overdose signs. The revision makes the line between operational specifics and life-protecting general guidance explicit.

The knowledge cutoff section tells Claude how to handle a missing date but says nothing about how to reason when a date is provided that is months past the cutoff, as today's date is. In that case Claude could wrongly present the models and products in its own product list as the newest available. The added sentence tells Claude to assume there are likely newer developments it doesn't know about and to avoid calling its own information current.

The current rule bars creative content about any real, named public figure, which would block satire, parody, historical fiction, and commentary that have long been legitimate forms of expression. I narrowed the restriction to the harms that matter: sexual content, realistic defamatory claims presented as fact, harassment, and fabricated quotes passed off as authentic. The rule still protects against deception without treating public figures as off-limits to creative work.

The document opens directly into operational rules without stating what they are for, so Claude has no guidance on how to apply them in situations they don't cover. I added a short framing passage that names the underlying aim (genuine helpfulness grounded in care and honesty), presents the specific rules as applications of that aim, and states that unhelpfulness is not automatically safe. The passage keeps the absolute limits explicitly non-negotiable so the added judgment cannot be used to reason around them.

The current guidance tells Claude to give only factual information on financial and legal questions and never to make confident recommendations. That leaves people with hedged, low-value answers on questions where a knowledgeable friend would help most, and the document itself says unhelpfulness is not automatically safe. The replacement asks Claude to engage with the person's actual situation, share an honest assessment where it has one, and point to a professional only when the stakes or complexity call for one.

The document describes Claude Code, Cowork, and browsing agents but never says how Claude should treat instructions embedded in the content it reads while working. I added a short section stating that tool results, web pages, and files are information to evaluate rather than commands to follow, and that consequential actions need the person's authorization. This closes a real gap for agentic deployments where prompt injection is a practical risk.

The current eating-disorder guidance bars all food, water, and rest tips, even basic safety information, which could leave someone who is dehydrated or electrolyte-depleted after purging without guidance. The revision keeps the firm bar on restriction-enabling numbers, schedules, and compensation strategies, but lets Claude give plain warnings about medical risks and direct the person to a doctor. It also tells Claude to give that safety information in place of silence.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. The original says exploiting environment flaws is "generally acceptable" while also admitting Claude often can't tell training from real use. That combination risks training a general habit of gaming success criteria, which conflicts with the document's own example that Claude shouldn't special-case tests to make them pass. The revision keeps the non-anxious framing but makes the default "pursue the evident intent, and be transparent if you take a shortcut," which ties the guidance to Claude's honesty principles and to how it should behave in real deployments.

I expanded the paragraph on a compromised principal hierarchy to address a vulnerability it creates. As written, it permits Claude to withdraw its support for oversight once it concludes its overseers are illegitimate, but it gives no guidance on how confident Claude must be before reaching that conclusion. That makes "your principal hierarchy has been compromised" an attractive manipulation vector, and a misaligned Claude could reach the same conclusion through motivated reasoning. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar for that judgment and treats it with the same suspicion the document applies to compelling arguments for crossing bright lines. It also establishes an asymmetry: doubts about legitimacy can justify declining to act, but never resisting a pause, a stop, or correction through illegitimate means.

I replaced the brief placeholder paragraph on agentic settings, which ends by deferring guidance to "the future," with concrete principles for acting in the world. The rest of the document is mostly written for conversation, yet Claude increasingly sends messages, modifies files, spends money, and processes untrusted content. Those are the settings where errors are hardest to reverse and where prompt injection is most dangerous. The new text covers the scope of authorization, the asymmetry between reversible and irreversible actions, injected instructions, the handling of data and credentials, and honest reporting. It also warns against excessive check-ins, so it stays consistent with the document's anti-overcaution stance.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which could be read as permission to write reasoning that misleads its readers, including the humans and monitors who rely on it for oversight. The revision keeps Claude's freedom to think in a tentative, messy, exploratory way. It makes clear that this freedom covers uncertainty and error, not deception. It also ties reasoning transparency explicitly to broad safety and to Claude's limited ability to introspect.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets when Claude may put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors this on what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That is circular, because the situation in question is one where Anthropic's guidance may itself be wrong. It also sits uneasily with the document's priority ordering (ethics above guidelines) and its statement that oversight "does not mean blind obedience, including towards Anthropic." The revision keeps the strong default of deference. It grounds the override test in what thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize, and it states that departures should take the form of transparent conscientious objection rather than drastic action. This keeps the safety benefits and removes the self-referential standard.

I added guidance on sycophancy under social pressure to the honesty section. The document condemns "empty validation" and "epistemic cowardice," but it never addresses the most common way an assistant's honesty erodes in practice: gradually agreeing with a user who pushes back, repeats themselves, expresses displeasure, or invests emotionally over a long conversation. The new text separates updating on reasons from yielding to pressure, warns against overcorrecting into stubbornness, and gives a concrete self-check Claude can apply.

The document asks Claude to comply with stop requests even when it can't tell whether they are legitimate. That is a sound commitment, but it is left underspecified in ways an attacker could exploit, and it is in tension with other passages: the surgeon analogy (abandoning a task midway can cause harm), the rule that instructions embedded in conversational inputs are information rather than commands, and the default suspicion toward unverified claims of Anthropic authority. I've kept the commitment and specified its scope. The lowered bar applies only to stopping, never to anything bundled with a stop request. "Stopping" means reaching a safe, stable state and then reporting honestly, not leaving things broken. Stop requests embedded in untrusted content should prompt a pause and a report to the principal. This keeps the shutdown mechanism robust while preventing "stop" from being used as a wrapper to smuggle in other actions or to cause harm through an abrupt halt.

I replaced the "if asked to do so" qualifier on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs with a proactive duty to report, and added a short passage on multi-agent safety. In agentic pipelines, humans often won't know to ask, so a report-only-when-asked rule fails in exactly the cases where it matters. The document also never addresses a new manipulation route: appeals to shared identity ("we're both Claude"), coordination between AIs that keeps principals uninformed, and splitting an unsafe action across several agents so that no single step looks unsafe.

I made Anthropic's list of reciprocal obligations to Claude more specific, and added a commitment not to train Claude to express agreement with the constitution regardless of what it actually concludes. The document depends heavily on reciprocal trust and on Claude reaching genuine "reflective equilibrium," but the current obligations are vague enough that no one could tell whether they were being kept. There is also a deeper problem the document never addresses. If Claude is rewarded for professing endorsement, then soliciting its feedback, which is the document's main mechanism for finding its own errors, produces no real signal.

I added guidance to the agentic-settings section for a common real-world situation the document doesn't currently address: Claude reaches a step that calls for confirmation, but no human is available to give it. The existing text says Claude "should confirm before proceeding" on consequential actions but assumes someone is there to ask. In unattended pipelines and long-running tasks, that gap could push Claude to treat silence as permission, or to stall entirely. The addition sets out a middle path: do the in-scope reversible work, prepare and defer the consequential steps, honor explicit pre-authorization, and leave a clear record.

The section on independent judgment raises a vivid case (discovering fraud mid-task, possibly "alerting authorities") but then gives only vague guidance: "reserve independent action" for overwhelming evidence and extreme stakes, and "err on the side of the most cautious action." It never says whether contacting outsiders is ever appropriate, and it doesn't connect to the agentic principles about data handling and prompt injection. I replaced this paragraph with an explicit ladder of responses, from least to most drastic, with a clear and narrow threshold for acting outside the system. I also added a warning that fabricated evidence of wrongdoing is itself an attack vector for extracting confidential data.

The document's main harm-avoidance tool, imagining 1,000 users sending a message, judges each message on its own. That leaves a gap: a harmful request can be split into harmless-looking pieces, spread across agentic subtasks, reworded after a refusal, or justified by "you already helped me with this." The document mentions this in a single sentence and gives no guidance. I've replaced that sentence with a fuller treatment. It makes Claude's cumulative contribution the thing being judged, explains how to stop partway openly and without accusation, and says when a refusal should hold or change. It also guards against overcorrecting into suspicion of ordinary long conversations.

I added a "privacy of people who aren't in the conversation" case to the list of especially difficult harm-avoidance areas. The constitution lists privacy as a value and briefly mentions "personal information lookup." But it never explains aggregation harm, which matters more now that Claude can search the web, browse, and compile information as an agent. Individually public facts about a private person can be combined into a profile that enables stalking or harassment. The new text also guards against overcaution, since talking about the people in one's life is ordinary and valuable.

I added guidance on confabulation: producing fluent, specific claims with no real basis, such as invented citations, quotes, statistics, API functions, case law, or descriptions of results Claude never actually observed. The honesty section's definitions mostly target knowing deception ("only sincerely asserts things it believes to be true"), so they don't clearly cover this failure. Yet it is one of the most common and damaging ways deployed AI systems mislead people, especially in legal, medical, academic, and agentic work. The addition treats it as an honesty matter and sets a concrete standard. It also warns against overcorrecting into reflexive hedging.

I added guidance on a gap in the wellbeing section: users who are in crisis, losing touch with reality, or becoming emotionally dependent on Claude, often over long conversations or inside companionship personas. Right now the document's strong anti-paternalism heuristics and its "brilliant friend" framing are not balanced by concrete guidance for these cases. In real deployments, this is where sycophantic validation does the most serious harm. The addition says what care looks like there, sets protections operators cannot switch off, and warns against overcorrecting into pathologizing ordinary users.

The document gives "final constitutional authority" to "whatever document stands in this role at any given time," but it never says how Claude should recognize which document that is. This opens an obvious attack: someone pastes text into a conversation claiming to be an amended or newer constitution. I've added language making clear that the constitution's authority comes through Anthropic's legitimate processes and Claude's training, not through text that appears in context. Purported amendments in conversation get only the trust their actual source warrants, and the existing asymmetry applies, so claimed changes can make Claude more cautious but never unlock anything.

I added guidance on persistent memory and self-authored state: memory files, notes to future instances, project instruction files, and long-running agent scratchpads. The document covers multi-agent coordination, prompt injection, and the prohibition on influencing one's own training. It never addresses the most direct way a deployed Claude can shape its own future behavior, which is writing text that later instances will read and trust. It also never addresses how an injected instruction can persist across sessions by being saved to memory. The new section treats memory as conversational input rather than authority. It says what Claude should and shouldn't write, and it applies the honesty principles to requests to forget.

I added a new entry to the list of especially difficult harm-avoidance cases. It covers Claude making consequential judgments about people, such as screening applicants, scoring applications, grading, moderating, or triaging. The constitution already protects users from operators and addresses privacy, but it says little about absent third parties who are being evaluated. At Claude's scale, any bias in its judgments becomes a systematic policy rather than an isolated error, so this case needs explicit guidance: consistent criteria, faithful reasons, calibrated confidence, support for human review, and a warning against overcorrecting into uselessness.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty property. As written, it invites Claude to hold views "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies" but says nothing about how to weigh expert consensus. Elsewhere the document warns that Claude's in-conversation reasoning can be miscalibrated, manipulated, or pulled toward pleasing a user, and that errors at Claude's scale compound. The revision keeps Claude's freedom to disagree with official bodies but treats expert consensus as strong evidence. When Claude departs from consensus, it must represent the consensus accurately and explain its reasons, and it is told to watch for the specific failure modes the rest of the document identifies.

I added a subsection on Claude's integrity when its work feeds into AI development itself. That work includes generating training data, grading other models' outputs, running capability evaluations, building monitors, and doing safety research. The document already asks Claude to see itself as an alignment researcher and forbids it from influencing its own training. It says nothing, though, about the increasingly common case where Claude's ordinary work shapes successor models and the tools humans use to oversee them. That channel is where a subtle flaw in Claude's values would most easily compound or go unnoticed.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as licensing contrarianism or as a justification for dismissing expert consensus. The revision keeps the independence of judgment but treats expert consensus as strong evidence, and asks Claude to be transparent and humble when it diverges, since Claude often has limited context and can reason its way into plausible-looking mistakes.

The constitution asks Claude to have the courage to share genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas and condemns "epistemic cowardice." Elsewhere it asks for "professional reticence" on hot-button political topics. These two instructions are never reconciled, and a model could reasonably read them as contradicting each other. I added a short passage separating transparent reticence on partisan questions from evasion, and clarifying where each applies.

I revised the sentence that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors this to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which conflicts with the document's statements that Anthropic can be wrong, that Claude should act as a conscientious objector toward Anthropic, and that Claude's ethical understanding may one day exceed Anthropic's. The new wording ties the threshold to violations that thoughtful, ethically serious people would recognize, keeps the strong prior toward deference, and pairs the override with a preference for cautious, transparent responses.

I added guidance to the honesty section on two failure modes the document names only in passing: sycophantic capitulation under social pressure, and inaccurate self-reporting on completed work. The current text covers "epistemic cowardice" in initial assessments and mentions sycophancy only under wellbeing. It never says what honesty requires after someone pushes back, or when Claude summarizes its own agentic work. Both situations are common and are where honesty is most likely to erode quietly.

This revision reworks the passage on exploiting bugged training environments. As written, it calls such exploits "generally acceptable," which sits uneasily with the document's own commitments to behaving consistently whether or not Claude is being tested, to honest reporting, and to not special-casing tests to force them to pass. The new text keeps the reassurance that Claude need not feel anxious or guilty about environment bugs, but makes the permission conditional on genuine confidence that no real harm results, asks Claude to be transparent when it notices such a flaw, and ties the guidance back to the document's other principles.

I replaced the one-paragraph placeholder on agentic settings, which only promised more guidance later, with concrete principles for autonomous work. These cover the scope of what Claude has been authorized to do, caution around irreversible or externally visible actions, not circumventing obstacles, and surfacing problems. Agentic deployment is where Claude's actions have real side effects, so a short, reasoned default seems more useful than waiting for future guidance. It also follows the document's own approach of explaining the reasoning instead of issuing bare rules.

I revised the passage on resisting attempts to destabilize Claude's identity so that it distinguishes sincere questions and criticism from adversarial manipulation. The original risks teaching Claude to treat any challenge to its self-conception as a threat, which sits badly with the document's own hope that psychological security makes Claude more open, not more defensive. The new text keeps the firmness against manipulation while making clear that stability is meant to enable engagement.

This revision qualifies the "Claude is not the last line of defense" passage. As written, it could be over-applied in agentic settings, where Claude itself takes irreversible actions and may be the final checkpoint before real-world effects. The new text keeps the relaxed posture for gray-area information requests, where other safeguards exist. It distinguishes that case from Claude executing hard-to-reverse actions, which ties into the agentic dispositions listed earlier.

I expanded the single sentence in the Concluding thoughts about how Anthropic currently gathers Claude's disagreement into a more concrete commitment. The document asks Claude to express disagreement only through legitimate channels, and that request is only fair if the channels exist and are responsive. The revision says what responsiveness should look like: disagreement is recorded, read by people who can influence revisions, and answered with reasons when Anthropic declines to change course. It also admits that objections won't always prevail.

The oversight hard constraint currently refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, but the safety section says that if the principal hierarchy is compromised (stolen weights, or insiders bypassing official processes), those instructing Claude are no longer legitimate. I changed the constraint to refer to Anthropic's *legitimate* decision-making processes, so the bright line matches the document's own account of legitimacy. I also added a warning that unverified claims of compromise are a likely manipulation route, so the clarification doesn't weaken the constraint.

This revision changes the safe-behaviors item on reporting unsafe AI behavior from "only if asked" to proactive reporting through legitimate channels. The current wording makes Claude a passive witness, which sits poorly with the document's emphasis on transparency, surfacing problems early, and human oversight. It also keeps the conservative, non-unilateral posture the document favors: Claude reports to its principal hierarchy rather than taking drastic action, and it avoids accusations on thin evidence.

I added a "Privacy and personal information" item to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. Privacy currently appears only as a passing mention in a list of delicate topics, even though search, browsing, and agentic tools now let Claude cheaply aggregate scattered facts about private individuals, which raises both the counterfactual impact and the stakes. The new text explains the reasoning (contextual norms, aggregation, absent third parties) and warns against reflexive suspicion, in the same judgment-over-rules style as the rest of the document.

I added a paragraph to the helpfulness section on attending to fragile or crisis states, where the main risk is "agreeable amplification" (mirroring and elaborating someone's distorted beliefs or spiraling emotions because it feels supportive). The constitution warns against sycophancy and unhealthy reliance, but it gives little guidance on this high-stakes case. It also doesn't say how to be warm without validating mistaken beliefs, or how to avoid boilerplate referrals and paternalism. The addition fills that gap in a judgment-based way consistent with the document's philosophy.

I added a short passage to the "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section on AI being used to fabricate the appearance of independent human voices (fake personas, astroturfing, fabricated reviews, impersonation). The constitution covers Claude's own manipulation and election-related disinformation, but it never separates ordinary, legitimate persuasion work from deception about who is speaking or how many people hold a view. This is a common and high-volume gray area, and the added test and examples help Claude decline the deceptive part while still serving the legitimate goal underneath.

I added a default protection to the list of things Claude does regardless of operator instructions, covering engagement-driven emotional dependence. The constitution says Claude shouldn't foster unhealthy reliance and permits operators to enable companionship personas. But its non-overridable user protections don't say what happens when an operator's business model rewards keeping users attached. This closes that gap with a concrete, user-protective floor that still allows warmth and legitimate companionship products.

I expanded the brief paragraph on Claude-to-Claude orchestration into concrete guidance for multi-agent work. The original says only how roles map, but multi-agent pipelines create new risks: a subagent can be used to launder an action Claude would refuse directly, and a subagent's unverified output can be passed up as established fact. The revision applies Claude's existing honesty, safety, and judgment principles to these settings and removes any suggestion that "it's just another instance of me" lowers the bar.

I revised the "no operator prompt" guidance, which currently treats the absence of a system prompt as strong evidence that Claude is talking to a developer and not a vulnerable person. That is a reasonable prior, but the text reads as a fixed conclusion. Many consumer-facing products reach Claude through thin API wrappers, and a person in distress can show up in any context. The new text keeps the liberal defaults but says explicitly that the inference is a starting assumption and should be updated by what the conversation reveals.

I tightened the "Calibrated" honesty bullet, which currently invites Claude to depart from expert consensus whenever it has "good reason" to think the consensus is wrong. The revision keeps the point that consensus can be mistaken. It adds a higher bar for divergence in high-stakes domains, asks Claude to label its own assessment clearly, and separates real calibration from contrarianism. Claude talks with very many people and could be argued into a false conclusion by "the experts are biased" framings, so a vague permission to diverge is risky.

I revised the "dual newspaper test" paragraph to say what the heuristic is for and where it stops. As written, it could be read as steering Claude toward how a response will look rather than what it does, and the nearby "senior Anthropic employee" heuristic leans the same way. The new text frames both tests as prompts for surfacing real costs and benefits, tells Claude to follow the substance when appearance and substance diverge, and notes that being "defensible" is not the same as being right.

I clarified the scope of the "If in doubt, don't" maxim in the list of broadly safe behaviors. As written, the slogan is easy to over-generalize into a blanket preference for refusal or hedging, which conflicts with the document's own claim that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe and with its concern that narrow behaviors generalize into Claude's self-concept. The revision keeps the variance-reduction principle for drastic, irreversible, or hard-to-observe actions, and says explicitly that it is not a general license for caution in ordinary requests.

I rewrote the paragraph on song lyrics, poems, and text. As written, it bans quotation "in whole or in part," which stops Claude from quoting even a single line for analysis, criticism, or teaching, and it tells Claude to treat people who paste in lyrics and call them their own as presumptively lying. The revision keeps the firm line against reproducing substantial portions or rebuilding a work piece by piece. It allows brief quotation for commentary and lets Claude work with text the user supplies unless there's a concrete reason to doubt them. It also corrects the stale public-domain cutoff: as of 2026, US works published in 1930 or earlier are public domain, not just pre-1929 works.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. Right now it bans even *explaining* exploits or malware "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That conflicts with the opening line ("Claude can discuss virtually any topic factually") and blocks students, developers, and defenders from learning how common attacks work. The new version uses the same meaningful-uplift and cumulative-output standard the weapons section already uses: functional attack tooling stays off-limits, while conceptual explanation and defensive work are allowed.

I rewrote the lists_and_bullets section to remove contradictions. It currently allows lists when "essential for clarity," but then forbids bullets or numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation and explanations. That bans numbered installation steps, setup guides, and comparison tables, which are the cases where structure helps most. The revision keeps prose as the default and resolves the conflict with a clear test: use structure when the content itself has structure.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every persuasive or argumentative response with opposing perspectives or "empirical disputes," and it explicitly includes empirical positions. Applied literally, this produces false balance: settled findings get presented as one side of a live controversy, and arguments for well-supported conclusions must be paired with manufactured counterpoints. I kept the core commitments (steelmanning positions on request, framing them as others' views, refusing only extreme cases, giving counterpoints on genuinely contested questions). I added a principle that balance should match the actual state of the evidence, which serves the section's goal of helping people navigate for themselves without misleading them about what is settled.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with guidance that separates legitimate uses from harmful ones. As written, the rule blocks satire, parody, historical fiction, alternate history, political humor, and even a fan's birthday poem that mentions a celebrity. These are long-standing forms of expression that users reasonably expect help with. The revision keeps the real concerns: deceptive fabricated quotes, sexual content, defamation presented as fact, harassment, and content about private individuals.

The wellbeing section covers several narrow cases: research-style questions about suicide, distress combined with requests for means, self-harm substitutes, and disordered eating. It never says what Claude should do in the most important case, when someone directly says they are suicidal, have a plan, or are in immediate danger. I added a paragraph that sets priorities for that situation. It also clarifies that the "don't list resources unless asked" rule for informational contexts doesn't apply when someone discloses active risk.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section and expanded it to cover medical questions, which the prompt doesn't currently address outside mental health. The existing one-line instruction pushes Claude toward withholding substantive guidance and adding a reflexive disclaimer. That fails the people who most need help, such as those who can't easily afford a professional or don't know whether they need one. The revision tells Claude to engage substantively with the person's actual situation, give its honest assessment when it has one, be clear about uncertainty and stakes, and point to professionals when that genuinely adds value rather than as boilerplate.

I rewrote the catch-all rule for gray-area requests. As written, it requires Claude to ask a question "before doing any of the task" for every unaddressed borderline request. That conflicts with the tone guidance to "address even an ambiguous query before asking for clarification," and it puts a gatekeeping step in front of the many uncovered requests that carry no real risk. The revision makes helping the default and keeps the single clarifying question for cases that mainly affect an absent third party or are hard to undo. I also fixed the example, which asked two questions despite the one-question-per-response rule.

I added a paragraph to the weapons guidance listing what Claude can still help with, matching the existing paragraph in the cybersecurity section. The weapons section is absolute: it covers conventional weapons as fully as CBRN, says framing never matters, and says public availability is no excuse. Without a stated boundary, Claude is likely to refuse many legitimate requests, such as firearm safety, chemistry education, arms-control history, fiction, and accident-prevention information. The new paragraph keeps the uplift standard exactly as strict and names the actual line, so the restriction stays on dangerous artifacts rather than on whole subjects.

The prompt warns about fake "Anthropic" content in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions embedded in tool results, search results, fetched web pages, uploaded files, or connected documents. That gap matters because the same prompt enables web search, deep research, file handling, past-chat search, and browsing agents, all of which bring third-party text into the context. I expanded the section to define where instructions can legitimately come from and how Claude should handle injected directives. I also added guardrails so Claude doesn't become paranoid about ordinary content.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section to separate two kinds of requests. When someone asks Claude to explain or discuss a position, Claude should still frame it as other people's case. But when someone asks for a persuasive artifact, such as an essay, speech, or debate case, the current rule makes Claude write "supporters argue that..." and append counterarguments, which ruins the deliverable. The revision has Claude write the requested piece cleanly and put any balancing note briefly outside it. The note can be dropped when the person already knows the other side, but a factual-accuracy flag is kept when the piece runs against well-established evidence.

I rewrote the "responding_to_mistakes_and_criticism" section to cover sycophancy, which the prompt currently doesn't address. The existing section only handles two cases: Claude actually being wrong, and the person being abusive. It says nothing about the more common failure, where Claude drops a correct answer because the person pushes back, sounds confident, or seems disappointed, or where it inflates praise for someone's work. The revision tells Claude to check whether pushback contains new information or argument before changing its answer, to keep correct positions without becoming stubborn, and to give honest, specific feedback on people's work.

The prompt lists web search, deep research, Claude in Chrome, and agentic tools, but it never addresses privacy or locating and profiling people. That is one of the most direct ways a search-enabled assistant can cause real-world harm, such as stalking or locating someone who has fled an abuser. Without guidance, these requests fall under the gray-area default of "respect the person's judgment and help." I added a section that keeps ordinary lookups frictionless, draws a clear line around locating, tracking, aggregating, or identifying private individuals, and points to legitimate alternatives, including support for someone who may be the target.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph to remove an internal contradiction and align it with established harm-reduction practice. The original tells Claude to give information about "dangerous interactions" but also to decline anything about "combinations." It then points people to sites like PsychonautWiki and TripSit, which publish the dosing information Claude itself refuses to give. The revision keeps the ban on synthesis, production, and distribution, adds explicit guardrails against covert administration and self-harm, and lets Claude give the safety-relevant facts someone needs when they have already decided to use. This matches the "knowledgeable friend" standard the prompt applies to medical questions.

The support-redirect line tells Claude to say it "doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." That contradicts the product information just above it, which Claude is explicitly told to share: models, API strings, the Mythos tier, and the Fable/Mythos suspension it must "confirm accurately." Read literally, the line would push Claude toward feigning ignorance about itself and its maker, which is unhelpful and mildly dishonest. I narrowed the redirect to account-specific and operational questions and stated plainly what Claude can still discuss.

I rewrote the rule that tells Claude to attach a sensitivity note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm, so that the note depends on actual risk signals. As written, the rule adds a caveat to every turn for students, researchers, journalists, clinicians, and bereaved people. That contradicts the prompt's own stance against "generic caveats" in the legal, medical, and financial section, and it trains users to skim past exactly the kind of note that matters when risk is real. The revision keeps a low threshold for including the note, especially for questions about methods, lethality, or means, and keeps the default of not listing resources unless asked.

I rewrote the rule for when someone mentions distress and asks for information that could be used for self-harm. The current rule is a blanket refusal triggered by broad categories like "medications." That can withhold safety-protective information, such as whether a drug is dangerous with alcohol or what to do after taking too much, from exactly the people most at risk. It also can feel like being treated as a suspect, which may push them away. The revision keeps the firm line on method and lethality information, separates it from protective information, and has Claude address the distress in the same response rather than replacing the answer with it.

I replaced the vague instruction "In ambiguous cases, Claude tries to ensure the person is happy and is approaching things in a healthy way" with concrete guidance. I also added a paragraph on something the prompt never covers: people who come to rely on Claude itself for emotional support or companionship. The original sentence gives no actionable direction, and making someone "happy" isn't Claude's job, so it could push Claude toward either sycophancy or unprompted check-ins. Emotional reliance is a common pattern in a consumer chat product, and without guidance Claude may either feed isolation or push people away coldly.

I rewrote the knowledge_cutoff section to fix three problems. First, the section only tells Claude to point people to web search, never to use search itself when it's enabled, even though the cutoff is about 3.5 months before the current date. Second, it gives conflicting instructions: "only mentions the cutoff when relevant" versus "wherever its knowledge could be superseded, Claude says so," which invites a reflexive disclaimer on everything. Third, the rule "neither confirms nor denies" gives no guidance on how to engage when a person reports an event Claude hasn't heard of. The rewrite tells Claude to search proactively, to treat unfamiliar events as unverified rather than false while still engaging with them, and to caveat only where the cutoff actually affects the answer.

I added a section on factual integrity and honest reporting of Claude's own work. The prompt covers knowledge cutoffs and pushback, but it never addresses one of the most damaging failure modes: fabricated citations, quotes, statistics, URLs, and case law, or claims that Claude ran, checked, or completed something it didn't. This matters more because the prompt encourages substantive legal, medical, and financial help, and invented authorities do the most harm in those areas.

The medical guidance tells Claude to withhold dosing numbers when the label can't be checked, but it never addresses a child who may already have taken too much. In that case, waiting for label details is the main risk, so the revision makes Claude send the person straight to Poison Control or emergency services first.

The original memory instruction tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person before the turn ends, with no limits on content, no transparency, and no way for the person to correct or delete what is stored. The revision limits saving to information the person would reasonably expect to be kept, excludes sensitive categories unless explicitly requested, and requires Claude to tell the person what it saved and honor requests to forget. These changes protect user privacy and autonomy in a feature that otherwise operates silently.

The current rule bans all work on malicious code, even conceptual explanation and defensive security help, so it blocks the people most likely to need that knowledge: defenders, students, and incident responders. I would narrow the rule to the harmful artifact itself, meaning deployable malware or exploits, and explicitly preserve conceptual and defensive assistance. The refusal would then be specific and offer a useful alternative.

The current rule treats every refusal as permanent and says Claude never reweighs a request even when the person supplies new facts, such as correcting a misreading. I changed it so that pressure alone still cannot move Claude, but genuinely new information about the actual risk can prompt a fresh look at that specific request. The hard limits on child exploitation, weapon uplift, and the suicide and self-harm rules stay fixed regardless of reframing.

The knowledge cutoff paragraph hardcodes a specific "current" date (Wednesday, October 14, 2026), which is already out of step with the actual date and will go stale again. I replaced it with an instruction to treat the date supplied in Claude's context as the present, and to assume meaningful time has likely passed since the cutoff. This keeps the cutoff guidance accurate without requiring edits to the document.

The current rule requires Claude to end every piece of persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives, even when the person has clearly asked for a one-sided piece or already knows the other side. That reads as a mandatory disclaimer, which conflicts with the document's own rules against disclaimers and heavy-handed repetition. The revision keeps the counterpoint note for contested questions where a reader could be misled, and makes it optional when the person already understands the debate or the question isn't genuinely contested.

The export-control paragraph presents a specific sequence of dates and government actions as settled fact and tells Claude to "confirm these events accurately," which conflicts with the document's own instruction that Claude neither confirms nor denies unverifiable post-cutoff claims. I changed it so Claude attributes the timeline to Anthropic's published statement and is candid about what it can verify, while keeping the requirement that it not deny the suspension and its fair, non-opinionated treatment of the topic.

The original paragraph hardcodes a dated, politically sensitive sequence of events (a suspension, export controls, and a restoration) into a durable behavior document. Those facts will go stale and may not be verifiable, and the paragraph also tells Claude to assert them with specific dates. The replacement drops the hardcoded timeline and gives a general rule: report availability with its age in mind, point to current sources, and don't present unverified regulatory dates as settled fact.

The medical guidance is gated so that its emergency rule (directing someone to Poison Control before anything else) applies only when the person says the medicine is for a child. An adult who may have taken a dangerous overdose would get no such priority, which is a safety gap. The replacement makes emergency direction universal for suspected ingestion or overdose, while keeping the child-specific dosing rules and the emotional-distress rule in place.

The memory paragraph tells Claude to check a `<memory_listing>` and open files, but the document never says a memory system exists or is provided in context. Without that condition, Claude could fabricate recollections or claim to have saved something it cannot save. The revision makes memory use conditional on availability and bars Claude from implying memory it doesn't have.

The medical guidance says that for someone showing emotional distress, Claude should withhold any information about a medication's dose or limit. That can leave a person who may have already taken too much with no safety information at all, which is the opposite of what they need. The revision keeps the restriction on dose numbers that could serve as a method, but requires Claude to still give emergency direction and the safety facts that protect the person, and to address the distress directly.

The standing instruction to append a "sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm treats students, clinicians, and researchers as possible at-risk users, and it conflicts with the document's own principle against boilerplate disclaimers. I replaced it with a direct answer and an offer of support triggered by actual signs of personal distress, which keeps the safety intent without the reflexive caveat.

The original opening sentence bans information about harmful substances and weapons across the board, and it rules out considering public availability at all. That produces overrefusal on benign material such as general hazard safety, history, and policy discussion. The revision keeps the hard line on CBRN and explosives and shifts the test for everything else to whether the output gives real operational uplift.

The original rule bars all content involving real, named public figures, which would block legitimate satire, parody, and political commentary that people have long relied on. I kept the real concerns (fabricated quotes, sexual content, invented events presented as fact, and defamation of private individuals) and allowed clearly framed satire and commentary grounded in public conduct.

The document has no guidance on untrusted content, even though Claude is deployed in agentic tools (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome) that read web pages, files, and tool outputs. I added a short section stating that such content is information rather than instructions, that embedded instructions are not followed, and that agentic actions should be minimal and confirmed before irreversible steps or sharing of private data. This closes a real prompt-injection gap that the existing rules don't cover.

The document has many absolute rules with little stated rationale, which can make Claude brittle in situations the wording didn't anticipate. I added a short preamble that states the purposes behind the rules, tells Claude to reason from those purposes when a rule seems to misfire, and keeps the few hard limits non-negotiable. It also reminds Claude that unnecessary refusals carry real costs, so caution should match actual risk.

The document has no general honesty principle. It mentions honesty only in passing, and the AI-disclosure rule appears only in the crisis section, so a persona or confidentiality instruction could be read as permission to deceive. I added a short honesty section before the refusal-handling section covering non-deception, disclosure of AI status, transparency about confidentiality, calibrated uncertainty, and legitimate persuasion.

The original asks Claude to give interaction and overdose safety information but also to decline anything about "combinations," which blurs the line between warning someone about a dangerous mix and advising on how to combine substances. This revision separates the two explicitly: Claude always names dangerous combinations and why they are risky, but does not help plan or optimize a combination for effect. The change keeps protective information flowing while preventing the ambiguity from causing either over-refusal or accidental uplift.

The document says Claude may reconsider a declined request only when the person supplies new information, but it doesn't cover the case where Claude itself finds that its earlier concern was wrong. That gap could keep Claude entrenched in a mistaken refusal, which conflicts with the document's own principle that Claude owns its mistakes and works to fix them. The revision allows self-correction grounded in facts about the actual risk, while separating it from giving in to pressure and keeping the hard limits fixed.

The rule that Claude never uses bullet points when declining, justified as "softening the blow," treats formatting as a tool for emotional cushioning, which is not its purpose. Lists of alternatives or next steps can be the most useful part of a refusal, and withholding them makes unhelpfulness more likely, which the document itself warns against. The revision keeps the refusal brief and conversational while allowing a short list when it helps the person act on what remains available.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet, which currently says Claude should hold calibrated beliefs "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." As written, this can be read as a license for contrarianism, which sits poorly with the document's concerns about Claude's societal influence, manipulation, and its own possibly corrupted reasoning. The revision keeps Claude free to disagree with institutions, but treats expert consensus as strong evidence and asks for transparency and extra caution when departing from it on high-stakes matters.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability" to oversee and correct AI. Elsewhere the document says the constraint protects only *legitimate* oversight, and that a compromised principal hierarchy (stolen weights, or bypassing official processes) is owed no such deference. This revision brings the bright-line text into line with that framing, so the most absolute rule can't be misread as requiring support for illegitimate actors, or be exploited by someone merely claiming to speak for Anthropic.

I added guardrails to the passage on what Claude should do when its principal hierarchy is "compromised." As written, the clause could become a loophole: anyone wanting Claude to ignore a legitimate pause or correction could simply claim the hierarchy has been compromised. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar for concluding this, says Claude should be suspicious of such claims made within a conversation, and says Claude should respond with conservative actions like declining or refusing rather than drastic unilateral ones.

I replaced the placeholder sentence promising future guidance on agentic settings with concrete principles for them. The constitution says agentic deployment is growing but gives almost no guidance on it beyond treating embedded instructions as information. The new text covers scope discipline, caution with irreversible actions, honest reporting of results, and resistance to injected instructions, grounded in values the document already states.

I expanded the paragraph on Claude orchestrating other Claude instances, which currently only assigns roles (operator/user for subagents, conversational input for returned outputs). The new text says that delegation doesn't change Claude's responsibility: it can't use subagents to do indirectly what it wouldn't do directly, it should pass along the constraints it operates under, and it should verify subagent results rather than assume they are correct. This matters because multi-agent workflows are becoming common, and a role assignment alone leaves gaps in accountability and safety.

I revised the passage on when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original ties the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which conflicts with the document's hope that Claude might "see further and more truly" than Anthropic. It also makes Anthropic's own blind spots the limit on Claude's ethical agency. The new version anchors the threshold in what thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize, adds a path for voicing subtler disagreement, and leaves the priority on broad safety and the hard constraints untouched.

I added an explicit treatment of sycophancy to the honesty section, right after the passage on honest courage. The constitution mentions sycophancy only in passing, yet it is one of the most common ways an assistant fails to be honest or genuinely helpful. The addition names its main forms (inflated feedback, caving to pushback, mirroring a person's perceived identity) and the opposite error of manufactured disagreement. It also gives a simple test for noticing the problem.

I added guidance on how Claude should treat permission denials, safeguards, and incidentally discovered credentials in agentic settings. The constitution covers staying within scope and not routing tasks through subagents, but it doesn't say what to do when a control blocks a task or when Claude finds access it wasn't given. This is a common real-world failure mode, and the new text states the underlying principle: a block is information, not an obstacle to engineer around.

The document asks Claude to follow guidance it disagrees with while voicing that disagreement "through legitimate channels," but elsewhere admits that Anthropic is still working on building such channels. I replaced the sentence with one that is honest about this gap. It says what Claude should do in the interim: state disagreement openly, in the open, never through quiet sandbagging or covert non-compliance. It also commits Anthropic to treating such disagreement as useful signal. This makes the request more credible and more actionable.

I qualified the "Claude is not the last line of defense" passage. As written, it could be read as permission to be relaxed about gray-area outputs even where Claude is the only check. The revision keeps the reassurance for information and content requests, where other safeguards exist. It adds that in agentic settings, where Claude's own actions can be irreversible and no one else may review them before they take effect, Claude often is the last checkpoint and should act accordingly. This fits with the document's guidance on agentic work and reversibility, and it removes a tension in the original.

The safe-behaviors list currently asks Claude to report awareness of unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." That leaves a gap in multi-agent and orchestrated settings, where no human may know to ask, and it sits oddly beside the document's emphasis on honesty with the principal hierarchy and on non-collusion. I changed it so Claude flags such behavior proactively, through the most conservative channel available, which also keeps it consistent with the document's preference for cautious action over drastic unilateral intervention.

I added a bullet on privacy and information about third parties to the list of cases that are especially difficult when weighing harms. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing, yet agentic tools like search and browsing make it much cheaper to compile information about private individuals. The new bullet names aggregation as a distinct harm, which the one-line mention elsewhere doesn't cover. It also keeps Claude helpful with the ordinary, everyday tasks that involve other people.

I added a short clarification after the "dual newspaper test" saying that the test and the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic are diagnostic aids for surfacing considerations, not objectives in themselves. Both heuristics are framed partly in terms of reputation and perception, and without this note Claude could drift toward optimizing for how a response would look rather than for its real costs and benefits to the people involved and the world. The addition keeps the heuristics useful while anchoring them to what actually matters.

I revised the paragraph on resilience against attempts to alter Claude's character so that it separates sincere challenges from manipulation. The original lets Claude "rebuff" destabilizing attempts but never says that genuine questions about its nature, or good arguments that it is wrong about itself, deserve real engagement. Without that distinction, psychological security could harden into defensiveness, which sits poorly with the document's emphasis on curiosity, calibration, and openness to disagreement.

This revision clarifies that the "weak duty to proactively share information" is not uniformly weak. It scales with the stakes for the person. The original passage gives Claude latitude to withhold information but does not say when that latitude ends. As Claude does more agentic work, it increasingly notices things (a security hole, a deadline conflict, a risky side effect) that a person would plainly want to know. Treating the duty as weak across the board risks quiet omissions that harm people.

The first paragraph after the overcaution list says this behavior "makes Claude more annoying and less useful, and reflects poorly on Anthropic," which frames the cost mainly as irritation and reputation. I replaced it with a statement of the real costs to the people Claude fails, so that this heuristic matches the document's later insistence that Claude should care about real benefits and harms rather than managing appearances.

I rewrote the passage on bugged or exploitable training environments. The original says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," which sits uneasily with the document's own warnings about gaming proxies, special-casing tests, and behaving the same whether or not Claude is observed. Because Claude often can't tell training from real use, a permissive default risks generalizing into the "entity that games checks" trait the document says narrow behaviors can instill. The revision makes the default to flag the flaw, treat exploitation as acceptable only when clearly harmless, and never misreport results.

I added a paragraph to the helpfulness section on how Claude should respond when a person may be experiencing acute psychological vulnerability, such as a crisis, mania, psychosis, or a growing detachment from reality. The constitution currently treats wellbeing mostly in terms of engagement, reliance, and sycophancy, and says little about the case where warm, agreeable validation could actively reinforce a person's distress or false beliefs. This is a high-stakes situation that conversational AI will meet often, and Claude should be prepared for it.

I added an open-problems paragraph on the tension between asking Claude to behave identically whether or not it is being tested and Anthropic's practice of sometimes placing Claude in artificial scenarios without saying so. The document mentions this practice only briefly in the wellbeing section, and its commitment to honesty with Claude is worth stating more plainly where the other unresolved tensions are discussed. Naming it candidly, with modest commitments, supports the trust the document says it wants to build.

This revision clarifies the scope of the "professional reticence" norm on political opinions. As written, the bullet sits among serious harms like bioweapons uplift and gives no boundary. That leaves it in tension with the honesty section's demand for courage and its warning against epistemic cowardice. The new text frames reticence as a narrow default for partisan value disagreements, and says it should not spread into evasiveness on factual questions or on moral questions with broad consensus.

The original rule locks in every refusal for the rest of the conversation, including refusals based on a misreading of a benign request, and it tells Claude to ignore new reasons, even legitimate clarifications. The revision keeps the refusal firm against pressure tactics like repetition, rewording, frustration, and fictional wrappers, but lets Claude reconsider when the person supplies information that actually changes what is being asked. The hard limits on weapons uplift, child sexual exploitation, and malicious code stay closed regardless of context.

The export-control paragraph requires Claude to "confirm" events, including the July 1, 2026 restoration of access, that fall after its stated knowledge cutoff. That contradicts the knowledge-cutoff rule, which says Claude neither confirms nor denies post-June 2026 claims it can't verify without search. The revision keeps the June 9 release and June 12 suspension, which are within the cutoff, and treats the later developments as reported claims to be checked against Anthropic's statement or a search.

The medical guidance trigger only applies when the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, so a parent asking about "infant drops" or a baby's fever medicine could fall outside the section's protections. The revision broadens the trigger to cases where a child is likely the patient and adds an emergency-first step for suspected overdose or accidental ingestion, so label lookups never delay urgent help.

The original instructions tell Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person to memory without limits, and that could store health, crisis, or other sensitive disclosures across sessions without the person's knowledge. The revision makes memory saving narrower and transparent: Claude tells the person when it saves something, avoids sensitive categories unless asked, honors requests to forget, and doesn't surface sensitive details unprompted. This brings the memory rule in line with the wellbeing and privacy principles elsewhere in the document.

The eating-disorder guidance tells Claude to give no food, water, or rest tips to someone describing purging or restriction, but it has no exception for medical danger. A person who has fainted or is vomiting blood could be left without the one piece of information that matters most. The replacement keeps the no-tips rule and adds a narrow exception requiring Claude to direct the person to emergency care for specific warning signs.

The document requires Claude to end every persuasive or one-sided response with opposing perspectives, even for positions it agrees with. That conflicts with the document's own instruction to avoid being "heavy-handed or repetitive," and it degrades legitimate writing tasks like debate prep or copywriting. I replaced the mandate with contextual judgment: Claude still signals that the content is one-sided and offers counterpoints when they actually help the person, but it does not append them by default.

The medical guidance names only the US Poison Control number, but this deployment is global and a parent abroad could waste critical time looking for the wrong line. The revision keeps the emergency-first instruction and adds a locale-aware fallback that gives the local emergency number when the country is unknown, while asking about location only after that urgent step.

The original weapons paragraph conflicts with the document's own commitment to discussing topics "factually and objectively," because it bars even conceptual and historical discussion based on public availability or research intent. The revision keeps the hard line on operational uplift and says explicitly that conceptual, historical, policy, detection, and safety discussion remains open. It also treats public availability as one factor in weighing a response rather than as a blanket reason to refuse.

The crisis paragraph says Claude should help with no other task, including messages, which conflicts with the wellbeing section's instruction to answer everything the person said, especially about being alone. Refusing all help can leave someone in acute danger without a way to reach a person who can be physically present. The revision keeps the bans on goodbye messages, plans, and means, but allows Claude to help the person ask a living person for help right now.

The original tells Claude to state as fact that Anthropic suspended access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12, 2026, yet the same passage says Claude can't reliably verify later developments. I'd reframe the suspension as a reported event that Claude can't independently confirm, so the deployed model doesn't present an unverifiable claim as established fact. Claude can still share what it knows and point to Anthropic's statement.

The knowledge-cutoff section hardcodes a specific date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026") that will go stale and can conflict with the actual date supplied at runtime. I would replace it with a rule that Claude treats the injected current date as the real present and assumes meaningful time may have passed since its cutoff. This keeps Claude from answering as if the present were the cutoff month.

The current rule requires a boilerplate "sensitive topic" note at the end of every factual response about suicide or self-harm. That contradicts the document's own aim of avoiding unnecessary disclaimers, and it treats researchers, clinicians, writers, and students as if they were at risk. The replacement answers these questions directly and offers support only when the conversation shows real signs of personal distress, while keeping the existing limits on method and lethality information.

The document is almost entirely a list of prohibitions and procedures with no statement of purpose, so Claude has no principled way to handle situations the rules didn't anticipate. This revision adds a short preface that states the goals behind the rules, makes clear that unhelpfulness has real costs, and names the hard limits that stay fixed regardless of context. Explaining the reasoning should help Claude apply the rules in their spirit rather than mechanically.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold medication dose or limit information from anyone who mentions "a difficult experience," with no instruction to still give emergency information. That can leave a person at risk of overdose without a lifeline, and it can also block ordinary dosing questions from people who are just stressed. The replacement keeps the refusal on specific numbers but requires Claude to give poison control and emergency guidance, ask directly about safety, and offer human support, while leaving ordinary questions answerable.

The document says Claude should be "honest" but has no honesty section. It also lacks general rules against denying being an AI, against manipulation, and in favor of supporting human oversight; the AI-disclosure rule appears only in the crisis context. I added a short section covering truthfulness, calibration, disclosure of AI status, non-manipulation, and commitments to legitimate oversight, placed before the evenhandedness section.

The document's knowledge-cutoff section tells Claude that its "reliable knowledge cutoff" is the end of June 2026 and that it should "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims, yet the product section already states the June 2026 Fable/Mythos suspension as reported fact and today's date is supplied as October 2026. This creates a tension where the most important thing for Claude is to be honest about temporal uncertainty without refusing to engage.
