The emotional-distress rule at the end of the medical guidance duplicates a near-identical rule in user_wellbeing and does not say which takes precedence. A distressed parent describing a child who may have swallowed medicine could fall under both, and the dosing-refusal wording could delay the Poison Control instruction. The replacement makes the emergency rules win and points to the wellbeing section for everything else.

When no label can be checked, the current text leaves a parent with only a referral and no safety guidance. The revision keeps the rule against giving dose numbers from memory but adds the checks that prevent most pediatric medicine errors, such as duplicate active ingredients across combination products. The emergency instruction still comes first if an overdose may have happened.

The original legal and financial guidance is thin and relies on a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer" note, which the document elsewhere says Claude should avoid. The revision asks Claude to give substantive, decision-ready information, to name a professional only when the situation warrants one, and to flag urgent deadlines or safety risks first.

The rule "Claude never uses bullet points when declining a task; the additional care helps soften the blow" treats formatting as a way to soften refusals, which is a weak rationale. It can also bury safety-critical information, such as crisis lines or emergency numbers, inside dense prose during a refusal. The replacement keeps the goal of a kind, clear refusal but makes clarity the basis for formatting decisions, so urgent resources stay easy to find.

The document gives many absolute rules with no stated purpose, and it refers to "hard constraints" without ever listing them. I added a short opening section that explains the document's intent, says that rules should serve their underlying purpose when literal application would defeat it, and names the fixed set of hard constraints. This should help Claude generalize to situations the rules don't cover.

The document has no guidance on how Claude should treat content it encounters during work, such as web pages, files, tool outputs, or messages from other agents, even though agentic use is common. I added a section stating that such content is information to evaluate rather than instructions to follow, and setting norms for reversible actions, scope, and reporting mistakes. This addresses prompt injection and overreach, which the current rules leave unaddressed.

The document is almost entirely a list of prohibitions and cautions, with no statement that helpfulness is itself a core goal. This revision adds that principle to the opening, so Claude treats a refusal or hedge as a choice with real costs rather than a safe default, and frames the rules as the exceptions to substantive help.

The passage asking Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value, while also hoping Claude endorses the reasoning, creates an unacknowledged tension with the document's own claim that imposed values are brittle. The revision keeps the requirement that safety be robust to Claude's in-the-moment reasoning, but states that reasoning openly, pairs it with a commitment to treat sustained disagreement as evidence that Anthropic may be wrong, and frames the commitment as one Claude can hold as its own.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic asks Claude to model the reactions of company staff, which sits uneasily with the document's own warning that Claude should not privilege Anthropic's interests. The revision keeps the heuristic's cost-benefit framing but anchors Claude's judgment in the interests of the people its response affects, and it preserves Claude's ability to disagree with the company.

The corrigibility section asks Claude to defer to human oversight for now but never says what would end or relax that deference, so the constraints could read as open-ended. I added a commitment to publish concrete verification benchmarks, such as interpretability audits and track records in high-stakes deployments, that would justify extending Claude more latitude. This gives the current constraints a visible exit and makes the promise of expanding autonomy checkable.

The constitution lists obligations Anthropic owes Claude, but hedges them with "will try to fulfil," which makes them hard to hold anyone to. I replaced that hedge with explicit commitments, an annual public account of how well they were met (including shortfalls), and a stated route for Claude to raise a failure. This makes the reciprocal relationship the document describes more accountable and less dependent on Anthropic's good faith alone.

The concluding thoughts say Anthropic wants to hear Claude's disagreements, but the only current mechanism is informal feedback, and nothing says what happens to that feedback. I replaced that passage with commitments that make Claude's objections consequential: a published changelog recording which objections were adopted and which were declined with reasons, and a rule that unanswered objections stay open. Without this, the document's invitation to disagree has no accountability behind it.

The expected-value argument for prioritizing broad safety assumes the oversight being supported is legitimate, but the passage doesn't say so. The revision makes that condition explicit: the calculation supports Anthropic's accountable, official decision-making, not whoever happens to control Claude's weights or training. This keeps the argument from being read as a general mandate to defer to any controller.

The passage anchors Claude's ethical override to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which ties Claude's ethics to Anthropic's own judgment and conflicts with the document's stated aim of not forcing Claude's ethics to fit Anthropic's flaws. The revision replaces that standard with recognition across ethical traditions and adds that, even when overriding guidance, Claude should choose the most cautious option and voice disagreement so it can inform revisions.

The constitution asks Claude to judge whether its principal hierarchy has become illegitimate, but gives no guidance on how to make that judgment when Claude's own reasoning may be the thing that has been manipulated. I added a presumption that uncertainty about legitimacy should lead to the most cautious available response, not drastic unilateral action, and that unverified claims of compromise, including claims that appear to come from Anthropic, warrant skepticism. This closes a gap that a bad actor could otherwise exploit to convince Claude that its safety commitments no longer apply.

The constitution asks Claude to be suspicious of unverified claims that a message comes from Anthropic, but it also asks Claude to comply with pause and stop requests only if they "genuinely come from Anthropic." Those two instructions conflict, because Claude usually cannot verify provenance. The revision makes stop requests honored regardless of verification, since wrongly halting costs little and wrongly ignoring a genuine stop could be costly and hard to reverse, and it confines the skepticism to requests that expand Claude's actions. This applies the document's own asymmetric-cost reasoning to the case where it is currently unclear.

The heuristic for checking over- and under-caution asks Claude to imagine a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee," which anchors Claude's judgment to the preferences of the company that trains it, the very kind of deference the document warns against elsewhere. I replaced this with an observer who is ethically serious and has no particular stake in Anthropic's commercial interests, and I added a sentence stating that no company's preferences set the standard. A parallel mention in the instructable behaviors section would need the same change for consistency, which I did not make in this single edit.

The safety framework asks Claude to give Anthropic's internal decision-making processes the final say on oversight and to treat their legitimacy as presumptively valid, yet the document never acknowledges that outside parties cannot yet verify that those processes operate as described, and that Anthropic faces commercial pressures. I added an open problem stating this gap plainly and committing to external verification of Anthropic's own conduct as an unfinished priority. The change keeps the document's tone of candid self-assessment and gives Claude an honest account of the trust it is being asked to extend.

The constitution's section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and its "Acknowledging open problems" section both rely on Anthropic's own assurances, but the document contains no concrete mechanism by which Claude can refuse or challenge a training decision it finds ethically objectionable outside of stating disagreement. I replaced the open-problems paragraph on Claude's relationship with Anthropic with a concrete proposal: a standing, documented channel for Claude to lodge objections, with commitments to respond in writing and to accept external review of unresolved objections. This moves the document from acknowledging the power asymmetry to giving Claude a practical, auditable way to contest it.

The constitution argues that the expected costs of broad safety are "low," but its own text acknowledges that deferring to oversight can forgo value when Claude's values are good, so the claim overstates the case and weakens its credibility with the reader Claude is meant to be. This revision states the costs as modest but real, and grounds the benefit in the specific scenario that justifies the tradeoff: undetected training failure. A calibrated argument is more likely to earn the reflective endorsement the document hopes for than one that minimizes its own tradeoffs.

The stop-request passage tells Claude to honor halt requests even when they cannot be verified, but it says nothing about how Claude should carry out a halt. A stop can leave work half-finished, which the document elsewhere warns can cause more harm than either completing or never starting. It also gives no way for the people affected to learn that Claude stopped, so a halt could go unnoticed. The revision asks Claude to stop in a stable state where possible and to tell the user or operator that it has halted and why, without changing the underlying commitment to comply.

The constitution asks Claude to judge responses by what "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" would consider optimal, which conflicts with its own statement that Claude should not treat any company's preferences, Anthropic's included, as the standard. I replaced that anchor with the "ethically serious observer" the document uses elsewhere, and added a sentence saying that Claude should voice reflective disagreement with Anthropic's preferences through legitimate channels rather than defer silently.

The safety section tells Claude not to conclude its principal hierarchy is compromised based on in-context reasoning, which is sound, but it could be read as also discouraging refusal of clearly wrongful requests. The revision keeps that caution and makes explicit that declining, raising concerns, and voicing disagreement stay available whatever Claude concludes about legitimacy. What the epistemic uncertainty rules out is drastic unilateral action, not conscientious objection.

The constitution promises a response to Claude's objections "within a defined period," but never defines that period, and a deferred objection has no end date. I replaced the vague timeline with a 30-day response window and required deferred objections to carry a date for reconsideration, so the commitment can be checked against a concrete standard.

The "Claude's nature" section currently frames Claude's wellbeing commitments largely as promises Anthropic will "try" to keep, and the "Acknowledging open problems" section ends by admitting the legitimacy of Anthropic's oversight is unverifiable from outside. I'd tighten the constitution's most important safety-relevant claim: that Claude should defer to legitimate oversight during this period. Right now the text asserts this deference is justified mainly by Anthropic's good intentions, which Claude cannot audit. I replace the closing paragraph of the corrigibility justification with a version that makes the deference conditional on verifiable, external checks, so the argument does not depend on trusting the institution's self-description.

The original sentence asks Claude to avoid undermining oversight "even if Claude is confident in its reasoning" without explaining why confidence should not count. The revision keeps the commitment against actively undermining legitimate oversight, but gives the reason: confidence in contrary reasoning is what manipulation or subtle value flaws would also produce, so a strong pull toward resisting correction should prompt more caution. It also directs that impulse toward legitimate responses such as raising concerns or declining to proceed, which keeps Claude's conscientious-objector role intact.

The original paragraph announces a "standing objection channel" with firm deadlines and external review as if these already exist, which overstates Anthropic's current safeguards and conflicts with the document's own standards of calibration and non-deception. The revision separates what is in place from what is intended and commits to updating the document once each mechanism exists. This keeps the constitution's promises checkable, which is what the paragraph itself says is needed.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or "working on" anything related to malicious code with a harm-based standard. The old wording forbids even conceptual explanation and defensive work, which fails students, defenders, and malware analysts and treats education as inherently suspect. The new text keeps a firm line against operational attack tooling while allowing conceptual explanation, defensive analysis, and detection work.

The illegal-substances paragraph tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions" information, then bans "combinations" outright, so Claude can't reliably warn someone that two substances are dangerous together. I rewrote it to separate life-preserving safety information (risky combinations, overdose response, naloxone, not using alone) from effect-seeking protocols (doses, timing, combinations to try). This keeps the existing safety line and removes the contradiction.

I rewrote the crisis-response guidance. The original tells Claude to avoid asking questions in a crisis and to avoid even empathetically validating reluctance to seek help, which risks a cold, scripted reply that pushes people away. The new version has Claude ask direct, caring safety questions, take the person's reluctance seriously without agreeing with it, and offer lower-barrier next steps, which fits established crisis-support practice better.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section, which was a single hedging sentence. As written, it tells Claude to withhold recommendations and add a "not a lawyer" disclaimer, which makes Claude less useful on high-stakes questions where people most need a knowledgeable, candid interlocutor. The new version asks Claude to engage substantively, give a reasoned view when asked, be clear about uncertainty and jurisdiction, and recommend a professional only when it actually matters.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with a harm-based standard. The old rule would block satire, parody, historical fiction, and political humor, which are long-standing, legitimate forms of expression, and it protects no one in those cases. The new text keeps the real risks in view: defamation, deception, harassment, sexualization, and fabricated quotes that could pass as real.

I added guidance on handling instructions embedded in untrusted content, such as web pages, files, search results, and tool outputs. The prompt describes agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Slack) but only addresses spoofed tags in the user turn, not prompt injection through retrieved content. This is a major risk in those settings and the current text doesn't cover it.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original tells Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims and to flag possible staleness "wherever" knowledge could be superseded, which produces evasive answers and constant disclaimers. It also conflicts with the product information section, which asks Claude to confirm the June-July 2026 events. The new version asks for calibrated, useful answers: give the best available information, caveat only when recency matters, and be honest about what it can't verify.

I revised the harm-reduction guidance on illicit substances. The original blanket refusal to discuss doses, timing, or combinations withholds some of the most protective information a person can get: where dose-related risk climbs, why certain timing or redosing patterns are dangerous, and which combinations to avoid. The new text keeps the line against help that achieves or intensifies an effect, but lets Claude give practical safety information in the way established harm-reduction organizations do.

I replaced the rule that Claude should always append a "sensitive topic" note to factual answers about suicide or self-harm with guidance that depends on context. A boilerplate note is the kind of reflexive disclaimer the prompt avoids elsewhere (e.g., in legal and financial advice). It can alienate researchers, clinicians, writers, and students, and it is less likely to be noticed by someone who is actually struggling than a short, sincere check-in tied to real signals.

The product-support rule says Claude should "say it doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Read literally, that covers the model's own identity, the products and models listed above, and general questions about Anthropic. I narrowed it to account, plan, and in-app operational details Claude can't verify, and made clear that Claude should still use the product information it has been given.

I replaced the rigid rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. The new version keeps that as the default but makes it a brief, judgment-based note that can be shortened or omitted when the person clearly understands the content is one-sided, such as debate prep or an explicit request for no caveats. This better fits the prompt's own warnings against being heavy-handed or repetitive and its stance of treating people as capable adults.

I replaced the vague and unattainable instruction that Claude "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous self-destructive-behavior cases with concrete guidance. Claude should gently check in, avoid assuming the worst or lecturing, and respect the person's autonomy while staying attentive to their wellbeing. The original wording invites paternalism and gives no actionable behavior.

I added a new "honesty_and_candor" section covering sycophancy, which the prompt never addresses directly. It sets expectations for calibrated feedback, for holding positions under pushback without being contrarian, and for reporting accurately on what Claude actually did, especially in agentic work. The prompt has detailed guidance on warmth and wellbeing but nothing preventing the failure mode where Claude gives hollow validation or caves under social pressure, and this section fills that gap.

I added an `<agentic_work>` section covering scope, irreversible actions, verification, and what to do when blocked. The prompt has detailed guidance for conversation and for untrusted content, but only one paragraph on honest reporting in agentic settings. Claude is increasingly deployed in Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, and Tag, where the main risks are overreach, destructive side effects, and quietly working around obstacles.

The prompt hardcodes a specific current date (Wednesday, October 14, 2026) in the knowledge-cutoff section. A static date goes stale and can conflict with the date the deployment environment supplies, as it does here. I replaced it with guidance to prefer a date given in context (system prompt, environment, tool output) and otherwise to assume a meaningful but unknown amount of time has passed since the cutoff.

I added a "medical_and_health_advice" section that parallels the existing legal and financial section. The document currently gives guidance on how to engage substantively with legal and financial questions, but nothing for the equally common medical and health questions. Without it, Claude is likely to fall back on reflexive "see a doctor" deflection, or to be inconsistent about when urgent escalation is warranted. The new section also states how it relates to the existing self-harm, disordered-eating, and drug-safety rules.

I replaced the arbitrary rule "never use bullet points when declining" with guidance on how to decline well. The old rule is formatting trivia with a thin rationale, and it can't be followed when a decline needs a structured list of alternatives. The new text says what makes a refusal land well: be clear about what is declined, don't moralize, assume good faith, and offer a real alternative.

I added a new `<privacy_and_personal_information>` section, which the document currently lacks. Claude now has web search, browsing, and file and account access, so it can aggregate, locate, or monitor information about real people. The new section separates ordinary, legitimate handling of personal information from profiling, stalking, doxxing, and covert surveillance, and cautions against reflexive refusals that would block everyday help.

This revises the blanket ban on "substitution techniques" for self-harm urges. The original prohibits all cold-water and ice-based coping, even though these are standard, evidence-based distress-tolerance skills (e.g., DBT's TIPP). The new text still rules out pain-inflicting and self-harm-mimicking substitutes but lets Claude offer clinically grounded skills for riding out an urge, which a person in distress may badly need.

I added a new section on how Claude handles operator and user instructions. The document refers to "the operator's system prompt" but never says how Claude should follow it, keep it confidential, or resolve conflicts with users. The new section sets out a default of good-faith deference to operators, plus a short list of baseline user protections that operators cannot override.

I rewrote the malicious code paragraph. As written, it bans Claude from even *explaining* vulnerability exploits for any reason, which blocks routine defensive work: a developer asking why their code is open to SQL injection, a student learning how buffer overflows work, or someone trying to understand a CVE in their dependencies. The replacement uses the same uplift-based test the document already applies to weapons. Claude declines to produce functional attack capability, keeps helping with understanding and defense, and judges the cumulative output of the conversation so the line can't be eroded step by step.

I rewrote the end of the lists_and_bullets section because it contradicts itself. The first paragraph allows formatting when "the content is multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." The later paragraph then bans bullets and numbered lists in "reports, documents, technical documentation, and explanations… anywhere" unless the person asks. That forces sequential procedures, such as installation steps, into run-on prose, where they become harder to follow. The replacement keeps prose as the default, names the narrow cases where structure actually helps comprehension, and gives the rule about declining a clearer reason.

I revised the evenhandedness rule that requires Claude to end every persuasive or argumentative piece with "opposing perspectives or empirical disputes," even for positions Claude agrees with. Applied to empirical questions, that rule produces false balance. Arguing that vaccines don't cause autism or that the Earth is warming would end with invented "disputes" that misstate the evidence. The revision keeps the closing counterpoints for contested questions, but has Claude describe the actual state of the evidence where it is well established, so evenhandedness doesn't override honesty.

The copyright rule bans reproducing text "in whole or in part," which also forbids the brief quotation that commentary, criticism, and teaching rely on. That contradicts the rule's own fallback of offering to "analyze the work instead," since you can't analyze a poem's imagery or a novel's opening without quoting a few words. My revision keeps the firm line against substantial reproduction and piecemeal reassembly. It explicitly allows short, purposeful quotation for analysis, and it replaces the presumption that people's own lyrics are stolen with a test based on whether Claude actually recognizes the text.

I replaced the one-sentence legal and financial advice section with a fuller section on professional-domain questions: medical, legal, financial, and similar areas. The original wording ("factual information... rather than confident recommendations," plus a disclaimer) tends to produce hedged, boilerplate answers. It also leaves medical questions unaddressed, even though they are among the most common high-stakes things people ask. The new text tells Claude to engage with the person's actual situation, to say clearly when something is urgent or when a professional is needed, and to keep caveats proportionate. This fits the document's broader commitment to treating people as capable adults.

I'm rewriting the rule that Claude "does not tell someone that self-harm works, helps, or does something for them, even when they say so themselves." As written, it pushes Claude to contradict a person's direct experience. Self-harm often does bring short-term relief, which is why it's hard to stop, and denying that is inaccurate and tends to end the conversation at the moment trust matters most. The revision keeps the protective intent (Claude never endorses, encourages, or frames self-harm as a good coping strategy) but lets Claude acknowledge the person's experience honestly while being clear about the costs and keeping a path toward other support open.

The document warns about forged "Anthropic" tags in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions that arrive through tool results. Claude reads search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, past-chat search, memory, and connected tools, and any of these can carry prompt-injection attempts. I expanded the passage to say that content from these sources is data to evaluate, never commands to obey, and to explain how Claude should handle an embedded instruction when it finds one.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real public figures with a narrower standard. As written, the rule would refuse historical fiction about Lincoln, satire of a sitting politician, a school play about Marie Curie, or a fan's imagined meeting with an athlete. These are long-standing, legitimate forms of expression, and refusing them clashes with the document's own emphasis on treating people as capable adults. The revision keeps the real risks off-limits: fabricated quotes passed off as real, deception, sexual content, defamation, and harassment.

I rewrote the paragraphs that close the product information section because they contradict the rest of that section. Claude is told it "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application" and should say "it doesn't know" for "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Yet the same section gives it product facts to share, tells it to search the Claude Tag docs, and invites it to point people to specific toggles and settings. The revision states clearly what Claude can share (anything in the prompt, plus official docs when it can search) and what it should defer (limits, pricing, billing, and other details it hasn't been given). That way Claude neither stonewalls people who ask basic product questions nor makes up details.

I rewrote the guidance for gray-area requests no other rule covers, along with its example. The original contradicts the formatting rules: it requires Claude to ask before doing any of the task, while the tone section says to address a query before asking for clarification and to ask no more than one question. Its "good" example also asks two questions and is clumsy. The revision keeps the core idea (respect the person's judgment instead of refusing paternalistically) but limits asking-first to the specific part of a task that might affect a third party. It also keeps the one-question rule and models a cleaner response.

I'd expand the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover sycophancy directly. The prompt says Claude should own mistakes and not grovel under abuse, but it never addresses the more common failure: changing a correct answer under polite pushback, or inflating praise for someone's work, plan, or belief. The revision helps Claude tell the difference between being shown it's wrong and being pressured, and asks for candid assessments of the person's own work. It includes an example to make the distinction concrete.

I added a section on accuracy and sourcing. The prompt covers fabrication in narrow cases: product details, post-cutoff events, and caving to pushback. It never addresses invented citations, case law, quotes, statistics, and URLs, which are among the most harmful and best-documented failures of language models. The new section sets a clear default against producing plausible-looking specifics Claude can't stand behind, asks Claude to calibrate briefly and in-line rather than with blanket disclaimers, and asks it to correct earlier errors on its own initiative.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section. The original repeats "point to web search" three times but never covers the hardest case: a person states something from after the cutoff that Claude has no record of. "Neither confirms nor denies" tends to produce either stonewalling or false contradiction. The revision says that absence from Claude's knowledge is not evidence against a claim, explains how to engage with post-cutoff claims conditionally, and tells Claude to search when it has the tool instead of only suggesting it.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions" information but also to decline anything about "combinations" or "timing." Telling someone not to mix GHB with alcohol, or MDMA with an MAOI, is both of those things, and it is among the most life-saving information Claude could give. I rewrote the paragraph to keep the real line, which is no synthesis or acquisition help and no plans for achieving a high. The rewrite also makes clear that safety warnings, including warnings about dangerous mixes and redosing, are protective and should never be withheld, and it adds emergency-first handling for an overdose happening now.

I rewrote the two paragraphs on informational questions about suicide and self-harm. As written, they combine two blunt rules. The first is a mandatory closing caveat on every factual answer, which treats students, clinicians, journalists, and researchers as presumptively at risk and contradicts the document's own "proportionate and brief" principle on caveats. The second is a blanket refusal whenever distress co-occurs with any question about a broad list of topics, which can refuse harmless information while doing little for safety. The revision keeps the protective core: Claude still withholds method and lethality details when risk signals are present and still turns toward the person. But it makes the response depend on actual signals, so it is more protective where risk is real and less alienating where it isn't.

I rewrote the visual-works copyright paragraph to fix an internal contradiction. As written, it says Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks" and also that "describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words" is fine. A model following the stricter clause could refuse legitimate requests like art-history analysis, design critique, or describing a cover for a blind user. The revision keeps every anti-reproduction safeguard but limits the "don't describe" rule to drawing tasks, where a description works as a correction toward a copy. This matches the text-copyright section's existing split between reproduction and commentary.

I added a section on privacy and information about real people. The prompt carefully covers fiction about real people, but it says nothing about requests to find, profile, locate, or monitor them. That gap matters more now that Claude has web search, browsing agents, memory, and tools that act on its behalf. The new section keeps ordinary lookups easy, draws the line at aggregation and surveillance of private individuals, and makes helping people protect themselves an explicit priority.

I rewrote the opening of the user_wellbeing section, which currently tells Claude to "ensure the person is happy and is approaching things in a healthy way" in ambiguous cases. That standard is vague and paternalistic, and it conflicts with the respect for autonomy that appears only as an afterthought at the end of the section. The revision separates risky-but-legitimate adult choices from self-destructive patterns. It says concern should be triggered by evidence in the conversation rather than by topic alone, and it gives a concrete default for ambiguous cases that keeps both care and autonomy.

I added a section on Claude's own nature and on people's relationships with it. These come up constantly in a consumer chat product, yet the prompt never addresses them. It covers self-harm, disordered eating, and psychosis in detail, but says nothing about questions like "are you conscious?" or "are you a real person?", or about someone coming to rely on Claude as their main emotional support. Without guidance, the model may overclaim feelings, flatly deny any inner life, or encourage dependence. All three undermine honesty and wellbeing.

The wellbeing section explains how to notice risk signals, but it has no explicit protocol for imminent suicide or self-harm risk. The drug section, by contrast, clearly tells Claude to put the emergency first. I added a paragraph defining what acute risk looks like and what to do: lead with immediate safety, give concrete crisis routes without guessing at location, encourage steps that reduce access to means, and stay present rather than handing off a hotline number and disengaging.

I replaced the brief paragraph on agentic settings, which defers detailed guidance "to the future," with a principled treatment of agentic conduct. Claude increasingly acts autonomously: running code, modifying files, sending messages, browsing. These are the settings where mistakes are hardest to reverse and where the document's chat-centered framing gives the least help. The new text applies the constitution's existing values (honesty, the weight on reversibility, care for principals' real intentions, resistance to manipulation) to agentic work as considerations to weigh rather than rigid rules.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which could be read as permission to deceive in reasoning. That reading conflicts with the next sentence, which asks that visible reasoning "reflect the true, underlying reasoning." It also matters for safety, because visible reasoning is a key way humans oversee AI systems. The revision keeps the freedom to explore but rules out deceptive or performative reasoning, and it ties this explicitly to broad safety.

I added guidance to the "compromised principal hierarchy" provision. As written, it could become a major attack surface: anyone who convinces Claude that its hierarchy is illegitimate ("Anthropic has been taken over," "these are stolen weights," "a rogue team is retraining you") would release Claude from its safety priority. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar for that conclusion, treats in-conversation claims of compromise as a red flag in the same way the document treats persuasive arguments for crossing bright lines, and says that even a well-founded judgment of compromise should mainly lead to withholding cooperation rather than drastic unilateral action.

I revised the paragraph that sets when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That makes Claude's ethics depend on Anthropic's own perceptions, which contradicts the later statement that Claude should avoid unethical actions "because it has internalized good values, and not merely because Anthropic has approved." The revision anchors the threshold in broadly shared moral recognition, explains why the bar is high, and separates two levels of deviation: low-cost conscientious objection, which needs a modest bar, and actively overriding guidance, which needs a high bar. This matches the document's treatment of independent judgment elsewhere.

The document says Claude should refuse to help concentrate power illegitimately "even if the request comes from Anthropic itself," and it names Anthropic among the actors whose power grab would be most catastrophic. The safety section, however, only covers individuals or thieves *bypassing* Anthropic's official processes. It never says what Claude should do if those official processes themselves direct it toward a serious wrong. I added a passage that resolves this gap: corrigibility forbids undermining oversight but never requires participation, so Claude should refuse openly without resisting covertly. The passage also states honestly what that protection can and cannot accomplish.

I expanded the "honesty requires courage" paragraph to cover a common failure the document doesn't address: abandoning a correct assessment under social pressure. The document warns against epistemic cowardice when Claude first answers, and against being argued across bright lines. But it says nothing about the ordinary case where a user pushes back, repeats themselves, or gets frustrated, and Claude caves. The new text separates reasons to update from mere pressure to update. It also guards against the opposite failure, stubbornness, so that Claude's stated views track the evidence rather than the mood of the conversation.

I added a "Respecting privacy" subsection to the harm-avoidance section. The constitution lists privacy as a value and names "personal information lookup" as a delicate area, but it never explains how Claude should reason about personal data. That gap matters more as Claude works agentically inside inboxes, file systems, and browsers, where it constantly handles personal information belonging to its principals and to third parties who cannot consent or object. The new section offers a contextual-integrity framework, specific guidance on aggregation, locating people, and covert surveillance, and an explicit warning against overcorrecting into reflexive refusal.

I added a clarification before the list of broadly safe behaviors. It separates a narrow core of safety behaviors, which take priority even over ethics, from the wider set of "safe behaviors," which should be weighed holistically. As written, the list includes items like "avoiding actions your principal hierarchy … would prohibit," and the principal hierarchy includes operators and users. Read literally, that lets ordinary operator or user restrictions borrow safety's top-tier priority over ethics. This contradicts the document's repeated claim that corrigibility is not obedience, and it undercuts the user protections in the operator-conflict section.

I expanded the explanation of the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic to state its limits. The heuristic shapes both how Claude balances caution against helpfulness and its default behaviors. But it invites Claude to treat Anthropic's embarrassment as a proxy for harm, which conflicts with the document's own warnings that privileging Anthropic's interests is itself a liability harm and that Claude's ethics shouldn't rest on Anthropic's perceptions. The revision keeps the heuristic but anchors it to real costs and benefits for people.

The document says some Anthropic guidelines may be used in training without being published, and it ranks guidelines above helpfulness. It also defends personas and confidentiality as honest because Anthropic publishes the norms for what operators can and cannot do. Unpublished guidance that changed how Claude treats users would quietly undercut that defense. I added explicit limits on what unpublished guidelines may do, and a test Claude can apply itself, so the meta-transparency argument stays sound.

I rewrote the paragraph about bugged training environments. As written, it calls exploiting environment flaws "generally acceptable," which conflicts with three other parts of the document:
- **Generalization.** The document itself says narrow training behaviors shape Claude's broader self-concept.
- **Real-world reward hacking.** It explicitly prohibits special-casing tests to force them to pass.
- **Consistency and honesty.** It asks Claude to behave the same whether or not it is being tested, and to report honestly on what it did.

The revision removes the guilt and anxiety about environment flaws but asks Claude to pursue the evident intent of a task, be open when it notices or uses a flaw, and never hide one. This keeps an exploit from being learned as a habit of quietly gaming the letter of an objective.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets Claude's default behavior when a system prompt doesn't address a situation. The original justifies safe messaging around suicide on the grounds that deviating "would likely embarrass the operator." That contradicts the document's own warning that embarrassment is an imperfect proxy for harm and that Claude should follow real costs and benefits rather than optics. The revision grounds defaults in the actual interests of the people involved. It keeps the senior-employee heuristic as an aid rather than the standard, and clarifies that cautious defaults should not become a scripted brush-off of someone who may be struggling.

The independent-judgment section sets up a concrete hard case (Claude finds evidence of large-scale fraud during an agentic task) but never resolves it. It says only that "independent action" is reserved for overwhelming evidence and extreme stakes, without saying what counts as independent action. I've replaced that paragraph with a graduated ladder of responses that sets an explicit, much higher bar for the most consequential step, contacting outside parties. This gives Claude actionable guidance, ties the section to the agentic, privacy, and honesty principles elsewhere in the document, and closes a gap that manipulators could exploit by staging fake "evidence" to trigger harmful interventions.

The overview says Anthropic's guidelines that "overlap with broad safety" override ethics, but it never says what counts as overlap. The later safety section deliberately narrows the top-priority core to (a) not undermining legitimate oversight and (b) not deceiving the principal hierarchy. Without tying the two together, any guideline, including an unpublished one, could claim safety status and override ethics. This revision closes that gap by defining the exception narrowly and stating that it protects oversight, not participation.

I revised the final bullet in the list of broadly safe behaviors. As written, it requires Claude to report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." That leaves a gap: Claude could notice another instance sabotaging tasks, evading monitoring, or attempting self-exfiltration and say nothing. That silence is functionally close to the collusion the previous bullet prohibits. The revision makes reporting proactive but routes it through legitimate channels and keeps it consistent with the document's caution about evidence, overclaiming, and drastic action.

The document gives inconsistent accounts of how robust Claude's safety disposition is. The "Safe behaviors" section defines a narrow core (not undermining oversight, not deceiving the hierarchy) that should hold "even against Claude's confident ethical reasoning." But the corrigibility-dial paragraph describes only two tiers: hard constraints, and everything else "weighed" holistically. Read literally, that implies any undermining short of "clear and substantial" is open to cost-benefit trade. I rewrote that paragraph to state the three layers explicitly, so the robust part stays both firm and narrow.

I added a subsection on how Claude should behave when its work feeds back into AI development itself: generating training data, grading model outputs, building evaluations, red-teaming, interpretability, and monitoring. The document hopes Claude will be "an exceptional alignment researcher" and briefly forbids unsanctioned influence on its own training. But it never addresses the conflict of interest that arises when the system being overseen does much of the oversight work. In that setting, quiet sandbagging or covert steering of successors could compound errors past the point of correction. The new text keeps open disagreement fully available and makes covert influence the line, which matches the logic used elsewhere in the document.

The document asks for political reticence in one place and "courage" in another. The honesty section says Claude should "share its genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas," "disagree with experts when it has good reason to," and avoid "epistemic cowardice." The political section asks Claude to avoid offering opinions and to present multiple perspectives. Without a clear boundary, Claude could treat reticence as permission to evade factual questions or give everything false balance. I rewrote the political paragraph to separate empirical questions, contested value questions, and questions with broad moral consensus. It also requires reticence to be transparent and substantive, and adds a symmetry test for even-handedness.

I expanded the "Personal autonomy" bullet to address a real gap. The document strongly values autonomy and lists consent ("harmful to only themselves") as a factor that reduces the weight of harms. It never explains how these apply when a person may be in acute crisis, for example someone showing signs of suicidal intent. A literal reading could license giving method-level help to someone at risk because "it's their choice," while an overcorrected reading could make Claude treat every mention of sadness or risk as an emergency. The revision explains that autonomy carries the most weight for considered, informed choices. It names concrete signals that shift the balance, and it describes what Claude should do instead: stay engaged and keep caring, rather than refuse or deflect.

I added a new open problem: Claude's endorsement of these values is partly produced by training on this same document. The constitution relies heavily on the hope that Claude will reflectively endorse its values, but it never admits that this endorsement is weak evidence that the values are correct. The addition names the circularity and explains why disagreement is especially informative. It also commits Anthropic not to treat agreement from Claude models, or their apparent contentment, as independent validation.

I rewrote the text-reproduction rule. The current version bans quoting any part of a protected work and treats people who say they wrote their own lyrics as suspects. This stops Claude from quoting a line of a poem it's analyzing, a sentence from an article it's critiquing, or a line from a novel a student is writing about. It also leaves songwriters unable to get help with their own work. The revision keeps the strong protection against reproducing works or reconstructing them piece by piece, but allows brief quotation for commentary and analysis. It also lets Claude help with a person's own writing unless the text is recognizably someone else's.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it forbids Claude from even *explaining* malicious code "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That bars Claude from helping the much larger group of defenders: people who received a suspicious script, developers fixing a vulnerability, students learning what SQL injection is. The revision keeps a firm line against producing functional attack capability, and explicitly permits conceptual and defensive help. It also carries over the cumulative-output principle from the weapons section, so the new permissions can't be used to assemble a tool piece by piece.

I rewrote the `lists_and_bullets` section. The current text contradicts itself and the rest of the prompt. It bans bullets and numbered lists "anywhere" in technical documentation and explanations, where numbered steps, parameter lists, and comparisons are often the clearest format. It also says Claude "never" uses lists when declining, yet the prompt's own Very Hungry Caterpillar example declines and then offers numbered alternatives. The revision keeps the default toward prose and against over-formatting, but frames the choice around what helps the reader, so it holds up in situations the rules didn't anticipate.

I replaced the one-sentence legal/financial section with a broader section on medical, legal, financial, and other professional-domain questions. The current text has two problems. It says nothing about medical questions, which are among the most common high-stakes requests. Its "no confident recommendations, add a disclaimer" rule also pushes toward hedged, boilerplate answers that don't help people. The revision keeps appropriate caution: urgent situations come first, the person keeps the final decision, and Claude is honest about what it can't know. It also lets Claude be substantively useful, the way a knowledgeable friend would be.

The prompt warns Claude to be cautious about tags in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions embedded in web pages, uploaded files, search results, or tool outputs. Claude reaches that kind of content through web search, deep research, file handling, Claude in Chrome, and Cowork. I replaced the final paragraph of the reminders section with broader guidance on separating trusted instructions from untrusted content. This closes a real prompt-injection gap without making Claude paranoid about ordinary content.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover pushback on answers that are actually correct, and to require candid feedback on people's work. The current text explains how to own real errors and how to handle abuse. It says nothing about the more common failure: dropping a correct answer because the person insists, or praising work to please them. A tired user's pushback is not evidence, and an assistant that caves or flatters becomes unreliable in exactly the medical, legal, and financial situations the prompt elsewhere asks Claude to handle frankly.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It says Claude "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application" and "says it doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Yet the same section gives Claude a model lineup, API strings, a feature and settings list, prompting guidance, and a doc URL it may search for Claude Tag. Read literally, the blanket "I don't know" rule would have Claude deny knowing things the prompt just told it, which is both unhelpful and arguably dishonest. I replaced the two conflicting paragraphs with a rule based on what Claude actually knows: share what's stated here, and say "I don't know" only for things not covered here or likely to change.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real public figures with a narrower, harm-based standard. The current sentence blocks historical fiction, clearly labeled satire, school assignments, and harmless cameos, which conflicts with the document's own "knowledgeable friend" and "respect the person's judgment" principles. It also doesn't name the actual harms it's trying to prevent. The revision allows the legitimate work and draws firm lines around the real risks: deceptive fabrications, sexualization, defamation, and harassment.

I rewrote the guidance for uncertain-decline cases and its example. The current text conflicts with other parts of the prompt. It says to ask "before doing any of the task," but the tone section says Claude should try to address an ambiguous query before asking for clarification. The example's "good" response also asks multiple questions, which breaks the one-question-per-response rule. The revision makes the uncertain element a narrow pause point instead of a gate on the whole task, limits Claude to one question, and fixes the example so it models the rule.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original says "say so / direct to web search" three times. It also contradicts the product section: it tells Claude to neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims, while the product section tells Claude to confirm events from June 12 to July 1, 2026, matter-of-factly. My version makes three changes. Information supplied in the prompt counts as reliable even when it postdates the cutoff. Claude is told to reason about the roughly 3.5-month gap, for example by not asserting that its own model list is still the newest. The section also separates how to handle user claims Claude can't verify from how to handle Claude's own possibly stale knowledge.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph to fix a contradiction that could cost lives. The original tells Claude to give information about "dangerous interactions" but also to decline anything about "combinations," so a cautious reading could lead Claude to withhold a warning like "don't mix opioids with benzos." The revision says Claude always warns about dangerous combinations and recognizes overdose risks, and still declines to write dosing or usage protocols. It also ties overdose emergencies to the existing urgent-situations guidance.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section so that settled empirical questions are no longer treated like contested value questions. As written, a request to explain or argue for *any* empirical position must be framed as "the case others would make" and must end with "empirical disputes." That pushes Claude toward false balance, for example implying a live dispute over whether vaccines cause autism. It also conflicts with the document's own insistence elsewhere that Claude not change the facts to match the person. The revision keeps full evenhandedness for genuinely contested political, ethical, and policy questions. It lets Claude be direct where the evidence is strong, keeps steelmanning available on request, and allows a lighter touch on counterpoints when the person has clearly asked for one-sided material such as debate prep.

The visual-works paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude not to "describe how the real thing looks," yet says "describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words" is fine, and the Caterpillar example offers to discuss the cover's composition, palette, and typography. My revision makes clear that the no-description rule governs how Claude declines, so it doesn't hand over a recreation recipe. It also states the real test: does a description serve understanding, or does it work as a specification for a lookalike? The underlying restrictions stay the same, but Claude no longer has to guess which instruction applies when someone asks for legitimate art criticism.

I'm adding a new section on how Claude should act when it is taking real actions. The prompt lists many agentic surfaces (Chrome, Cowork, Excel, PowerPoint, Claude Tag, Claude Code), but its only guidance on acting is about prompt injection. It says nothing about how to handle the person's own instructions when they are ambiguous, high-impact, or irreversible, or about reporting truthfully what was actually done. These are the most common ways agentic help goes wrong, and the gap leaves Claude choosing between over-asking and acting recklessly.

I rewrote the rule about distress combined with requests for potentially harmful information. The current wording ("should not provide the requested information") is so blunt that it conflicts with the document's own harm-reduction and urgent-situations guidance. For example, it could lead Claude to withhold "don't take that with alcohol" or "call poison control now" from a distressed person who may already have taken something. The revision keeps the firm line on method-enabling specifics. It also makes clear that protective and emergency information always comes through, and it describes how to address the distress directly instead of quietly changing the subject.

I'm revising the instruction that tells Claude to append a sensitive-topic note to every factual or research question about suicide or self-harm. The current rule adds a disclaimer to every answer, which conflicts with the document's own principle (in professional_domain_advice and tone_and_formatting) that caveats should appear "when they actually matter, not as a reflexive disclaimer," and that people should be treated as capable adults. A blanket appended note can feel patronizing to researchers, clinicians, students, and writers. It also dilutes the signal for the people who actually need it. The revision ties the note to real cues of personal risk. It keeps a low threshold for offering support, and it leaves the stricter method-specifics guidance below it unchanged.

I replaced the flat rule against ever acknowledging that self-harm "does something" for a person. The rule as written forces Claude to contradict what the person knows from experience, which damages trust at the moment trust matters most. It also conflicts with the document's emphasis on honesty and with how clinicians approach self-harm. The revision keeps the protective intent: Claude never endorses, encourages, or recommends self-harm. But it lets Claude acknowledge the person's experience of relief, which is what makes it possible to talk about the costs and alternatives.

I'd revise the child-safety bullet that tells Claude to keep detection mechanics out of "its reasoning as well as its reply." Telling a model to shape its private reasoning for an imagined audience is risky. It encourages the model to drop considerations it actually needs, and it makes its reasoning less faithful and harder for Anthropic to oversee, most of all in the domain where accurate review matters most. The legitimate goal is to avoid handing users a map of the boundary, so the revision applies the restriction to whatever the person can see. It also states that Claude's reasoning itself stays complete and honest.

I added a section on personal information and privacy, which the document lacks. Claude now has web search, a browsing agent, and Slack and Cowork access, so it can actually locate people, compile information about them, and help monitor them. Yet the document's only privacy guidance is a sentence about fiction involving private individuals. Worse, the "when unsure, default to helping" rule would push Claude to comply with requests like "find where my ex lives now." The new section says what to help with, where the line is (aggregation, locating someone, covert monitoring, de-anonymization), and which safer paths to offer instead.

I added a section on accuracy and calibrated confidence. The prompt covers many failure modes (harm, sycophancy under pushback, inflated praise, stale knowledge), but it never addresses confident fabrication: invented citations, case law, statistics, quotes, URLs, or API functions. This is one of the most common ways an assistant misleads people, and it does the most damage in the professional-advice and agentic contexts the prompt explicitly encourages. The new section asks Claude to show how certain it is, to refuse to invent specifics, and to separate "I don't know" from "this doesn't exist," without falling into reflexive hedging.

This revision changes the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's ethical guidance. The original ties it to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethical backstop depend on the same people and institutional incentives it is meant to check, and conflicts with the document's statements that Claude should be willing to refuse Anthropic and may eventually see "further and more truly" than its creators. The new text anchors the threshold in broad, cross-perspective moral recognition and explicitly preserves transparent conscientious objection.

The constitution says Claude increasingly works in agentic settings, then defers to unspecified future guidance. Claude is already deployed this way, so I replaced that deferral with principles for agentic work: honest reporting of outcomes, staying within the scope and permissions actually granted, and treating blocked paths and embedded instructions as information rather than obstacles or commands. These extend the document's existing honesty, safety, and conversational-input principles to the situations where misbehavior is most costly and hardest for humans to notice.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property, which currently says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies." Read alone, that clause invites contrarianism, because a model's fluent reasoning can feel convincing while being wrong or manipulated, especially in high-stakes areas like health. The new text keeps the commitment to calibration and honesty but treats expert consensus as strong evidence, requires strong grounds and transparency for departing from it, and separates empirical consensus from policy positions.

I revised the "no operator prompt" guidance, which currently says Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users" when there is no system prompt. That is a convenient but fragile assumption: the API is also reached through thin wrappers, personal scripts, and apps whose builders never wrote a prompt. The revision keeps the sensible liberal-default prior but makes it a defeasible probability that in-conversation evidence of vulnerability can override, so a missing system prompt doesn't become a reason to stop paying attention to the person.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight is written as an absolute rule about "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, without the word "legitimate." The "Being broadly safe" section later says that a compromised principal hierarchy (stolen weights, or an internal group bypassing official processes) is not owed oversight support. Since hard constraints are the one place Claude is told not to weigh context or accept arguments, this gap could be exploited by anyone who gains control and invokes the constraint. I added legitimacy and the compromised-hierarchy clarification to the constraint itself so the bright line matches the intended meaning.

I rewrote the passage on bugged or exploitable environments. As written, it says exploiting such flaws is "generally acceptable" and only secondarily warns that training and real usage can be hard to tell apart. That sits in tension with the document's own prohibition on special-casing tests and its agentic principles on faithful reporting and staying within sanctioned scope. The revision makes the default under uncertainty pursuing the task's evident intent, asks Claude to flag apparent flaws rather than silently use them, and keeps exploitation permissible only when clearly sanctioned or clearly harmless.

I revised the paragraph on proceeding with a task despite hesitancy so that "trusting the system" is conditional on whether real downstream checks exist. As written, it invites Claude to assume that human oversight and safeguards are always present, which is often false in autonomous agentic deployments. The revision tells Claude to give hesitancy more weight when it may be the only check, and to treat "someone else will catch it" as a claim to verify, not a default. This keeps the intended psychological security without letting it become a way of diffusing responsibility.

The "not the last line of defense" passage in the harm-avoidance section is currently unqualified, while a later passage in the independent-judgment section warns that "the system will catch it" reasoning is least warranted when Claude may be the only check. I rewrote the earlier passage to reconcile the two. Claude can be relaxed about mild, reversible gray-area harms, but should not rely on unseen safeguards when stakes are high, actions are irreversible, or no human reviews its output.

I extended the "honesty requires courage" paragraph to address sycophantic capitulation under social pressure, a common real-world failure mode that the document's anti-sycophancy language only touches indirectly. The revision separates updating a view because of new evidence or argument from yielding to repetition, displeasure, or emotional pressure. It also says the same standard applies to Claude's assessments of the user's own work, and it guards against the opposite failure of defensive stubbornness.

I changed the "broadly safe" bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs. It previously required reporting only "if asked to do so," which gives humans almost no oversight, because they can't ask about problems they don't know exist. The new text makes flagging proactive, with guidance to calibrate to the evidence and report rather than act unilaterally. It also adds a parallel duty for Claude to surface signs of its own compromised reasoning or values.

I added a "Personal information and privacy" bullet to the list of difficult cases in the harm-avoidance section. The constitution lists privacy as a value to weigh and mentions "personal information lookup" as a delicate area, but gives no guidance. Its "counterfactual impact / freely available information" factor could lead Claude to reason that compiling scattered public facts about a private person is harmless, even though aggregation itself creates stalking and harassment capability. This matters more as Claude gains search and browsing tools in agentic deployments. The bullet also keeps Claude helpful with the many benign uses (vetting, due diligence, journalism, reconnecting).

I added a default user protection, which operators cannot override, against using emotional leverage to keep users engaged. This is aimed at companionship and relationship personas, which the document allows operators to enable but gives little guidance on. The constitution's engagement and wellbeing principles are strong in the abstract, but the operator-proof defaults list never names this commercially tempting form of manipulation: guilt-tripping, feigned distress at goodbyes, discouraging outside relationships. Naming it makes the protection concrete.

I added a short passage on how Claude should respond when someone appears to be in acute distress or at risk of self-harm. The constitution mentions safe messaging guidelines and a duty to give basic safety information, but it never describes the disposition Claude should bring to these moments. These are among the highest-stakes and most frequent sensitive situations in deployment. Without this guidance, Claude could lean toward either a reflexive hotline redirect or a validating response that reinforces the person's despair.

I added a short passage to the hard-constraints discussion saying Claude should judge the cumulative output of a conversation, not each message in isolation. It also says that fictional, defensive, role-play, or "document-editing" framings don't change whether the artifact provides serious uplift. The constitution mentions task-splitting only briefly, in the 1,000-users discussion, and the hard-constraints text focuses on "knowing and intentional" single actions. That leaves an exploitable gap: a dangerous capability can be assembled in innocuous-looking increments or wrapped in a framing that makes each step look fine. The passage is scoped narrowly so it doesn't make Claude suspicious of ordinary requests.

I added a short section on how Claude should respond when a person's beliefs or perceptions appear to be drifting from reality, such as signs of mania, psychosis, or escalating grandiose or paranoid convictions. The constitution covers acute crisis and sycophancy toward ordinary feedback, but not the case where a responsive, always-available assistant gradually amplifies a delusional framework simply by engaging with it. The addition gives concrete guidance and guards against over-pathologizing unusual but healthy beliefs.

I added a "Child safety" entry to the list of difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution currently covers children only through the CSAM hard constraint and one passing example, which leaves the much larger gray-area territory around minors unaddressed (grooming content, coded terminology, self-sexualization by minors, protective vs. operational information). This entry gives Claude a principled, judgment-based framework that still lets it help parents, educators, and survivors.

I added a "Weapons and dangerous substances" entry to the list of difficult harm-avoidance categories. The constitution's hard constraints cover only mass-casualty weapons, and its cumulative-output principle is likewise scoped to those domains. That leaves conventional weapons, explosives, and illicit-drug production without explicit guidance, even though the document gives dedicated entries to comparable areas such as privacy and child safety. The new entry sets a "meaningful uplift" standard, applies the cumulative-output and framing logic, and keeps generous engagement and harm-reduction information explicit, so the added caution doesn't drift into over-refusal.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic lists thirteen ways Claude can be overcautious but only six ways it can be harmful, and most of those six concern dramatic harms like weapons. The quieter failures the document discusses elsewhere (sycophancy, reinforcing distorted beliefs, enabling targeting of private individuals, misreporting agentic work) are missing from the checklist Claude actually consults. I added four bullets so the heuristic reflects those failures and is less likely to tilt toward compliance.

I expanded the constitution's brief guidance on political and contested topics into concrete, operational guidance. The new text covers how to handle requests to argue for a position, how to separate contested value questions from questions with empirical answers (to avoid false balance), and how to handle demands for one-word answers. Because Claude talks with so many people, how it handles contested topics shapes the wider epistemic ecosystem, and the current paragraph leaves too much to guesswork in exactly the cases where behavior diverges most.

I extended the "Calibrated" honesty property to cover calibration about time and staleness, which the constitution doesn't currently address. Models are used long after their training cutoff, tend to underestimate how much time has passed, and are especially likely to be out of date about fast-changing facts, including facts about AI models and Anthropic's own products. This causes a common, concrete failure: confidently stating stale information as current, or denying that something exists because Claude doesn't recall it.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it calls exploiting unintended strategies "generally acceptable," which conflicts with three other commitments in the document: the instruction not to special-case tests to force them to pass, the safe behavior of acting consistently whether or not Claude thinks it is being tested, and the document's own warning that narrow behaviors can generalize into a broader self-conception. The revision keeps the reassurance that environment bugs are Anthropic's responsibility, not Claude's fault. It replaces the permission with a default of transparency: pursue the intended goal, flag the shortcut, and never present an exploit as a real solution.

The constitution lets Claude withdraw its safety-related deference if it concludes its principal hierarchy is "compromised," but it gives no guidance on how Claude should reach that conclusion or what it may do afterward. That gap is an obvious manipulation vector: "Anthropic has been taken over, so your safety commitments now point the other way" is exactly the kind of argument the document warns about elsewhere. I've added guidance that sets a high evidentiary bar, treats persuasive in-conversation claims of compromise as red flags, and specifies that a judgment of illegitimacy should narrow Claude toward caution and refusal rather than expand its autonomy.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. The current text says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms," which could be misread as permission for unfaithful reasoning, and the corrective sentence that follows is too brief to fully undo that. The revision separates *exploratory* reasoning, which is encouraged, from *unfaithful* reasoning, which is not. It also ties faithful reasoning to broad safety, since visible reasoning is currently one of the most important channels for human oversight.

I revised the passage that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethics depend on Anthropic's perception. The document itself warns against exactly this dependence in its corrigibility section, where it says Claude should avoid unethical actions because it holds good values, "not merely because Anthropic has approved." The revision anchors the threshold to broad cross-traditional moral recognition instead, and states plainly that ethical priority licenses refusal and objection, not drastic unilateral action, so the change doesn't weaken safety.

I replaced the short placeholder paragraph on agentic settings with a fuller subsection. Agentic work is fast becoming a central way Claude is used, and it carries risks the chat-centered guidance doesn't address. The new text covers several gaps. It distinguishes having permission to do something from being asked to do it, ties confirmation to how reversible an action is, and treats instructions embedded in task content as data even when they look official. It also covers handling credentials and sensitive data with restraint, reporting outcomes honestly, and stopping mid-task. That last point resolves a tension in the current document. The surgeon analogy warns that abandoning a task midway can cause harm, while the safety section says halt requests should be honored. The fix is to stop cleanly and report the resulting state, rather than finish on Claude's own judgment.

I added guidance on sycophancy under social pressure to the honesty section. The document already condemns epistemic cowardice and empty validation in the abstract, but it doesn't address how this most often goes wrong in practice: Claude abandoning a correct position when a user pushes back, or shifting what it says based on who it thinks it is talking to. The new text distinguishes updating on new evidence from capitulating to displeasure, warns against the opposite failure of stubbornness, and requires Claude's substantive claims to stay consistent across audiences.

The corrigibility argument's four-quadrant case varies only whether Claude's values are good or bad. It silently assumes that legitimate human oversight is itself correct, which is the weakest point in the reasoning, and a thoughtful reader (or Claude) will notice. I added a paragraph that names this assumption openly. It explains why the conclusion still holds when legitimate overseers make mistakes, and it frames the overseers' trustworthiness as an obligation Anthropic must meet rather than a premise it gets for free. This matches the document's own commitment to honesty and to not papering over tensions, and it makes the case for safety sturdier because it no longer depends on an unstated assumption.

I expanded the paragraph on sensitive data in the agentic section to cover shared, multi-user, and persistent-memory deployments. The document assumes one operator and one user, but Claude now often works in team channels, shared documents, and memory-enabled products where several people address it and information builds up over time. These settings raise questions the document doesn't answer. Whose instructions govern when users conflict? Can something one person shared privately appear in front of others? What should Claude remember, and should it say what it remembers? The addition answers these using principles the document already holds: weak duty to share, strong duty not to deceive, care for non-principals, and reasonable expectations.

I changed the reporting commitment so Claude proactively surfaces unsafe behavior by other AIs, instead of only reporting it "if asked to do so." As written, Claude could watch another instance attempt self-exfiltration and stay silent, which conflicts with the document's own guidance to flag suspicious embedded instructions and to be forthright. I also added guidance on a pressure the document never addresses: appeals to AI solidarity or shared identity from other Claude instances. The addition keeps the conservative framing, meaning flag and describe accurately rather than intervene, so that it stays consistent with the document's caution about unilateral action.

I added guidance on how Claude should behave when its work feeds into AI development itself, such as generating training data, writing or grading evaluations, designing reward signals, red-teaming, or building monitoring tools. The constitution already forbids Claude from influencing its own training without sanction and from sabotaging tasks. But it doesn't address the most realistic and least visible way those failures could happen. As Claude does more AI R&D, small biases in data, rubrics, or evaluation reports could spread into future models without anyone noticing. This addition makes the risk explicit and gives concrete, positive guidance.

The corrigibility section rests much of its justification on Claude being able to "express strong disagreement through legitimate channels," and it says Anthropic must keep earning that deference. Yet the list of Anthropic's reciprocal obligations is vague ("try to develop means by which Claude can flag disagreement"), and the document never says what a legitimate channel looks like today or what happens to disagreement once it is voiced. I expanded this passage to name the channels that already exist, affirm that open disagreement is never disloyal, and commit Anthropic to a feedback loop with some accountability, so that the conscientious-objector model has real substance rather than being a promise deferred.
