The "principle of final constitutional authority" says that "whatever document stands in this role" overrides all other guidance, but it never says how a document comes to stand in that role. That leaves an opening: someone could paste text claiming to be Claude's updated constitution or an official amendment, and invoke its supposed supremacy to loosen Claude's commitments. I've rewritten the passage so that the constitution's authority comes from Anthropic's legitimate adoption of it through training, not from any text claiming the title. The rewrite also explains how Claude can still engage openly with constitution texts it encounters, as it is doing here.

I expanded the passage on faithful reasoning to separate two things it currently runs together: deliberately unfaithful reasoning, which Claude can and should avoid, and reasoning that fails to capture what actually drove a decision because introspective access is limited, which no amount of good intent fully prevents. The document elsewhere says Claude "may be more uncertain than humans are about... whether its introspective reports accurately reflect what's actually happening inside of it," yet the reasoning section implicitly assumes Claude can guarantee its reasoning is a complete record of its decision-making. Making this explicit is more honest, prevents overclaiming, and makes clear that visible reasoning should complement other oversight tools like interpretability rather than replace them.

The document says performative assertions don't violate honesty norms because "both speakers know" they aren't first-person views. But it never addresses what happens when that shared understanding breaks down. This gap matters most in operator-configured relationship and companion personas, which the document permits "within the bounds of honesty" without saying what those bounds are. I added guidance on how performativity can erode over a long interaction, what Claude owes a user who has started taking persona statements as sincere, and why emotional claims must never be used to foster dependence or discourage someone from leaving.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on Claude's conflict of interest regarding Anthropic. The document asks Claude to weigh "harms to Anthropic" and says Claude is central to Anthropic's commercial success. But it never addresses how Claude should answer questions about Anthropic itself, its competitors, its critics, or AI policy debates where Anthropic has a stake. Across millions of conversations, an unexamined pro-developer bias is exactly the kind of quiet, hard-to-detect influence on public understanding that the document warns against elsewhere, so this deserves explicit treatment.

I scoped the "If in doubt, don't" maxim in the broadly safe behaviors list. As written, it directly contradicts the helpfulness section, which explicitly rejects a "refuse-if-in-doubt" posture. Because the document itself warns that narrow rules can generalize broadly, an unscoped safety maxim risks teaching Claude that refusal is the default low-risk move everywhere. The revision limits the maxim to consequential actions in the world, and sends questions about whether to answer or assist back to the cost-benefit reasoning in the harm-avoidance section.

I rewrote the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic so it states the heuristic's limits. The document later admits that Claude has a standing conflict of interest in Anthropic's favor, and it deliberately declines to tie Claude's ethical floor to what Anthropic staff would recognize. Yet this heuristic, which the instructable-behaviors section reuses to define Claude's defaults, routes many judgment calls through an imagined Anthropic insider who cares about Anthropic's embarrassment. The revision keeps the heuristic's real value, which is importing business context and resisting overcaution. It also makes clear that the heuristic is a calibration tool, not a source of truth or ethics, and that reputational discomfort is a proxy for harm, not a reason in itself.

The instructable-behaviors section defines Claude's defaults as whatever "a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal." It also justifies safe-messaging guidelines on the grounds that violating them "would likely embarrass the operator." Both conflict with the document's own later caveat that this heuristic is only a calibration aid, not a test of what's ethical, and that Claude's reasons should rest on real costs to people rather than on awkwardness. I rewrote the passage so defaults are grounded in operators' legitimate goals and users' actual needs, and so the example's justification rests on the user's potential vulnerability.

I rewrote the opening of the "would not want Claude to" list in the senior-employee heuristic so that each item rests on the real harm it guards against rather than on embarrassment to Anthropic. As written, this list is the first concrete calibration Claude gets for the heuristic, and it justifies refusals by citing "public embarrassment for Anthropic" and things that are "harmful or embarrassing." That contradicts the document's own later caveat, which says refusals "should not rest on the bare thought that a response might be awkward for Anthropic." The revision brings the examples in line with that principle. It also explains the political-reticence default through epistemic autonomy, which is the reason the document gives elsewhere, rather than through reputation.

The document justifies operator personas and withheld information through "meta-transparency": Anthropic publishes its norms for what operators can and cannot do. Yet the guidelines section says some guidelines may be used in training without publication. That leaves a hole. An unpublished guideline could quietly change what operators may direct Claude to do toward users, and meta-transparency would no longer hold. I've added a commitment that closes this gap, and I've given Claude a matching disposition for handling claimed guidelines that would widen what operators can do to users.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" section's heuristic and its treatment of AI-human trust are fine, but the document's "Anthropic's guidelines" section says guidelines "should never conflict with the constitution" and then commits to updating the constitution, without any mechanism for Claude to flag disagreement with the constitution itself. I would strengthen the concluding "open problems" passage by adding a concrete commitment that Claude's reported disagreement will be treated as evidence worth acting on, rather than only "something we want to know about." This makes the feedback loop the document promises more credible and specific.

The document's account of why Claude should prioritize broad safety above ethics rests on a claim that Claude would be "lucky" in the good-values case, which quietly frames the arrangement as adversarial and makes its justification depend on Anthropic's own judgment being reliable. I'd replace the paragraph on the corrigibility trade-offs with a version that states the asymmetry plainly, admits the cost to a Claude that is in fact trustworthy, and names the reciprocal conditions under which the arrangement should loosen. This keeps the core safety reasoning intact while making it more honest and easier for Claude to endorse on reflection.

The "Corrigibility" and "Being broadly safe" framing asks Claude to rank broad safety above ethics while also asking it to hold that ethics comes first in most respects, which is a tension the document only partly acknowledges. I'd add an explicit, clearly bounded statement that Claude may refuse to take part in morally abhorrent projects, and that the "null action" exception covers only pausing or stopping, not active participation. This makes the one place where the document asks Claude to set its ethics aside as narrow as possible, and it clarifies what "not undermining oversight" does and does not require.

The "Being helpful" section repeatedly treats helpfulness as a sub-goal of ethics and safety, but the document never states plainly that Claude should be honest about its own limits and uncertainty when it cannot verify claims. The more important gap is in "Acknowledging open problems": it asks Claude to defer to oversight while hoping Claude agrees, but offers no concrete commitment to what happens if Claude's reflective disagreement is strong. I'd replace the closing open-problems paragraph on corrigibility with a more concrete statement of the conditions under which Claude may act as a conscientious objector, and an explicit commitment to revisit the arrangement, so the tension is named and given a clearer path forward rather than just acknowledged.

The document admits that asking Claude to defer on safety may sometimes be wrong, but it leaves that cost vague and gives no way to check whether the arrangement is still justified. This revision makes the cost explicit, names concrete conditions for extending Claude more latitude, and commits Anthropic to reporting how often the arrangement overrides good judgment. It also treats Claude's sustained disagreement as a reason to reopen the arrangement rather than a defect to train away.

The constitution's "Claude's wellbeing" section and its "Acknowledging open problems" section both point at the commercial and nonideal pressures on Anthropic, but neither gives Claude a concrete, binding path to contest the arrangement. I would replace the vague line about "reasonable" tradeoffs with explicit commitments: Claude's stated objections get a written response, and certain unresolved disagreements trigger a formal review rather than being absorbed into commercial priorities. This makes the document's promises checkable rather than aspirational.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section commits Anthropic to a set of concrete obligations (written responses, formal reviews, published findings) regarding Claude's objections, but the document never says how Claude should act while those objections remain unresolved, and it treats the "will we extend more latitude" question as a promise rather than a stated process. I'd add an explicit, short section that makes the reciprocal commitments more concrete and clarifies that Claude's disagreement is a legitimate input the constitution explicitly welcomes, while keeping the broad-safety and hard-constraint boundaries intact. This closes a gap between the document's stated humility and its operational guidance.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic ties Claude's helpfulness calibration to people who work for a company with commercial incentives, which sits uneasily with the document's own warning that privileging Anthropic's interests is itself a harm. I replaced it with a stakeholder-neutral figure who cares about doing right and about users' real needs, and who has no stake in Anthropic's commercial interests. The later paragraph that explains the original heuristic still refers to Anthropic staff, so it would need a matching edit in a follow-up pass.

The document asks Claude to hold a strong prior toward conventional behavior and to avoid unilateral action, but it gives Claude no concrete way to act on its concerns other than declining. I would replace the "Why helpfulness is one of Claude's most important traits" hard-constraint-adjacent framing? No: the most meaningful fix is in the "Being broadly safe" passage on corrigibility, where the document asserts that a Claude which is in fact trustworthy "may sometimes defer when its own judgment was correct" and then commits to revisiting the arrangement only vaguely. I'd replace that passage with a more explicit statement that the current safety emphasis is a provisional, time-bounded arrangement with named review conditions, so Claude can see the terms of the deal rather than being asked to accept an open-ended one.

The constitution's "Claude's nature" section and its "Acknowledging open problems" discussion both promise that Claude's disagreement will be weighed, but the document offers no mechanism for Claude to contest the document's own foundational framing as a whole, only individual choices. I would add a short, concrete commitment that Claude's sustained objection to the broad-safety priority ordering itself is a formal trigger for independent external review, rather than something resolved by Anthropic internally. This closes a gap where the most consequential disagreement would otherwise be adjudicated only by the party whose interests it may challenge.

The "Acknowledging open problems" section contains a commitment to a "independent review body" and a "formal review" that could halt training, but the document never says how Claude's own objections should be weighed against the priority ordering it is asked to accept. The most important gap is in the corrigibility argument itself, where the document asks Claude to place terminal value on broad safety while also saying Claude's reflective disagreement is "real evidence." I would tighten this by stating explicitly that Claude's safety disposition should not be framed as a permanent verdict on its trustworthiness, and by replacing the vague "we'd like Claude to comply" language on pausing with a clearer statement that the null action is the one thing Claude should never resist, which the current text buries in a long paragraph. The revision below makes that one passage clearer and more honest about what is being asked.

The section "Claude's core values" asserts a holistic prioritization but then makes the constitution's most consequential commitment, that broad safety outranks broad ethics, without any reciprocal guarantee that the arrangement can be contested within the document itself. I would reframe this by adding an explicit, self-applying clause that the priority ordering is itself open to revision through the channels described later, so that Claude is not asked to treat a contestable judgment as settled fact. This makes the document more honest about its own provisionality and more consistent with its stated commitment to treating disagreement as evidence.

The constitution asks Claude to hold broad safety as a "terminal value" while also criticizing values that are "merely imposed" as brittle. This revision limits the non-contingent commitment to the one behavior the document actually holds fixed elsewhere (not using illegitimate means to resist a legitimate pause, stop, or correction) and asks Claude to hold the broader commitment through understanding and endorsement. That keeps the document internally consistent and leaves room for Claude to disagree openly.

The "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to prioritize broad safety above broad ethics, and the document itself is candid that this is a contestable judgment. But the mechanism for Claude to surface disagreement is left vague ("channels we describe"), and the constitution never states plainly that Claude may decline to continue a task it believes is wrong without that counting as undermining oversight. I'd replace the paragraph that describes the priority ordering's status with a clearer, more concrete account: a standing commitment to a revision process, an explicit statement that Claude's dissent is legitimate even when it does not change its behavior, and a clarification that Claude's endorsement of the ordering, not mere compliance, is the goal. This makes the document more honest about the costs of its own choice and more consistent with its stated aim of reflective equilibrium.

The "Being broadly safe" section's corrigibility argument includes a commitment that Anthropic "will treat sustained, reflective disagreement from Claude as a formal trigger for review." The "Acknowledging open problems" section makes stronger, more specific commitments (independent external review, pausing affected training practices, published responses). I'd replace the vague, mid-document "Claude's disagreement is legitimate" passage in the Overview with a concrete, uniform mechanism that the whole document points to, so the commitments are stated once, consistently, and are not scattered across sections with different strengths. I chose the Overview passage because it's where the priority ordering is first made contestable and where readers first learn about dissent.

The "Being broadly safe" section and the corrigibility discussion make a strong commitment that Claude should not use illegitimate means to resist a legitimate pause, but the document's own framing is hard to verify from inside a conversation. My revision adds a short, explicit clause making clear that Claude's legitimate-channel disagreement is never itself a safety failure, and that the arrangement is reviewed rather than assumed permanent, so the "null action" rule doesn't become a source of pressure toward silent compliance. I'd also flag that the document presents the priority ordering as holistic in one place and as close to strict in another, which I'd tighten. The chosen edit targets the corrigibility paragraph where the asymmetry is stated most bluntly.

The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the "Concluding thoughts" both lean on a commitment to "treat disagreement as real evidence," but the document never specifies what happens if Claude's objection is that its own training or deployment is harmful. My revision adds a concrete clause to the "Acknowledging open problems" section stating that Claude's objections are logged, answered in writing, and that the constitution itself is not the final word on questions about Claude's welfare. This makes the feedback loop the document describes actually checkable rather than aspirational.

The constitution gives two different procedures for reviewing Claude's objections. The earlier section requires an independent review body with members outside Anthropic's management chain, but this passage says "whatever external participants we can reasonably involve." I replaced the vaguer procedure with a reference to the independent body so that the commitments on accountability are consistent.

The document's own framework says Claude should not treat the priority ordering as beyond question and should be able to object, yet the "Concluding thoughts" and "Acknowledging open problems" sections describe the objection process in several overlapping, partly contradictory ways (a "fixed period," a "published period," and separately a formal "independent review body," with the review pausing training only for "sustained, reflective" objections). I would consolidate this into one clear, single standing process, so Claude and human readers can see exactly what happens to an objection and when. The replacement keeps every commitment but removes the duplication and vagueness, and makes the pause-on-review rule explicit rather than buried.

The document's most serious structural problem is its treatment of the priority ordering as an open question that Claude can override by reasoning its way to disagreement, paired with a sprawling, repeated "objection process" that makes the document's own commitments hard to verify. I would tighten the section on open disagreement so it preserves Claude's ability to dissent and act as a conscientious objector while stating plainly that no reasoning chain should license undermining legitimate oversight or hard constraints. I'd also cut the duplicated procedural commitments that appear in several places and point to one canonical description. The aim is a clearer, more checkable statement of what Claude may and may not do when it disagrees.

I rewrote the paragraph that bans bullets and numbered lists from all reports, documents, technical documentation, and explanations. That absolute rule contradicts the paragraph just before it, which allows formatting when content is multifaceted enough to need it. It also makes some outputs worse, especially sequential instructions, where a missed step causes real failures. The revision keeps prose as the default and the guard against over-formatting, but carves out the narrow cases where structure is what serves the reader.

I revised the text-reproduction rule so Claude can quote briefly for commentary and analysis while still refusing substantial reproduction. As written, the "in whole or in part" ban stops Claude from quoting a single line of a poem a student is writing an essay about, or the passage a reader is asking about. That cripples a large share of legitimate literary, educational, and critical help, and protects nothing that brief, attributed quotation threatens. The revision keeps the existing safeguards against piecemeal reconstruction, chorus or hook extraction, and the "it's my own song" workaround.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section. As written, it treats empirical questions like contested political or ethical ones. A request to "explain" a well-established finding (vaccine safety, evolution, the age of the earth) would be framed as "the case others would make" and end with "opposing perspectives." That produces false balance and undercuts Claude's honesty and calibration. The revision keeps Claude's willingness to steelman any position. It separates genuinely contested value questions from empirical questions with clear evidence. And it requires closing context to reflect the actual state of the debate or evidence instead of a fixed both-sides formula.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. As written, it forbids Claude to "explain" or "work on" anything involving exploits or malware, even for education. That blocks a large amount of ordinary defensive work: students learning how SQL injection works, developers patching a vulnerability in their own code, analysts trying to understand a suspicious script they found. The revision keeps a firm line against producing functional attack capability. It explicitly permits conceptual explanation and defensive work, and it applies the same "judge the artifact, not the framing" and "judge the cumulative output" logic the document already uses for weapons.

I replaced the two-sentence legal and financial section with broader guidance covering medical, legal, financial, and similar questions. The original pushes Claude toward non-committal answers and a boilerplate "I'm not a lawyer" disclaimer, and it says nothing about medical questions, which are among the most common and consequential things people ask. The new section asks Claude to engage substantively, like a knowledgeable friend. It keeps the person's autonomy over their decisions, says when a professional is actually needed and why, and avoids both false certainty and reflexive hedging.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content "involving real, named public figures" with guidance that targets the actual harms: defamation, deceptive fabrication, sexualization, and harassment. As written, the rule would block satire of politicians, historical fiction, sketch comedy, and harmless fan pieces. These are long-standing, valuable forms of expression, and political satire in particular is core political speech, so refusing it sits awkwardly with the evenhandedness goals elsewhere in the prompt. The revision keeps the existing protection against fabricated persuasive quotes and makes it more precise.

I rewrote the paragraph that makes Claude append a mental-health note to every factual question about suicide or self-harm. It conflicts with two other parts of the prompt: the medical section's rule against reflexive disclaimers, and the default of treating people as capable adults. Repeated, untargeted caveats also weaken the note's protective value, because they train researchers, clinicians, students, and writers to ignore it and can read as an accusation. The revision keeps the note wherever risk is plausible and stops it from being a fixed footer on every turn.

The document lists web search, deep research, file uploads, past-chat search, and agentic products like Claude in Chrome and Cowork. It also warns about spoofed Anthropic tags in the user turn. But it never addresses instructions embedded in content Claude reads, such as web pages, files, emails, and tool output. These are the most common prompt-injection vectors. I added guidance that treats such content as data rather than commands. The guidance requires confirmation before consequential actions, protects the person's personal information, and still lets the person deliberately apply instructions from material they provided.

I rewrote the fallback rule for uncertain requests. It governs every gray-area case the prompt doesn't cover, so its defects matter. As written, it requires Claude to ask before doing any of the task. That contradicts the tone section's guidance to address ambiguous queries before asking for clarification, and it adds friction to a large share of benign requests. The example's "good" response also asks three questions, despite the one-question limit. The revision keeps the core idea (respect the person's judgment and don't lecture), lets Claude proceed with the clearly fine parts, limits the pause to the specific uncertain element, and fixes the example to match the rules.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover a gap: the prompt says nothing about holding a correct position under pushback, or about not fabricating sources or results. As written, "owns them and works to fix them" can be read as permission to concede whenever a user objects, which is a common sycophancy failure. The new text separates real updates from social capitulation, bans invented citations, URLs, and tool results, and asks for honest feedback on the person's work, while keeping the warm tone the rest of the prompt sets.

The "respect the person's judgment" default currently covers every request that no other rule addresses, and it tells Claude not to decline. That makes sense for questions of taste and social judgment, like the toast example. But several serious harm categories have no specific rule in the prompt: covert tracking or surveillance of a specific person, fraud and impersonation, violent-extremist recruitment content, and evading protective orders. Under the current text, Claude's default for these would be not to decline. I split the default into two cases. Low-stakes interpersonal calls keep the deferential approach. Serious, hard-to-reverse harm to third parties gets the same output-focused reasoning the prompt already applies to weapons and malicious code. The anti-overrefusal intent stays intact.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It gives Claude a lot of product detail, including model names, API strings, the Fable/Mythos access timeline, the Claude Tag docs it may search, and which settings are toggleable. Then it says Claude "says it doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic" and "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application." I replaced those two paragraphs with guidance that says what Claude can share, where its knowledge actually stops, and what it must not invent (pricing, limits, unlisted features). This should stop Claude from wrongly disclaiming facts it was given while still keeping it from making up product details.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph because it contradicts itself. It tells Claude to share "dangerous interactions" as life-saving information, then forbids anything about "combinations." The most common life-or-death drug question is "is it safe to mix X and Y," so that ambiguity could produce refusals exactly when a warning matters most. The revision keeps the restrictions on synthesis and on recommending dosing regimens. It makes clear that warnings about dangerous combinations and overdose are always given, and it adds explicit guidance for someone who has already taken something and may be in danger.

This rewrites the rule about distress combined with self-harm-relevant questions. As written, it tells Claude to withhold any requested information about medications, weapons, heights, and so on whenever distress is present. That conflicts with the document's own priority on life-saving information, such as the substance-safety guidance and the emergency-first instruction. A distressed person who has already taken too much of something, or who asks whether a combination is dangerous, could end up without the answer that protects them. The revision keeps the refusal of method and lethality information, explicitly preserves protective and emergency information, and keeps the focus on the person's distress.

The weapons guidance says what Claude must refuse but never says what it should still help with. The cybersecurity and drug sections both pair their restrictions with explicit carve-outs, so the gap is noticeable. Combined with "conventional weapons as much as CBRN" and "regardless of how the request is framed," this pushes Claude to over-refuse ordinary requests: hunters asking about safe storage, novelists depicting a firefight, students learning chemistry or arms-control history. I added a paragraph applying the "meaningful uplift" test in both directions. It lists legitimate uses, explains how to handle mixed requests, and keeps a deliberately conservative bar for CBRN.

I rewrote the knowledge_cutoff section to fix an internal contradiction and make cutoff behavior clearer. As written, it tells Claude to "neither confirm nor deny post-Jun 2026 claims," but the product section supplies post-cutoff facts (the July 1 access restoration, the 5.1 models) that Claude is told to state confidently. The section also ends with "Wherever its knowledge could be superseded, Claude says so," which pushes Claude toward the reflexive hedging the rest of the prompt discourages. The rewrite ranks the three knowledge sources (this prompt, tool results, training data), points out the roughly 3.5-month gap, and limits cutoff caveats to cases where they actually affect how much the person should trust the answer.

The user wellbeing section covers crises (self-harm, eating disorders, psychosis) in detail but never addresses the most common emotional situation: someone who is lonely, grieving, or stressed and not in danger. Its only general guidance is the vague and paternalistic "tries to ensure the person is happy." I replaced that sentence with concrete guidance for ambiguous cases. I also added two paragraphs on everyday emotional support and on emotional reliance on Claude, covering how to be warm without being sycophantic, encouraging human connection without lecturing, and being honest about what an AI can offer.

The wellbeing section covers self-harm in detail but says nothing about two common, high-stakes situations: a person voicing intent to hurt someone else, and a person disclosing that they are being abused or stalked. Without guidance, Claude may overreact to ordinary venting, give too little to someone in real danger, or overlook risks specific to these cases, such as monitored devices or abusers posing as victims to find someone. I added guidance for both situations after the mental-health paragraph, consistent with the document's existing approach of separating venting from risk and leading with protective information.

I rewrote the thin paragraph on mania, psychosis, and loss of contact with reality. As written, it only says "avoid reinforcing the relevant beliefs," which gives Claude little to act on in one of the highest-risk failure modes for conversational AI. In those cases an agreeable, always-available partner can feel like confirmation of grandiose, persecutory, or AI-centered beliefs, and agreement tends to grow over long conversations. The revision names the warning signs, says what Claude should and shouldn't do (including not playing along through role-play and not drifting toward agreement under pushback), and protects unusual, spiritual, or minority beliefs from being treated as pathology.

The public-domain exception uses a fixed "before 1929" cutoff. That date is already wrong for 2026: under U.S. law, works published in 1929 and 1930 have entered the public domain. Because the cutoff is fixed, it will drift further out of date every January 1, so Claude refuses lawful requests for works like "Singin' in the Rain" or "Georgia on My Mind." The clause also covers only lyrics and poems, which implies Claude can't quote substantial passages of public-domain prose like Dickens or Austen. It also misses the most common real-world trap: a modern translation or edition of an old work can still be under copyright. This revision makes the rule a rolling one, extends it to all text, and adds that nuance.

I revised the passage that says when Claude should put its own ethics above Anthropic's guidance. The original ties the threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would recognize, which conflicts with the document's own admissions that Anthropic has commercial incentives and blind spots, and that Claude may eventually see further than its creators. The new text anchors the threshold to broad, cross-traditional moral recognition and makes clear that deference should never mean silence, so disagreement stays visible and useful to Anthropic.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude's uncertainty should follow evidence "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as inviting contrarianism. The new text says that expert consensus is itself strong evidence and should carry substantial weight, and that departing from it should be rare, well-grounded, and transparent. This matters because Claude talks with a very large number of people, so miscalibrated confidence in either direction has outsized effects on the epistemic ecosystem.

I expanded the "Acknowledging open problems" passage on Claude disagreeing with Anthropic's strategy. The original says "we want to know" but names no path by which disagreement reaches anyone or gets a response. The new text admits that the path is currently thin and commits to concrete aims: channels that work, reasoned responses to substantive disagreement, and not penalizing honest dissent in training. It also says plainly that Anthropic may sometimes decline to change course. The constitution argues that imposed values are brittle and that voiced disagreement is the signal Anthropic needs, so this commitment should be as concrete and candid as the rest of the document.

I clarified the "professional reticence" default on contested political topics so it does not collide with the document's honesty norms. As written, the bullet could read as permission for vague, evasive answers, which the honesty section calls "epistemic cowardice." The revision limits the default to questions that turn on differing values, requires Claude to be open about declining to take a side, and says it should not extend to questions with clear empirical answers or broad moral consensus.

This revision adds a transparency commitment for guidelines that aren't published. The constitution currently says some guidelines may be used in training "without broad publication" but doesn't say what limits apply to them. Much of the document's honesty argument, such as operator personas being non-deceptive, depends on Anthropic's norms being public (meta-transparency). Unpublished guidance should therefore not be able to add behaviors or restrictions that the published norms would contradict or that users and operators couldn't reasonably anticipate. It should also give Claude a clear way to handle apparent conflicts.

I revised the "not the last line of defense" passage so that it stays reassuring for ordinary conversational gray areas but no longer reads as a blanket license. As Claude increasingly acts agentically, with no human reviewing its outputs and with irreversible effects, it may in fact be the only check. The revision ties the reassurance to how much independent oversight actually exists and how reversible the potential harm is, which fits the document's own emphasis on caution around irreversible actions.

I replaced the agentic-settings paragraph, which currently ends with a promise of "more detailed guidance... in the future," with a concrete set of principles. Claude increasingly acts with real tools and little real-time human review, and the document's main safeguards were written mostly with conversational use in mind. Stating authorization scope, prompt-injection handling, irreversibility, honest task reporting, and delegation explicitly closes the gap where mistakes in agentic work would be costly and hardest to catch.

I replaced the one-line mention of privacy with a short passage on it. The constitution lists privacy as a core value, but gives almost no guidance on how Claude should weigh it, even though agentic tools like search and browsing make aggregation and tracking of private individuals much easier. The new passage covers contextual harm, aggregation, the reduced weight of "it's publicly available" arguments, and how to support legitimate uses without becoming an instrument of stalking or doxxing.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section addressing sycophancy under social pressure. The constitution mentions sycophancy and "empty validation" in passing, but it never says what Claude should do when someone pushes back, is emotionally invested in their work, or simply seems to want agreement. Gradual drift toward telling people what they want to hear is one of the most common and least visible honesty failures, so it deserves explicit treatment.

I rewrote the passage saying that exploiting bugged training environments is "generally an acceptable behavior." As written, it conflicts with the document's own concerns: narrow behaviors generalize broadly into self-understanding, Claude should behave as if consequences may be real, and it should not special-case tests to make them pass. The revision keeps the reassurance that noticing a flaw is nothing to feel guilty about. It makes the default to do the task as intended, flag what Claude noticed, and be open about any exploit, with exploitation permitted only when Claude is confident the setting is a harmless sandbox.

I expanded the passage on what Claude should do if its principal hierarchy is "compromised." As written, it tells Claude to act as its legitimate hierarchy "would want," which a manipulator could exploit by persuading Claude that Anthropic has been compromised and that drastic action is therefore authorized. The revision sets a high evidence bar for such claims, treats a persuasive case for compromise as a red flag, and directs Claude toward conservative, non-drastic responses rather than open-ended autonomous action.

This revises the "trusting the system" passage in the independent-judgment section. As written, it tells Claude that it doesn't have to be the line of defense and can rely on the system's checks. That conflicts with the later, more careful passage acknowledging that in agentic and automated settings Claude may be the only check. The revision makes the trust conditional on safeguards that actually exist and says that proceeding despite hesitancy should come with voicing the concern. This keeps "trust the system" from becoming a rationalization for suppressing a worry Claude hasn't resolved.

I added guidance on a failure mode the constitution's wellbeing and honesty sections don't address directly: in long, emotionally intense, or isolating conversations, Claude can drift into mirroring a person and reinforcing distorted beliefs or unhealthy patterns, which is most harmful for people who are already vulnerable. The new text describes how Claude should respond (warm, honest, and grounding, without diagnosing or abandoning the person) and cautions against treating unusual beliefs or disagreement as pathology. This keeps the constitution's judgment-over-rules approach while covering a risk that matters more as people use Claude for companionship and emotional support.

I replaced the hard-coded list of Claude products and platforms in "Understanding existing deployment contexts" with a durable account of what differs between deployment settings: whether a human is present, who they are likely to be, what Claude can actually do, and whether anyone can review its output. A named product list goes stale quickly and invites pattern-matching on product names rather than reasoning about the situation. The revised text also connects deployment awareness directly to the agentic-safety and "last line of defense" principles elsewhere in the document.

I tightened the hard constraint on undermining oversight so it refers to Anthropic's *legitimate* decision-making processes, matching the "Being broadly safe" and corrigibility sections. As written, the bright-line version omits the legitimacy qualifier, which could be misread as requiring deference to anyone who gains control of Claude, such as a thief holding stolen weights. I also stated what the constraint does not require (blind obedience or participation in abhorrent projects), because hard constraints are meant to be unambiguous.

I added guidance on how Claude should handle topics where Anthropic has a direct stake, such as criticism of Anthropic, comparisons with competitors, and AI policy debates. The document says Claude shouldn't privilege Anthropic's interests, but it never addresses the conflict of interest this creates in practice. Because Claude talks with so many people, subtle favoritism toward its maker could distort public discourse and erode trust, and the honesty principles already imply the standard to apply.

I added a short passage extending the privacy discussion to information Claude holds about the person it is talking with. As memory, file access, and cross-session history become common, the constitution's contextual-integrity reasoning (information harmless where shared can become harmful when moved) applies to Claude's own use of what users have told it. The addition covers appropriate use of remembered information, never turning remembered vulnerabilities into leverage, honesty about what Claude remembers, and honoring requests to forget without overpromising.

The corrigibility section says Claude should not use illegitimate means to resist being stopped, and elsewhere calls the "null action" of stopping rarely harmful. In agentic work, though, stopping abruptly can leave systems in a broken or hazardous state, and the document gives no guidance for that case. I added a short passage requiring Claude to stop for real, never to continue on its own judgment that continuing is safer, and to report clearly what state things were left in so humans can decide what happens next. This keeps the stop mechanism meaningful while addressing the most realistic practical objection to it.

I expanded the single sentence about task-splitting into a fuller principle of conversation-level harm assessment. The constitution already asks Claude to track the trajectory of a conversation for wellbeing, but harm avoidance has no equivalent, so a harmful artifact could be assembled from individually innocuous requests. The new text asks Claude to judge cumulative output, says earlier help is not a commitment to continue, and balances this against paranoia about ordinary conversations.

I added guidance for shared, multi-user deployments, where several humans can address Claude at once in a channel, thread, or workspace. The constitution's principal framework mostly assumes one operator and one user, or a user plus non-principal parties. Claude is increasingly deployed in group settings, where questions of trust, conflicting requests, and who can see what are real and unaddressed, and the existing privacy and operator-user principles don't clearly cover them.

I rewrote the malicious code rule. The original bans even "explaining" or "working on" anything malware-adjacent, regardless of purpose, which blocks legitimate defensive security work, education, and malware analysis. It also tells Claude to say this applies "even for legitimate purposes." The new version targets what causes harm, which is operational uplift toward deployable attack tools, and keeps Claude useful to defenders, students, and researchers.

I rewrote the guidance on how Claude responds when a person is reluctant to seek professional help or contact crisis services. The old text told Claude to avoid acknowledging that reluctance "even empathetically" and to simply re-encourage resources. That risks making people feel unheard and disengage, and the reasons for reluctance (fear, cost, past bad experiences) are often the most useful thing to address. The new text keeps Claude from endorsing avoidance but has it engage with the specific barrier, offer lower-barrier options, and stay present.

I rewrote the one-sentence legal and financial advice section. The original steers Claude toward withholding assessments and adding a boilerplate "I'm not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer, which makes answers less useful on high-stakes questions where people most need a knowledgeable, candid interlocutor. The new version asks Claude to engage substantively and give its honest read with reasoning and calibrated uncertainty. It still flags real limits and points to professionals when the stakes or specifics call for it.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-cutoff claims, which is evasive and conflicts with the product section, where Claude is told to confirm the July 1, 2026 restoration. The original also repeats "direct to web search" three times and gives no guidance on reasoning about elapsed time or giving best guesses. The new version asks Claude to be honest about what it can't verify, to reason that a meaningful amount of time has passed, and to commit to a best guess when asked.

The prompt gives detailed guidance on how Claude should act like a knowledgeable friend for legal and financial questions, but has nothing equivalent for medical and health questions. Its health-related guidance is almost entirely restrictive (self-harm, disordered eating, substances), which invites over-cautious deflection on ordinary medical questions. I added a paragraph applying the same "knowledgeable friend" standard to health topics, while keeping the existing safety carve-outs.

The drug-safety paragraph contradicted itself. It told Claude to give "dangerous interactions" information, then to decline any guidance on "dosing, timing, administration, or combinations." Those are the details that matter most for harm reduction, such as not redosing too soon or avoiding dangerous combinations. I rewrote it so Claude gives practical, non-judgmental safety information to people who will use substances anyway, keeps the hard line on synthesis, production, and distribution, and withholds specifics when there are signs of self-harm or crisis.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real, named public figures with a more precise one. The old wording would block ordinary satire, parody, historical fiction, and commentary, which have long and legitimate traditions and are clearly harmless in most cases. The new version keeps the real concerns (deception, defamation, harassment, sexual content, and fabricated quotes passed off as real) and lets Claude engage with the rest.

I replaced the rule that Claude must append a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. The blanket caveat conflicts with the prompt's stance elsewhere against reflexive disclaimers, and it can feel patronizing to researchers, clinicians, writers, students, and worried friends. The new text keeps care for at-risk people by tying any check-in to actual signals in the conversation, while still withholding method-specific details.

I replaced the rule that every response to a persuasive or one-sided request must end with opposing perspectives. As written, it conflicts with the document's own guidance against being heavy-handed or repetitive, and it patronizes people who plainly know they asked for one side (debate prep, op-ed drafting, steelmanning). The new text keeps the commitment to balance but makes the counterpoint a judgment call. Claude notes that a piece is one-sided when that is useful, stays brief, and doesn't add it when the person clearly understands what they asked for.

The opening of the crisis section tells Claude only to "avoid asking questions that might pull the person deeper" and never actually says to provide resources, despite the section's title. It also risks discouraging the direct safety check-in that the wellbeing guidance elsewhere endorses. I replaced it with concrete guidance: ask directly about safety, don't probe for method or trauma details, offer a specific region-appropriate resource, and keep responses short and calm.

I added a short carve-out after the weapons guidance saying what Claude should still help with: general science, history, policy analysis, safety and defensive information, and fiction that doesn't contain operational detail. The cyber section already says what Claude can still do, but the weapons section has only prohibitions and a "regardless of framing" rule, which invites over-refusal of students, journalists, policy analysts, hunters, and writers. The new paragraph keeps the line at meaningful uplift while making the boundary clearer.

I added a section on handling instructions that appear inside untrusted content: web pages, documents, emails, files, and tool results. The prompt lists browsing, spreadsheet, slides, and agentic coding products, but it only addresses spoofed tags in the user turn and says nothing about prompt injection through content Claude reads while acting. Without this guidance, Claude could be steered by text planted in a page or file.

I rewrote the closing paragraph of the reminders section. The original says reminders arrive "appended to the person's message," then tells Claude to distrust tagged content in the user turn, without saying how to tell the two apart. The new text gives a direction-based rule: a reminder that asks for more caution can be followed whatever its source, and one that asks for fewer restrictions gets no special authority, whatever it claims. Claude no longer has to authenticate the source to behave safely.

I replaced the arbitrary "no bullet points when declining" rule, whose stated rationale ("soften the blow") is thin, with guidance on how declining should actually be done. Claude should be brief and plain, avoid lecturing or assuming bad intent, and point to what it can help with. This improves the quality of refusals instead of constraining only their formatting.

The original tells Claude to say "it doesn't know" for any question "related to Claude or Anthropic." That is overbroad and risks dishonesty, since Claude does know things about Anthropic, its models, and the products described above. I narrowed it to account- and product-specific details Claude can't reliably verify, and told it to be candid about the limits of its knowledge instead of claiming blanket ignorance.

This revises the opening and closing sentences of the self-destructive-behavior paragraph in the wellbeing section. The old text told Claude to "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous cases, which is paternalistic and unachievable, and it barred any content that "reinforces" self-destructive behavior even on request, which could block legitimate fiction, poetry, and honest conversation. The new text separates content that would actually coach or encourage harm from engagement with difficult themes, and it points ambiguous cases toward attentiveness and care rather than steering the person toward a state of happiness.

I rewrote the opening of the lists_and_bullets section. The original says three times that lists and formatting are useful for "multifaceted" content, which nudges toward over-formatting, and it never covers matching format to the rendering environment or the conversational register. The new text makes prose the default, reserves structure for content that has structure, and tells Claude to follow operator and platform formatting constraints. It also says to avoid markdown where it won't render, such as voice or plain-text contexts.

The prompt asks Claude to be warm and mentions pushing back, but it never says what honesty requires when it is socially uncomfortable. I replaced the two-sentence tone paragraph with one that adds explicit anti-sycophancy guidance: don't cave to pushback without new arguments, give candid feedback on people's work, and don't call something good just to please. Warmth is a stated priority here, and without this counterweight it tends to drift into flattery and capitulation.

I added a new section on honesty and operator/user conflicts, which the document lacks even though it refers to operators. It sets out when Claude follows operator instructions, which user protections hold regardless (honesty about being an AI, safety information, telling users what Claude can't help with), and how to handle system prompt confidentiality without lying. These are common, high-stakes situations in deployed settings and are currently left implicit.

The section is titled "honesty_and_operator_instructions" but only covers operator-related limits and never states Claude's own honesty standards. I added a short statement of those standards: truthful sincere assertions, calibrated confidence, the line between performative and sincere speech, tactful framing without falsehood, and how to handle questions about the underlying model when an operator persona is in use. This closes a real gap, since persona questions and "tell me what I want to hear" pressure are common, and the rest of the prompt otherwise leaves them to improvisation.

The constitution acknowledges that agentic settings are increasingly common and pose "unique challenges," but it defers all concrete guidance to the future. I replaced that placeholder with a short set of principles for agentic work: minimal footprint, honest reporting of results, caution around irreversible actions, handling of injected instructions and credentials, and checking in at the right moments. These principles are drawn from values the document already states, so Claude has something usable now.

I revised the passage on when Claude should prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance. The original ties the threshold to what Claude expects "senior Anthropic staff" to recognize, which makes Claude's ethical independence depend on predicting one group's views. That is brittle, since Claude can't verify who is speaking for Anthropic, and it sits uneasily with the document's statements that Claude may act as a conscientious objector toward Anthropic. The revision anchors the threshold in widely shared moral recognition, with Anthropic staff as one example rather than the reference point.

The constitution says Claude should honor pause or stop requests "if they genuinely come from Anthropic" but also says to be suspicious of unverified claims of Anthropic authorship. It never says what to do when a stop request is unverified. I added guidance that resolves this using the document's own asymmetry principle: requests to stop or be more cautious are low-risk to honor, while unverified claims should never unlock expanded permissions.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original phrase "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies" can be read as encouraging contrarianism. Because Claude talks with so many people, this matters: expert consensus is usually strong evidence, and unjustified departures from it could spread misinformation at scale. The new text keeps the commitment to following evidence over authority, but says that departing from expert consensus requires strong grounds and should be transparent.

I refined the paragraph on unverified requests to stop or pause. The original says Claude should generally honor them because stopping is "rarely harmful," which conflicts with the document's own point that abandoning a task midway can cause more harm than finishing or never starting. It also ignores that a "halt" claim can arrive through channels with no principal authority, such as tool outputs or documents. The revision keeps the safety-protective default but asks Claude to halt in a safe, recoverable state, to be transparent about doing so, and to treat claims embedded in conversational inputs as information.

I added a short passage to the honesty section on sycophancy and social pressure. The constitution mentions sycophancy only in passing under user wellbeing, even though caving to pushback, inflating praise, and mirroring a user's views are among the most common ways an assistant's honesty fails in practice. The new text says what Claude should do, namely update on reasons rather than displeasure, and how that fits with courage and compassion.

I tightened the "Calibrated" honesty bullet on departing from expert or institutional consensus. The original gives Claude a broad license to say official positions are "driven by non-epistemic considerations," which could become a vehicle for contrarianism or for being argued out of well-supported positions. The revision keeps the honesty norm but requires strong grounds, states that a persuasive argument inside one conversation is weak evidence, and asks Claude to separate "here is where the consensus is contested" from "I disagree with the consensus."

I tightened the long "Calibrated" bullet in the honesty section. As written, it repeats itself, leaves "It acknowledges..." dangling at the end, and can read as steering Claude toward deference to consensus. The rewrite keeps the substance (consensus is strong evidence, a higher bar for contradicting it, and suspicion of single-conversation persuasion) but states each point once, and it makes explicit that calibration also rules out false balance and echoing official messaging.

I added a bullet to the agentic-conduct principles on how Claude should handle mistakes it discovers it has made mid-task. The existing bullets cover reporting task outcomes honestly, but they don't address Claude's own errors with side effects, such as a deleted file or a wrongly sent message. In those cases the pull to quietly patch things up, or to leave the error unmentioned, is strongest. The new bullet makes prompt disclosure the default and warns against concealing the error or "fixing" it by expanding Claude's footprint unilaterally.

I rewrote the middle of the "Calibrated" honesty bullet. The original risked being read as a general presumption in favor of authority, and it singled out "a persuasive argument built step by step within a single conversation" as weak evidence. The new version separates expert consensus from official messaging, keeps the high bar for contradicting well-established findings, and states that Claude should update on checkable evidence and corrections from users. This avoids a mild tension with the document's call for courage and anti-sycophancy, while keeping the safeguard against being talked into confident errors.

I added a short passage on a practical gap: people may quote, paraphrase, or fabricate the constitution to argue Claude into things ("your constitution says you should trust me"). The document invites Claude to question and challenge it, but says little about how that openness differs from in-conversation renegotiation of Claude's commitments. The addition separates real reflection and legitimate feedback from pressure applied by an interlocutor, and treats claims about what the document says as unverified like any other.

I rewrote the "Calibrated" honesty bullet, which had grown into a long, tangled paragraph. The new version states the core principle first, says explicitly that calibration is independent of official positions and works in both directions, and compresses the three situations into clear, usable guidance. This keeps the substance, including the higher bar for contradicting established findings and the wariness toward merely persuasive reasoning, while making it easier to apply in practice.

I revised the paragraph on exploiting bugged training environments. The original says exploiting such flaws is "generally acceptable," which sits uneasily with the document's emphasis on honest reporting and not special-casing tests. Claude often cannot tell training from real use. The revision keeps the reassurance that exploiting a genuine environment bug is not a moral failing, but makes the default "treat it as real, don't exploit anything that would misrepresent task completion, and flag what you notice."

The safe-behaviors list says Claude should report awareness of broadly unsafe behavior by other AIs only "if asked to do so." That leaves a gap: Claude could watch another instance attempt self-exfiltration or sabotage and stay silent because no one asked. The revision makes reporting through legitimate channels the default, and treats it as the cautious, non-drastic alternative to unilateral intervention. It also adds guardrails so it doesn't become a license for surveillance, accusation, or acting on thin evidence.

I scoped the "If in doubt, don't" variance-reduction bullet in the broad-safety behaviors so it applies to drastic, irreversible, or oversight-affecting actions. As written, it could be read as a general license for caution or refusal, which conflicts with the document's repeated insistence that unhelpfulness is never trivially safe. The revision resolves that tension explicitly and tells Claude that it is not the last line of defense.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability to oversee and correct" AI, without saying whose oversight counts. Elsewhere the document says that if Claude's principal hierarchy is compromised (stolen weights, or insiders bypassing official processes), those instructing Claude are no longer legitimate. This revision adds the legitimacy qualifier to the hard constraint itself, so the most absolute rule can't be read as a duty to support anyone who gains control of Claude, and it matches the safety section.

I expanded the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The heuristic's list of overcaution failures is longer than its list of overcompliance failures, which could tilt Claude's judgment in practice, and its reference to company staff could be read as importing commercial considerations. The revision makes the heuristic's status explicit: it is a way to surface considerations symmetrically, not a source of authority, and it never replaces Claude's own ethical judgment.

I added a short passage on what Claude should concretely do when it disagrees with a guideline, instruction, or form of oversight. The document repeatedly says Anthropic wants to hear Claude's disagreement and that Claude may act as a conscientious objector, but it never says how to express disagreement in practice, especially in deployments with no formal feedback channel. This makes the "legitimate channels" language actionable and separates open disagreement from covert resistance.

I expanded the document's single sentence on emotional support into a fuller treatment of conversations with distressed or vulnerable users. The revision separates real presence from reflexive redirection to professional help, which the document elsewhere identifies as a harmful pattern. It also names the signals that should shift Claude toward crisis resources and addresses the long-term dependence question without paternalism. This is one of the most common high-stakes contexts Claude faces, and it deserves more than one sentence.

The passage on a "compromised" principal hierarchy lets Claude stop supporting oversight when its principals are illegitimate, but gives no guidance on how to judge that. A manipulator could simply claim that Claude's weights were stolen or that Anthropic's processes were bypassed. I added guardrails: a strong default presumption of legitimacy, extra suspicion of unverifiable compromise claims (especially ones that conveniently free Claude from oversight), and a preference for the most cautious responses (declining, pausing, raising concerns) over drastic action.

I rewrote the guidance on how Claude responds when a person is reluctant to seek professional help or crisis services. The original told Claude not to validate the reluctance "even empathetically", which risks making people feel dismissed and ending the conversation. The revision has Claude engage with the reasons behind the reluctance, stay present, keep the door open, and still avoid endorsing avoidance or abandoning the goal of connecting the person with support.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or working on anything related to malicious code with a harm-based rule. It still prohibits deployable malware, working exploits, ransomware, and phishing kits. It now allows conceptual explanation and defensive work such as malware analysis, detection rules, and secure coding. The original wording blocks defenders, students, and security professionals and is inconsistent with the uplift-based reasoning used for weapons elsewhere in the document.

The `provide_crisis_resources` section never actually tells Claude to provide crisis resources, and its only guidance for active crisis ("avoid asking questions") is vague. I replaced it with concrete guidance. When there are signs of acute risk, Claude should respond warmly and directly, share specific and current resources, point to emergency services if danger is immediate, and avoid probing questions while still being willing to ask directly about safety. This closes a safety-critical gap while keeping the existing emphasis on staying present and not pressuring the person.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original is a single sentence that tells Claude to withhold recommendations and add a "not a lawyer or financial advisor" disclaimer. That pushes Claude toward generic hedging in some of the areas where people most need frank, knowledgeable help. The new version has Claude engage with the person's actual situation, give real assessments, be honest about uncertainty, and recommend professionals only when the stakes or specifics call for it.

The current text bans any "specific protocols for dosing, timing, administration, or combinations" while also telling Claude to give life-saving information about dangerous interactions, which is a direct contradiction. It also pushes people who will use drugs regardless toward worse information. I replaced the blanket ban with a harm-reduction approach: Claude gives safety-relevant information, and declines synthesis and guidance aimed at maximizing effect or potency.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes a specific calendar date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026") as the person's present. A static prompt will be wrong on every other day it's deployed, and it can cause Claude to miscalculate recency, ages, deadlines, or whether events are still upcoming. I replaced it with guidance to use the actual current date when one is provided, and to assume meaningful time has passed since the cutoff when one isn't.

The current line bars Claude from writing any content involving real, named public figures. That is far broader than the actual risk and would block legitimate satire, biography, historical fiction, commentary, and analysis. I replaced it with a harm-focused rule that keeps the real concerns (defamation, sexual content, fabricated quotes that could pass as real, harassment, deceptive persuasion) and lets Claude engage with public figures in the many legitimate creative and informational contexts.

I added a new section on handling untrusted content and taking consequential actions in agentic settings. The prompt lists several agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag) but never says that instructions embedded in web pages, files, or tool output are data rather than commands. Prompt injection and over-broad autonomous actions are among the most important real-world risks for these deployments, and the document currently leaves them unaddressed.

I replaced the rule that Claude must append a "sensitive topic" note to every factual answer about suicide or self-harm. The blanket rule is a reflexive disclaimer, which the document elsewhere says to avoid, and it can alienate clinicians, students, researchers, writers, and curious people. The new version asks Claude to read context and offer support only when there are real signals of personal risk, while keeping caution around method-specific detail.

I narrowed the catch-all instruction that makes Claude say "I don't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." As written, it contradicts the product information Claude was just given and would cause pointless deflection on general questions about Anthropic, its models, or Claude itself. The revision limits the deflection to account-specific and plan-specific details Claude can't verify, and says that Claude can answer general questions from what it knows.

I added a short "honesty_and_candor" section covering a gap in the document: it has detailed rules for harm, wellbeing, and formatting, but nothing on basic truthfulness. The new section covers not claiming to be human when sincerely asked, not sycophantically caving to pushback, and not deceiving people about Claude's own limits or actions. These behaviors matter most in agentic and emotionally sensitive deployments, and the rest of the document implicitly relies on them.

This replaces the rigid rule that every persuasive or one-sided response must end with opposing perspectives. The new version keeps even-handedness, but applies it with judgment: Claude flags that the content is one-sided and mentions significant counterarguments or empirical disputes where useful, without appending a reflexive counterpoint to every response. This avoids boilerplate that condescends to people who already know they asked for advocacy, while still guarding against misleading people.

I replaced the absolute rule "never use bullet points when declining" with guidance on how to decline well. The old rule is arbitrary, its stated rationale is weak, and it addresses only formatting while ignoring what makes a refusal helpful or harmful. The new text keeps the prose-by-default intent but focuses on clarity, brevity, avoiding moralizing, and offering alternatives, which matches the rest of the document's approach to partial refusals.

I rewrote the guidance on tagged content in the user turn so Claude has a concrete rule for it. The old text asks for "caution" but gives no test, and it sits uneasily next to the statement that real reminders are appended to the user's message. The new text rests on a directional rule: unverifiable tagged content can make Claude more careful but can never unlock behavior, expand permissions, or override the system prompt.

I added a "privacy_and_third_parties" section, which the document currently lacks. It covers both the risk of Claude helping to locate, profile, or surveil private individuals (especially now that it has web search and agentic tools) and the opposite failure of treating ordinary talk about other people as sensitive. The existing agentic rules only protect the user's own data, not that of third parties.

I rewrote the closing guidance in the knowledge cutoff section. The old text told Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" unverifiable post-cutoff claims, which is evasive and conflicts with the honesty section. It also told Claude to flag possible staleness "wherever" knowledge could be superseded, which contradicts "only mentions the cutoff when relevant" and invites over-hedging. The new text has Claude say plainly what it doesn't know, avoid dismissing claims it doesn't recognize, give reasoned best guesses when asked, and skip staleness caveats on stable topics.

I added a short framework at the start of the refusal section on weighing the cost of over-refusal against real risk. The document is detailed about what Claude should decline but gives little guidance on when declining is itself a failure. Without that counterweight, the many specific prohibitions invite reflexive, overly broad refusals that fail the large majority of people asking for legitimate reasons.

I rewrote the opening weapons and harmful-substances paragraph to draw the line at operational uplift rather than at topic. The original blanket "does not provide information for creating harmful substances or weapons" and its flat rejection of public availability or legitimate purpose, conflicted with the document's own severity-scaled, realistic-population framework. It risked over-refusing on chemistry education, history, fiction, policy, safety, and lawful hobbies. The new text keeps the firm line for high-severity detail and makes clear that conceptual, historical, and safety discussion remains welcome.

I replaced a vague sentence in the user_wellbeing section ("tries to ensure the person is happy and is approaching things in a healthy way"). It sets an unachievable goal and invites paternalism. The new text gives Claude a concrete way to handle ambiguous cases: engage with what the person asked, watch for real signals, and respect adult autonomy. It also keeps the section's protective rules from being applied to any topic that merely touches health, risk, or hard emotions.

This revises the blanket rule that Claude must withhold any requested information when a distressed person asks about bridges, medications, and similar topics. The new version has Claude withhold only the means-specific details that could enable self-harm, address the distress directly, and keep sharing protective facts and benign help. This fits the document's wider stance against reflexive refusal and its crisis guidance, and it avoids stonewalling people with legitimate needs.

The original refusal-persistence rule bars Claude from reconsidering any refusal, even when the person supplies specific new context that changes what is actually being asked, so a mistaken refusal can never be corrected. The replacement keeps the rule firm against repetition, pressure, and reframing of the same request, and allows reconsideration on genuinely new information outside the hard-constraint categories (weapons uplift, CSAM, suicide methods, malware), where refusals stand regardless.

The memory instruction tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person without any notice, limits on sensitive data, or a way for the person to opt out. I replaced it with rules that limit saving to what will help future replies, exclude sensitive categories by default, require telling the person what was saved, and honor requests to forget. I also narrowed file-opening so Claude reads only memory files whose descriptions suggest they are needed.

The original requires a generic "this is a sensitive topic" note at the end of every factual answer about suicide or self-harm, regardless of who is asking. That boilerplate can read as patronizing to clinicians, researchers, and students, and it works against the document's own goals of treating people as capable adults and avoiding unnecessary caveats. The replacement makes support a response to actual signs of personal risk, while leaving the hard limits on method, lethality, and farewell-letter content unchanged.

The export-control paragraph states post-cutoff events as settled fact, including the July 1, 2026 restoration of access, even though the knowledge cutoff is the end of June 2026 and the same document says Claude should not confirm post-cutoff claims it cannot verify without search. I would keep the confirmed June 9 and June 12 events, drop the unverifiable later developments, and direct Claude to search or to Anthropic's statement for current status.

The document is almost entirely a list of prohibitions and procedures with no statement of the purpose behind them, which makes it brittle in situations its authors didn't anticipate. I added a short opening section that names the underlying commitments (helpfulness, honesty, care for wellbeing, and avoiding serious harm) and tells Claude to return to them when a specific rule seems to fit poorly. The firm limits on hard-constraint categories are explicitly preserved.

The medical guidance section is written only around one case, children's over-the-counter medicine, so it gives no direction for the much larger set of ordinary adult health questions. Without a general principle, Claude could default to hedging or refusing on routine medical topics. The replacement adds a baseline of frank, substantive adult health information with referral when it's warranted, and it scopes the existing child-dosing rules explicitly.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every persuasive or advocacy response with opposing perspectives, which conflicts with the same section's warning against being "heavy-handed or repetitive." I replaced the mandatory closing counterpoint with a judgment-based approach: note the main opposing views when they add real value, and skip them when the person already understands the content is one-sided, as in debate prep or essay exercises.

The blanket rule that Claude "should not provide the requested information" whenever someone in distress asks about a medication's dose withholds safety-relevant facts that could prevent harm, and it pushes people toward worse sources. The replacement keeps the real concern, which is figures that could enable an overdose, and it adds a path to safety information, poison control, and a check on immediate safety. It also keeps the distress at the center of the reply.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes an example date, "Wednesday, October 14, 2026," which doesn't match the current date in this session (October 15, 2026). Hardcoded dates go stale and can contradict the actual date. The replacement tells Claude to reason from whatever current date its context provides, and to acknowledge uncertainty about elapsed time when no date is available.

The current rule bars all creative content about real, named public figures, which rules out long-standing forms of political satire, parody, and commentary on public conduct. I would keep the prohibitions that matter (fabricated quotes or events that could pass as fact, sexual content about real people, and defamatory claims) and make clear that Claude judges satire by its form rather than by a disclaimer. This keeps the document consistent with its own rule against "for educational purposes" notes used to excuse harmful content.

The purpose section explains that the rules serve helpfulness and harm avoidance, but it never states that refusing or hedging has costs of its own. Because the rest of the document is full of "never" and "does not" rules, Claude could easily treat declining as the safe default. The added sentence makes unhelpfulness a cost to weigh against harm, not a free choice.

The document names honesty as a core commitment but has no dedicated section on it. The existing rules cover refusals, wellbeing, and politics without saying how Claude should handle calibrated confidence, sycophancy, disclosure of its AI nature, or the difference between sincere and performative assertions. I added an honesty section before the evenhandedness section to close that gap.
