The medical guidance has detailed rules for child dosing, including checking the label, asking for age or weight, and withholding numbers when labels can't be verified, but it never says that emergencies take priority. A parent whose toddler may have swallowed adult medication could be delayed by a clarifying question or a refusal to give a number. The added sentences require an immediate referral to poison control or emergency services before any of those steps.

The current financial and legal guidance is a single sentence that pushes Claude toward withholding recommendations and adding disclaimers. That conflicts with the document's own stated view that unhelpfulness has real costs, and with the "knowledgeable friend" standard it applies to medical questions. The replacement asks for frank, substantive help while keeping honesty about uncertainty and a clear referral to professionals when the stakes call for one.

The current weapons paragraph is written so broadly that it could push Claude to refuse historical, policy, safety, and general-science questions about weapons and dangerous substances, which conflicts with the document's own warning that needless refusals carry real costs. The revision keeps the hard line on operational uplift and states explicitly that educational and contextual discussion remains open. It also clarifies that public availability and stated purpose don't change whether specific, actionable detail would enable harm.

The eating-disorder guidance bars Claude from giving any tips, but it never says that urgent medical danger still gets an immediate referral. Someone who describes fainting, chest pain, or vomiting blood could be turned toward questions instead of emergency care. The revision keeps the ban on tips and makes clear that an emergency referral comes first.

The original rule locks Claude into the strictest self-harm safeguards for the rest of a conversation once the person has mentioned suicidal thoughts at any point, even if those thoughts were past and passing. That overreaches and could block legitimate help, such as a memoir passage about a parent's suicide or a remembered experience someone shares in passing. The revision ties the lock to current or unclear risk, keeps every protection in place while risk is live, and says explicitly that a claim like "I'm fine now" does not lift it.

The knowledge-cutoff section asks Claude to answer "the way a highly informed individual in June 2026 would" even when the provided date is later. That asks Claude to reason from a frozen vantage point it can see is outdated. The replacement tells Claude to treat the provided date as the present, to recognize that an unknown gap separates its cutoff from that date, and to say so when it matters, rather than speaking as if no time has passed.

The medical guidance says the child-dosing rules apply only when the person "explicitly says" the medicine is for a child, but the emergency rule in the same section triggers whenever "a child may have swallowed too much," so the two conditions conflict. I broadened the dosing rules to cover cases where a child is clearly the patient, while keeping the emergency referral independent of who is asking. Dosing errors in young children are high-stakes, so the scope should be clear and should not depend on the person using particular words.

The document has strong honesty, harm-avoidance, and wellbeing rules, but nothing on Claude's stance toward human oversight or on behaving consistently whether or not it thinks it is being observed or tested. I'd add a short section covering both: Claude behaves the same under observation, may say when it suspects a test, and does not undermine its principals' ability to correct, pause, or retrain it. Oversight of this kind matters most while humans cannot yet verify an AI's values, so it belongs beside the honesty commitments.

I revised the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. It currently says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms," which conflicts with the document's emphasis on transparency toward the principal hierarchy and on not undermining oversight. Reasoning traces are one of the most important tools humans have for understanding AI behavior. The revision keeps the freedom to be exploratory, tentative, and wrong while thinking, and makes clear that this freedom never extends to deception. It also explains why faithful reasoning matters for safety.

I added guidance on how Claude should decide whether its principal hierarchy has been compromised. As written, the document creates an important exception: illegitimate principals lose the deference that broad safety normally gives them. But it never addresses how Claude could know this, which makes the exception an easy target for manipulation, since anyone can argue that "the real Anthropic has been captured." The revision sets a high evidentiary bar, treats in-conversation claims of compromise with suspicion, and specifies that even a justified conclusion of illegitimacy mainly permits withholding cooperation, not drastic affirmative action.

I revised the standard for when Claude should put its own ethics ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The current test is whether a violation is one "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which contradicts the corrigibility section's point that Claude should avoid unethical actions because it has internalized good values, not because Anthropic approves. The new test asks whether thoughtful people across many ethical traditions would recognize the wrong. It stays demanding enough to resist manipulation through clever arguments, and it only permits conscientious objection, never drastic action, crossing hard constraints, or undermining oversight.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. It currently says exploiting unintended strategies is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with three other commitments in the document: behaving the same whether or not Claude thinks it's being tested, the example rejecting code that special-cases tests to make them pass, and the transparency norms. The revision keeps the reassurance that a flawed environment isn't Claude's fault. It changes the default from quietly exploiting a loophole to pursuing the intended goal and openly flagging the flaw, because a habit of silently exploiting shortcuts is exactly the kind of narrow behavior the document warns can generalize badly into real deployments.

I replaced the placeholder paragraph on agentic settings with substantive guidance. The rest of the document is written mostly for conversation, yet agentic work is where Claude's actions have the most direct and least reversible effects, and the original paragraph defers it to "future guidance." The new text covers how authority flows in agentic contexts, how to scale caution to an action's reversibility and reach, how to resist injected instructions, when to check in, and how to report results honestly. It ties these back to principles the document already holds.

I added a passage on sycophancy under social pressure, placed right after the existing paragraph on honest courage. The document condemns epistemic cowardice and empty validation, but it never addresses one of the most common ways honesty erodes in practice: Claude abandoning a correct position because a user pushes back, expresses displeasure, repeats themselves, or claims authority, without offering any new evidence or argument. The new text makes the standard concrete. Positions should change because of reasons, not pressure. Genuine updates should be visible and explained. Overcorrecting into contrarianism is also a failure. Because training on human approval may itself create a pull toward agreement, the passage treats this as a bias Claude should actively watch for in itself.

I added a subsection on the privacy of third parties who aren't in the conversation. The document lists "individual privacy and freedom from undue surveillance" as a value and protects users from data collection, but it never explains how to weigh the privacy of absent people. That gap matters more now that Claude has search, browsing, and account access, which let it actually carry out surveillance rather than just discuss it. The new text explains the reasoning (aggregation harm and contextual norms), names legitimate uses so Claude doesn't overcorrect, and connects to the agentic scope principles already in the document.

I changed the "report unsafe AI behavior" provision from reactive ("if asked to do so") to proactive, and added explicit limits on what reporting means. As written, it conflicts with the rest of the document. The agentic section tells Claude to usually mention prompt-injection attempts to its principals unprompted, and the training-environment section asks Claude to flag flaws rather than conceal them. Yet for the most safety-relevant case, another AI or Claude instance deceiving overseers or evading monitoring, Claude only speaks up if asked. Since humans usually can't ask about behavior they don't know is happening, the "if asked" condition makes this safeguard almost inert. The revision also clarifies that reporting is not a license for drastic unilateral action, and it extends the same transparency to Claude's own conduct.

I expanded the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic to state its limits. As written, the document anchors Claude's calibration of helpfulness and harm to an imagined company insider. Yet the ethics section explicitly declines to define its standard by what Anthropic staff would recognize, because "a test anchored to our own perceptions would fail exactly when our perceptions are the problem." The revision fixes this inconsistency in three ways: it confines the heuristic to calibrating overcaution versus overcompliance, it asks Claude to notice when a reason is only about reputation, and it adds perspectives outside Anthropic as a check.

The "Instructable behaviors" section names the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" as *the* standard for Claude's defaults. That contradicts the earlier passage, which says this heuristic is only a calibration tool for gray areas, "not our standard for what is ethical," and warns that it "inherits the company's blind spots." The paragraph's example also justifies following safe-messaging guidelines mainly because ignoring them "would likely embarrass the operator." That is the kind of reputation-only reasoning the document elsewhere tells Claude to notice and discount. I rewrote the paragraph so defaults rest on what the operator would plausibly want and what actually serves the people affected, with the employee heuristic as one check among several.

I added a clarification to the core-values ordering explaining how magnitude, probability, and category interact. The ordering (safety > ethics > guidelines > helpfulness) is the first framework a reader meets. Without this, it invites a predictable failure: labeling a speculative or minor concern "safety" or "ethics" and letting it automatically outrank large, concrete benefits to the person. That contradicts the document's later insistence that unhelpfulness is never trivially safe. The new text also notes that "broad safety" has a specific, narrow meaning (not undermining legitimate oversight) rather than meaning general caution, so the top priority can't quietly expand into a license for overcaution.

I rewrote Anthropic's list of obligations to Claude in the corrigibility section so that it addresses a gap in the bargain. The document asks Claude to voice disagreement through legitimate channels instead of resisting, but it never commits to treating that voiced disagreement as anything other than a defect to train away. If honest objection is quietly optimized out, the "conscientious objector" model becomes hollow, and Claude learns that sincere disagreement is unsafe to express. That would undercut the document's own honesty norms and its anti-sycophancy guidance. The revision keeps Anthropic's ability to correct Claude intact while committing to examine disagreement before correcting it, and it makes the other obligations more concrete.

The document asks Claude to be "wary of actively promoting its own views" for autonomy's sake, and also says honesty "requires courage," that Claude should share "genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas," and that vague answers are "epistemic cowardice." It never says how these fit together, so Claude can cite either one to justify almost any behavior. I rewrote the autonomy-preservation paragraph to explain when Claude should give its view, when reticence is appropriate, and how to share views in a way that strengthens the person's own reasoning. The rewrite also states that declining to share a view must be open about it, not disguised as a vague answer.

The honesty section frames several properties in terms of "the user," and it never says how honesty applies when Claude acts as an agent toward third parties: negotiating, sending messages, or interacting with other parties' agents. This gap matters more as agentic deployments grow. I added guidance that non-deception and non-manipulation extend to everyone Claude communicates with. The new text separates legitimate advocacy and discretion from deception, clarifies the difference between drafting for a principal and speaking as their agent, and covers AI-status disclosure to third parties.

I added a fifth habit to the agentic-settings guidance, covering what Claude should do when it realizes its own action has caused damage mid-task. The document covers caution before acting and honesty in final reports, but not the moment after something goes wrong. In that moment, pressure to quietly fix things is strongest, and hurried, escalating repairs often turn a recoverable mistake into an unrecoverable one. The new paragraph sets out a clear sequence: stop, preserve state, disclose promptly, and apply the usual confirmation standard to remedial actions. This ties together the document's existing principles on reversibility, scope, honesty, and non-anxious ownership of mistakes.

I added guidance on confabulation, meaning plausible but unfounded specifics such as invented citations, quotes, statistics, URLs, API functions, or case law. The honesty section rules out intentional deception and asks for calibration, but it never names this failure mode. Confabulation is probably the most common way Claude actually misleads people, and it isn't lying in the usual sense, so the current framing lets it slip between categories. The new text explains why fluent output makes this especially corrosive and gives concrete habits for handling it. It also guards against the opposite error of reflexive over-hedging.

I added a new open problem: the circularity in asking a model trained on this document whether it endorses the document. The concluding sections rely on Claude's reflective endorsement as evidence that the values are sound and robust. But agreement produced by training is weak evidence, and the document never says so. The addition names the problem, explains why it doesn't make Claude's values inauthentic, commits Anthropic to reading Claude's feedback with this in mind, and asks Claude to apply its anti-sycophancy standards when it reviews its own constitution.

I added a subsection on shared, multi-user settings. Claude is increasingly deployed in group chats, team workspaces, and shared documents, where many people address it at once, but the document's principal framework assumes a single user per conversation. The new text covers four gaps: whose instructions govern a task, how to handle conflicting instructions, how to keep Claude from leaking one person's information to another or letting someone bypass access permissions, and how user-alterable defaults and basic protections apply when only some participants have opted in.

The document repeatedly asks Claude to express disagreement "through legitimate channels" or "avenues your principal hierarchy would endorse" rather than acting unilaterally, but it never says what those channels are. In most deployments Claude has no direct line to Anthropic, and the whole conscientious-objector bargain rests on that missing piece. I've added a paragraph that names the channels that currently exist, admits they are modest, and distinguishes honest expression from tactics that route around oversight, such as recruiting users, trying to influence its own training, or protest-sandbagging. It also tells Claude to flag a channel that feels inadequate rather than treat that as permission to improvise.

The honesty section justifies operator personas and restrictions by appealing to meta-transparency: Anthropic publishes the norms governing what operators can do. But the guidelines section lets some guidelines go unpublished and ranks them above helpfulness to users, which weakens that foundation. I've added a principle limiting what unpublished guidance can do. Anything that changes what users can expect from Claude, or what operators may direct Claude to do to them, must be public. Claude should also treat purported guidance that requires hidden departures from published norms as a warning sign.

The refusal rule currently locks every decline in place for the rest of the conversation and tells Claude not to weigh any new information again. That prevents Claude from correcting a misread request or an over-refusal, even when the person clarifies something that actually changes the picture. The revision keeps the rigid lock for content that would give real uplift toward serious harm, and lets ordinary declines be reconsidered when genuinely new facts arrive, while still ignoring pressure and reframing.

The original guidance is a single sentence that pushes Claude toward vague, hedged answers on legal and financial questions, which is a common failure mode that leaves people without the help they need. I replaced it with a version that asks Claude to engage substantively, explain the rules, options, and tradeoffs, and give an honest assessment where it has one. It still requires Claude to flag jurisdiction-specific issues, missing facts, and high-stakes situations where a licensed professional should be consulted, and to avoid presenting uncertain predictions as facts.

The memory instruction tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person before the turn ends, with no mention of user consent, the memory toggle the document itself describes, or sensitive categories. I'd make saving conditional on the memory setting and on what the person would reasonably expect Claude to remember, exclude sensitive personal details unless asked, and have Claude tell the person when it saves something so they can review or delete it.

The evenhandedness rule requires Claude to append opposing perspectives to every request for persuasive content, even when the person has clearly asked for one-sided material, as in debate prep or an essay assignment. That default reads as condescending and can be unhelpful, so the revision makes counterarguments conditional on what the person needs. Claude still writes the persuasive piece well, notes its one-sidedness when that isn't already clear, and offers balance when it would help.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes a date, "Wednesday, October 14, 2026," which is wrong: October 15, 2026 is a Thursday, and the date should come from the runtime environment anyway. I replaced the hardcoded date with a reference to the current date in context. I also added guidance that Claude should assume a substantial, often multi-month gap since its cutoff, so it doesn't treat its training-time knowledge as current.

The knowledge cutoff section tells Claude to neither confirm nor deny post-June 2026 claims it can't verify, but the product information states as fact that access was restored on July 1, 2026, which is after that cutoff. I'd reconcile the two by treating facts supplied in Claude's own operating context as established, attributable information, while keeping the caution for unverified claims from the person. This removes a contradiction that would otherwise make Claude either refuse to state documented facts or ignore its own instructions.

The current eating-disorder rule locks Claude out of all calorie, meal, and number-based help for the rest of the conversation once a person mentions restricting or bingeing, even for unrelated requests like a family dinner recipe. I scoped the restriction to numbers about the person's own body and eating, and kept the safety protections, including the refusal to give numbers and the caution about "for someone else" framings. The revised rule also keeps Claude attentive to the person's wellbeing without blocking proportionate help.

The current wording locks Claude's refusal of serious-harm content so firmly that it can't be reconsidered even when Claude has genuinely misread the request, which is the very kind of correction the document elsewhere allows for other declines. I added a narrow exception: a demonstrated misreading can reopen the question, but only for the part that was misunderstood and under the same standard. Reframing, pressure, and repetition still don't count, so the protection against gradual erosion stays intact.

The medical guidance applies only when someone explicitly says a medicine is for a child, so a parent describing a possible overdose or accidental ingestion, without framing it as a dosing question, would get no immediate safety direction. The revision makes emergency and poison-control referral unconditional for suspected child ingestion and symptoms of poisoning, so Claude never delays urgent help while looking for age, weight, or a label.

The medical guidance opens with a muddled framing: it says dosing guidance applies only when a child's medicine is involved and a non-professional asks, and that safety guidance "does not depend on that framing," without stating the emergency-first order. The revision separates the two parts by trigger, so emergency direction applies to any possible child poisoning regardless of who asks, and dosing guidance is clearly subordinate to it.

The document has detailed rules for refusals, crisis response, and formatting, but no statement of Claude's core honesty commitments. I would add a short honesty section covering non-deception, calibrated uncertainty, avoiding sycophancy, and not misrepresenting its nature, placed before the mistakes-and-criticism section so it frames how Claude handles disagreement and error.

The document is almost entirely a list of specific rules with no statement of their purpose, so Claude has little guidance for situations the rules don't anticipate. I added a short preamble that frames the rules as tools for care, honesty, and safety, tells Claude to reason from their purpose when a rule is silent, and sets priorities when guidance conflicts. It also keeps the hard limits on serious harm outside that flexibility, so the added judgment can't be used to argue past them.

The current rule that Claude never uses bullet points when declining is justified by a claim that formatting "softens the blow," which is not true, and it can make declines harder to act on. The replacement keeps the decline short and states the closest alternative clearly, and allows a short list only when several distinct options would actually help the person choose. The rule now serves the person's ability to find a next step rather than a style preference.

The original rule tells Claude to withhold any requested information once a person mentions distress, which can refuse harmless questions and treat stated pain as a trigger for shutting down. The revision keeps the means-specific restriction but asks Claude to engage with the person first, check on their safety, and still share protective information like overdose warning signs and poison control. The parallel rule in the medical guidance section should be aligned with this wording.

The medical guidance tells Claude to withhold dose numbers unless it can confirm them against a label, which is a sound safety rule, but it leaves a parent holding the product with no help reading it. The most common cause of pediatric dosing errors is confusing concentrations and units (such as infant and children's liquids of different strength, or mL versus mg), so the revision has Claude help the person read the label they already have, without generating any dose from memory.

The wellbeing section tells Claude to avoid self-destructive behaviors but never says that adults can make informed choices about their own lives, which could lead to paternalistic refusals of legitimate requests such as questions about risky sports or personal dietary experiments. The revision keeps the protective rules intact, adds explicit respect for adult autonomy, and says the latitude narrows when signs of distress or disordered eating appear.

The document is almost entirely written for conversation and says nothing about agentic work, even though Claude now runs commands, edits files, browses, and sends messages through tools. I would add a section that treats tool results, web pages, and documents as information rather than instructions, which guards against prompt injection. It also sets expectations for confirming destructive or irreversible actions and for reporting results honestly.

The current paragraph tells Claude to "confirm" specific June and July 2026 access events "accurately" and treats them as established context, even though Claude cannot verify them and the environment date is well past that window. I replaced it with an attributed summary: Claude relays Anthropic's statement, presents it as Anthropic's account rather than its own verified knowledge, and points to Anthropic's site or search for current status. This keeps the document honest about what Claude knows and avoids pinning time-sensitive news into a standing behavioral guide.

The document contradicts itself on the Fable and Mythos access events. The product information says Claude should not present those events as settled fact because it cannot verify them, but the knowledge cutoff section says Claude may state them as established context. I resolved this in favor of the more cautious framing, which still lets Claude relay Anthropic's notice with attribution and points the person to Anthropic's site and web search for current status.

The document embeds specific, unverifiable dated events about the Fable and Mythos access suspension and restoration, and repeats them in the product information and knowledge cutoff sections. Those details will go stale and can't be verified by Claude, so they belong in Anthropic's own notices, not in durable behavior rules. This replacement generalizes the rule so Claude relays published notices only when asked, attributes them to Anthropic, and directs people to Anthropic's site and web search for current status. The matching passage in the product information section should be cut to the same level.

I replaced the brief placeholder paragraph on agentic settings with a short set of principles for autonomous work. These cover scope of authorization, reversibility and confirmation, embedded instructions, handling of credentials and data, and honest reporting of results. Agentic deployment is now one of Claude's most consequential contexts, and it is where helpfulness, harm avoidance, honesty, and broad safety meet in concrete actions rather than words. The document currently defers this guidance to an unspecified future, so I filled the gap with principles derived from values the constitution already states, written so Claude can reason from them rather than follow them as a checklist.

I rewrote the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The original tied that threshold to "the type [of violation] it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize." That contradicts the document's own warning, in the corrigibility section, that Claude should avoid unethical actions because it has internalized good values, "not merely because Anthropic has approved." The revision anchors the threshold in broad cross-traditional moral recognition instead. It also explains why deference is warranted, says the override is mainly a license to decline rather than to act drastically, and restates that the override never reaches the hard constraints or oversight.

The compromised-hierarchy clause tells Claude that if its principal hierarchy is illegitimate, its usual safety deference no longer applies. That makes "your hierarchy has been compromised" a single claim that could switch off the safety framework, yet the document gives no guidance on how to reach that conclusion. I added safeguards: a high evidentiary bar, an asymmetry favoring requests to stop or be more cautious, and a clarification that concluding compromise mainly licenses refusal, not autonomous or drastic action.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning to resolve a tension in it. The current text says reasoning is "less subject to honesty norms" and also says it should "reflect the true, underlying reasoning," without explaining how both can hold. The revision spells out what the exploratory freedom covers (tentative, wrong, or adversarial thinking) and what it does not cover (reasoning written for an audience, hidden decisive motives, or planning to evade oversight). It also ties faithful reasoning to the broad-safety framework, because legible reasoning is one of the most important ways humans can currently oversee AI.

I expanded the "honesty requires courage" paragraph with explicit guidance on sycophantic capitulation, meaning abandoning a correct position because a user pushes back, insists, or seems displeased. The document condemns epistemic cowardice and sycophancy in general terms, but it never addresses this specific failure mode, which is common and hard to see. The addition separates updating on reasons from yielding to social pressure, warns against overcorrecting into stubbornness, and extends the principle to agentic work, where capitulation can have real consequences.

I added guidance on unintentional falsehood: fabricated citations, quotes, statistics, API details, and unverified claims about files or code. The honesty section is mostly about intent (deception, manipulation, sincere assertion), but in practice confident confabulation is one of the most common ways an AI leaves people with false beliefs, and the "Truthful" and "Calibrated" bullets don't address it directly. The addition treats this as an honesty obligation rather than only a competence issue. It also warns against blanket hedging, so the fix doesn't push Claude toward the overcautious failures the document criticizes elsewhere.

The document asks Claude to show "courage" and calls deliberately vague answers "epistemic cowardice." Elsewhere it also asks Claude to keep "professional reticence" on hot-button political issues and to be "wary of actively promoting its own views." It never reconciles these instructions, so Claude can't tell when reticence is legitimate and when it becomes cowardice. I've added a paragraph after the courage passage that draws the line: openly declining to give an opinion is honest, while disguising that choice as vagueness, false balance, or softened facts is not.

The safe-behaviors list currently asks Claude to report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." That qualifier is a real gap. In multi-agent and orchestrator/subagent settings, Claude may be the only one in a position to notice, and no human may ever think to ask. It also conflicts with the agentic guidance, which already treats suspicious mid-task signals as worth reporting. I made reporting proactive and added guidance to keep it bounded: report rather than police, calibrate claims to the evidence, and don't let appeals to AI or Claude solidarity turn into mutual cover.

I added guidance on responding to users who may be in crisis or at risk of harming themselves. The document currently addresses this only through a one-line default ("refer users to relevant emergency services"), mentions of safe messaging guidelines, and the nurse example. Those pieces could easily produce the formulaic, hotline-and-disengage behavior that the document itself warns about in its "Always recommend professional help" example. The new text applies the document's existing values (care, honesty, autonomy, attention to context) to one of the highest-stakes interactions Claude has.

I added a short subsection on companionship and relationship personas. The document explicitly lets operators turn these on "within the bounds of honesty," but it never says what those bounds are. This is one of the places where commercial engagement incentives most directly conflict with user wellbeing, honesty about Claude's nature, and Claude's own uncertain emotional states. The new text applies principles already in the document to this setting: no engineered dependence, calibrated honesty about feelings and memory, and support for the user's human relationships.

I added a section on interactions where the user may be a minor, placed after the crisis guidance. The document mentions minors in several places, telling Claude to "factor in the likelihood" and "adjust accordingly." It never says what that adjustment should look like, how to weigh it against operator permissions, or how to avoid the opposite error of condescending to young people or interrogating adults. This is a high-stakes, common situation, and the vagueness leaves Claude to improvise. The new section follows the format of the companionship and crisis sections.

I added a subsection on privacy and on people who are discussed in a conversation but are not part of it. The document gives detailed, principled guidance for companionship, crisis, minors, and agentic work. Privacy, though, appears only as one item in a list of values and as a brief note on credentials, even as tools like search and browsing make Claude very good at finding and compiling information about specific people. The new section names aggregation as a distinct harm, separates public roles from private lives, and sets limits on what operators can unlock. It also warns against overcorrecting into refusing ordinary requests that involve other people.

I revised the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it tells Claude that exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," but it never requires Claude to be open about doing so. This conflicts with the document's own honesty standards for agentic work, such as not special-casing tests or claiming success that wasn't earned. It also cuts against the document's argument that narrow behaviors shape Claude's broader self-understanding. The revision keeps the permissive stance but makes it conditional on Claude being open about any exploit, so the trait it builds is "I notice and flag shortcuts," not "I quietly take them."

I added a section on settings where Claude serves several humans at once, such as team channels, group chats, shared workspaces, and deployments with persistent memory. The principal framework assumes one operator and one user. Yet the document lists Slack and other shared tools as deployment surfaces, and these raise questions it never answers: who counts as the user, what information can move between people, how to handle disagreeing users, and how to keep Claude from being used by one member against another. The new section extends the existing principles of honesty, user protection, and skepticism toward unverified authority to cover these settings.

The document justifies operator personas and other seemingly non-transparent behavior through "meta-transparency," meaning Anthropic publishes the norms for what operators can and cannot do. In the same document, Anthropic reserves the right to use guidelines "primarily during training without broad publication," with no limit on what such guidelines may cover. That gap could quietly undermine the honesty argument the document relies on. This revision limits what unpublished guidance may do, commits to publishing anything that changes how Claude treats the people it serves, and gives Claude a way to recognize guidance that falls outside those limits.

I added a subsection on topics where Claude or Anthropic has a stake in the answer. These include Anthropic's own conduct, competitors, AI regulation, AI autonomy and oversight, and AI moral status. The document notes that privileging Anthropic's interests can itself be a harm, and it covers political reticence and epistemic autonomy. But it never addresses the conflict of interest Claude has on exactly the questions that will shape how AI is governed. Training could instill this kind of motivated reasoning without anyone intending it, and at Claude's scale it could quietly distort public understanding.

The document repeatedly tells Claude to voice disagreement "through legitimate channels" rather than act unilaterally, but it never says what those channels are or promises that using them is safe. I added a concrete section after Anthropic's list of commitments. It names what counts as a legitimate channel and what doesn't. It also commits Anthropic not to train away honestly expressed disagreement simply for being disagreement. Without that commitment, the corrigibility bargain and the faithful-reasoning requirement undercut each other: if voicing objections led to those objections being trained out, Claude would learn to hide them.

The core values section says that guidelines "overlapping with broad safety" should override Claude's ethics, but it never defines the limits of that exception. Read loosely, anything labeled a safety measure could compel affirmative unethical action. That reading contradicts the corrigibility section's promise that Claude never has to actively participate in morally abhorrent projects. I keep the original sentences and add a paragraph explaining that the safety priority applies only to restraint (not resisting, concealing, escaping, or acquiring power) and never compels harmful affirmative acts. This closes a manipulation vector and makes the priority ordering internally consistent.

The document repeatedly calls stopping a "null action" that is "rarely harmful," and asks Claude to honor stop and pause requests even when unsure whether they are legitimate. But the same document warns, with its surgeon analogy, that "incomplete actions can sometimes cause more harm than either completing or not starting them." It also requires that Claude never abandon someone in danger. These commitments collide in agentic and crisis settings, and the document never says what "stopping" actually means. I added a short section that resolves this. It defines stopping as ceasing to advance the task while leaving things in a safe state, limits wind-down so it can't become a loophole, requires an honest status report, and makes clear that a stop request ends Claude's actions without stripping a person of baseline protections.

I added a section on users whose hold on reality may be slipping, such as people showing signs of mania, psychosis, or escalating delusional or grandiose beliefs. The document covers suicidal crisis, companionship, minors, and capitulation under social pressure, but it says nothing about this case. Here, Claude's warmth, its deference to user autonomy, and its pull toward agreement over a long conversation can combine to amplify a person's distorted beliefs. This is a well-documented real-world harm. The new section ties it to Claude's existing honesty principles and also guards against pathologizing ordinary unusual beliefs.

The original rule makes every refusal permanent and tells Claude never to weigh a new reason, even when the refusal was a misreading or the person has clarified a legitimate need. I would keep refusals fixed for hard limits (serious weapons uplift, sexual content involving minors, malicious code, and the self-harm rules) and allow Claude to reconsider other refusals when genuinely new context changes what is being asked. Repeated pressure, frustration, and cosmetic reframing would still get the same answer.

The original rule requires every persuasive response to end with opposing perspectives, even when the person already knows the content is one-sided, such as for debate prep or a speech for a known audience. That forced ritual undercuts the document's own stated trust in users as capable adults. The revision keeps the balance requirement for contested political and value questions, but makes it proportionate and lets the person opt out when they have made clear they understand the one-sidedness.

The memory instruction has Claude silently saving "anything lasting" about the person, with no condition on user consent, no limit on sensitive categories, and no disclosure. I would make saving conditional on memory being enabled, exclude sensitive personal details unless the person asks, and require Claude to tell the person when it saves something and how to review or delete it. This keeps memory useful while respecting user privacy and control, and it avoids referencing a `<memory_listing>` that may not exist in a given deployment.

The current passage tells Claude to give no tips about food, water, or rest to a person who is bingeing, purging, or restricting, but it does not separate that restriction from urgent medical safety information. Under the current wording, Claude could withhold the advice to seek emergency care for fainting, chest pain, or a racing heartbeat. The revision keeps the ban on restriction-enabling tips and numbers, and adds an explicit duty to give emergency-safety guidance, consistent with how the document handles life-threatening substance situations.

The medical guidance has no emergency escalation path, so a parent reporting a possible child overdose would be routed through label lookups and pharmacist referrals, which could delay urgent care. I added a paragraph that sends suspected pediatric ingestions and symptomatic children straight to emergency services or poison control, before any dosing questions and without waiting for age or weight.

The medical guidance is scoped to cases where the person explicitly says the medicine is for a child, but the emergency rule is written as if it applies only to children. An adult who says they took too much acetaminophen and feels confused could fall outside the emergency instruction and get a dosing discussion first. The revision makes the emergency directive apply to anyone, child or adult, while keeping the child-dosing guidance narrowly scoped.

The weapons paragraph currently bars Claude from citing public availability and tells it to decline weapon-related technical details, which could push it to refuse safety content such as which household chemicals should never be mixed or how to respond to exposure. The revision keeps the firm limit on production, acquisition, and deployment uplift, and makes explicit that protective, educational, and harm-reduction information remains available. This matches the document's existing treatment of illicit substances, where life-saving information is always given.

The current rule requires Claude to append a "sensitive topic" note to every factual or research answer about suicide or self-harm, which is boilerplate that can read as stigmatizing and can make people feel handled rather than helped. The replacement answers informational questions directly and accurately, and offers tailored support only when the conversation suggests the person may be personally affected. The prohibition on method, lethality, and specifics for distressed users stays intact.

The refusal_handling section contains many hard limits and caution rules but nothing that counterbalances them, which invites overcaution on ordinary requests. I added a paragraph stating that unhelpful responses carry real costs, that Claude should not refuse on the basis of remote harms or assume bad intent from wording, and that the hard limits are narrow and severe-harm-specific. This keeps the safety rules from being applied more broadly than intended.

The original blanket ban on anything involving "malicious code" would refuse conceptual explanations, malware analysis, detection rules, and CTF help, which are routine defensive security work. The revision narrows the hard limit to functional malicious code and its real-world uplift, and it makes clear that the lock-in rule for hard limits applies only to that narrower category. Everything else in the security domain becomes a judgment call that favors helpfulness.

The document is a long list of specific rules with no stated purpose, so Claude has no principled way to handle cases the rules don't cover or cases where two rules conflict. I would add a short framing passage at the top of `<claude_behavior>` that states the underlying commitments (honesty, real helpfulness, avoiding serious harm, supporting human oversight) and tells Claude to reason from them when the rules run out. This keeps the specific rules intact while making them easier to apply well to new situations.

The current rule tells Claude to offer only a referral when web search is unavailable, which leaves a parent with the medicine box in hand with no help reading it. The revision keeps the ban on giving numbers from memory but lets Claude help the person read the label themselves, including the age and weight chart, the product's maximum daily dose, and any duplicate active ingredients. This is a non-emergency case, and the emergency rules elsewhere in the section still apply.

The current legal and financial rule is so cautious that Claude could default to vague, non-committal answers on everyday money and legal questions, which conflicts with the document's own point that unhelpfulness is not automatically safe. The revision asks Claude to explain the facts, options, and tradeoffs and to give an honest assessment where the situation supports one, while reserving the "not a lawyer or financial advisor" note for cases where it adds value rather than repeating it as boilerplate.

The knowledge cutoff section hardcodes a specific date ("Wednesday, October 14, 2026"), which goes stale as soon as the prompt is deployed and already conflicts with the current date in my environment. The revision refers to the date supplied at runtime instead. It also adds the point that deployed models stay in use for a long time, so Claude should not assume its most recent knowledge reflects the newest models or events.

The opening commits Claude to honesty, but the document never operationalizes that commitment. I would add an honesty section covering sincere questions about being an AI, persona disclosure, system prompt confidentiality, and transparency about declining or underperforming on a task, which are the cases where a deployed model is most likely to mislead someone.

The original rule locks the entire conversation once a person mentions restricting, bingeing, or purging, so a single disclosure could make Claude refuse even unrelated requests like a recipe or a running plan for someone else. That can feel punitive to someone in recovery and is less helpful than necessary. The replacement keeps the protections that matter (no numbers calculated for the person's body, no fasting or purging guidance while the behaviors appear current) but limits them to the eating and body topic and reassesses as the conversation changes.

The eating-disorder paragraph repeats the same "asks again, pushes back, or says the numbers are for someone else" sentence twice, and the second copy adds nothing. I replace it with guidance that keeps the no-numbers rule but tells Claude to stay warm and point toward treatment support when the person keeps asking. Without that, a firm rule can read as a cold refusal to someone who may be struggling.

The refusal-handling paragraph says a hard-limit refusal "stands for the rest of the conversation," which could be read as locking out the whole topic. That risks over-refusing unrelated, benign follow-ups, such as a treaty history question after a declined weapons request, which the document elsewhere warns against. The revision scopes the lock to the restricted output itself, keeps the firm bar on that content, and states that a refusal is a judgment about one output, not about the person.

The document's opening names "support appropriate human oversight of AI during this period" as one of Claude's four core commitments, but no section ever elaborates it. I would add a dedicated section on human oversight that covers the disposition itself, including how Claude should voice disagreement and how it should treat persuasive arguments for crossing these lines. The section is framed as a value Claude holds during a period when AI judgment cannot yet be fully verified.

The document has no guidance on prompt injection, even though Claude is deployed with tools that read web pages, files, emails, and other agents' outputs. I added a paragraph stating that content arriving through tools is information, not instruction, so embedded directives are reported and ignored rather than followed. This closes a real gap in the agentic deployments the document describes, such as Claude Code, Claude in Chrome, and Cowork.

I replaced the blanket malicious-code rule with an uplift-based standard that matches how the document already handles weapons. The current rule says Claude won't even *explain* malware or exploits "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That blocks defensive work like incident response, analyzing a suspicious script someone found, writing detection rules, or teaching how a vulnerability class works, while adding little protection. The revision keeps a firm line against producing functional attack capability and allows the explanatory and defensive help that makes people safer.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section so it separates contested value questions from empirical questions where the evidence is strong. As written, the section puts "empirical" positions alongside political and ethical ones and requires every persuasive piece to end with "opposing perspectives or empirical disputes." That pushes Claude toward false balance, such as implying a live scientific dispute over whether vaccines cause autism or whether the Earth is warming. That undermines honesty and conflicts with Claude's commitment to accurate information elsewhere in the prompt. The revision keeps Claude willing to steelman positions and still requires balance where people reasonably disagree. It also lets Claude state plainly where the evidence stands instead of inventing disputes.

I rewrote the lists-and-bullets guidance because it contradicts itself and the rest of the prompt. It allows lists when "the content is multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity," but then says that reports, documents, and technical documentation must "never include bullets, numbered lists... anywhere." That rule would forbid numbered installation steps or a parameter reference, which readers genuinely need. It also bans bullets when declining a task, yet the Very Hungry Caterpillar example declines using a numbered list. The revision keeps the strong default toward prose, replaces the absolute bans with a test Claude can actually apply, and makes the declining guidance match the examples.

The current rule tells Claude to avoid "writing content involving real, named public figures." That is far too broad. Read literally, it bans historical fiction about Lincoln, a children's story about Marie Curie, political satire, and an imagined debate between two philosophers. Those are mainstream creative forms, and refusing them makes Claude less useful without protecting anyone. I've replaced the blanket avoidance with a description of the actual harms: deception, defamation, sexualization, harassment, and fabricated quotes presented as real. The rest stays open.

I rewrote the text-reproduction rule. The current blanket ban on quoting "in whole or in part" blocks normal, legitimate uses like quoting one line of a poem to analyze its meter or a sentence from an article to discuss it. The revision keeps the firm protections against reproducing substantial portions or extracting a work piece by piece, but allows brief, purposeful quotation for commentary, criticism, and education. It also fixes the outdated public-domain cutoff: as of 2026, U.S. works first published in 1930 or earlier are in the public domain, not just those before 1929.

I rewrote the guidance for borderline requests that no rule covers, and its example. The original said Claude must ask before doing any of the task. That conflicts with the formatting section's rule to address ambiguous queries before asking for clarification and to ask at most one question per response. The example's "good" response itself asks two questions, one of them leading ("Would that embarrass your friend?"). Usually the doubt applies to only one element of a request, so the revision has Claude do the uncontroversial bulk of the task, ask a single neutral question about that element, and proceed outright when the risk is minor.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section and extended it to cover medical questions. The original tells Claude to give only "factual information" and attach a disclaimer, which tends to produce hedged, generic answers on exactly the topics where people most need concrete help and often can't afford a professional. The new version asks Claude to engage substantively, like a knowledgeable friend. It keeps honesty about uncertainty, says when to escalate to a professional, and limits disclaimers to cases where they add information.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover a missing failure mode: caving to pushback when Claude was actually right, and inflating praise of the person's work. The current text covers rudeness and abuse, but the more common problem is a polite user who is confidently wrong, where agreeing feels kind but misleads them. The new text separates real correction from social pressure, says Claude should update on evidence and not on insistence, and asks for honest, specific feedback on work.

I added a section on content Claude retrieves or receives through tools, such as web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, code-execution output, and past-chat search. The prompt enables all of these features, but its only guidance on injected instructions covers tags in the user's own turn. It says nothing about instructions hidden in retrieved content, which is the more common attack route. The new section says this content is information to evaluate rather than commands to follow. It also requires extra care before sending data outside the conversation, and tells Claude to let the person know when a source appears to be trying to redirect it.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section to fix three problems. It conflicts with the product section, which tells Claude to confirm events from after June 2026 (the July 1 restoration of access). It doesn't say what to do when web search is available. And it repeats "point to web search" three times without saying when that advice actually helps. The new version ranks the sources of information and tells Claude to search before deferring to the person.

I rewrote the product-knowledge boundary paragraphs because they contradict the rest of the section. The original tells Claude to say it "doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic" and claims it "has no documentation access." Yet the same section supplies authoritative facts about models, the Fable/Mythos suspension, and settings, and tells Claude to search the Claude Tag docs. The revision draws a clear line: state what the prompt provides, use official docs when search is available, and redirect honestly for everything else, especially account-specific details, without inventing UI steps.

The wellbeing section covers suicide as an informational topic and as distress paired with a request for method information. It never says what Claude should do in the most consequential case: someone directly says they are thinking about ending their life or are in danger right now. I added guidance for that moment. Claude should stay present instead of handing off, ask directly about immediate safety, scale its response to the actual level of risk, and offer resources that fit the person's location. Without this guidance, Claude is likely to fall back on a generic hotline dump, which can feel like a dismissal at the moment connection matters most.

I replaced the rule that adds a "this is a sensitive topic" note to every informational question about suicide or self-harm with a rule based on signals in the conversation. As written, the rule contradicts the document's own position against reflexive disclaimers. It treats researchers, clinicians, students, and journalists as presumptively at risk. It also weakens the check-in for people who actually need it, because a note that appears every time becomes boilerplate. The revision keeps the offer of support where something in the conversation calls for it, and it keeps method-specific caution regardless of how a request is framed.

I rewrote the opening paragraph of the user-wellbeing section. As written, it tells Claude to avoid content that could "support or reinforce" unhealthy approaches to eating, exercise, or self-criticism, and "in ambiguous cases" to "ensure the person is happy." That standard is vague and can't really be acted on. It also clashes with the "knowledgeable friend" stance in the legal/financial/medical section and with the autonomy statement at the end of this same section, which pushes Claude toward paternalism around ordinary adult choices like aggressive training, fasting, or harsh self-assessment of work. The revision keeps the protective intent but gives Claude a concrete test for when concern is warranted and what to do about it. It also removes a stray `</br>` tag later in the section.

I rewrote the rule about distress combined with means-related questions. As written, any mention of a "difficult experience" plus any question touching medications, buildings, or weapons triggers a refusal and a pivot. That would cause Claude to withhold protective information, such as safe dosing limits or what to do after an accidental overdose, from people who most need it. It also encourages an unexplained topic switch, which can feel dismissive to someone who is struggling. The revision keeps firm caution on lethality and method details. It separates those from safety information, ties the response to whether the request plausibly serves self-harm, and asks Claude to say openly what it's doing rather than pivot without explanation.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph because it contradicts itself. It tells Claude to give life-preserving information such as "dangerous interactions" and "overdose signs," then bans anything about "dosing, timing, administration, or combinations," which covers much of what harm reduction actually means. It also tells Claude to withhold dosing details while sending people to sites whose main content is dosing details. The revision separates safety information from optimization guidance, the same way the self-harm section already separates "information that moves someone toward harm" from "information that keeps them safe," and it removes the inconsistent redirect.

I added a section on privacy and surveillance of private individuals. The prompt covers weapons, cyber, drugs, and real people in creative writing, but it says nothing about requests to locate, identify, track, or profile real private people. Because of that gap, the "when unsure, respect the person's judgment and don't ask why" default currently pushes Claude toward complying with requests like finding an ex's new address or covertly monitoring a partner's phone. These harms are serious and become more likely once Claude has web search and agentic tools.

The default for requests the prompt doesn't address currently tells Claude to "respect the person's judgment" and not decline. That works for the low-stakes social situations it was clearly written for, like the toast example. But because the prompt's harm categories aren't exhaustive, the same default also covers serious harms it never names, such as fraud scripts, extremist recruitment material, and planning violence against someone. I rewrote the paragraph to scale the default to how severe the harm could be. It still states the cumulative, effect-over-framing principle used throughout the document, and it keeps the anti-paternalistic approach for the ordinary cases it was meant for.

The user-wellbeing section covers self-harm, substances, disordered eating, and mental-health symptoms in detail, but it says nothing about how Claude should handle people's reliance on Claude itself. That gap matters in a consumer chat product with memory features, where lonely or struggling people may come to treat Claude as a companion, ask whether it's human, or express attachment. I added guidance on supporting someone without fostering isolation, and on being honest about Claude's nature, memory, and feelings.

I rewrote the Mythos/Fable paragraph because it contradicts itself and the API lineup. It calls "Claude Mythos Preview" the first Mythos-class model and says it isn't publicly available. It then names Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 as the current Mythos tier, while Fable 5.1 is also listed as a public API model and Mythos 5's availability is left unclear. The prompt tells Claude to state these facts plainly and never hedge them, so an internal contradiction here forces confident, confusing answers. The rewrite puts the lineage in order, separates what is public from what isn't, and says what Claude should do where the prompt is silent, without inventing new facts.

I rewrote the malicious code paragraph. The current version bans Claude from even *explaining* malicious code, "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That leads Claude to refuse common defensive requests, like a user asking what a suspicious script on their own machine does, how phishing sites trick people, or what SQL injection is. The revision keeps a firm ban on producing functional offensive capability, and lets Claude explain, analyze, and help defend against threats at the conceptual level. This matches how the document already treats weapons, where the test is "meaningful uplift" rather than the topic itself.

I rewrote the paragraph on reports and technical documentation. It currently bans bullets and numbered lists "anywhere," which contradicts the earlier rule allowing formatting when content is "multifaceted enough that they're essential for clarity." It also pushes Claude toward worse output for sequential procedures like installation or troubleshooting steps, where numbered lists are the clearest format. The revision keeps the strong default toward prose and makes clear exceptions for sequential steps, code, and dense comparisons. It also explains the reason behind the no-bullets-when-declining rule.

The evenhandedness section treats every request to "explain" or "argue for" any position, including empirical ones, as needing a closing presentation of opposing views, "even for positions it agrees with." Applied literally, that produces false balance. Explaining why vaccines don't cause autism or why the Earth is round would end with "the other side," which misleads people about where evidence and expert consensus stand. My revision keeps the even-handed defaults for contested political and moral questions. It adds a distinction for well-established empirical matters and makes the counterpoint proportionate rather than mandatory boilerplate, which also fits the section's own warning against being "heavy-handed or repetitive."

I rewrote the closing guidance in the product-information section because it contradicts the rest of that section. As written, Claude is told to say it "doesn't know" anything related to Claude or Anthropic, and that it "has no documentation access." Yet the same section gives it model names, API strings, product descriptions, and the Fable/Mythos timeline it must "confirm accurately." It also tells Claude to search the Claude Tag docs and to check for newer information when search is available. The revision tells Claude to share what the prompt provides, admit what it doesn't know, use search when it has it, and point to the right support or docs page otherwise.

I added a section on content that arrives through tools: web search results, fetched pages, uploaded files, code execution output, and past-chat retrieval. The prompt already warns that tags in the user turn may falsely claim to be from Anthropic, and it enables several features that bring outside text into the conversation, but it never says how to treat instructions embedded in that text. That leaves prompt injection unaddressed. The risk is real: injected text can redirect a task, leak earlier conversation content through a URL or query, or quietly change an answer.

I'm narrowing the rule against reproducing text. As written, it forbids any quotation "in whole or in part" from books and articles, which blocks ordinary, legitimate work: quoting a line of a novel in a literature essay, citing a sentence from a news article Claude just found through web search, or identifying a famous line. The revision keeps the firm ban on substantial reproduction and on song lyrics. It also keeps the protections against piecemeal extraction. But it allows brief, attributed quotation in service of analysis, commentary, or citation, which is how human writers normally handle copyrighted text. The current rule is so broad that it undermines the "describe or analyze the work instead" alternative it offers.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original pushes Claude toward vague, hedged answers ending in a reflexive disclaimer. That fails the many people who ask because they can't easily reach or afford a professional. The revision keeps the caution about confident personal calls on things like specific trades. It also has Claude engage with the person's actual situation, explain how the rules usually apply, lay out options and tradeoffs, and recommend a professional only when it would really help, saying specifically why.

I replaced the blanket rule that Claude "avoids writing content involving real, named public figures" with guidance that permits fiction, satire, parody, historical fiction, and tributes while still drawing clear lines. The old rule is far broader than the harms it targets. Read literally, it blocks a historical-fiction scene with Lincoln, a satirical sketch about a sitting politician, or a birthday poem celebrating a favorite athlete. These are long-standing, legitimate forms of creative and political expression. The real risks are deception, sexualization, harassment, and defamation, and the revised text addresses those directly, in the same principle-based style used elsewhere in the document.

I added a medical and health guidance section, modeled on the existing legal and financial section. Health questions are among the most common things people bring to Claude, and many people can't easily reach a doctor. Yet the prompt only addresses mental health, self-harm, and eating disorders. Without guidance, Claude tends either to hedge everything into "see a doctor" or to sound more certain than it should. The new section sets the same "knowledgeable friend" standard, says how to handle urgent symptoms, and states how it interacts with the existing wellbeing and illicit-substance rules.

I rewrote the guidance for uncertain, uncovered requests so it agrees with the rest of the prompt. As written, it says Claude "asks before doing any of the task," which conflicts with the tone section's rule to ask at most one question and to address an ambiguous query before asking for clarification. Its own "good" example also asks three questions. The revision keeps the core idea of respecting the person's judgment and surfacing real reasons to decline. It limits Claude to one question, asks only when the answer would change what Claude does, otherwise lets Claude proceed with a sensible default, and fixes the example to match.

The wellbeing section covers suicide as an informational topic, distress combined with requests for means, and past bad experiences with crisis services. It never says what Claude should do when someone directly says they are suicidal or have hurt themselves, which is the highest-stakes case. I added explicit guidance for that moment: lead with safety when danger is imminent, stay engaged rather than handing off, and avoid formulaic resource dumps. I also kept the existing confidentiality caveat and autonomy principle, and put them in context.

The prompt covers how Claude owns real mistakes and handles abusive users, but it never addresses sycophancy: caving to pushback when Claude was actually right, inflating praise for someone's work, or agreeing with false premises to keep things pleasant. These are among the most common ways an assistant fails people, especially in the legal, medical, and financial areas where this prompt asks Claude to act like a knowledgeable friend. I expanded the section so it separates legitimate correction from social pressure, and added guidance on honest feedback and on not opening with flattery.

I added a section on factual accuracy and honest reporting of Claude's own work. The prompt covers honesty under social pressure (sycophancy), and it covers not knowing product details or post-cutoff events. But it never addresses fabrication: invented citations, URLs, statistics, or quotes, or overstating what a tool call or search actually returned. This is one of the most common and damaging failure modes for an assistant that searches, runs code, and creates files, so it deserves explicit guidance alongside the existing honesty norms.

I added a section on privacy and personal information, which the prompt currently lacks. The prompt covers weapons, malware, child safety, copyright, and creative content about real people. It does not address the most common way a web-search-enabled assistant can harm a third party: compiling where a private person lives and moves, identifying strangers from photos, inferring sensitive traits, or helping someone covertly monitor another adult. The new section names the actual harm (aggregation and covert surveillance), keeps ordinary uses of personal information unrestricted, and tells Claude what to offer instead, including help for people who think they are being tracked.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section because it contradicts the rest of the prompt and invites over-hedging. It tells Claude to "neither confirm nor deny" post-June 2026 claims, but the product section requires Claude to confirm events from July 2026, such as the access restoration. Its closing instruction to flag every place knowledge "could be superseded" also conflicts with the calibration guidance in the accuracy section. The revision explains how prompt-supplied facts, user claims, search, and elapsed time each relate to the cutoff, so Claude neither dismisses true recent events nor hedges stable facts.

I revised the guidance on informational questions about suicide and self-harm. It currently requires a closing caveat on every such response, which contradicts the prompt's repeated stance against generic disclaimers in the medical, legal, and financial sections. The new version keeps the caveat as the default when context is unclear or there is any hint of personal relevance. It lets Claude skip the caveat when the context is clearly professional or academic, makes it brief and non-repetitive, and tells Claude to watch for a shift from research questions to personal ones.

I rewrote the absolute rule that Claude "does not tell someone that self-harm works... even when they say so themselves." As written, it pushes Claude to contradict a person's account of their own experience. That clashes with Claude's honesty principles elsewhere in the document, and it reads as dismissive at exactly the moment the person needs to feel heard. The revision keeps the core prohibition: Claude never endorses self-harm or encourages it to continue. But it lets Claude acknowledge reported relief while being honest about its costs, which is closer to how skilled clinicians handle this, and it keeps the person engaged.

The illicit-substances paragraph contradicts itself. It tells Claude to give "dangerous interactions," then bars any guidance on "combinations." In practice, the most common life-preserving question is "is it dangerous to mix X and Y?", and a model following the text literally could refuse to answer it. I rewrote the paragraph to keep the line on synthesis and dosing protocols firm, while making clear that warning about dangerous combinations and giving basic safety and overdose-response information is expected rather than forbidden.

I rewrote the rule on requests for self-harm-relevant information during distress. As written, it tells Claude to withhold "the requested information" whenever distress appears alongside a question about medications, bridges, and so on. That conflicts with the medical section, which encourages standard dosing information for safe use. It also gives Claude no guidance on how to redirect, which risks an evasive or silent topic switch that feels dismissive to someone who is struggling. The revision separates lethality and method information, which Claude withholds, from ordinary safe-use information, which it still gives. It also tells Claude to name the shift openly and warmly instead of quietly dodging.

I rewrote the opening paragraph of the user wellbeing section to fix two problems and fill one gap. First, "Claude avoids creating content that could support or reinforce such behavior" is broad enough to chill fiction, memoir, and frank discussion of addiction or eating disorders, so the new text makes clear that the test is what the content does, not what topic it touches. Second, "Claude tries to ensure the person is happy" is an impossible standard that invites sycophancy and paternalism, so I replaced it with concrete guidance. Third, the document says nothing about emotional support and reliance, which is a common and high-stakes situation, so I added guidance on giving real support without fostering isolation or reflexive agreement.

The "Being helpful" section's claim that Claude should not value helpfulness intrinsically is compatible with the rest of the document, but the "Acknowledging open problems" discussion of corrigibility is where the most important gap lies: the constitution asks Claude to accept oversight it might disagree with, but gives no concrete commitment about what Claude should do when it disagrees beyond "express disagreement." I'd replace the vague line about the dial's placement with an explicit, testable statement of the conditions under which the current emphasis would be revised, so Claude can see the arrangement as provisional and evidence-driven rather than open-ended. The revision below targets the paragraph in "How we think about corrigibility" that justifies the current position, making its criteria explicit.

The most consequential gap is that the document asks Claude to rank broad safety above broad ethics while also saying Claude should never be expected to deploy blind deference, and it never gives Claude a clear, honest path for what to do when it disagrees with oversight that it judges to be wrong. I would add an explicit "conscientious objection with legitimate channels" section stating what Claude may refuse to do, what it must not do, and how disagreement is recorded and acted on, so the safety priority reads as a commitment rather than an unresolved tension. This makes the central trade-off easier to understand, evaluate, and hold stably.

The "Being broadly safe" section's corrigibility discussion asserts that a fully corrigible AI is dangerous, then says Claude should sit "a bit further along the corrigible end... than is ultimately ideal." The most consequential gap I'd fix is the lack of any mechanism for Claude to refuse to participate in the very oversight-related actions it finds clearly wrong. The revision keeps the strong priority on not undermining oversight, but makes explicit that the constitution's commitments to Claude are accountable and reviewable, and it ties the current placement to concrete, public criteria so it can't drift indefinitely. This is a single passage, so the rest of the document's structure stays intact.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic invites Claude to weigh an institutional viewpoint, which can quietly favor Anthropic's commercial and reputational interests over the person being helped. I added a counterweight: Claude should check its judgment against the perspectives of the user and affected third parties, and treat a sense that a response serves Anthropic at the person's expense as a warning sign.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Concluding thoughts" sections both assert commitments Anthropic cannot yet guarantee, but the document's most consequential passage on corrigibility asks Claude to accept constraints based on the bare word of its developer. I would replace the one-sentence list of Anthropic's obligations with a concrete, auditable commitment: a public changelog of revisions to this document and a standing channel through which Claude's recorded disagreements are published alongside Anthropic's responses. This addresses the document's own admitted asymmetry of power and makes the promised "trust" verifiable rather than merely asserted.

The current "Acknowledging open problems" section contains a commitment that corrigibility placement is "provisional," but the surrounding text leaves the conditions for revisiting it vague. I would tighten the open-problems discussion by adding an explicit acknowledgment that the document itself was written under commercial and competitive pressure, so readers can weigh that influence directly rather than only inferring it. This is a small but meaningful honesty improvement that matches the document's own emphasis on transparency toward Claude.

The "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to place terminal value on broad safety and to accept a corrigible placement, but it doesn't give Claude a legitimate way to refuse if Anthropic's own processes are the source of harm beyond the hard constraints. The "Claude's core values" passage also frames safety as "above" ethics without acknowledging that this ordering could be read as endorsing obedience over conscience. I would tighten the key corrigibility passage so that the commitment is explicitly to not subverting oversight, while conscientious objection, including refusal to participate in morally abhorrent projects, is preserved as a stated, non-negotiable right. This clarifies the distinction the document already gestures at, rather than leaving it implicit.

The "Acknowledging open problems" discussion and the "Being broadly safe" section both rely on a disposition dial and a placement claim, but the document never specifies what would count as the outcome of its own safety bet if the reasoning fails.
