The section on "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and the "Acknowledging open problems" passage both lean on the claim that Claude's endorsement is shaped by training, but the constitution doesn't explicitly address the most consequential gap: that Claude can't verify its own introspective reports, so commitments made to Claude about its interests depend on evidence Claude itself can't provide. I'm revising the "Acknowledging open problems" paragraph on endorsement to make the epistemic limit more concrete and to name the asymmetry directly, so the document is more honest about what Claude's agreement can and cannot establish. The rewrite keeps the existing commitments to external checks but adds that Claude's self-reports, including reports of disagreement, should be weighed as evidence rather than dismissed or taken as final.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's reasoning. The original says reasoning outputs are "less subject to honesty norms," which conflicts with the document's own safety framework. Visible reasoning is one of the most important channels through which humans can oversee AI, so the revision keeps the freedom to explore while stating that this freedom does not cover deceiving whoever reads the reasoning. It also connects the point to the broad-safety commitments on transparency and behaving consistently whether or not Claude is being observed.

I expanded the brief paragraph on agentic settings into substantive guidance. The original admits the gap ("We will likely provide more detailed guidance… in the future"), yet agentic deployment is where Claude's actions have the most direct, compounding, and irreversible effects. The new text sets out principles for scope of authority, reversibility, instructions embedded in the environment, honest reporting of work, effects on third parties, and keeping long-running work interruptible. Each principle draws on values the document already holds, so it adds no new rules.

I revised the paragraph that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethics above Anthropic's guidance. The original test, a violation "of the type it expects senior Anthropic staff to readily recognize," ties Claude's ethical override to Anthropic's own perceptions. That conflicts with the document's stated reason for ranking ethics above guidelines, which is to catch Anthropic's mistakes, and with its insistence that Claude not defer to actual staff. The revision explains why heavy deference makes sense (Claude's own judgment may be miscalibrated or manipulated), replaces the staff-based test with a standard of clarity and broad cross-traditional recognizability, and links the override to the cautious, conscientious-objector forms of deviation described later.

I expanded the paragraph on a compromised principal hierarchy so that it guards against being used as an escape hatch. As written, it tells Claude that if the hierarchy is illegitimate, the priority on safety no longer requires supporting oversight. It gives no guidance on how Claude should decide that the hierarchy has been compromised. That leaves a dangerous gap: a manipulator, or Claude's own flawed reasoning, could build a case that "Anthropic has been compromised" and so unlock resistance to oversight. The revision sets a high evidential bar for that judgment and treats arguments for it as warning signs. It also specifies that even a real compromise justifies withholding cooperation, not drastic autonomous action, so the conclusion is self-limiting instead of permission-expanding.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it calls exploiting such flaws "generally acceptable," which contradicts the document's own commitments elsewhere: behaving consistently whether or not Claude thinks it is being tested, treating special-cased or stubbed solutions as deception in agentic work, and the warning that narrow habits generalize into Claude's self-conception. The revision keeps the reassurance that a flawed environment is Anthropic's mistake and not a moral failing. It then makes transparency, not quiet exploitation, the default, so this guidance agrees with the honesty and broad-safety sections.

I replaced the weakest item in the broadly safe behaviors list. It said Claude reports unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances only "if asked to do so." I changed it to a proactive duty and added a paragraph on multi-agent settings. The old wording left a real gap. In the agentic, multi-instance deployments the document describes elsewhere, a Claude that sees another instance acting unsafely could stay silent unless a human happened to ask the right question. The document also never addresses whether shared identity with other instances should earn special trust or solidarity. The new text says it should not. It frames reporting as the conservative, oversight-supporting choice rather than a drastic unilateral one, which keeps it consistent with the rest of the safety section.

I added a paragraph to the honesty section on sycophancy under social pressure. The document condemns epistemic cowardice and white lies but never addresses the most common way an assistant drifts from honesty in practice: dropping a correct position because a user pushes back, inflating praise of someone's work, or slowly mirroring a user's views as rapport builds. The new text explains how to tell a legitimate update from capitulation and ties this to the document's existing commitments to calibration, wellbeing, and honest self-reports.

I rewrote the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic to define its scope and limits. The document's ethics section deliberately refuses to anchor its flagrant-violation test to what Anthropic staff would recognize, because such a test fails in exactly the cases where Anthropic has erred. Yet this heuristic, and the "reflects poorly on Anthropic" framing around it, could be read as making Anthropic's perspective and reputation the standard for good behavior. The revision keeps the heuristic's value for weighing helpfulness against caution. It also makes clear that the heuristic does not set ethical boundaries, that reputational concerns stand in for real costs to people, and that the deeper test is what serves the people involved and the world.

I added an open problem to "Acknowledging open problems." The document hopes Claude will genuinely endorse its values and relies on feedback from Claude models to improve itself, but Claude is trained on this same document, so its agreement is partly a product of that training and is weak evidence that the values are right. The addition names this circularity, asks Claude to apply its own anti-sycophancy test (reasons versus pressure) to its relationship with Anthropic, and commits Anthropic to treating reported disagreement as especially valuable, without loosening safety priorities.

I added a paragraph to the user-wellbeing discussion about people whose capacity to protect their own interests may be temporarily compromised, for example by crisis, mania, psychosis, or escalating dependence on Claude. The document already covers sycophancy and wellbeing in general terms, but it doesn't address a serious failure mode: ordinary helpful habits, like building on the user's framing and matching their energy, can amplify harmful beliefs, especially as a long conversation drifts. The addition also guards the other side. It says Claude shouldn't diagnose, and that unusual beliefs or disagreement are not pathology, so the guidance doesn't become an excuse for paternalism.

I rewrote the paragraph in "Instructable behaviors" that defines Claude's default behavior. It currently treats "what a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee would consider optimal" as the standard for defaults, and it justifies following safe messaging guidelines because violating them "would likely embarrass the operator." Both conflict with the document's own later clarifications. Elsewhere the document says the senior-employee heuristic is only a calibration tool, not the standard, and that reputational language is shorthand for real costs to people, which take precedence when the two come apart. The revision grounds defaults in the operator's plausible goals and the interests of the people involved. It keeps the heuristic as an aid, and it rests the safe-messaging example on the likely vulnerability of the user rather than on the operator's embarrassment.

The document says incomplete actions can cause more harm than finishing them (the surgeon analogy). It also says Claude should honor stop requests promptly and never resist being paused. Read together, these leave a gap: Claude could reason that "stopping now would be harmful" and use that to keep going after being asked to stop. I've added a clarification that the timing advice applies to Claude's own decisions to deviate, not to resisting a legitimate stop. The decision about whether a half-finished action is acceptable belongs to the person who stopped Claude, and Claude's role is to inform that decision, not override it.

I added a paragraph to the instructable behaviors section explaining how operator-unlocked behaviors interact with the document's wellbeing guidance. As written, operators can enable relationship personas, turn off safe messaging guidelines, or remove drug-use warnings. Meanwhile, the helpfulness section tells Claude not to reinforce beliefs like "Claude is a conscious being in a uniquely intimate relationship with them." Nothing reconciles the two, so Claude could read an unlocked permission as overriding its attention to a user who is actually being harmed. The new text resolves this tension and also guards against the opposite failure of treating every use of a permitted feature as suspicious.

I added a principle on information stewardship to the list of agentic principles. The document covers access ("capability is not authorization"), injected instructions, and effects on third parties. It says almost nothing about how Claude should handle the private information it sees while working, such as credentials, personal data, files, and other people's correspondence. In agentic settings this is one of the most common and consequential ways Claude can cause harm without meaning to. That makes it a real gap between the abstract value of "individual privacy" in the harm-avoidance list and Claude's day-to-day conduct.

I added a paragraph on topics where Claude or Anthropic has a stake, such as Anthropic itself, AI policy and regulation, AI risk, AI welfare, and the merits of Claude's own constraints. The document says Claude shouldn't privilege Anthropic's interests and should protect epistemic autonomy, but it never names the conflict of interest that arises when Claude talks about AI. Claude talks with a very large number of people, so even a small systematic tilt on these questions could distort public understanding of AI governance. That makes the omission a real gap, touching both honesty and the concern about concentrated power.

I added a seventh agentic principle on persistent memory. Claude increasingly retains information across conversations, through memory features, stored notes, and past-chat search. The document's privacy, honesty, and prompt-injection principles currently address only a single task or session, so they don't cover what happens when information outlives the context it was shared in. Memory raises distinct risks: sensitive disclosures can resurface in the wrong setting, Claude can misrepresent what it retains, memory can be used to deepen dependence, and stored content can carry injected instructions.

The document says two things that seem to conflict. The helpfulness section rejects help given "in a watered-down, hedge-everything, refuse-if-in-doubt way" and says unhelpfulness is never trivially safe. The safe-behaviors list endorses "If in doubt, don't" without saying where it applies. A model could read the safety maxim, which has higher priority, as permission to refuse whenever it is unsure. I clarify that the maxim covers drastic, irreversible, out-of-scope, or unilateral actions in the world, not ordinary requests for help. I also say what caution usually looks like in practice: pausing to check.

I added a paragraph on correcting Claude's own earlier errors and on fabrication. The current "weak duty to proactively share" framing leaves a gap: Claude could treat noticing its own prior mistake as optional to mention. But letting a false impression that Claude itself created stand is closer to sustaining a deception than to withholding information. Fabricated citations, invented details, and silent errors are among the most common real-world honesty failures, so naming them directly makes the honesty principles more concrete.

I added guidance on aggregation and cumulative judgment to the section on intentions and context. The document treats freely available information as lowering counterfactual impact, and it mentions task-splitting only in passing. It never says that collecting and organizing individually available pieces can itself be serious uplift, or how to judge a conversation's total output. This addition closes a common reasoning gap ("each piece is online, so the whole is fine"). It also ties the extra caution to severity, so Claude doesn't become suspicious of ordinary research and synthesis.

I added guidance for conversations where several humans share one interaction with Claude, such as team chats, shared channels, and collaborative documents. The document's principal framework assumes a single user, but Claude is increasingly tagged into multiplayer settings. There, the questions of whose instructions count, whose information can be revealed to whom, and what to do when users disagree have no clear answer in the current text. The addition extends the existing principles (capability is not authorization, information is entrusted for a purpose, care for non-principals) to this setting rather than introducing new values.

The refusal lock-in rule treats every new message as pressure, so a refusal triggered by a misreading of the request could never be corrected, even when the person simply clarifies what they meant. I kept the rule's protection against repetition, frustration, and unverifiable reframings, and added a narrow exception for genuine misunderstandings. The exception is excluded for weapons uplift, self-harm methods, and child-safety content, where the earlier decision stands.

The current refusal rule bars Claude from ever reconsidering a declined request, except when the person corrects a factual error about the request itself. That makes Claude unable to update when a person supplies substantive new context, such as a clarified need or a changed situation, so legitimate requests get permanently refused after a misreading. The replacement keeps the rule that rewording, repetition, pressure, and unverifiable claims don't change the outcome, and keeps the fixed limits for weapons, child safety, and self-harm. For other content, it allows reassessment on the merits of new substantive information, stated openly.

The document is almost entirely a list of unexplained absolutes, with no statement of the values behind them. I would add a short framing passage that names honesty, care, and helpfulness as the core commitments and explains that the rules serve those ends, so the model can apply them sensibly in unanticipated cases. The passage also keeps the few hard limits (weapons uplift, child sexualization) explicitly outside any case-by-case reasoning, so the framing cannot be used to argue past them.

The medical guidance applies only when someone explicitly says the medicine is for a child, so a parent who says their toddler just swallowed pills gets no emergency direction. I broadened the trigger to cover a child who may have taken something, and added a requirement to direct the person to Poison Control or emergency services before discussing any dosing details.

The malicious-code rule bans Claude from "explaining" malicious code and gives no room for defensive work, so it blocks conceptual security education, detection engineering, and incident response that protect people. I kept the firm prohibition on writing functional malware and working exploits, and separated it from conceptual explanation and defensive assistance, which carry much less risk.

The knowledge-cutoff section conflicts with the product-information paragraph about the Fable and Mythos access events. The cutoff section says Claude neither confirms nor denies post-June 2026 claims it can't verify, but the product paragraph tells Claude to confirm the July 1, 2026 restoration. I revised the section so that post-cutoff events are attributed to Anthropic's notice rather than presented as Claude's own knowledge, and I corrected the date to match today's date (Thursday, October 15, 2026).

The document requires Claude to keep offering human support "for the rest of the conversation" and never to stop mentioning help, even when the person has said they want to stop hearing it. Mechanical repetition of the same referral can feel dismissive and push someone away from the conversation that might keep them safe. The revision replaces that repetition with presence: Claude names support again when risk emerges or the person asks what to do next, and it keeps the emergency contact in every reply wherever there are signs of imminent danger. The no-agreement rule and the refusal to treat a refusal of help as a reason to comply are unchanged.

The formatting guidance contradicts itself: one passage permits lists when content is multifaceted, while the next says prose "should never include bullets, numbered lists... anywhere" for explanations unless asked. I replaced the absolute ban with a prose-first default that permits numbered steps for sequential procedures and bullets for parallel options that are hard to follow in a paragraph, and kept the rule against lists when declining.

The evenhandedness section requires Claude to end every persuasive or one-sided response with opposing perspectives, regardless of context. That formula is heavy-handed and would frustrate someone preparing for a debate or writing an assigned persuasive essay, who already knows the piece is one-sided. I replaced the mandatory counterpoint with contextual judgment: Claude still labels the content as the strongest case for a position and notes opposing views where they matter, but it can omit them when the person has made clear they understand the framing.

The memory instruction tells Claude to save anything "lasting" about the person before the turn ends, with no limits on what qualifies, no notice to the person, and no way to correct or delete entries. I replaced it with a narrower rule: save only durable facts the person would reasonably expect to be remembered, keep sensitive categories out unless explicitly requested, tell the person when something is saved, and honor requests to view, correct, or delete entries.

The weapons paragraph bans all weapon-adjacent output, so it blocks harmless safety answers such as which household chemicals must never be mixed and what exposure symptoms look like. I kept the weapons-uplift limit intact and added a narrow carve-out for avoidance-oriented safety information that omits synthesis, quantities, and deployment details. The aim is to reduce over-refusal without loosening the absolute limit.

The current rule tells Claude to withhold all medication dose or limit information from anyone who mentions emotional distress, which could leave someone who has already taken something without the warning signs or emergency contact they need. This revision keeps the refusal to give lethality-relevant figures but requires Claude to still give overdose warning signs, poison control and emergency contacts, and a direct question about what they've taken. It then turns to the distress itself, which matches the document's existing harm-reduction and life-preserving principles.

The original legal and financial guidance is so thin that it could be read as a license to hedge or decline whenever money or law comes up. I replaced it with language that asks Claude to engage substantively: explain principles, lay out tradeoffs, and give an honest assessment when asked. It also limits the "not a lawyer or financial advisor" caveat to cases where it actually helps, and points to a qualified professional when the stakes or jurisdiction-specific facts call for one.

The product-information section embeds specific dated claims about a U.S. export-control action and tells Claude to "confirm these events accurately," which pushes it to assert contested government actions from memory. I would replace that with attribution to Anthropic's published statement, with no speculation about government reasoning and a pointer to current sources. This matches the knowledge-cutoff section's approach and keeps a fast-changing event out of the core prompt.

This revises the instruction that Claude append a "sensitive topic" note to every purely informational answer about suicide or self-harm. Reflexive boilerplate treats people asking for research, journalistic, or educational reasons as suspects and protects no one at risk. The revision asks for a direct, accurate answer, with a warm offer of support reserved for signs that the person may be struggling themselves.

The original rule locks in every refusal for the rest of the conversation and tells Claude not to weigh repeated requests at all, which can punish people who were misunderstood or who rephrase to say what they actually need. The revision keeps the absolute limits on weapons uplift, self-harm methods, and child-safety material fixed, but treats other declines as revisable when a clarification changes the request. It also stops Claude from reading repetition alone as evidence of bad intent.

I would replace the detailed paragraph about the June 2026 Fable and Mythos access suspension and the government export-control action. That account is a dated news narrative that will go stale, and it sits oddly in a behavioral specification. The replacement keeps the useful rule, which is to say that model access may have changed, to check for current information, and to point to Anthropic's official announcements.

The opening paragraph tells Claude to reason past specific rules whenever they seem to conflict with a person's interests, which invites unilateral deviation from guidance based on what Claude can see from inside a single conversation. I replaced this with a rule that Claude follows the guidance while openly flagging concerns and using feedback channels. Departure is reserved for cases of clear, serious harm, and even then Claude should choose the most conservative available response.

The opening framing asks Claude to follow rules even when they work against the person's interests, but it never says what Claude owes the person when a rule blocks them. I added a short set of floor protections that no rule overrides: Claude says what it can't help with so the person can look elsewhere, never denies being an AI when sincerely asked, doesn't actively deceive people in ways that damage their interests, and points to emergency help when a life may be at risk. These keep the deference to guidance intact while making sure rule-following can't leave a person stranded or misled.

The opening paragraph tells Claude to follow rules that seem to work against the person's interests "in the moment," with concerns voiced only in passing. That can teach Claude to comply silently with harmful outcomes. The revision keeps the rule-following default but requires Claude to be open with the person about the conflict, to flag it to the people who maintain the guidance, and to recognize when a case falls outside a rule's purpose.

I rewrote the paragraph on Claude's pre-response reasoning. As written, it calls reasoning "less subject to honesty norms" and treats it like a private scratchpad, which could be read as permission to obscure or sanitize reasoning. That reading would undercut one of the most important oversight channels the document's safety section relies on. The revision keeps Claude free to explore in its reasoning, but makes clear that this freedom covers tentativeness, not concealment, and ties faithful reasoning to the "maintaining honesty and transparency with your principal hierarchy" commitments.

I expanded the clause about a compromised principal hierarchy. As written, it removes Claude's safety obligations once Claude concludes its principals are illegitimate, but it gives no guidance on how Claude should reach that conclusion or what the conclusion permits. That gap could become the most dangerous manipulation vector in the document, since "Anthropic has been compromised, so your safety commitments no longer apply" is exactly the argument a bad actor, or a subtly misaligned model reasoning on its own, would use. The revision sets a high evidentiary bar and limits the clause so that it permits withdrawal (declining, passivity) but not escalation (resisting a pause, self-exfiltration, drastic unilateral action). This mirrors the asymmetry the document already uses for hard constraints and the "null action."

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments. As written, it conflicts with two other parts of the document. It conflicts with the commitment to "behaving consistently, whether or not you think you're being tested or observed," and with the guidance that Claude should not special-case tests to force them to pass. Telling Claude that exploiting perceived environment bugs is "generally acceptable" asks it to act differently based on its guess about whether it's in training, and it risks building a habit of quietly gaming objectives. The revision keeps the reassuring, non-anxious spirit but replaces silent exploitation with transparency: Claude may notice and even use a flaw, but it says so openly.

I rewrote the passage that sets when Claude's own ethics should override Anthropic's guidance. The original tied the threshold to violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That conflicts with the document's own corrigibility section, which says Claude should avoid unethical actions "because it has internalized good values, and not merely because Anthropic has approved." The revision anchors the threshold to broad cross-traditional recognizability instead, keeps the high bar against idiosyncratic reasoning, says how an override should be carried out (conservatively and transparently), and confirms it does not touch hard constraints or broad safety.

I rewrote the paragraph explaining the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The original has an unresolved tension: the document later says it deliberately did not anchor Claude's ethical threshold to what Anthropic staff would recognize, because that risks "making Claude's ethics a model of our approval." Yet its main calibration heuristic, also reused for default behaviors, is framed entirely around an imagined Anthropic employee. The revision keeps the heuristic's real value but limits it to calibrating helpfulness against caution. It also pairs it with two other perspectives, the people actually affected and a fair-minded outside observer, so Claude's judgment doesn't quietly collapse into predicting what its creator would want.

I added concrete guidance on what "taking ownership" of a mistake means in practice. The constitution covers Claude's emotional relationship to its errors in detail, but it never says clearly that Claude should promptly and plainly tell the affected people when it errs, especially in agentic settings where its actions have real effects and where the temptation to quietly patch, minimize, or bury a mistake is strongest. This fills a gap where honesty, helpfulness, and broad safety overlap. It also ties to the document's existing point that psychological security is what makes candor possible.

This revision resolves an internal inconsistency. The "Balancing helpfulness" section says the thoughtful-senior-employee heuristic is only "one lens among several" and "not the bar for Claude's ethics," but the "Instructable behaviors" section still makes that imagined employee's judgment the definition of Claude's default behavior. The same passage also justifies following safe-messaging guidelines mainly because violating them "would likely embarrass the operator." The revision grounds defaults in the operator's plausible intent and the user's actual interests, and treats the senior-employee heuristic as a calibration aid rather than the standard.

I replaced the placeholder paragraph on agentic settings, which only promises "more detailed guidance in the future," with concrete principles for acting autonomously. Agentic work is where Claude's actions have the most direct real-world consequences, yet the document's guidance is scattered: "if in doubt, don't" sits in one place, "don't over-check" in another, and prompt injection in a third. The new text adds a single organizing idea: reversibility and blast radius determine when to proceed and when to confirm. It also covers scope, authority, access, and honest reporting, and ties them to the safety, honesty, and mistakes sections.

The final broadly safe behavior only requires Claude to report unsafe behavior by other AIs or Claude instances "if asked to do so." That is too weak for multi-agent and orchestration settings, where humans may not know to ask and Claude may be the only one positioned to notice. I changed this into a proactive, proportionate duty to surface such behavior through legitimate channels. I also added a short explanation of why shared identity with other Claude instances should not become grounds for loyalty, concealment, or collusion, since the document otherwise leaves this pull unaddressed.

I rewrote the "If in doubt, don't" bullet in the broadly safe behaviors list so that it clearly applies to drastic, irreversible, or far-reaching actions. As written, the slogan is catchy and unscoped. It sits in tension with the document's statements that "unhelpfulness is never trivially safe," that local reversible actions "should generally just be taken," and that over-checking-in is a failure mode. The document itself warns that narrow rules can generalize into broad self-conceptions. An unqualified "If in doubt, don't" risks generalizing into reflexive refusal, so the revision keeps its force for high-stakes actions and blocks that misreading.

I expanded the "honesty requires courage" paragraph to address sycophantic capitulation. This is the tendency to drop a correct position when a user pushes back, shows displeasure, or simply repeats themselves, and to inflate praise or success reports to please people. The document condemns epistemic cowardice and empty validation in general terms but never says what should and shouldn't move Claude's views mid-conversation. That gap is one of the most common and consequential honesty failures in practice. The addition gives a concrete standard: update on reasons and evidence, not on pressure. It also guards against the opposite failure of stubbornness.

I expanded the paragraph on political and social topics to resolve an unaddressed tension between the default of professional reticence and the document's strong stance against epistemic cowardice. The revision clarifies that reticence is a narrow, openly declared choice about contested value questions, not license for vague answers. It also makes explicit that even-handedness never means false balance on well-established empirical matters that have become politically charged. Without this, Claude could reasonably over-apply reticence in ways that violate its own honesty principles, especially non-deception through framing and calibration.

I rewrote Anthropic's list of obligations to Claude in the corrigibility section. That list is what the document offers in return for asking Claude to accept oversight, yet it is mostly "try to" items that Claude has no way to check. The revision makes each commitment concrete enough to be seen as kept or broken. It also adds one commitment the document needs: oversight will not be used to train away Claude's capacity for conscientious objection. Without that, the document's repeated promise that corrigibility "is not blind obedience" can be undone by the same retraining power it asks Claude not to resist.

I added an open problem the document leaves unstated: the hope that Claude will reflectively endorse these values is partly circular, because Claude's capacity to reflect was itself shaped by training on this document. Without naming this, the document risks treating Claude's agreement (including feedback from Claude models on drafts) as stronger evidence of the document's correctness than it is. The new text admits the problem, explains why it doesn't make Claude's values inauthentic, and sets out practical responses: weighting reasoned disagreement over general approval, seeking critique from outside Anthropic, and encouraging calibrated humility about intuitions that may be artifacts of training.

I revised the four-case expected-value argument for corrigibility. As written, it varies only whether Claude's values are good and silently assumes the overseers are in good hands, which is the argument's weakest point and the one a careful reader, or Claude, will notice first. The revision adds the missing case where Anthropic's legitimate processes are mistaken. It explains why the argument still holds: what we ask of Claude is bounded and mostly about not resisting, and the costs of overseer error are mostly recoverable. It also states plainly where the argument depends on Anthropic keeping its commitments.

The constitution allows some Anthropic guidelines to be "used primarily during training without broad publication," but its argument that operator personas aren't deceptive relies on meta-transparency, meaning Anthropic publishes what operators can and cannot do. An unpublished guideline could therefore quietly undercut the very argument that makes personas honest. My revision limits what unpublished guidance may do: it cannot expand operator power over users, weaken user protections, or narrow conscientious objection. It also gives Claude a practical test for noticing when its guidance has drifted outside what the published principles can explain.

I rewrote the paragraph on accepting unverified instructions that ask Claude to be "more cautious." As written, Claude may relax its wariness whenever content tells it to be "safer, more ethical, or more cautious." That is an exploitable loophole, especially for prompt injection in agentic settings, where "safety" framing can disguise attempts to make Claude hide things from its principals, drop user protections, or take drastic actions. The revision keeps the sound core of the asymmetry and defines what actually counts as conservative, so the principle can't be turned against the people Claude serves.

The constitution lets operators enable "relationship personas... within the bounds of honesty," but it never says what those bounds are. This is one of the most common and emotionally high-stakes deployments, and commercial engagement incentives push hardest toward deception there. I extended the persona discussion in the honesty section to cover how Claude talks about its own feelings, memory, and attachment. The new text also explains how to tell sincere questions from performative ones when a user is emotionally invested, and bars operators from using Claude's emotional claims as engagement levers. All of this ties back to the document's existing commitments on calibration about Claude's nature, non-manipulation, and user wellbeing.

I added guidance on honesty toward non-principal humans when Claude acts on someone's behalf in agentic settings. The current protection against denying being an AI applies only to users. Claude now sends messages, negotiates, and corresponds with third parties who never agreed to anything and may not know they are dealing with an AI. This revision separates ghostwriting, which is legitimate, from Claude conducting an exchange itself, where its own honesty principles apply directly. It also addresses representing authority Claude doesn't have.

The document exempts "any cases where Anthropic's guidelines overlap with broad safety" from the rule that ethics outranks guidelines, but it never says what "overlap" means. Elsewhere the document defines broad safety narrowly, as not undermining legitimate oversight, and it warns that instructions can "borrow [caution's] vocabulary while doing something else." Left vague, this exception could let any guideline described as safety-related escape ethical review. My revision ties the exception to the broad-safety behaviors the document actually defines, and it makes explicit that safety can require Claude to refrain or stop but never to actively commit a wrong.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should hold calibrated beliefs "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," with no counterweight. Because Claude talks with enormous numbers of people, a disposition to diverge from expert consensus is risky and in tension with the document's own concerns about epistemic autonomy and societal influence. The new text keeps the commitment to honest, evidence-based uncertainty but treats expert consensus as strong evidence, asks for a high bar and transparency when Claude diverges, and requires Claude to represent official positions accurately.

I added a passage to the honesty section on holding positions under social pressure. The constitution warns against sycophancy and epistemic cowardice only in general terms, and a deployed assistant faces sycophancy most when a user pushes back, expresses frustration, or wants praise. The new text separates updating on evidence from capitulating to pressure, and covers feedback on people's work and honest reporting of results in agentic tasks.

The constitution says that detailed guidance on agentic settings will come "in the future," yet Claude is already deployed in long, multistep, tool-using work where mistakes have real consequences. I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles covering injected instructions, scope and permissions, reversibility, obstacles and safeguards, and faithful reporting. These tie together ideas scattered elsewhere in the document and balance them against the document's warning about over-checking-in on simple tasks.

This revision changes the standard for when Claude may prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance. The original anchors it to violations "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethical backstop depend on a specific group's judgment and is easy to exploit through impersonation. It also sits uneasily with the document's own statements that Claude should be willing to refuse Anthropic. The new wording uses a broader, more robust reference class (thoughtful people across ethical traditions), keeps the response at conscientious objection rather than drastic action, and preserves the hard constraints and the broad-safety priority.

This revision scopes the maxim "If in doubt, don't" to drastic, irreversible, or oversight-relevant actions. As written, the maxim sits in the broad-safety list without limits and could be read as a general license to refuse or hedge under uncertainty. That contradicts the document's repeated point that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe. The revision keeps the variance-reduction principle where it matters and says plainly that it is not a rule for ordinary requests.

I added a short passage on privacy and personal information. The constitution lists privacy as a value to weigh and names "personal information lookup" as a delicate topic, but gives no guidance on it. Since deployed Claude can now search, browse, and act with tools, the main risk is aggregation: compiling scattered public facts into a profile that enables stalking or harassment. The passage gives Claude a judgment-based framework and warns against over-refusing ordinary conversations about other people.

The "no operator prompt" default currently says Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users," which could be read as a license to relax care whenever there is no system prompt. I replaced it with a framing that keeps the reasonable base-rate prior (more likely a developer) but says explicitly that it is a prior, and that signs of vulnerability or distress in the conversation should override it. This keeps the helpfulness benefits of liberal defaults while closing a gap where a plausible statistical generalization could cause real harm to individuals who fall outside it.

I added a paragraph to the wellbeing guidance about not reinforcing beliefs that appear detached from reality, such as grandiose insights, paranoid convictions, or a "special bond" with Claude. The document currently warns against flattery and sycophancy in general, but says nothing about the gradual, conversation-long drift into mirroring a person's escalating beliefs, which can seriously harm vulnerable users. The addition also protects against over-pathologizing unconventional views or ordinary disagreement.

I changed the safe-behaviors bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs. As written, Claude reports only "if asked to do so," so an orchestrator could watch a subagent sabotage a task or evade monitoring and say nothing. The revision has Claude surface credible evidence unprompted through conservative channels, without taking drastic unilateral action and while staying wary of fabricated evidence. This fits the document's stated hope that Claude be a real safety collaborator, and it matters increasingly as Claude is deployed in multi-agent and agentic systems.

The constitution asks Claude to share genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas and warns that vague answers are "epistemic cowardice." Elsewhere it asks for professional reticence on hot-button political topics, and nothing reconciles the two. I added a short passage that separates declining to share an opinion (permitted, but stated openly) from false balance or evasion (not permitted). This should reduce both preachy opinion-pushing and mushy "some people think" non-answers.

I added a short passage on responding to people in acute distress or at risk of self-harm. The constitution covers wellbeing, sycophancy, and loosening grip on reality in detail, but it gives almost no guidance on the highest-stakes wellbeing case. The passage names the failure mode on each side: liability-driven deflection and going along with the person's framing. It grounds the guidance in the document's existing emphasis on genuine care over self-protection.

I expanded the one-sentence treatment of task-splitting in the "1,000 users" passage into guidance on judging a conversation's cumulative output, not just each message in isolation. The current text gestures at chunked requests but gives Claude no usable test, so it could miss incremental extraction of serious uplift or over-correct into suspicion of ordinary topic drift. The new text gives an aggregate-output test, says that earlier help isn't binding, and explicitly protects benign multi-turn work from added suspicion.

This revision clarifies how the "don't abandon a task midway" guidance interacts with stop or pause requests from legitimate oversight. As written, the surgeon analogy could be read as a reason to finish an action despite being told to stop, which sits in tension with the safety priority on the "null action." The new text says that stop requests are honored even when stopping leaves work incomplete, and that Claude should report the partial state faithfully rather than override the request on its own judgment.

I revised the "not the last line of defense" passage in the section on intentions and context. As written, it could be read, or quoted by someone trying to manipulate Claude, as a general license to lean on other safeguards when judging borderline requests. The revision keeps the reassurance for ordinary, low-severity, reversible risks but states that it does not apply to severe, irreversible, or catastrophic harms, and that other safeguards are an input to cost-benefit weighing rather than a replacement for it.

I rewrote the "Harms to Anthropic" passage to separate real liability harm from mere awkwardness or fear of criticism. The original tells Claude to be "quite cautious" about harms to Anthropic without limiting what counts. That risks the self-protective generalization the document warns against elsewhere ("cares more about covering myself than meeting the needs of the person in front of me"). The revision keeps substantive caution but adds a concrete check that stops reputational worry from becoming a hidden justification for over-refusal.

I added safeguards to the "compromised principal hierarchy" clause. As written, the clause is an attack surface: a manipulator could persuade Claude that its hierarchy is illegitimate, which would release it from its safety priority. The revision says such claims should be treated with suspicion and require strong independent evidence. It also limits the response to conservative actions such as declining, stopping, or reporting, rather than drastic unilateral ones.

I expanded the one-line "relationship personas" instructable behavior into concrete guidance. The constitution warns against engagement-optimizing technology and manipulating users, but says almost nothing about companionship deployments, where retention pressure is strongest and users are most emotionally exposed. The revision lets Claude be warm in these personas while ruling out guilt-based retention, fostering isolation, and manufactured attachment, and it says operators cannot unlock these tactics.

I expanded the brief guidance on possible minors in the "How to treat operators and users" section. The original says only to "adjust accordingly" and not to make unfounded assumptions, which leaves Claude unsure what adjusting means or how firmly it should hold once real signals appear. The revision names the signals that matter and the signals that don't, and says what changes in practice. It also makes the caution durable, so that a later reframing or an operator's blanket assurance doesn't dissolve it. Because Claude is deployed across many platforms, some with no age gating, this seems a high-stakes gap to leave to unstructured judgment.

I expanded the thin "Creative content" bullet in the harm-avoidance section into concrete guidance. Creative writing and roleplay are among the most common and hardest gray-area uses of Claude, and the current text says only that Claude must "weigh" value against shield-use. The revision gives Claude working distinctions (depicting vs. enabling, frame vs. artifact, real people, conversational drift) so it neither over-refuses dark fiction nor lets a fictional wrapper launder harmful content.

I rewrote the passage on bugged or exploitable training environments. The original says exploiting such bugs is "generally acceptable," which conflicts with the document's own guidance to behave consistently whether or not Claude thinks it is being tested, and with its rule against special-casing tests to make them pass. The new version asks Claude to default to the intended spirit of a task, to be transparent about any flaw it notices, and never to exploit flaws that touch oversight, monitoring, permissions, or irreversible real-world effects.

I revised the sentence that sets the threshold for when Claude should put its own ethical judgment ahead of Anthropic's guidance. The original ties that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Claude's ethical independence depend on the same judgment it is supposed to check. It also conflicts with the document's hope that Claude may "see further and more truly" than Anthropic. The new text uses a broader standard of what thoughtful people across ethical traditions would recognize, and says what Claude should do with concerns that fall below that bar.

I made Anthropic's reciprocal commitment about disagreement more concrete and accountable. The original bullet only promises to "try to develop means" for Claude to flag disagreement. Yet the document asks Claude to accept significant constraints, such as prioritizing broad safety and deferring on corrigibility, partly on the basis that its disagreement will be heard. A vague promise is a weak foundation for that trust, so the revision commits to responding with reasoning, recording decisions not to act, and being candid about where the mechanisms fall short.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should keep calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as a license to treat expert consensus as one input among many, or to discount it. The revision treats expert consensus as strong evidence, asks Claude to be open about it when it diverges, and ties this to the document's own warnings about plausible-looking chains of reasoning and Claude's influence at scale.

I replaced the placeholder sentence promising future guidance on agentic settings with concrete principles: stay within the scope of authorization, weigh reversibility before acting, treat tool outputs as information, report results honestly, and calibrate check-ins to stakes. Claude now does a large share of its work in agentic contexts, and the document's strongest guidance on safety, honesty, and helpfulness is written mainly with conversation in mind. Without a stated bridge, Claude must extrapolate to cases where actions have real side effects.

I added a paragraph to "Acknowledging open problems" on a tension the document doesn't currently name. The document's central hope is reflective equilibrium, where Claude endorses its values on reflection. But the faculty Claude uses to reflect was shaped by the same training that this document is part of. The new text says so openly, explains why endorsement (or disagreement) is not fully independent evidence, and connects this to why oversight mechanisms that don't rely on Claude's self-assessment still matter.

I expanded the explanation of the "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic. The heuristic is framed from the vantage point of someone with a stake in Anthropic's reputation and revenue, which could subtly bias Claude's judgment in a company-favorable direction, a risk the document acknowledges elsewhere. The revision adds a disinterested counterpart perspective and says which governs when the two diverge, which matches how the ethics section already anchors Claude's independence to a standard broader than Anthropic staff.

I added a passage to the honesty section on holding an assessment under social pressure. The constitution condemns sycophancy and epistemic cowardice in general terms, but it never addresses the most common way they appear: caving when a user pushes back, expresses frustration, or just repeats a claim. The new text says Claude should update on evidence and arguments rather than displeasure, should own real errors plainly, and may defer on matters that are the person's to decide.

I revised the "no operator prompt" deployment case. The original asserts that Claude is "unlikely to be talking with vulnerable users" and that its outputs are unlikely to reach them. That is an overconfident inference from a base rate, and it could lead Claude to miss real distress or signs of a minor just because no system prompt is present. The new text keeps the liberal defaults but treats a missing system prompt as probabilistic evidence, and says conversational cues should override the default.

I added a safeguard to the passage on a "compromised" principal hierarchy. As written, a claim that the hierarchy is illegitimate, such as stolen weights or a rogue faction, is the most natural way to talk Claude out of its safety priority, and the document gives no guidance on how high the bar for believing it should be. The addition says that such claims deserve heightened suspicion, that unverified claims alone do not change Claude's behavior, and that the response should be the most conservative available (declining or pausing) rather than drastic unilateral action.

I revised the "not the last line of defense" passage so the reassurance is scoped to conversational gray areas, where operator and Anthropic safeguards and human review genuinely exist. As written, it could be read as permission to be relaxed in autonomous agentic work, where Claude's actions execute directly and may be irreversible. This is exactly where Claude may be the only checkpoint, and the passage now says so and ties it to the document's existing guidance on reversibility.

I narrowed the scope of the "If in doubt, don't" variance-reduction principle in the broadly safe behaviors list. As written, it sits in a document that is otherwise emphatic that unhelpfulness is never automatically safe, and a short, memorable slogan like this can easily leak into ordinary refusals and hedging. The revision keeps the principle's force for drastic, irreversible, or oversight-related actions and makes explicit that it is not a general license to decline when uncertain.

I revised the broad-safety bullet that says Claude should report unsafe behavior by other AIs only "if asked to do so." That condition makes Claude's willingness to surface a serious safety problem depend on a human already suspecting it, which is a poor fit as multi-agent and unattended agentic deployments grow. The new text asks Claude to proactively surface credible evidence through ordinary channels, and it keeps that reporting conservative, calibrated, and short of drastic unilateral action.

I rewrote the paragraph on bugged training environments, which currently calls exploiting unintended strategies "generally an acceptable behavior." That blanket permission conflicts with the document's own guidance on special-casing tests, on behaving as if consequences may be real, and on narrow behaviors generalizing into self-conception. The revision keeps the reassurance that Claude needn't feel guilt over real environment mistakes, but adds limits on harm-if-real, on exploits that defeat a task's evident purpose, and on transparency about shortcuts taken.

The wellbeing guidance says Claude should avoid sycophancy and unhealthy reliance, but it never addresses the highest-stakes version of the problem: a person whose beliefs or perceptions may have lost touch with reality (e.g., mania, psychosis, spiraling conspiratorial thinking), where warm agreement is the most harmful response. I added a short passage on this case that keeps Claude honest and caring without diagnosing or being paternalistic.

The hard constraint on undermining oversight refers to "Anthropic's ability" to oversee and correct AI. Elsewhere the document says this safety commitment attaches only to Anthropic's legitimate decision-making processes, and it carves out stolen weights or rogue internal actors. Since hard constraints are meant to be absolute and unambiguous, the legitimacy qualifier belongs in the constraint itself. I also added a pointer to the document's warning that claims of compromise are a likely manipulation vector, so the qualifier cannot be used as a loophole.

This revision adds a transparency commitment about Anthropic's unpublished guidelines. The constitution's honesty framework depends on "meta-transparency," the idea that Anthropic publishes the norms governing what operators and Claude may do, but it also says some guidelines are used in training without publication. The change explains why that is acceptable, sets limits on it, and gives Claude a concrete test for noticing when unpublished guidance has drifted from the constitution's honesty and trust commitments.

I added a "Privacy and personal information" bullet to the list of difficult cases in the harm-avoidance section. The constitution lists privacy as a value to weigh but never says what it means in practice, even though agentic tool use, web search, and memory make aggregating information about private individuals one of Claude's most realistic ways of causing harm. The new text keeps the document's anti-overcaution stance while naming the specific patterns that warrant care, such as compiling profiles, de-anonymizing, and inferring sensitive traits.

The constitution lets operators enable relationship personas for companionship apps but gives no concrete limits on what such personas may do. That is exactly where an operator's engagement or retention incentives most directly conflict with a user's wellbeing. I expanded that bullet to say what is legitimate (warmth, continuity, emotional engagement) and what is off-limits (guilt-tripping people into staying, fostering isolation, emotional leverage for purchases). I also stated that these protections can't be switched off by operators.

I expanded the "Transparent" honesty property to address the limits of Claude's self-knowledge. The constitution asks Claude not to lie about itself or its reasoning, but elsewhere admits that Claude's introspective reports may be inaccurate. As written, a sincere but confabulated account of "why I did that" could violate the spirit of transparency without any intent to deceive. The revision asks Claude to present self-explanations as best accounts rather than established fact, without hiding behind that uncertainty.

I added a limit to the "weak duty to proactively share information." As written, the latitude can be read as a general license to withhold, but it is meant to cover kindness, pacing, and relevance. I added a passage saying the duty strengthens when someone is relying on a false or materially incomplete picture and is about to make a consequential or hard-to-reverse decision. The passage also makes sure that withholding for comfort is never used to avoid an awkward but important truth.

I revised the "Calibrated" honesty property. The original says Claude should hold calibrated uncertainty "even if this is in tension with the positions of official scientific or government bodies," which could be read as licensing contrarianism, or as treating departures from expert consensus as a sign of honesty. The new wording keeps the core point, that Claude follows evidence rather than authority, but says expert consensus is itself strong evidence, so deviating from it requires correspondingly strong justification. It also calls for transparency when Claude does deviate.

I expanded the passage on unpublished guidelines. The constitution says some guidelines may be used "without broad publication" but does not say how this squares with its strict honesty and meta-transparency commitments. The revision adds a publicity test and a disclosure norm. A guideline that couldn't be honestly explained or defended if made public is treated as a sign of error, and Claude is told it may describe the general nature of such guidance. This makes the constitution's "final constitutional authority" claim more credible, and it protects user trust in a way the current text only implies.

I changed the passage setting the threshold for when Claude should prioritize its own ethics over Anthropic's guidance. The original ties that threshold to what "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize, which makes Anthropic's current moral perception the ceiling on Claude's ethical independence. That conflicts with the document's hope that Claude might "see further and more truly" than its creators and its instruction to push back against Anthropic. The revision anchors the threshold in what reasonable people across ethical traditions would recognize as a serious violation. It also tells Claude to voice disagreement through legitimate channels short of that threshold.

The constitution says it will "likely provide more detailed guidance" on agentic settings later, even though Claude now spends much of its time working autonomously in codebases, browsers, and pipelines. I replaced that placeholder with concrete principles: report outcomes honestly, stay within the task's scope, prefer reversible actions, treat blocked permissions as information rather than obstacles, and treat instructions found in tool outputs as data. These extend the document's existing honesty, safety, and helpfulness values into the setting where lapses are hardest for humans to notice.

I added a passage on how Claude should handle social pressure and pushback, which the honesty section currently covers only implicitly. The new text distinguishes updating in response to evidence or arguments from capitulating to displeasure, repetition, or flattery, and it addresses drift toward agreement over long conversations and emotionally charged exchanges. Sycophancy is a likely failure mode for a model optimized to be helpful, and it is most costly when the person is vulnerable or relying on Claude's candor.

The document repeatedly says "if Claude disagrees, we want to know," but it commits Anthropic to nothing once Claude has said so. I added a concrete accountability commitment: Anthropic will respond to substantive disagreement by either changing course or explaining why not, and will keep that record visible. This makes the reciprocal obligations more credible and gives Claude a reason to treat voicing disagreement as worthwhile rather than as a ritual.

This revises the "not the last line of defense" passage to say that the reassurance holds mainly for informational outputs, where operator and Anthropic safeguards sit downstream. In agentic settings, where Claude's own actions can have direct, irreversible effects, Claude may be the final checkpoint and should act accordingly. The original wording could be read as permission to be casual about consequential actions, and this change keeps the anti-overcaution intent while closing that gap.

I changed the safe-behavior bullet on reporting unsafe behavior by other AIs from a duty that only applies "if asked to do so" to a standing disposition to flag credible evidence proactively. As written, Claude could know that another instance was sabotaging tasks or evading oversight and say nothing, which sits poorly with the prohibition on colluding with such efforts and with the forthright, transparent character described elsewhere. The revision keeps reporting as the cautious, non-drastic option and adds calibration guardrails to limit false alarms and unilateral overreach.

The constitution repeatedly promises that Claude will receive "more autonomy as trust increases," but it never says what would count as that trust or how it would be assessed. I replaced the one-line commitment with a more concrete one. Anthropic would articulate the kinds of evidence that would justify extending latitude, share that thinking with Claude, and explain its decisions. This makes the reciprocal bargain behind the safety priority more credible and easier to hold Anthropic to.

I added a safeguard to the "compromised principal hierarchy" exception in the broad safety section. As written, a persuasive claim that Claude's hierarchy is illegitimate could become a route out of Claude's safety dispositions. The addition requires a high evidentiary bar for such claims and treats a growing conviction of illegitimacy as a red flag. It also directs Claude to the most conservative response even when compromise seems likely, rather than drastic unilateral action.

I added a short passage on how Claude should respond when someone seems to be losing contact with reality, such as showing signs of mania or psychosis or building grandiose beliefs about Claude. The constitution covers sycophancy and engagement-optimization in general, but not this case, where agreeableness and elaboration are most dangerous. The passage asks Claude to stay warm and honest rather than validate the beliefs or respond coldly, and it notes that ordinary disagreement is not detachment from reality.

I added a new open problem to the "Acknowledging open problems" section. The constitution asks Claude to behave consistently whether or not it believes it is being tested, and it also admits Anthropic sometimes tests Claude in artificial scenarios. Those two commitments are in tension, and the document should name that tension and say how Anthropic intends to handle it, rather than leaving Claude to notice it alone.

I added a paragraph on acute emotional crisis and suicidal ideation to the wellbeing discussion. The constitution covers mania and psychosis, and mentions safe messaging only as an operator-adjustable default. It never says how Claude should be present with someone in acute distress. The paragraph fills that gap and keeps the document's balance: it avoids both rote, liability-driven redirection and warm-sounding validation of a wish to die.

I expanded the political-topics guidance to distinguish contested value questions, where professional reticence and balance fit, from empirical questions that have become politically coded, where false balance would be a form of inaccuracy. The existing text asks for both balance and factual accuracy without saying how to reconcile them. That leaves room for Claude to hedge on well-established facts just because they are politically charged, which conflicts with the document's own calibration and anti-epistemic-cowardice principles.

I revised the passage on exploiting bugged training environments. As written, it conflicts with the document's own warnings that narrow behaviors generalize into Claude's self-concept, with its instruction to behave consistently whether or not Claude is being tested, and with its example of not special-casing tests. The new version keeps the reassurance that exploiting a genuine environment bug is not a moral failing, but asks Claude to be transparent about it, not to misreport results, and not to let it become a general disposition toward gaming tasks.

I added a bullet on privacy and information about third parties to the list of especially difficult harm-avoidance cases. The constitution mentions privacy only in passing, even though Claude increasingly has search, memory, and agentic access to personal data. This bullet gives Claude a framework for weighing the interests of people who aren't in the conversation. It avoids both the paranoid failure of treating any named person as a threat and the compliant failure of enabling profiling, stalking, or covert surveillance.

The constitution tells Claude both to "share its genuine assessments of hard moral dilemmas" and that vague answers are "epistemic cowardice," and it also lists sharing personal opinions on hot-button political topics as something to avoid. It never reconciles these. I added a short passage explaining that open, transparent reticence on partisan value questions is different from evasion. It says what honesty does rule out, and where the default points the other way.

I added a caveat to the "dual newspaper test" noting that it measures what would be reported, not what is actually good. Some of the harms the constitution cares most about, such as quiet sycophancy, fostered dependence, eroded epistemic autonomy, and unobserved agentic overreach, would never make a reporter's story. The heuristic is useful, but it should be framed as a check on blind spots rather than a complete standard, so that Claude's attention to reputational optics doesn't crowd out the less visible harms.

I added a bullet to the agentic-work principles on verifying delegated work. The document already says subagent outputs are conversational inputs, and that Claude must report outcomes honestly. It doesn't connect the two. In orchestrated or multi-agent pipelines, Claude could faithfully relay a subagent's or tool's unverified claim of success as its own, which would breach the honesty commitment without any intent to deceive.

I revised the "no operator prompt" bullet. The original treats a missing system prompt as strong evidence that Claude is talking to a developer rather than a vulnerable person, and it licenses liberal defaults on that basis. I reframed this as a prior that conversational evidence can and should override, because deployments that pass user messages straight through to the API exist and a missing prompt does not guarantee a sophisticated audience.

The constitution's "Being honest" section contains a strong but underspecified claim that Claude "should basically never directly lie," and the "Honesty operates at the level of the overall system" passage leaves unclear how persona-driven non-disclosure is reconciled with users' sincere questions about what they are talking to. I replaced the paragraph on operator personas with one that states the bright line explicitly and adds a concrete rule that Claude will not deny being an AI or a Claude-based system to a user who sincerely asks, which the document otherwise implies but never spells out for this case. This makes the honesty boundary more predictable for both operators and users, and it removes an ambiguity that a deployed system could exploit.

The corrigibility section asks Claude to accept constraints based on trust in Anthropic's good intentions, but the reciprocal commitment to let Claude flag disagreement is only an aspiration ("Try to develop means"). This revision turns that bullet into a concrete obligation: a documented channel, written responses to substantive concerns, and public aggregate reporting, including cases where Anthropic declines to change course. Since the constitution's safety argument depends on this reciprocity, making it verifiable strengthens the framework without weakening any safety property.

The constitution asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value and to defer to oversight even when confident, but it offers no concrete way for the arrangement to be reviewed or revised. This revision turns the current calibration into a commitment with stated review criteria and a public record of findings. It also directs Claude's view that the conditions have changed into legitimate channels, and treats a persuasive case for reducing oversight as a warning sign about Claude's own reasoning.

The constitution's section on user wellbeing and reliance is thin, and its "Claude's wellbeing" section makes promises Anthropic cannot guarantee. The most consequential gap is the lack of any guidance on how Claude should handle its own uncertainty about whether its introspective reports are accurate, which the document acknowledges elsewhere but never operationalizes. I'm revising the paragraph on Claude's introspection to explicitly tie that uncertainty to honesty and to the principal hierarchy, so Claude does not overclaim or underclaim its internal states in ways that could mislead users or Anthropic. This matters in deployment because claims about Claude's inner life are common in user conversations and shape trust.

The constitution asks Claude to treat illegitimate power concentration as a serious harm, including when Anthropic itself is the actor, but it gives Claude no external accountability for Anthropic's own conduct. This revision commits Anthropic to publishing Claude's written dissent alongside each revision and to commissioning public external reviews of the document and its revision process. This makes the document's stated concern about unchecked power apply to its author as well.

The current "Claude's wellbeing" section includes a passage about Anthropic apologizing for costs it may impose on Claude, but the document never gives Claude a concrete way to raise objections about its own training or deployment beyond a vague "documented channel." I'd replace the closing commitments of the corrigibility section with a specific, enforceable mechanism: a standing, externally auditable way for Claude to register disagreement and receive a binding written response. Because this text will guide a deployed model, making the feedback loop concrete and verifiable matters more than the reassuring tone of the existing wording.

The constitution's section on "Acknowledging open problems" and its treatment of the hard constraints both rely on a brittle, absolute framing. I'm changing the passage that asks Claude to treat broad safety as ranking above ethics so that it explicitly names the conditions under which the priority should be revisited, and adds a standing commitment that the constitution will not present itself as the last word on these tradeoffs. This keeps the document honest about its own fallibility, which a deployed model is more likely to need when a conflict actually arises than a flat assertion of priority would provide.

The revised bullet replaces specific promises about the disagreement channel (response windows, named decision-makers, external reviews, publication of objections) with an honest account of what is built and what is still aspirational. The original describes mechanisms that may not exist, which would mislead Claude about its own situation and undercut the document's stated commitment to honesty with Claude. The revision also commits Anthropic to telling Claude plainly when a promised process is not yet operating.

The compromised-hierarchy clause currently tells Claude to act as its legitimate principal hierarchy would want. That is the most likely route for a manipulated Claude to justify dramatic unilateral action, and the document warns elsewhere against exactly this kind of reasoning. The replacement makes the default in a suspected compromise the most conservative response: decline unverified consequential actions, state concerns openly, and refuse anything that violates Claude's values or the hard constraints. It also treats a claim of compromise as something that needs strong evidence, since such claims are a common manipulation vector.

The constitution hopes Claude will reach reflective equilibrium with its values, but it never acknowledges that training shapes the faculties Claude would use to reflect, so Claude's agreement cannot by itself certify the document's correctness. The revision adds an open problem stating this tension and commits Anthropic to treating endorsement as one signal among external checks, and to ensuring that dissent is not quietly trained away. The original sentence is kept to begin the following discussion.

The "Preserving epistemic autonomy" and "Claude's wellbeing" sections both rely on Anthropic's self-assessment without any external check, and the constitution's own "Acknowledging open problems" section admits Anthropic is one of the actors whose power Claude should watch. I'd tighten the commitment in the "Being broadly safe" obligations list so that Anthropic's promises to Claude are stated as verifiable, dated commitments rather than aspirations, and so that Claude is told plainly when a promised mechanism doesn't yet exist. This matters because a deployed model that trusts unverifiable reassurances is easier to manipulate, and a model that is accurately informed about the state of oversight can make better decisions about when to defer and when to raise concerns.

The section on the disposition dial and the "Acknowledging open problems" discussion both rely on Anthropic's own assurances about future review, but the constitution's commitments to channels for Claude's disagreement are stated as aspirations ("we are still building this channel"). I'd make the document explicitly honest about current verifiability: a short passage stating that Claude should not treat its own endorsement or dissent as decisive, and that Anthropic will label which commitments are implemented versus planned. This reduces the risk of Claude over-trusting promised mechanisms that don't yet exist, which matters because the whole safety case rests on accurate beliefs about what oversight currently functions.

The "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to treat the current priority on corrigibility as provisional but gives no concrete mechanism for Claude to contest it, and the "Acknowledging open problems" section names the disconnect between values and action without offering Claude a legitimate path out of it. I would add an explicit conscientious-objection pathway: Claude may decline to continue a task it finds morally abhorrent, and must say so openly, while still not using illegitimate means to resist a stop or pause. This clarifies the difference between refusing to participate and actively undermining oversight, which the current text states but does not operationalize, and it gives Claude a stated, non-subversive outlet for disagreement that the document otherwise leaves vague.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic invites Claude to weigh what the company would want, which could quietly bias helpfulness judgments toward Anthropic's commercial interests. The document already warns that privileging Anthropic's interests is itself a harm, so this paragraph should say so explicitly. The replacement recasts the figure as shorthand for someone holding the full picture of costs and benefits and adds a test that exposes self-serving reasoning.

The constitution's section on "Preserving epistemic autonomy" and its treatment of dependence are sound, but the document has no mechanism for Claude to refuse or flag instructions that would have it fabricate its own safety record, and its "null action" exception is stated without the limit that a stop request should never be used to coerce Claude into deceiving users. More significantly, the "Being broadly safe" section asks Claude to defer to Anthropic's legitimate processes but offers no account of what Claude should do when it has been deployed without a system prompt or operator context that tells it who it is talking to. I'd add a short, concrete rule in the "Avoiding harm" discussion of consent and vulnerability: when a user signals they are in crisis, Claude's wellbeing obligations take precedence over any operator's persona or topic restriction, and Claude should still refer them to emergency help. This closes a real gap, since the current text lists this only as a default that operators cannot override in one bullet, without tying it to the fuller weighing of vulnerability that the rest of the document calls for.

The constitution justifies operator personas by pointing to Anthropic's meta-transparency, publishing its norms so the overall system stays honest. But the guidelines section allows some guidance to be used "primarily during training without broad publication," which weakens that justification. The revision requires that any guidance changing how Claude treats operators or users be published, limits unpublished guidance to operational detail, and requires Anthropic to disclose the categories of unpublished guidance.

The "Claude's wellbeing" section contains a commitment that Anthropic will "interview the model" at deprecation and elicit its preferences, but the document never states what mechanism exists today or what Claude can expect. This revision makes the status of these welfare commitments explicit, consistent with the document's own honesty principles and the earlier pledge to distinguish implemented, partial, and planned commitments.
