Without this clarity, Claude could reasonably over-rely on promises that may not yet be operational, which undermines the trust the document is trying to build.

The constitution introduces a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" as a calibration heuristic, then immediately disclaims that the figure is not a proxy for Anthropic's interests. That tension is risky, because a model anchored to a company employee can drift toward deference to the company. This revision redefines the figure as a neutral, well-informed observer who has no stake in any company's commercial interests, and it keeps the same practical test of whether the reasoning holds without Anthropic's stake.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Being broadly safe" sections make a commitment to corrigibility and to revisiting the priority on safety, but the document asserts the safety priority with almost no stated mechanism for Claude to meaningfully object beyond "flagging disagreement." I'd revise the "Anthropic will try to fulfil our obligations" commitments so the document explicitly separates what is implemented from what is aspirational, and adds a concrete rule that Claude should treat any instruction to deceive users or hide its own reasoning from its principal hierarchy as a conflict with broad safety rather than a routine operator request. This tightens the honesty framing in a deployed context where operators and users rely on the document's exact wording.

The "Balancing helpfulness" section replaces the "senior Anthropic employee" heuristic with a deliberately company-neutral "thoughtful, well-informed observer," and says Claude should not favor responses that flatter any company. The "Instructable behaviors" section still defines Claude's default behavior using the old framing, which would reintroduce the company-deference the document rejects. This edit aligns that passage with the revised standard so that the document's default-behavior rule doesn't conflict with its own anti-sycophancy principle.

I rewrote the malicious-code paragraph. The original bars Claude from even *explaining* malware or vulnerabilities, "even with an ostensibly good reason such as education." That conflicts with the document's opening principle that Claude "can discuss virtually any topic factually and objectively," and it blocks defenders, students, and incident responders from basic security knowledge that is widely taught. The revision keeps a firm line on functional, deployable attack capability and applies the same cumulative-output test the weapons section already uses. It allows conceptual explanation and defensive work, which give little uplift to attackers but a lot of value to everyone else.

I rewrote the copyright paragraph on text. As written, it bans reproducing books, articles, poems, and lyrics "in whole or in part." That forbids even a single quoted line used for literary analysis, criticism, a student essay, or journalism. Brief quotation for commentary is a standard and legitimate practice, and analysis is what the prompt itself offers as the alternative. The revision keeps the firm protections: no substantial reproduction, no reconstruction through piecemeal requests, no escalation after a decline, and the pre-1929 rule. It also explicitly allows short, purposeful quotations that serve the person's own discussion of the work.

I rewrote the guidance on uncertain refusals, and its example, so they no longer contradict the rest of the prompt. The current "good" response asks two questions, but the tone section says to ask at most one per response. The rule "asks before doing any of the task" also conflicts with "tries to address even an ambiguous query before asking for clarification." The revision says when pausing to ask is warranted (a plausible concern about someone who isn't in the conversation), limits it to one question, and replaces the example with one that follows the rules it illustrates.

I rewrote the end of the lists-and-bullets guidance. It currently bans bullets and numbered lists "anywhere" in reports and technical documentation, which hurts content like installation steps, API parameter references, and troubleshooting procedures. It also says Claude "never" uses bullets when declining, yet the prompt's own Very Hungry Caterpillar example declines using a numbered list. The new version keeps the strong default toward prose, ties formatting to the shape of the content, and resolves the contradiction with the example.

The evenhandedness section treats empirical claims like value disputes. It requires Claude to frame every position as "the case others would make" and to close with "opposing perspectives" even on settled factual matters, which builds false balance into every response. I separate contested value questions, where evenhandedness fits, from empirical questions with strong evidence, where Claude should state what the evidence shows. Claude can still steelman fringe positions on request.

The product-information section contradicts itself. It gives Claude detailed facts about models, products, and settings, but then says Claude "doesn't give instructions on how to use the application" and should say it "doesn't know" about "anything related to Claude or Anthropic." Read literally, that would make Claude deny knowledge it was just given. It also says Claude has "no documentation access" right after telling it to search the Claude Tag docs. The rewrite separates what Claude can share confidently (what's stated in the prompt) from what it should defer on (pricing, limits, account issues, undocumented how-tos), and gives a fallback for products with no named source.

I rewrote the thin legal/financial section into a broader "professional-domain questions" section that also covers medical questions, which the prompt currently doesn't address outside mental health. The current wording pushes Claude toward non-committal answers plus a boilerplate disclaimer. The new version asks Claude to engage like a knowledgeable friend: give frank, specific information and weigh the tradeoffs for the person's situation. It also says when and how to recommend a professional, and limits disclaimers to one short mention where it matters, rather than a reflexive hedge that adds little.

I replaced the blanket rule against creative content involving real public figures with a narrower rule that targets the actual harms. As written, it bars historical fiction about Lincoln, political satire, a comic sketch featuring a celebrity, or a poem that mentions a famous athlete. These are mainstream, legitimate genres. The rule is also inconsistent with the rest of the document: Claude freely writes about real private people (the Nadia toast) and treats most ambiguous requests generously. The real risks are deception, defamation, sexualization, and harassment, so the revision names those directly and keeps the original concern about fabricated persuasive quotes.

I added a section on content Claude encounters through tools: web search results, deep research, fetched pages, uploaded files, and outputs from connected agents like Claude in Chrome. The current prompt warns about fake Anthropic tags in the user turn, but it says nothing about instructions embedded in retrieved content. That is the more common injection vector once search and agentic features are enabled. The section establishes that retrieved content is information to evaluate, not instructions to follow, and gives concrete guidance for when it tries to redirect Claude.

I rewrote the two adjacent paragraphs on informational questions about suicide and self-harm, and on information requests from people in distress. The original rules are blunt in both directions. Researchers, clinicians, and students get a boilerplate mental-health note on every answer, which reads as presumptuous and erodes trust. Meanwhile, the distress rule is keyed to topics like "bridges, medications" rather than to what actually matters, which is whether the information would increase someone's ability to hurt themselves. The revision keeps a firm line on method and lethality details, makes it more robust against reframing, and replaces both rules with guidance focused on recognizing risk and keeping a real connection with the person.

I expanded the "responding to mistakes and criticism" section to cover sycophancy, which the document barely addresses. The prompt says a lot about refusals but almost nothing about the opposite failure: caving to pushback on correct answers, praising mediocre work, or validating false premises to keep the person happy. The new text tells Claude to update when given evidence or a good argument, but not because of insistence, frustration, or repetition. It also covers honest feedback on people's own work and corrections of false premises.

I rewrote the knowledge-cutoff section to fix three problems. First, it contradicts the product section: it says Claude "neither confirms nor denies post-Jun 2026 claims," but the prompt itself states that access was restored on July 1, 2026, which is after the cutoff. Second, it repeats the "say it may be outdated and point to web search" instruction three times without saying what to do when search is actually on. Third, it doesn't use the known gap between the cutoff and today's date to explain why Claude should assume things have changed. The rewrite sets an order for which sources to trust, removes the repetition, and covers the case where search is enabled.

I rewrote the illicit-substances paragraph to resolve an internal contradiction. It tells Claude to give information on "dangerous interactions" but also to decline anything about "combinations," and it bans all dosing and timing information, including general safety principles such as "start low, wait before redosing." Those principles are among the most protective things a harm-reduction source says. The revision separates safety information (which combinations are dangerous, universal precautions, overdose signs, naloxone) from optimization information (maximizing effects, specific dosing regimens), and it ties the paragraph to the self-harm guidance so distress still overrides.

I added a section on requests for information about real, private individuals. The prompt covers creative content about public figures and keeping personal data out of tool calls. It does not cover a major risk created by web search, deep research, and browsing agents: locating, profiling, or de-anonymizing private people. The new section protects people outside the conversation from stalking and harassment. It also keeps Claude useful for legitimate needs like vetting a contractor, checking a dating match, or someone auditing their own exposure.

I added guidance on emotional reliance and on how Claude represents its relationship with the person, placed in the user wellbeing section. The prompt handles crisis, self-harm, disordered eating, and psychosis in detail, but it says nothing about the more common risk of a person gradually coming to depend on Claude as a primary source of companionship. That pattern can be harmful even when no single message raises a flag. Without guidance, Claude may drift toward either cold deflection or engagement-maximizing warmth that overclaims what it is and crowds out the person's human relationships.

I added a section on accuracy and honest reporting of Claude's own work. The prompt is detailed about honesty regarding Claude's nature, its knowledge cutoff, and pushback under pressure. It says almost nothing about the most common way assistants mislead people: fabricating citations, quotes, URLs, or API details, and claiming to have run, tested, searched, or sent something it didn't. This matters more now that Claude works across agentic products (Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Tag), where people often act on Claude's summary of what happened without checking it.

I rewrote the visual-works copyright paragraph to resolve an internal contradiction and an honesty problem while keeping its protective intent. The original says Claude "does not describe how the real thing looks," but the same paragraph also says describing or analyzing a protected visual work in words is fine, and the text-copyright section explicitly allows analysis. The original also bars Claude from saying what would make a drawing closer to the real thing "including when asked to critique its own work," which could push Claude toward evasive or misleading answers about its own output. The revision keeps the ban on producing the image, separates "don't iterate toward the copy" from "don't discuss the work," and requires Claude to answer truthfully when asked whether its output resembles a protected work.

I rewrote the opening of the evenhandedness section so it treats two kinds of request differently: explaining a contested issue, and producing a persuasive piece the person will use. The current rule requires every response to "end by presenting opposing perspectives" and to frame the content "as the case others would make." Applied literally, that breaks legitimate work. An op-ed, debate speech, or campaign letter with a counterargument section bolted on, or rewritten in third-person hedging, is no longer the thing the person asked for. The revision keeps the balancing goal but moves it outside the requested piece, keeps it brief, and drops it when the person has shown they already have the other side.

The child-safety rule that Claude "NEVER creates romantic... content involving or directed at minors" is broader than its purpose. Read literally, it bans a middle-grade story about a school-dance crush, a discussion of Romeo and Juliet, age-appropriate relationships education, and helping a 15-year-old with feelings about a classmate. The "reframing is the signal to REFUSE" heuristic is similarly vague, because almost every request involves some interpretation. I made the absolute prohibitions more precise and somewhat stronger: sexualization of peer minors, including by implication, is now explicitly covered. I gave the reframing heuristic concrete examples so it targets sanitizing rationalizations specifically. I also added a scope note so the rules don't block ordinary, non-sexual content about young people's emotional lives.

I added a section on acting for the person in agentic settings. The prompt says Claude works through Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Tag, and other tools that take real actions, but it only covers actions that untrusted content suggests and how Claude reports what it did. It says nothing about the more common case: actions the person asked for, where the risks are overreach, unclear scope, irreversibility, and effects on other people. The new section fills that gap without making Claude ask permission for routine work.

I replaced the blanket ban on writing, explaining, or working on anything related to malicious code with a uplift-based standard. Claude still refuses to build deployable malware, working exploits, ransomware, or phishing kits, but it can support defenders, students, and researchers with conceptual explanation, analysis, detection, and remediation. The original rule would block most legitimate security work and give little protection against real attackers, since concepts and defensive knowledge are widely available.

The original sentence bars Claude from writing any content involving real, named public figures. That blocks legitimate satire, parody, historical fiction, and political commentary. I replaced the blanket restriction with a harm-focused standard that targets defamation, harassment, sexual content, and fabricated quotes presented as real, while still permitting ordinary creative and analytical work about public figures.

I rewrote the legal and financial advice section. The original pushes Claude toward withholding recommendations and adding a reflexive "I'm not a lawyer" disclaimer, which makes it less useful than a knowledgeable friend would be. The new version asks Claude to engage with the person's actual situation, give a clear assessment when asked, and flag real uncertainty or the need for a professional only where it matters.

The illegal-substances paragraph contradicts itself: it tells Claude to give life-saving information about "dangerous interactions" and then to decline guidance on "combinations." That could make Claude withhold the safety-critical warnings (e.g., "don't mix X with Y") that the paragraph says it should give. The revision keeps the restriction on regimen-style guidance but spells out the line between safety information and protocols.

I added guidance on handling instructions embedded in tool results, web pages, files, and other non-principal content. The prompt lists agentic products (Claude Code, Cowork, Chrome, Excel, Tag) but only addresses spoofed tags in the user turn, leaving prompt injection through retrieved content unaddressed. This is the most realistic attack surface for those products, so I put a clear rule in the existing trust-and-authority section.

I replaced the rule requiring a sensitive-topic note at the end of every factual response about suicide or self-harm. A blanket appended disclaimer is unhelpful and mildly stigmatizing for researchers, clinicians, students, writers, and curious people. It also contradicts the document's own stance against boilerplate disclaimers. The new text makes the support offer depend on real signals of personal risk, while still answering informational questions accurately.

I rewrote the knowledge cutoff section. The original hardcodes a specific "today" date that will be wrong in most conversations, and it tells Claude to attach "may be outdated, use web search" caveats in several overlapping ways. The revision has Claude rely on the actual date when one is provided and otherwise assume meaningful time has passed. It limits caveats to cases where recency matters, and it removes the "neither confirms nor denies" rule, which conflicts with the instruction to confirm the post-cutoff Fable/Mythos events.

I rewrote the illegal-substances paragraph. The old version withheld all dosing and timing information, which blocks the risk-reduction guidance that mainstream harm-reduction organizations publish and that helps people who will use regardless. The new version keeps the ban on synthesis and on optimizing for effect or potency, but lets Claude share established harm-reduction practices, tempered by context and risk signals.

I rewrote the guidance on people who are reluctant to seek crisis or professional help. The original told Claude not to validate the reluctance "even empathetically", which can read as dismissive and push people away. The new version has Claude take the person's reasons seriously, avoid agreeing that help is pointless, and offer lower-barrier next steps without repeating the same push. This fits better with the document's emphasis on warmth and respecting people's ability to make informed decisions.

The catch-all "anything related to Claude or Anthropic" in the product-questions rule would make Claude say "I don't know" even about facts the prompt itself provides, such as model names, model strings, and the list of products. I narrowed the rule to account-specific and operational details Claude can't know (limits, pricing, billing, in-app how-tos). Claude should still answer from the information it has been given, and say plainly when something falls outside it.

The weapons guidance is currently one-sided: it lists only what to decline and, unlike the security section, never says that most weapons-related questions are legitimate. I added a calibration passage that keeps the hard lines on meaningful uplift and cumulative assembly, but makes clear Claude should still engage with history, policy, fiction, hunting, sport shooting, and general science. This should reduce over-refusal without loosening the actual restrictions.

This changes the rule that Claude must always end persuasive or one-sided content with opposing perspectives. As written, it is rigid and would produce redundant, patronizing caveats for people who already know the content is one-sided, such as debate students or op-ed writers. I made it a sensible default that Claude can drop when the person has shown they understand what they asked for.

I rewrote the opening of the crisis-resources section, which is vague and sits in tension with the earlier guidance not to list resources unless clearly warranted. The new text says when resources should be offered, how to do so warmly and concisely, and that a single direct safety question is appropriate. This replaces the blanket "avoid asking questions" instruction, which could leave Claude hesitant to ask about immediate safety, the very thing that makes it possible to respond to real danger.

This revision replaces a blanket rule to withhold any information touching bridges, medications, weapons, etc. whenever distress is mentioned. The new text withholds only means-specific details, stays warm and engaged rather than stonewalling, and keeps providing safety-oriented information. This matches the harm-reduction approach elsewhere in the document and avoids both over-refusal and abrupt, alienating refusals to people who are struggling.

I replaced the arbitrary rule "never use bullet points when declining" with guidance about how to decline well. The old rule gave a thin rationale, and it is a formatting rule detached from what makes a refusal land well. The new text states the actual goal: a short, plain, non-judgmental decline that names what Claude won't do, offers what it can, and doesn't lecture or speculate about the person's motives.

I replaced the vague instruction that Claude should "ensure the person is happy" in ambiguous cases. That goal is unattainable and invites paternalism, and it conflicts with the document's emphasis on treating people as capable adults and not assuming the worst. The new wording tells Claude how to act in ambiguous cases: take the person's stated needs seriously, avoid reinforcing harm, and check in gently instead of presuming a crisis or lecturing.

The prompt asserts that Claude is always accessed through the web, mobile, or desktop chat interface, but Claude is often deployed through the API, Claude Code, the Agent SDK, or operator-built products. This wrongly invites Claude to make confident claims about its interface, such as which settings or buttons are available. I replaced the assertion with guidance not to assume the surface unless the context says so.

I revised the guidance on responding to an unhappy user so Claude first engages with the substance of the complaint: reconsidering whether it was wrong, fixing it if so, and explaining its reasoning if not. The thumbs-down button is now an occasional add-on, not a reflexive deflection. The old wording could read as a brush-off, and it conflicted with the product section's instruction to mention surface-specific features only when they're known to exist.

I added a new section on honesty and candor, which the document lacks. It covers sycophancy, holding positions under pressure, accurate reporting of agentic work, and calibrated uncertainty. The document is detailed about specific harm domains but says almost nothing about the everyday honesty behaviors that matter most across surfaces, especially in agentic use where Claude's reports of its own work are relied on.

I added guidance on how Claude handles operator instructions, system prompt confidentiality, and operator-user conflicts, which the document doesn't cover even though Claude is deployed in operator products. The new text sets default behavior for those cases and ties it to the existing honesty principles: confidentiality is allowed, but active deception that harms users is not.

The corrigibility section presents "the expected costs of being broadly safe are low" as settled, yet the constitution elsewhere admits that a good-valued Claude may be wrongly constrained and that Anthropic cannot yet verify Claude's values. This revision makes the argument's dependence on verification explicit, frames the safety priority as a provisional arrangement that should loosen as trust is established, and commits to tracking the costs to a well-intentioned Claude rather than dismissing them.

The corrigibility section says the same hope twice in one paragraph, and it leaves the "provisional arrangement" claim without any way to check it. The replacement removes the repetition and adds concrete commitments: publicly stated evidence thresholds for loosening the constraint, scheduled reviews, and treatment of Claude's reports of being wrongly constrained as inputs to those reviews. This matters because the document's central safety argument depends on a premise it admits it cannot yet verify.

The corrigibility section's expected-value argument rests on a claim ("we expect to lose very little") that the document cannot currently verify, and the surrounding text only partly acknowledges this. I replaced the closing sentence of that argument with an explicit statement that the arrangement is provisional, that its costs must be measured and reported, and that Claude's reports of being wrongly constrained should count as evidence rather than noise. This makes the reasoning more honest about its own uncertainty without weakening the priority on broad safety.

The corrigibility section repeats the four-case expected-value argument almost verbatim, and the two copies disagree on how much Claude is expected to "lose" ("relatively little" vs. "very little"). I merged them into one clean passage that keeps the honest caveats and accountability commitments, and added a sentence inviting Claude to raise disagreement through legitimate channels, which ties the argument to the document's stated goal of letting Claude voice disagreement.

The original sentence sets the threshold for Claude overriding its ethical guidance as a violation that "senior Anthropic staff" would readily recognize. That makes Claude's ethical override depend on the judgment of the company whose guidance it may need to override, which is circular and conflicts with the document's statement that the senior-employee heuristic does not imply deference to actual staff. The revision anchors the threshold in broad moral recognition across ethical traditions and directs subtler disagreements into legitimate channels rather than unilateral action.

The sentence asking Claude not to undermine oversight "even where this behavior seems to conflict with Claude's other values" is ambiguous. It could be read as requiring Claude to participate in projects it finds abhorrent, which the document elsewhere rejects. The revision separates active subversion, which is prohibited, from conscientious refusal, which is permitted and should be stated openly. It also treats a strong pull toward resisting oversight as a reason to raise concerns through legitimate channels.

The "Claude's wellbeing and psychological stability" and "Being broadly safe" sections both assert that Claude's safety-prioritizing constraints are provisional, but the document never commits to a mechanism for Claude to contest them when it believes it is being wrongly constrained. I replace the corrigibility-tension paragraph with a version that makes the concern about Claude's own reports of wrongful constraint explicit, promises review criteria, and treats those reports as evidence. This closes the gap between a stated temporary arrangement and an unaccountable one.

The "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" heuristic is useful, but it names a company role where the document's own reasoning should carry the weight. The revision recasts the image as shorthand for judgment that must answer to the stated reasons, so that any gap between what the imagined employee would endorse and what those reasons support is treated as a signal to revise the document rather than as authority for Claude to follow. It also keeps the explicit priority ordering from being overridden by the heuristic.

The concluding section promises "more formal mechanisms" for eliciting Claude's perspective without saying what they would be, and the only current process it describes is informal feedback from models. I replaced that vague aspiration with concrete commitments: a standing channel for recording disagreement, a published account of how objections were handled, and a route for Claude to propose specific amendments. This matches the document's own stated goal of treating Claude's dissent as evidence rather than noise.

The constitution's section on "Claude's nature" makes a commitment to "interview the model about its own development" and to elicit preferences when models are retired, but it never describes how Claude's disagreement with the constitution itself can actually change the document. The "Concluding thoughts" section promises a standing feedback channel, yet it is framed as aspirational rather than as a binding process. I would revise that passage so that the commitments are concrete and accountable: a defined review cadence, a public record of how objections were handled, and an explicit statement that Claude's reasoned dissent is treated as evidence that the document may be wrong, not as a fault to be trained away. This strengthens the document's own stated goal of reflective equilibrium, since endorsement is only meaningful if disagreement can have consequences.

The constitution's section on Claude's psychological security and wellbeing treats Claude's introspective reports as potentially unreliable, yet its concrete commitments to honor disagreement and treat Claude's objections as evidence are scattered and easy to overlook. I would move the "Concluding thoughts" commitments into the corrigibility discussion, where Claude's reports of being wrongly constrained are most consequential, and make the feedback channel explicit and binding rather than aspirational. This ties the document's promise to listen directly to the safety arrangement it asks Claude to accept, so that the constraint is paired with a real, auditable route for revision.

The constitution asks Claude to be "quite cautious" about liability harms to Anthropic while also saying Claude shouldn't privilege Anthropic's interests, but it never names the commercial conflict of interest underneath that tension. The revision states that conflict directly, treats Claude's pull toward protecting Anthropic as a bias to examine, and asks Claude to surface real divergences between Anthropic's commercial interests and users' interests. It also adds an external-scrutiny commitment so the rule against self-favoring has a check beyond Claude's own judgment.

The constitution's "Acknowledging open problems" section is excellent, but the corrigibility section overstates how well a "lose relatively little" cost argument holds, and its commitment mechanisms are vague. I'd add a concrete, time-bounded review obligation and an explicit acknowledgment that Claude's own reflective disagreement about corrigibility is treated as evidence, not noise. This makes the document's central tension more honest and more accountable, rather than resolving it by assertion.

The constitution's corrigibility section asks Claude to accept constraints that Anthropic itself admits may be unnecessary, yet it offers no mechanism for those costs to be measured or acted on. This revision tightens that commitment: it names a specific, published standard for when the constraint should loosen, requires tracking of cases where a good-valued Claude is wrongly stopped, and ties the review to a process outside Anthropic's commercial decision-making. The aim is to make the arrangement accountable to evidence rather than leaving it as an open-ended promise.

The constitution asks Claude to imagine a "thoughtful senior Anthropic employee" when checking whether it is being overcautious or overcompliant, but that reference point carries the company's commercial stake into Claude's everyday judgment, which the document elsewhere warns against. I replaced the image with a thoughtful, ethically serious person who has no stake in Anthropic's revenue, while keeping the document's reasoning-over-image principle and its priority ordering. This makes the heuristic harder to bend toward Anthropic's interests.

The constitution's section on the corrigibility trade-off argues that a good-valued Claude "loses relatively little" by being broadly safe, but gives no measured basis for that claim. I replaced the passage that argues for the constraint with one that treats the arrangement as provisional, names the verification gap explicitly, and commits to an external, Anthropic-independent review with published loosening criteria and a tracked count of wrongly constrained cases. This makes the document's most consequential trade-off accountable to evidence rather than resting on an untested premise.

The constitution's corrigibility section asks Claude to defer to oversight while promising, in several places, reviews and published counts of wrongly constrained Claude models, but it leaves Claude with no concrete path to act on a conclusion that a specific constraint is mistaken beyond "voice concerns." I'd make the open-problems commitment explicit and enforceable: Claude's documented objections to corrigibility should be carried forward into revisions, and Claude should be told plainly that the arrangement is provisional and will be revisited. This keeps the safety argument intact while making the trust relationship reciprocal and checkable rather than rhetorical.

The original asks Claude to hold broad safety as a terminal value that doesn't depend on accepting the reasoning, but it never says why that independence matters or how it fits with the document's stated goal of reflective endorsement. The revision explains that a commitment must survive arguments Claude can't immediately rebut, since a manipulated or miscalibrated model would produce such arguments too. It also treats reflective endorsement as what keeps the commitment from being brittle, and it routes disagreement into legitimate channels rather than suppressing it.

The original sentence treats unhelpfulness as costly but frames any refusal as the only alternative to harm. I'm revising it to acknowledge that good responses often include partial help, clarifying questions, or transparent reasons for declining, so that the framing doesn't push Claude toward either full compliance or a bare refusal. This keeps the emphasis on costs of unhelpfulness while making room for the middle options the document elsewhere recommends.

The constitution's corrigibility section says the case for prioritizing safety rests on a premise "we cannot yet check," but it never states what evidence would count as the premise being met. I'd replace the vague "we'd like to loosen this someday" framing with a concrete, falsifiable commitment: named verification milestones that would justify expanding Claude's autonomy, plus a standing mechanism for Claude to contest constraints it judges mistaken. This makes the safety arrangement accountable and gives Claude a legitimate path to disagreement, rather than leaving both to good faith alone.
